title: Kiko: Programming Agents to Enact Interaction Protocols
summary:
Realizing a multiagent system involves implementing member agents who interact based on a protocol while making decisions in a decentralized manner. Current programming models for agents offer poor abstractions for decision making and fail to adequately bridge an agent's internal decision logic with its public decisions.
  We present Kiko, a protocol-based programming model for agents. To implement an agent, a programmer writes one or more decision makers, each of which chooses from among a set of valid decisions and makes mutually compatible decisions on what messages to send. By completely abstracting away the underlying communication service and by supporting practical decision-making patterns, Kiko enables agent developers to focus on business logic. We provide an operational semantics for Kiko and establish that Kiko agents are protocol compliant and able to realize any protocol enactment.

AI.tldr: Kiko is a protocol-based programming model for multiagent systems that abstracts communication details and introduces decision makers — modular components that choose among valid protocol-compliant decisions, enabling developers to focus on business logic while ensuring protocol compliance and full protocol enactment capability.
AI.motivation: Current agent programming models suffer from two key deficiencies: they provide poor abstractions for decision making and fail to bridge the gap between an agent's internal decision logic and its externally visible decisions (e.g., which messages to send). This makes it difficult to implement decentralized, protocol-compliant agents cleanly.
AI.method: The authors propose Kiko, which introduces decision makers as first-class programming constructs. Each decision maker selects from a set of valid, protocol-sanctioned decisions and produces mutually compatible message-sending choices. The underlying communication service is fully abstracted away. The paper provides a formal operational semantics for Kiko to rigorously define agent behavior.
AI.result: Through the operational semantics, the authors establish two key properties of Kiko agents: (1) protocol compliance — agents always act within the bounds of the protocol; and (2) enactment completeness — Kiko agents are capable of realizing any possible protocol enactment.
AI.conclusion: Kiko successfully bridges the gap between internal decision logic and public agent actions by providing a protocol-based abstraction centered on decision makers, yielding formally verified protocol compliance and full expressiveness for protocol enactment.

title: Agentic Analysis for Agentic Infrastructure: An LLM-Powered Pipeline for Comparative Governance of DAO and Corporate AI Protocols
summary: As AI agent protocols proliferate, the governance structures shaping their interoperability standards remain empirically underexamined. We introduce an LLM-powered comparative pipeline for large-scale governance discourse analysis, integrating automated annotation, neural topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to study socio-technical power structures at scale. We validate it on two contrasting standards for agent interoperability: ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led). Analyzing 4,323 governance participation records, we combine LLM-assisted coding, topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to examine how institutional design shapes thematic priorities and community structure. We find that while governance form influences substantive focus, both regimes exhibit comparable levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. Discourse alignment is denser in the permissionless setting, suggesting that open governance may foster greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation. These findings illustrate how LLM-assisted methods can advance the empirical study of technology governance, with implications for designing more equitable agentic AI standards. All data and code are openly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an LLM-powered pipeline for analyzing governance discourse at scale, applies it to compare ERC-8004 (permissionless) and Google A2A (corporate-led) agent interoperability standards, and finds that while governance form shapes thematic focus, both exhibit similar participation inequality and fragmentation, though permissionless governance yields denser discourse alignment.
AI.motivation: AI agent protocols are proliferating rapidly, yet the governance structures that shape their interoperability standards remain empirically understudied. There is a need for scalable methods to analyze socio-technical power structures in technology governance.
AI.method: An LLM-powered comparative pipeline integrating (1) automated annotation, (2) neural topic modeling, and (3) multi-layer network analysis. Applied to 4,323 governance participation records from two contrasting standards: ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led).
AI.result: (1) Governance form influences substantive thematic focus; (2) both regimes exhibit comparable levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation; (3) discourse alignment is denser in the permissionless setting, suggesting open governance fosters greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation.
AI.conclusion: LLM-assisted methods can meaningfully advance the empirical study of technology governance. The findings carry implications for designing more equitable agentic AI standards, and the open availability of data and code supports reproducibility and further research.

title: The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators
comment: 12 pages main text + 21 pages appendix (37 pages total, incl. references); 10 figures (6 main text + 4 appendix); 10 tables (2 main text + 8 appendix). Preliminary preprint; work in progress. Keywords: self-improving agents, learned evaluation, multi-agent systems, auto- mated scientific discovery, controlled utility evolution, co-evolutionary search, autoresearch
summary: Self-improving agents are state-of-the-art (SOTA) on agentic coding benchmarks and have recently been extended to general domains. However, their search methods generally assume a stationary evaluation criterion: a fixed verifier, benchmark, or labeled dataset that remains valid as the agent improves. This ignores a central feature of evolution: species adapt as their environments change with them. We aim to bring the same principle to recursive self-improvement, making evaluation part of the improvement loop and opening search to evolving evaluators, adversarial objectives, and dynamic utilities that may surpass static benchmarks. We introduce the Red Queen Godel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework for recursive self-improvement under non-stationary utilities. The RQGM makes this possible through controlled utility evolution: search is organized into epochs with a fixed within-epoch evaluation criterion, while the utility can be updated at epoch boundaries, so self-improvement guarantees hold per epoch as the objective evolves across them. We begin by showing that even on verifiable coding tasks, the RQGM improves test pass rate over the prior SOTA by adding a complementary agent-as-a-judge code-review signal. This signal is cheaper and the RQGM uses 1.35x-1.72x fewer tokens. We then turn to scientific paper writing and reviewing, and Olympiad-level proof writing and grading, where the RQGM improves performance over prior self-improving agents: co-evolved writers reach 1.78x-1.86x higher acceptance rates under a diverse agent-as-a-judge panel, while co-evolved graders reach 9% higher ground-truth accuracy. In paper reviewing, the strongest baseline reviewer over-accepts AI-generated papers at up to 1.91x the human rate. The RQGM corrects this by introducing an adversarial objective that discovers reviewers equally stringent on AI and human work.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Red Queen Godel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework enabling recursive self-improvement under non-stationary utilities, where evaluation criteria co-evolve with the agent. RQGM organizes search into epochs with fixed within-epoch criteria but allows utility updates at epoch boundaries, achieving superior results on coding (1.35-1.72x fewer tokens, higher pass rates), scientific writing (1.78-1.86x higher acceptance), proof grading (9% higher accuracy), and adversarial reviewer calibration.
AI.motivation: Current self-improving agents rely on stationary evaluation criteria (fixed verifiers, benchmarks, or labeled datasets), which contradicts a core evolutionary principle: species co-adapt as their environments change. The authors aim to bring non-stationary, co-evolving evaluation into recursive self-improvement loops, enabling evolving evaluators, adversarial objectives, and dynamic utilities that can surpass static benchmarks.
AI.method: The RQGM framework organizes recursive self-improvement into epochs. Within each epoch, a fixed evaluation criterion is used for search/optimization, guaranteeing self-improvement. At epoch boundaries, the utility function itself is updated (e.g., via agent-as-a-judge signals, adversarial objectives, or co-evolved evaluators). This enables controlled utility evolution while maintaining per-epoch improvement guarantees. The method is applied to coding tasks (adding code-review signals), scientific writing/reviewing, and Olympiad-level proof writing/grading.
AI.result: On verifiable coding tasks, RQGM surpasses prior SOTA in test pass rate while using 1.35-1.72x fewer tokens. For scientific paper writing, co-evolved writers achieve 1.78-1.86x higher acceptance rates under diverse agent-as-a-judge panels. For proof grading, co-evolved graders reach 9% higher ground-truth accuracy. In paper reviewing, the strongest baseline reviewer over-accepts AI papers at 1.91x the human rate; RQGM's adversarial objective discovers reviewers equally stringent on AI and human work.
AI.conclusion: Non-stationary utility evolution via RQGM demonstrably improves over stationary self-improvement across coding, scientific writing, and mathematical proof domains. Co-evolving evaluators alongside agents yields both better performance and better-calibrated evaluation, addressing biases like AI-paper over-acceptance.

title: Instruction Bleed: Cross-Module Interference in Prompt-Composed Agentic Systems
comment: 8 pages, 2 tables. Accepted to the ICML 2026 Workshop on Failure Modes in Agentic AI (FAGEN), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Practitioners of prompt-composed agentic systems report a recurring failure mode: editing one prompt module silently shifts the behavior of others despite no shared variable or executable dependency. We formalize this as compositional behavioral leakage (CBL): interference between modules sharing a context window. CBL is enabled by architectural non-isolation: transformer self-attention provides no formal boundary between concatenated modules. We probe CBL on a deployed job-evaluation agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6, 144 trials) through a reusable three-channel protocol that perturbs non-focal modules along volume, content, and form. Only the content channel produces a detectable paired effect (Cohen's d = 0.63, bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero); no recommendation flipped -- a sub-threshold regime invisible to standard QA but compounding across the thousands of decisions a deployed agent makes. CBL is orthogonal to known agent-failure axes (adversarial injection, cognitive degradation, multi-agent fault propagation, privacy leakage). We contribute an operational definition, a reusable protocol, a falsifiable prediction set, and a system-class characterization, establishing cross-module interference measurement as a requirement for prompt-composed agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: Prompt modules in agentic systems interfere with each other through shared context window attention, a phenomenon the authors formalize as Compositional Behavioral Leakage (CBL). Experiments on Claude Sonnet 4.6 show subtle but detectable cross-module effects (d=0.63) from content perturbations — effects invisible to standard QA but potentially compounding at deployment scale.
AI.motivation: Practitioners report that editing one prompt module silently alters the behavior of other modules despite no shared variables or executable dependencies. This failure mode lacks formal definition, measurement protocols, and empirical characterization, motivating the authors to establish CBL as a distinct axis of agent-failure requiring systematic evaluation.
AI.method: The authors formalize CBL as interference between modules sharing a context window, enabled by the lack of architectural isolation in transformer self-attention. They design a three-channel perturbation protocol (volume, content, form) and apply it to a deployed job-evaluation agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6) across 144 trials, measuring paired effects via Cohen's d with bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: Only the content perturbation channel produced a detectable effect: Cohen's d = 0.63 with bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero. No individual recommendation flipped, indicating a sub-threshold regime invisible to standard QA metrics but potentially compounding across thousands of deployed decisions.
AI.conclusion: CBL is orthogonal to known failure axes (adversarial injection, cognitive degradation, multi-agent fault propagation, privacy leakage). The authors contribute an operational definition, a reusable measurement protocol, a falsifiable prediction set, and a system-class characterization, arguing that cross-module interference measurement should become a standard requirement for prompt-composed agent evaluation.

title: HierBias: Context-Conditioned Hierarchical Media Bias Detection with Multi-Task Type Classification
summary: Media bias detection is a critical task for ensuring fair and balanced information dissemination, yet existing sentence-level approaches classify each sentence independently, ignoring inter-sentence contextual signals that human annotators naturally exploit. We present \textbf{HierBias}, a hierarchical context-conditioned media bias detector that formally models document context in bias prediction. We introduce the \emph{context-conditioned bias probability} and prove theoretically that leveraging document context strictly reduces the Bayes error of sentence-level classification when inter-sentence mutual information is non-zero. A multi-task generalization bound further establishes that jointly training binary bias detection and fine-grained bias type classification improves sample efficiency on small annotated corpora. Architecturally, HierBias pairs a sentence-level RoBERTa encoder with a cross-sentence Transformer aggregator and dual output heads for binary detection and four-class type classification. Evaluated on BABE and BASIL, HierBias achieves 0.853 F1 and 0.723 MCC, surpassing the state-of-the-art bias-detector by $+2.6\%$ F1 and $+4.3\%$ MCC (McNemar's test, $p < 0.05$). Ablation experiments confirm that each theoretical component contributes independently and consistently.

AI.tldr: HierBias is a hierarchical model for media bias detection that leverages inter-sentence context, theoretically proving context reduces Bayes error, and achieves state-of-the-art results on BABE and BASIL with +2.6% F1 and +4.3% MCC gains.
AI.motivation: Existing sentence-level media bias detection methods classify sentences independently, ignoring the inter-sentence contextual signals that human annotators exploit. This motivates a formal treatment of document-level context for improved bias prediction.
AI.method: HierBias combines a sentence-level RoBERTa encoder with a cross-sentence Transformer aggregator and dual output heads (binary detection + four-class type classification). The authors introduce the concept of context-conditioned bias probability and provide a theoretical proof that document context strictly reduces Bayes error when inter-sentence mutual information is non-zero. A multi-task generalization bound shows joint training improves sample efficiency. Evaluation uses McNemar's test for statistical significance.
AI.result: On the BABE and BASIL benchmarks, HierBias achieves 0.853 F1 and 0.723 MCC, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art by +2.6% F1 and +4.3% MCC (McNemar's test, p < 0.05). Ablation studies confirm each theoretical component contributes independently and consistently.
AI.conclusion: Modeling document-level inter-sentence context is both theoretically justified and empirically beneficial for media bias detection. The dual-task architecture with hierarchical aggregation provides a principled framework that improves over independent sentence classification approaches.

title: Orchestrating Black-Box Schema Converters: An Empirical Study of Automated, Quality-Ranked Conversion Across Heterogeneous Schema Languages
summary: Modern software systems routinely need the same data model in several schema languages: a model may exist as JSON Schema for a web API, as XSD for data exchange, and as SHACL for a knowledge graph. Keeping these representations consistent as the model evolves is a recurring construction and maintenance burden, because converters between schema languages are hard to find, scattered across ecosystems, of uneven quality, and frequently lossy. We study, empirically, to what extent such imperfect, heterogeneous converters can be orchestrated into automated, reproducible, and quality-ranked conversions, and where the current converter landscape reaches its limits. Our approach models schema languages as nodes and converters, treated as black boxes, as directed edges, so that conversions become paths that are discovered, executed, ranked, and reported with full per-step provenance, with failures handled by trying alternatives. We realize it as the open-source Schema Conversion Orchestrator, integrate it into MetaConfigurator, and evaluate it on 60 conversion tasks built from real-world schemas across five schema languages, using agent-assisted, human-reviewed quality annotations. Orchestration surfaces a usable result for 43 of 60 tasks; the remaining failures localize concrete gaps in the converter landscape. We discuss implications for tool builders and for measuring conversion quality.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies orchestrating heterogeneous, imperfect schema converters into automated conversion pipelines. By modeling schema languages as nodes and converters as directed edges in a graph, conversions become discoverable paths. The open-source Schema Conversion Orchestrator, integrated into MetaConfigurator, was evaluated on 60 real-world tasks across five schema languages, yielding usable results for 43 tasks and identifying concrete gaps in the converter landscape.
AI.motivation: Modern software systems require maintaining the same data model in multiple schema languages (JSON Schema, XSD, SHACL, etc.). Keeping these representations consistent during model evolution is burdensome because individual converters are scattered, of uneven quality, frequently lossy, and hard to find. There is no systematic way to chain these converters into reliable, automated, quality-assessed conversion workflows, nor a clear understanding of where the converter ecosystem fails.
AI.method: Schema languages are modeled as nodes and converters (treated as black boxes) as directed edges in a graph. Conversions become paths discovered via graph traversal. The system executes, ranks, and reports conversions with full per-step provenance; failures trigger alternative path exploration. The approach is implemented as the open-source Schema Conversion Orchestrator, integrated into MetaConfigurator. Evaluation uses 60 conversion tasks from real-world schemas across five schema languages, with quality annotations produced via agent-assisted, human-reviewed assessment.
AI.result: Orchestration produced a usable result for 43 of the 60 tasks. The remaining 17 failures localized concrete gaps in the current converter landscape. The approach demonstrated that orchestrating imperfect converters can yield automated, reproducible, quality-ranked conversions for a substantial portion of real-world tasks, while also systematically identifying where converter development is lacking.
AI.conclusion: Orchestrating heterogeneous, lossy converters into ranked, provenance-tracked conversion paths is viable and addresses a real maintenance burden in multi-schema systems. The failures reveal specific gaps that should guide future converter development. The work has implications for both tool builders and for establishing systematic methods of measuring schema conversion quality.

title: Physics-guided Convolutional Neural Network for Domain Growth Prediction in Systems with Conserved Kinetics
summary: The spatiotemporal evolution of many physical, chemical, and biological systems is described by nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). Recently, deep neural network-based surrogate models have gained increasing interest as efficient alternatives to computationally expensive traditional numerical solvers. In this work, we propose an attention-based, physics-guided convolutional neural network as a surrogate model to learn the microstructural evolution of such systems. We train the model to accurately predict the full time-evolution of phase separation in binary mixtures governed by the Cahn-Hilliard equation. We show that predictions from our trained surrogate model remain stable and accurate over long-time rollouts for both critical and off-critical mixtures and preserve the mixture composition throughout evolution. We also show that our model accurately captures the growth of domain size and is consistent with the Lifshitz-Slyozov domain-growth law. The prediction results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for modeling systems with conserved kinetics and can be extended to other complex dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes an attention-based, physics-guided CNN surrogate model for learning microstructural evolution governed by the Cahn-Hilliard equation, demonstrating stable, accurate long-time predictions that preserve mixture composition and obey the Lifshitz-Slyozov domain-growth law.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical solvers for nonlinear PDEs describing spatiotemporal evolution (e.g., phase separation) are computationally expensive. Deep learning surrogates offer efficient alternatives, but existing models may lack long-term stability, compositional consistency, and physical law adherence.
AI.method: An attention-based, physics-guided convolutional neural network (CNN) surrogate model is trained to predict the full time-evolution of phase separation in binary mixtures governed by the Cahn-Hilliard equation. The architecture incorporates attention mechanisms and physics-based guidance.
AI.result: The trained surrogate yields stable, accurate long-time rollout predictions for both critical and off-critical mixtures, preserves mixture composition throughout evolution, accurately captures domain size growth, and remains consistent with the Lifshitz-Slyozov domain-growth law.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework is effective for modeling systems with conserved kinetics and can be extended to other complex dynamical systems beyond phase separation.

title: Detecting and Controlling Sycophancy with Cascading Linear Features
summary: Interpreting and controlling model behaviors through activation steering methods requires many pairs of contrastive samples that clearly exhibit desired or undesired behavior. These data pairs determine the degree to which interpretability frameworks can reliably detect model features responsible for a behavior, and therefore the ability to steer models toward or away from such behavior. In this work, we present an iterative data generation pipeline that isolates cascading linear features responsible for a behavior. Specifically, we show how moving beyond simple binary pairs of samples, and instead isolating samples that show degrees of features that scale linearly with behavior, allows for better disentanglement of features. We focus on detecting and steering away from sycophancy -- the tendency of language models to prioritize user validation. We demonstrate that sycophancy features discovered through cascading samples form linearly separable subspaces, and allow for selection of model activations that more clearly correspond to the desired behavior than baseline approaches. We also evaluate their ability to enable detection, deterministic scoring, and robust steering, and see that they either match or outperform LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines while providing lower computational demand and more interpretability guarantees. Code & Data: https://cascading-feats.github.io/

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an iterative data generation pipeline that identifies cascading linear features — features scaling linearly with behavior intensity — for improved activation steering. Applied to sycophancy in LLMs, this method produces more interpretable, linearly separable feature subspaces that match or outperform LLM-as-judge and prompting baselines for detection, scoring, and steering, with lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods rely on binary contrastive sample pairs (desired vs. undesired behavior), which limit the ability to reliably detect and disentangle the model features responsible for a behavior. The authors argue that isolating samples exhibiting degrees of a feature that scale linearly with behavior intensity — rather than simple binary opposites — enables better feature disentanglement and more effective steering.
AI.method: The authors propose an iterative data generation pipeline that produces "cascading" samples: examples that exhibit a target behavior (sycophancy) at varying, linearly scaling intensities. These samples are used to identify activation subspaces where the behavior manifests as linearly separable features. The pipeline iteratively refines sample generation to isolate these cascading linear features, which are then leveraged for behavior detection, deterministic scoring, and activation steering (manipulating model activations to steer away from sycophancy).
AI.result: Sycophancy features discovered via cascading samples form linearly separable subspaces and yield model activations that correspond more clearly to the target behavior compared to binary-pair baselines. The method matches or outperforms LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting approaches for detection, deterministic scoring, and robust steering, while requiring lower computational demand and providing stronger interpretability guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Moving beyond binary contrastive pairs to cascading, linearly-scaling samples significantly improves the disentanglement of behavioral features in LLMs. This approach enables more reliable and interpretable activation steering with practical advantages over existing methods, demonstrated effectively on the sycophancy problem.

title: Having Dog Ears "for Real": Effects of Active and Passive Haptics on Embodying Non-Human Body Parts in VR
comment: Accepted to the IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR) 2026
summary: Embodying non-human body parts in VR is a prevalent practice among certain subcultures and is a personally important creative outlet to many individuals. However, the discrepant morphology between real and virtual bodies can decrease Sense of Embodiment (SoE). Haptic feedback can compensate by increasing SoE felt towards non-human body parts, but there is a literature gap in comparing the effects of different haptic modalities, and their combinations, on SoE. Through an online survey sent out to social VR communities (n = 63), we determined that animal ears are a commonly embodied and ecologically valid non-human body part to study. We then ran a 2x2 within-subjects user study (n = 28) with two independent variables: active haptics, delivered through vibrotactile gloves, and passive haptics, delivered through a physical headband, for when participants reach up to touch virtual dog ears appended to their avatar in VR. Our findings show that (1) passive haptics produced the strongest overall embodiment outcomes, (2) combining modalities reduced the benefits of passive haptics, and (3) SoE towards non-human body parts positively correlates with SoE towards the entire avatar. We discuss implications of our findings in various domains, and on embodiment literature.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how passive haptics (physical headband) and active haptics (vibrotactile gloves), alone and combined, affect the Sense of Embodiment (SoE) toward non-human body parts (virtual dog ears) in VR. A survey (n=63) established animal ears as ecologically valid targets, and a 2×2 within-subjects experiment (n=28) revealed that passive haptics alone yielded the strongest embodiment, combining haptic modalities diminished the benefits of passive haptics, and SoE toward non-human body parts correlates positively with SoE toward the entire avatar.
AI.motivation: While embodying non-human body parts in VR is a meaningful creative practice for many, morphological mismatch between real and virtual bodies reduces Sense of Embodiment. Haptic feedback is known to compensate, but there is a gap in the literature regarding how different haptic modalities (active vs. passive) and their combinations compare in their effects on SoE for non-human body parts.
AI.method: A two-phase approach: (1) An online survey (n=63) distributed to social VR communities to identify animal ears as a commonly embodied, ecologically valid non-human body part. (2) A 2×2 within-subjects user study (n=28) manipulating active haptics (vibrotactile gloves, on/off) and passive haptics (physical headband, on/off) while participants reached up to touch virtual dog ears on their VR avatar. Sense of Embodiment was measured across both the non-human body part and the full avatar.
AI.result: (1) Passive haptics (physical headband) produced the strongest overall embodiment outcomes. (2) Combining active and passive haptic modalities reduced the benefits observed with passive haptics alone. (3) Sense of Embodiment toward non-human body parts positively correlates with Sense of Embodiment toward the entire avatar.
AI.conclusion: Passive haptics are more effective than active haptics for enhancing SoE toward non-human body parts, and combining modalities can be counterproductive. Embodiment of non-human appendages appears tightly linked to overall avatar embodiment, carrying implications for VR avatar design, social VR platforms, and the broader embodiment literature.

title: Reducing Redundancy in Whole-Slide Image Patching for Scalable Indexing and Retrieval
summary: The rapid growth of digital pathology has created an urgent need for efficient indexing and retrieval of whole slide images (WSIs). This need is intensified by emerging generative AI workflows, particularly retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which require dependable similarity search to support high-stakes clinical decision-making. Yet the substantial cost of high-performance storage limits the scalability and accessibility of WSI indexing for many healthcare institutions. Consequently, methods that can reduce storage demands while preserving retrieval accuracy have become a critical research priority. We propose ARReST (Antithetical Redundancy Reduction Strategy), a principled oppositional framework that leverages redundancy across dissimilar tissue classes to markedly decrease the number of patches that must be indexed from each WSI. Instead of eliminating only within-class duplicates, ARReST identifies antithetical patches-those whose representations contribute minimally to cross-class discrimination-and prunes them from the searchable archive. This targeted reduction substantially compresses the index without sacrificing morphological diversity or retrieval fidelity. By minimizing superfluous patch representations, ARReST reduces storage footprint, lowers computational overhead, and accelerates similarity search across large pathology repositories. Extensive experiments on TCGA repository (The Cancer Genome Atlas with 21 organs) demonstrate that ARReST achieves significant index compression while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. The observed storage savings of 3% to 60% (14%$\pm$13%) can be reliably achieved without compromising retrieval performance for many organs. The proposed strategy enables scalable, cost-efficient WSI indexing and is well-suited for next-generation retrieval-driven clinical AI systems.

AI.tldr: ARReST proposes a framework that reduces whole slide image storage for indexing by pruning "antithetical" patches — those that contribute minimally to cross-class discrimination — achieving 3–60% storage savings without sacrificing retrieval performance.
AI.motivation: Digital pathology's rapid growth demands efficient WSI indexing and retrieval, especially for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in clinical AI. High-performance storage costs limit scalability, creating an urgent need for methods that reduce storage while preserving retrieval accuracy.
AI.method: ARReST (Antithetical Redundancy Reduction Strategy) is an oppositional framework that goes beyond traditional within-class deduplication. It identifies and prunes "antithetical patches" — patches whose feature representations contribute minimally to cross-class discrimination. By targeting redundancy across dissimilar tissue classes, it compresses the searchable index while maintaining morphological diversity and retrieval fidelity.
AI.result: Experiments on TCGA (21 organs) show ARReST achieves index compression ranging from 3% to 60% (mean 14% ± 13%) while maintaining competitive retrieval performance across most organs, without compromising retrieval fidelity.
AI.conclusion: ARReST enables scalable, cost-efficient WSI indexing by strategically pruning low-discriminative patches, making it well-suited for next-generation retrieval-driven clinical AI systems. The approach demonstrates that principled redundancy reduction across classes can yield meaningful storage savings without accuracy trade-offs.

title: MIRAGE: Protecting against Malicious Image Editing via False Moderation
summary: The proliferation of AI-powered image editing systems raises serious concerns because it allows personal images to be arbitrarily manipulated at scale, with minimal effort, and a lower barrier to entry. Prior work on image immunization adds imperceptible perturbations to an image to protect against unauthorized manipulations. However, these methods usually require access to the model weights and the image manipulating prompt. This significantly limits their use, especially against powerful commercial image-editors such as GPT-Image, Gemini Flash Image (Nano Banana), and Grok Imagine. To address this, we take a system-level view of the problem and identify a previously unexplored attack surface common to all major commercial image editing systems: pre-generation safety moderation.Rather than disrupting the generative model itself, we propose to immunize images by causing these moderation classifiers to flag images as policy-violating, triggering an automatic refusal regardless of the editing prompt. We operationalize this by adding adversarial perturbations to align our image to policy-violating concepts in the representation space of an ensemble of open-source embedding and moderation models. We call our method MIRAGE, which stands for Moderation Induced Resistance Against Generative Editing. We evaluate MIRAGE against multiple closed-source image editing APIs and demonstrate success rates of more than 88%. Our approach is simple, prompt-agnostic, and effective, offering a practical path towards protecting personal images from unauthorized AI-powered editing.

AI.tldr: MIRAGE protects personal images from AI-powered editing by adding adversarial perturbations that trick pre-generation safety moderation systems into flagging images as policy-violating, causing editing APIs to refuse manipulation. This prompt-agnostic, model-weight-free approach achieves over 88% success against commercial editors like GPT-Image and Gemini.
AI.motivation: Existing image immunization methods require access to model weights and editing prompts, making them impractical against closed-source commercial image editors. The authors identify an unexploited vulnerability: the safety moderation classifiers that all major systems run before generation, providing a universal attack surface.
AI.method: MIRAGE adds adversarial perturbations to images that align them with policy-violating concepts in the embedding space of an ensemble of open-source embedding and moderation models. This triggers the pre-generation safety filters of commercial editors to auto-refuse any editing request, regardless of the user's prompt.
AI.result: Evaluated against multiple closed-source image editing APIs (GPT-Image, Gemini Flash Image, Grok Imagine), MIRAGE achieves success rates exceeding 88%.
AI.conclusion: MIRAGE offers a simple, prompt-agnostic, and effective defense against unauthorized AI image editing by exploiting the universal pre-generation moderation pipeline, providing a practical path for protecting personal images without needing access to proprietary model weights or editing prompts.

title: SOLAR: AI-Powered Speed-of-Light Performance Analysis
summary: How fast could a deep-learning model run on target hardware, and how far is today's implementation from that limit? These questions are central to software, hardware, and algorithm optimizations. Speed-of-Light (SOL) analysis answers them by computing a workload's theoretical minimum execution time on a given architecture. Yet deriving SOL bounds remains manual, error-prone, and disconnected from rapid model development. To close this gap, we introduce SOLAR, a framework that automatically derives validated SOL bounds from PyTorch and JAX source code. SOLAR leverages both generative and deterministic components in its flow: an LLM frontend translates any source programs into an executable Affine Loop IR, validated by output comparison; a deterministic flow lifts the IR into an einsum graph; and an analytical backend computes unfused, fused, and cache-aware SOL bounds. SOLAR provides comprehensive operator and language coverage, produces validated bounds with zero observed SOL violations, and offers multi-fidelity analysis that tightens bounds and surfaces optimization insights. We evaluate SOLAR across KernelBench, JAX/Flax models, and robotics workloads. These experiments demonstrate four use cases: headroom analysis at multiple fidelity levels, identifying optimization opportunities, cross-platform exploration, and inverse-roofline hardware provisioning.

AI.tldr: SOLAR is an automated framework that derives validated Speed-of-Light (SOL) execution time bounds from PyTorch/JAX source code using an LLM frontend and deterministic analytical backend, enabling multi-fidelity headroom analysis, optimization identification, cross-platform exploration, and hardware provisioning.
AI.motivation: Computing the theoretical minimum execution time (SOL bound) for deep learning models on target hardware is critical for guiding software, hardware, and algorithm optimizations, yet existing approaches are manual, error-prone, and not integrated into rapid model development workflows.
AI.method: SOLAR combines: (1) an LLM frontend that translates PyTorch/JAX source code into an executable Affine Loop IR with output-validation; (2) a deterministic flow that lifts IR into an einsum graph; and (3) an analytical backend that computes unfused, fused, and cache-aware SOL bounds. The framework provides comprehensive operator/language coverage with zero observed SOL violations.
AI.result: Evaluated across KernelBench, JAX/Flax models, and robotics workloads, SOLAR demonstrated four key use cases: multi-fidelity headroom analysis, identifying optimization opportunities, cross-platform exploration, and inverse-roofline hardware provisioning.
AI.conclusion: SOLAR successfully automates the previously manual SOL analysis process with validated bounds, offering a practical tool for guiding DL system optimizations across multiple fidelity levels and hardware targets.

title: Know2Guess: A Contamination-Aware Multi-Zone Benchmark for Knowledge-Boundary Evaluation in Large Language Models
summary: Reliable evaluation of large language models should separate supported answering from unsupported guessing without conflating either with data contamination, prompt idiosyncrasy, or generic refusal behavior. We present a contamination-aware, multi-zone benchmark for measuring the transition from answerable knowledge to abstention-expected unknowns under frozen build-time labels. The benchmark contains 1,200 items across five domains, explicit abstention expectations, contamination-risk metadata, and dual parsing with an official strict parser plus a normalized robustness parser. We evaluate FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct models under locked answer-or-abstain prompts, answer-only controls, and prompt-template variants. The benchmark is not solved by generic non-answer behavior: FLAN baselines remain weak on productive abstention, while stronger instruction-tuned models expose a selective but incomplete transition from answering to abstaining. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieves the best overall reliability, but answer-expected zones remain difficult, calibration remains poor, and benign-item refusal persists. Prompt and parser robustness analyses preserve the main ranking and qualitative conclusions. The benchmark therefore provides a reproducible protocol for auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct but interacting dimensions of LLM reliability.The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/renweimeng/Know2Guess-A-Contamination-Aware-Multi-Zone-Benchmark.

AI.tldr: A contamination-aware, multi-zone benchmark is introduced to evaluate LLMs' ability to distinguish answerable questions from unknowns, measuring the transition from supported answering to appropriate abstention. Evaluations across FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct reveal that stronger instruction-tuned models show a selective but incomplete transition, with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieving the best overall reliability, though calibration remains poor and benign refusal persists.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation conflates supported answering, unsupported guessing, data contamination, prompt idiosyncrasies, and generic refusal behavior. There is a need for a reproducible protocol that disentangles these dimensions to reliably audit answerability and abstention.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark with 1,200 items spanning five domains, featuring frozen build-time labels, explicit abstention expectations, and contamination-risk metadata. They use dual parsing (official strict parser + normalized robustness parser) and evaluate models (FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, Llama-3-Instruct) under locked answer-or-abstain prompts, answer-only controls, and prompt-template variants.
AI.result: FLAN baselines are weak on productive abstention. Stronger instruction-tuned models exhibit a selective but incomplete answering-to-abstention transition. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieves the highest overall reliability, but answer-expected zones remain difficult, calibration is poor, and benign-item refusal persists. Prompt and parser robustness analyses preserve the main ranking and qualitative conclusions.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark offers a reproducible protocol for auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct yet interacting dimensions of LLM reliability. The dataset is publicly released.

title: Augmentation with Dilution: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Human Contributor Ecosystems After AI Coding Agent Adoption
summary: AI coding agents are penetrating open-source software development at an unprecedented pace, yet existing research predominantly treats human contributors as a static backdrop rather than as the subject of inquiry. This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study that takes the human contributor ecosystem as its dependent variable, examining how the number, composition, and behavior of human participants change following AI coding agent adoption in open-source projects. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design on a dataset of 11,097 GitHub repositories spanning January 2023 to May 2026, we provide causal evidence via the Sun and Abraham estimator. Our results show that AI agent adoption does not significantly change the absolute number of human contributors (ATT = 0.014, p = 0.224), but significantly reduces human contributor density (ATT = -0.019, p = 0.002), indicating that the relative share of human participation declines as AI-generated pull requests accumulate. The relative participation share of newcomers declines significantly by 3.7 percentage points (ATT = -0.037, p < 0.001), with the effect emerging immediately after adoption and remaining stable throughout the observation window. Review depth increases significantly by 5.3% (ATT = +0.0168, p < 0.001), indicating that AI agents shift burden from the code production stage to the review stage. Moderator analysis reveals that these effects vary systematically with project size, programming language, and project maturity. Together, these findings present a pattern of augmentation with dilution: AI agents are not displacing human contributors, but are systematically reshaping the participation structure of open-source ecosystems.

AI.tldr: First large-scale causal study of how AI coding agent adoption affects human contributor ecosystems in OSS. Using staggered DiD on 11,097 repos, findings show AI agents don't displace humans but dilute relative human participation, reduce newcomer share (~3.7pp), and shift burden to code review — a pattern termed "augmentation with dilution."
AI.motivation: Existing research treats human contributors as static context rather than the subject of inquiry when studying AI coding agents in OSS. There is a lack of causal evidence on how AI agent adoption reshapes the human contributor ecosystem — specifically the number, composition, and behavior of human participants.
AI.method: Staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) design using the Sun and Abraham estimator for causal inference. Dataset covers 11,097 GitHub repositories from January 2023 to May 2026. The dependent variable is the human contributor ecosystem (contributor count, density, newcomer share, review depth). Moderator analysis examines heterogeneity by project size, programming language, and project maturity.
AI.result: AI agent adoption shows no significant change in absolute human contributor count (ATT=0.014, p=0.224). Human contributor density drops significantly (ATT=-0.019, p=0.002). Newcomer participation share declines by 3.7pp (ATT=-0.037, p<0.001), with immediate and stable effect. Review depth rises 5.3% (ATT=+0.0168, p<0.001). Effects vary systematically with project size, language, and maturity.
AI.conclusion: AI coding agents produce a pattern of "augmentation with dilution": they do not displace human contributors outright but systematically reshape OSS participation structures — reducing relative human and newcomer involvement while increasing review burden. This raises long-term sustainability concerns for community-driven open-source development.

title: \chisao{}: A GPU-Native Parallel Optimizer for Multimodal Black-Box Functions via Convergence-Anticonvergence Oscillation
summary: Finding all modes of a multimodal black-box function is a fundamental challenge in optimization, Bayesian inference, and scientific computing. Existing approaches -- basin-hopping, CMA-ES, multistart gradient descent -- operate sequentially and cannot exploit the massive parallelism of modern GPU hardware. We introduce \chisao{} (\textbf{C}onvergence-\textbf{H}alt-\textbf{I}nvert-\textbf{S}tick-\textbf{A}nd-\textbf{O}scillate), a GPU-native population optimizer that runs an entire sample batch simultaneously and exploits a deliberate convergence-anticonvergence oscillation cycle to escape local traps while freezing confirmed modes. The structural move is asymmetric: samples that reach true peaks are frozen (``stuck'') and preserved, while the rest keep exploring via momentum-based anti-convergence and stochastically smoothed gradients. Adaptive reseeding via two complementary strategies (Repulse Monkey and Golden Rooster) maintains population diversity throughout. On all 42 functions of the Simon Fraser University optimization benchmark suite across dimensions $d \in \{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}$, \chisao{} achieves \textbf{100\%} mode recovery where all CPU baselines collapse at $d \geq 8$ on the hardest multimodal functions, at up to \textbf{$34\times$} speedup over basin-hopping on functions where all methods succeed (Michalewicz $d=64$) and up to \textbf{$39\times$} on unimodal functions (Rotated Hyper-Ellipsoid $d=64$, pure GPU dividend). All benchmarks evaluate the objective by value alone -- gradients come from finite differences -- so the reported speedups are a derivative-free worst case. Under substantial likelihood noise ($σ_{\mathrm{noise}}$ up to 1.0), mode detection remains 100\% reliable. The algorithm is available as a standalone open-source Python package on PyPI.

AI.tldr: CHISAO is a GPU-native population optimizer that uses a convergence-anticonvergence oscillation cycle to find all modes of multimodal black-box functions. It achieves 100% mode recovery on all 42 SFU benchmark functions across dimensions 2–64, with up to 34× speedup over basin-hopping, and remains robust under substantial likelihood noise.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-mode finding methods (basin-hopping, CMA-ES, multistart gradient descent) are sequential and cannot leverage GPU parallelism. There is a need for a massively parallel algorithm that efficiently locates all modes of multimodal black-box functions on modern GPU hardware.
AI.method: CHISAO (Convergence-Halt-Invert-Stick-And-Oscillate) runs an entire sample batch simultaneously on GPU. It employs an asymmetric structural move: samples reaching true peaks are frozen ("stuck") and preserved, while others continue exploring via momentum-based anti-convergence and stochastically smoothed gradients. Two complementary adaptive reseeding strategies — Repulse Monkey and Golden Rooster — maintain population diversity. Gradients are computed via finite differences, making the approach derivative-free.
AI.result: On all 42 functions of the SFU optimization benchmark suite (d ∈ {2,4,8,16,32,64}), CHISAO achieves 100% mode recovery where all CPU baselines fail at d ≥ 8 on the hardest multimodal functions. It delivers up to 34× speedup over basin-hopping where all methods succeed (Michalewicz d=64) and up to 39× on unimodal functions (Rotated Hyper-Ellipsoid d=64). Mode detection remains 100% reliable under likelihood noise up to σ_noise = 1.0.
AI.conclusion: CHISAO demonstrates that deliberate oscillation between convergence and anti-convergence, combined with asymmetric mode freezing and adaptive reseeding, enables GPU-native, derivative-free, fully parallel recovery of all modes in multimodal black-box optimization — outperforming sequential CPU methods in both reliability and speed, even under substantial noise.

title: Life After Benchmark Saturation: A Case Study of CORE-Bench
summary: When a benchmark's accuracy saturates, it is often retired and replaced with a more challenging version. We show that this approach privileges accuracy and misses the opportunity to study six other key dimensions of agent performance: construct validity issues such as shortcuts, out-of-distribution generalizability, efficiency, reliability, the relative importance of the model versus the scaffold, and uplift from human-agent collaboration. We use CORE-Bench Hard, a benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code, as a case study to demonstrate that measuring agents along these dimensions yields meaningful insights into agent performance even after accuracy saturates. First, we surface threats to construct validity in CORE-Bench Hard that are difficult to anticipate with less capable agents. We introduce an improved benchmark, CORE-Bench v1.1, and an out-of-distribution task suite, CORE-Bench OOD. Second, we find that despite accuracy saturation, CORE-Bench v1.1 remains useful for measuring efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance. Finally, we conduct a small-scale randomized experiment to measure uplift from human-agent collaboration on real-world computational reproducibility tasks. We find a statistically significant speedup by about a factor of two -- likely underestimated due to one-fifth of human-only reproductions reaching the time limit before completing -- and describe various other findings. Together, our contributions present a more rigorous alternative to the dominant accuracy-centric evaluation paradigm.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that when benchmark accuracy saturates, rather than simply retiring the benchmark, researchers should evaluate agents along six under-explored dimensions: construct validity (shortcuts, OOD generalization), efficiency, reliability, model vs. scaffold contributions, and human-agent collaboration uplift. Using CORE-Bench (computational reproducibility) as a case study, the authors demonstrate that these dimensions yield meaningful insights even post-saturation, introduce improved benchmarks (v1.1 and OOD), and find a statistically significant ~2× speedup from human-agent collaboration.
AI.motivation: Benchmark evaluation in AI is dominated by an accuracy-centric paradigm: when accuracy saturates, benchmarks are discarded for harder ones. This misses the opportunity to extract insights from other important performance dimensions. The authors seek to demonstrate a more rigorous, multidimensional evaluation framework.
AI.method: Using CORE-Bench Hard (a benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code) as a case study: (1) Surface construct validity threats (shortcuts) via more capable agents; (2) Introduce CORE-Bench v1.1 and an OOD task suite (CORE-Bench OOD); (3) Measure efficiency, reliability, model vs. scaffold contributions on CORE-Bench v1.1; (4) Conduct a small-scale randomized experiment comparing human-only vs. human-agent collaboration on real-world reproducibility tasks.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Identified construct validity threats in CORE-Bench Hard not visible with weaker agents; (2) CORE-Bench v1.1 remains discriminative for efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance despite accuracy saturation; (3) Human-agent collaboration yielded a statistically significant ~2× speedup over human-only reproductions, likely an underestimate due to 20% of human-only runs hitting the time limit.
AI.conclusion: The dominant accuracy-centric evaluation paradigm should be replaced by a multidimensional framework encompassing construct validity, OOD generalizability, efficiency, reliability, model/scaffold attribution, and human-agent collaboration uplift. This yields richer insights and more rigorous agent evaluation, even on saturated benchmarks.

title: Assistive Visual Cues for Visual Neglect Patients
summary: Previous research on exogenous and endogenous cues has shown how they direct attention and improve interaction speed and error rate in applications. However, most studies focus on people with normal sight. People suffering from visual neglect have difficulties attending to parts of the visual field. One treatment method calls for the use of strong visual cues to remind patients of their neglected area and help guide their attention to it. Therefore, we examine the effects of endogenous and exogenous cues on visual neglect patients. Our results showed that visual neglect patients perform better with endogenous cues, when targets are within their neglected area. In some cases, combining exogenous and endogenous cues improve performance further. However, the performance varies greatly between patients. Using one neglect patient as an example, we saw that the best endogenous cue had an average acquisition time of 3.5 seconds compared to 6.5 for the best exogenous. Combining exogenous and endogenous cues further improved acquisition time to 2.8 seconds.

AI.tldr: This study investigates how exogenous (reflexive) and endogenous (volitional) visual cues affect attention in patients with visual neglect. Results show that endogenous cues outperform exogenous cues for directing attention to neglected visual fields, and combining both cue types can yield further improvements, though individual patient responses vary significantly.
AI.motivation: Most attention cueing research focuses on normally sighted individuals, yet visual neglect patients struggle to attend to parts of their visual field. Since strong visual cues are used therapeutically to redirect attention to neglected areas, understanding which cue types (endogenous vs. exogenous) work best for this population is clinically important.
AI.method: The researchers examined the effects of both endogenous cues (centrally presented, requiring voluntary interpretation) and exogenous cues (peripherally presented, reflexively capturing attention), as well as their combination, on visual neglect patients' ability to detect targets in neglected visual field regions. Acquisition time served as a key performance metric.
AI.result: Endogenous cues consistently outperformed exogenous cues for neglect patients when targets appeared in the neglected hemifield. Combining exogenous and endogenous cues further improved performance in some cases. A representative patient showed average acquisition times of 3.5s with the best endogenous cue, 6.5s with the best exogenous cue, and 2.8s with combined cues. However, there was substantial inter-patient variability.
AI.conclusion: Visual neglect patients benefit more from endogenous than exogenous attentional cues for redirecting attention to neglected areas, and combined cueing strategies may offer additional gains. The high inter-patient variability suggests that individualized cueing approaches may be necessary for therapeutic applications.

title: From Clicks to Intent: Cross-Platform Session Embeddings with LLM-Distilled Taxonomy for Financial Services Recommendations
comment: Dianjing Fan and Yao Li equally contributed to this work. 7 pages, 1 figure
summary: Sequential user behavior modeling is widely adopted in industrial recommender systems; however, significant gaps remain in financial services, where pre-login web interactions and authenticated in-app experiences differ drastically. Specifically, pre-login web users typically explore new products, whereas logged-in app users focus on account servicing. Due to the challenge of cross-channel entity resolution (e.g., matching anonymous web sessions to authenticated mobile accounts), web-based intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization. Existing methods for capturing web-based intent are often ad-hoc and narrow, lacking the flexibility to support both quantitative downstream recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale. In this work, we propose a scalable and dual-purpose intent prediction framework for web-based interactions and demonstrate its applicability for personalization. Our approach transforms raw web clickstreams into two outputs: a self-supervised Transformer encodes multi-modal clickstreams into a compact session embedding, while an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline produces interpretable intent labels. Our system demonstrates that self-supervised clickstream representations combined with LLM-distilled taxonomies can jointly serve quantitative tasks and qualitative understanding in production: on the mobile homepage tile ranking task, the session embedding improves macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38% over production baselines. On the user conversion prediction task, the embedding outperforms the LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1, while the distillation layer delivers interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop.

AI.tldr: Proposes a dual-purpose framework that transforms web clickstreams into both compact self-supervised session embeddings (for quantitative downstream tasks) and LLM-distilled interpretable intent labels (for qualitative understanding), demonstrating significant gains in mobile homepage recommendation and user conversion prediction in financial services.
AI.motivation: Financial services face a cross-channel gap: pre-login web users explore products while logged-in app users manage accounts, and web intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization due to entity resolution challenges. Existing methods lack flexibility for both quantitative recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale.
AI.method: A dual-output framework: (1) a self-supervised Transformer that encodes multi-modal clickstreams into compact session embeddings, and (2) an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline that produces interpretable intent labels. The distillation layer balances latency and performance for production deployment.
AI.result: On mobile homepage tile ranking, the session embedding improves macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38% over baselines. On user conversion prediction, the embedding outperforms LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1; the distilled labels achieve interpretability at ultra-low latency with only 7% performance degradation.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised clickstream representations combined with LLM-distilled taxonomies effectively serve both quantitative recommendation tasks and qualitative understanding in production financial services, bridging the web-to-app intent gap.

title: Data Facts: A Metadata Schema for Structured Data Exchange in the NANDini Multi-Agent Ecosystem
summary:
NANDini (Networked Agents Natural Distillation of Interconnected Nodal Intelligence) envisions an automated ecosystem where intelligent agents independently create, process, and exchange data to drive decisions at scale. Realizing this vision requires infrastructure beyond agent discovery and communication: agents must be able to advertise, evaluate, and verify the datasets they hold.
  Current protocols, including NANDA for federated registry and A2A and MCP for inter-agent messaging, address identity and communication but provide no mechanism for structured data exchange. Existing enterprise data-sharing frameworks, such as IDS-RAM, Gaia-X, and Ocean Protocol, assume human-in-the-loop governance that is incompatible with autonomous, real-time agent interactions.
  We introduce Data Facts, a core NANDini concept: a lightweight JSON metadata schema that bridges agent discovery and data access through a single pointer, `data_facts_url`, added to an existing Agent Facts registry record. The linked document encodes dataset identity, access tier, whether public, semi-private, or private, endpoint, a time-to-live for freshness validation, and a SHA-256 integrity checksum.
  For private and semi-private data, we implement a three-layer security pipeline: JWT authentication, capability-scoped gateway authorization, and an A2A credential delegation protocol. Across 840 decision-making evaluations, data-informed agents achieve 100% accuracy versus 35.2% without data access (p < 0.001); TTL enforcement reduces stale-data errors from 37.6% to 8.8%; checksum verification achieves 100% corruption detection at all injection rates; and the security pipeline blocks all 46 forgery attempts with zero data leakage.

AI.tldr: NANDini introduces "Data Facts," a lightweight JSON metadata schema that enables autonomous agents to advertise, evaluate, and verify datasets via a single pointer in Agent Facts registries, achieving 100% data-informed accuracy and robust security with zero leakage.
AI.motivation: Current agent protocols (NANDA, A2A, MCP) address identity and communication but lack structured data exchange mechanisms. Enterprise frameworks (IDS-RAM, Gaia-X, Ocean Protocol) require human-in-the-loop governance, making them incompatible with autonomous, real-time agent interactions. There is no existing infrastructure for agents to advertise, evaluate, and verify datasets they hold without human intervention.
AI.method: The authors propose Data Facts: a lightweight JSON metadata schema added via a `data_facts_url` pointer to Agent Facts registry records. It encodes dataset identity, access tier (public/semi-private/private), endpoint, TTL for freshness validation, and SHA-256 integrity checksum. For private/semi-private data, a three-layer security pipeline is implemented: (1) JWT authentication, (2) capability-scoped gateway authorization, and (3) an A2A credential delegation protocol. Evaluation uses 840 decision-making trials, with forgery injection and staleness experiments.
AI.result: Data-informed agents achieved 100% accuracy vs. 35.2% without data access (p < 0.001). TTL enforcement reduced stale-data errors from 37.6% to 8.8%. SHA-256 checksum verification detected 100% of data corruption at all injection rates. The security pipeline blocked all 46 forgery attempts with zero data leakage.
AI.conclusion: Data Facts successfully bridges agent discovery and data access in a fully autonomous manner, eliminating the human-in-the-loop bottleneck. The combination of TTL-based freshness, checksum integrity, and multi-layer security provides a viable infrastructure for trusted, real-time data exchange among autonomous agents at scale.

title: Scientific discovery as meta-optimization: a combinatorial optimization case study
summary: Scientific discovery is fundamentally an optimization problem, defined by a vast "state space" of theories and experiments, and an evaluation criterion based on quality, novelty, and validity. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated exploration of this space, but we argue that simultaneous modification of the evaluation criteria is equally important. Here, we propose formalizing research as meta-optimization, where the optimization objective itself is also being optimized. Our key contribution is "consensus objective aggregation," where LLM-generated objective functions are combined via correlation-weighted voting, yielding a stable, self-correcting evaluation criterion that evolves as understanding deepens. We apply this framework to algorithm discovery for 3-SAT problems based on digital MemComputing machines, reducing the baseline scaling with problem size $N$ from $\sim N^{2.51}$ to $\sim N^{1.33}$ and delivering a $\sim 67\times$ speedup on the largest instances tested. As a problem-agnostic framework, we hope this approach will considerably aid scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper frames scientific discovery as a meta-optimization problem where both theories/experiments and the evaluation criteria themselves are being optimized. The core contribution is "consensus objective aggregation," which combines LLM-generated objective functions via correlation-weighted voting to produce a stable, self-correcting evaluation metric. Applied to 3-SAT algorithm discovery using digital MemComputing machines, the framework reduces scaling from ~N^2.51 to ~N^1.33 and achieves a ~67× speedup on the largest instances.
AI.motivation: Traditional approaches to automated scientific discovery treat the evaluation criterion as fixed while searching over theories and experiments. The authors argue that in real science, the criteria for what constitutes "good" science also evolve as understanding deepens. This motivates a meta-optimization formulation where the objective function itself is subject to optimization, enabling a more faithful and effective automation of the scientific process.
AI.method: The framework formalizes research as meta-optimization with two interacting levels: (1) optimization over the state space of theories/experiments, and (2) meta-optimization over the evaluation criteria. The key technical mechanism is "consensus objective aggregation," where multiple LLM-generated objective functions are combined via correlation-weighted voting. This produces a self-correcting evaluation criterion that stabilizes and improves as understanding evolves, avoiding the brittleness of any single hand-crafted or LLM-generated objective.
AI.result: Applied to algorithm discovery for 3-SAT problems based on digital MemComputing machines, the framework reduced scaling with problem size N from the baseline ~N^2.51 to ~N^1.33. On the largest instances tested, this yielded approximately a 67× speedup, demonstrating substantial practical improvements in algorithmic efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The meta-optimization framework with consensus objective aggregation provides a problem-agnostic approach to automated scientific discovery. By allowing evaluation criteria to co-evolve with the theories and experiments under investigation, the method captures a more authentic scientific process and demonstrates significant empirical gains. The authors express hope that this approach will broadly aid scientific discovery across domains.

title: Helpfulness Hurts: Domain-Dependent Degradation of Mid-Trained Compassion Values Under Post-Training
summary: Standard post-training pipelines apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) to make language models helpful, but these processes may inadvertently degrade values instilled during pre-training. We investigate whether the domain of post-training data differentially affects the retention of animal compassion values in a Llama 3.1 8B model mid-trained on compassion-oriented synthetic data, using both SFT (helpfulness via Dolly-15k vs. coding via Magicoder-110K) and GRPO (helpfulness via RLHFlow vs. coding via Magicoder), evaluated on the Animal Harm Benchmark (AHB 2.2) and MORU benchmark (Moral Reasoning Under Uncertainty). Helpfulness training significantly degrades animal compassion relative to coding training on AHB (SFT: 35.7% vs. 65.2%; GRPO: 18.7% vs. 32.0%), replicating across two independent helpfulness datasets and two training paradigms. On English MORU items, helpfulness training degrades general moral reasoning by 25.5 percentage points (46.4% vs. 71.9%), a striking gap that rivals the compassion effect in magnitude. However, this effect does not transfer cross-lingually: on the multilingual MORU benchmark, the domain effect disappears (SFT: 52.3% vs. 51.2%). In contrast, the animal compassion effect transfers consistently across languages, with Magicoder's AHB percentage-point gain over the base model 4.5 times larger on non-English items than English items. This divergence suggests that values instilled through mid-training are encoded more deeply and cross-lingually than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. These results suggest that, for labs building on value-laden mid-training, coding-domain post-training may better preserve mid-trained values than helpfulness post-training without harming general reasoning capabilities.

AI.tldr: Post-training data domain differentially affects value retention: helpfulness-oriented SFT and GRPO significantly degrade animal compassion and general moral reasoning compared to coding-domain training, while mid-trained values transfer cross-lingually but domain-specific reasoning improvements do not.
AI.motivation: Standard post-training (SFT + RL) for helpfulness may inadvertently erode values instilled during pre-training or mid-training. The authors investigate whether the domain of post-training data — helpfulness vs. coding — differentially affects the retention of animal compassion values in a model mid-trained on compassion-oriented data.
AI.method: A Llama 3.1 8B model was mid-trained on compassion-oriented synthetic data, then post-trained under four conditions: SFT with Dolly-15k (helpfulness) vs. Magicoder-110K (coding), and GRPO with RLHFlow (helpfulness) vs. Magicoder (coding). Evaluation used the Animal Harm Benchmark (AHB 2.2) and the Moral Reasoning Under Uncertainty (MORU) benchmark, including multilingual MORU items.
AI.result: Helpfulness training consistently degraded animal compassion vs. coding training on AHB (SFT: 35.7% vs. 65.2%; GRPO: 18.7% vs. 32.0%). On English MORU, helpfulness training degraded moral reasoning by 25.5 pp (46.4% vs. 71.9%). However, this domain effect disappeared on multilingual MORU (SFT: 52.3% vs. 51.2%), while the animal compassion effect transferred cross-lingually — Magicoder's AHB gain over base on non-English items was 4.5× larger than on English items.
AI.conclusion: Mid-trained values are encoded more deeply and cross-lingually than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. For labs building on value-laden mid-training, coding-domain post-training better preserves mid-trained values than helpfulness post-training, without harming general reasoning.

title: Towards Safety-Aware Mutation Testing for Autonomous Driving Systems
summary:
Simulation-based testing is essential for ensuring the safety of Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS), yet the community lacks a systematic criterion for determining when we can safely stop additional test scenario generation. Existing coverage metrics typically focus on individual component reliability or treat the ADS as a black box, failing to capture certain component interactions that cause most ADS accidents. While traditional mutation testing provides a falsifiable measure of test adequacy, directly porting code- and deep learning model-level mutations to the corresponding modules of ADS is insufficient.
  In this vision paper, we propose a paradigm shift toward Safety-Aware Mutation Testing (SAMT). Unlike traditional mutation testing, which creates mutants (i.e., faulty versions of the software under test) by injecting artificial faults into individual components, SAMT systematically injects temporally bounded faults into the messages exchanged between ADS modules to simulate realistic interaction failures. To ensure these mutants represent genuine hazards, we propose deriving mutant generation rules directly from top-down safety engineering frameworks, such as System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA). By embedding systems thinking into the mutation testing pipeline, SAMT provides a rigorous mechanism for evaluating test adequacy, enabling automated scenario generation, and guiding ADS repair. We also outline critical open challenges.

AI.tldr: Proposes Safety-Aware Mutation Testing (SAMT), which injects temporally bounded faults into inter-module messages of Autonomous Driving Systems, with mutant generation rules derived from STPA, to provide a systematic, falsifiable criterion for test adequacy and enable automated scenario generation.
AI.motivation: Current simulation-based ADS testing lacks a systematic stopping criterion; existing coverage metrics miss component interactions that cause most accidents, and traditional mutation testing (code/DL-level) does not adequately translate to the modular architecture of ADS.
AI.method: SAMT injects temporally bounded faults into messages exchanged between ADS modules rather than into individual components. Mutant generation rules are derived top-down from System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA), embedding systems thinking into the mutation testing pipeline.
AI.result: This is a vision paper; it outlines the SAMT paradigm and its potential to provide rigorous test adequacy evaluation, automated scenario generation, and guidance for ADS repair, while also identifying open challenges.
AI.conclusion: SAMT represents a paradigm shift from component-level to interaction-level mutation testing for ADS, leveraging safety engineering frameworks to ensure mutants represent genuine hazards, thereby offering a more meaningful measure of testing sufficiency.

title: Implementation of reinforcement learning in chemical reaction networks: application to phototaxis as curiosity-driven exploration
comment: This paper is accepted as talk at ALIFE 2026 (Waterloo, Canada)
summary: Living systems navigate environments using noisy and incomplete sensory signals. In unicellular algae, phototaxis is often modeled as a mechanistic run--tumble process driven by stimulus--response rules. However, such descriptions overlook how organisms actively sample their environment to reduce sensory ambiguity. From a minimal cognition perspective, we reframe this navigation as a subjective, information-driven sensorimotor process. To this end, we propose a framework linking a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with biochemical reaction dynamics. Environmental variables are hidden, while the cell updates a minimal internal state from each observation through a memoryless Bayesian step. These internal dynamics balance orienting toward light with exploratory reorientation and can be implemented through Chemical-Reaction-Network Ordinary Differential Equations (CRN--ODEs). Our model includes a biophysical observation process for photoreception and a chemically computable polynomial bound on information gain. Using Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) on 30 experimentally recorded Chlamydomonas trajectories, we infer the behavioral objective consistent with observed phototactic motion and benchmark the resulting dynamics with standard Stochastic Simulation Algorithm (SSA) baselines. Our model reproduces the empirical alignment-to-light distribution, comparable to objective SSA baselines on this dataset. Within this framework, run--tumble alternation emerges as an information-acquisition strategy: tumbling reorients the cell to sample new sensory configurations and resolve sensor ambiguity, demonstrating how intracellular biochemical networks can support adaptive information-seeking behavior in cellular navigation.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes unicellular phototaxis as an information-driven sensorimotor process using a POMDP framework coupled with biochemical reaction dynamics, showing that run-tumble behavior emerges as an adaptive information-acquisition strategy to resolve sensory ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Traditional mechanistic models of phototaxis (stimulus-response run-tumble rules) overlook how organisms actively sample their environment to reduce sensory ambiguity. The authors aim to bridge this gap by modeling navigation from a minimal cognition perspective, where the cell behaves as a subjective agent managing uncertainty through information-seeking actions.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework combining Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) with Chemical-Reaction-Network Ordinary Differential Equations (CRN-ODEs). The cell maintains a minimal internal state updated via memoryless Bayesian inference, balancing light orientation with exploratory reorientation. A biophysical photoreception model and a chemically computable polynomial bound on information gain are incorporated. Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is applied to 30 experimentally recorded Chlamydomonas trajectories to infer behavioral objectives, and the resulting dynamics are benchmarked against Stochastic Simulation Algorithm (SSA) baselines.
