AI.result: The IRL-inferred model successfully reproduces the empirical alignment-to-light distribution observed in experimental data, performing comparably to objective SSA baselines. Run-tumble alternation emerges naturally within the framework as an information-acquisition strategy, where tumbling serves to reorient the cell and sample new sensory configurations to resolve sensor ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: Run-tumble behavior can be understood not merely as a mechanistic reflex but as an adaptive information-seeking strategy. The POMDP + CRN-ODE framework demonstrates how intracellular biochemical networks can support such behavior, linking minimal cognition concepts with biochemically plausible computation in cellular navigation.

title: Refusal Lives Downstream of Persona in Chat Models
comment: Accepted to the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability workshop
summary: Linear directions in activation space have been identified for both refusal and persona traits in instruction-tuned chat models, but the two have been studied as separate mechanisms. We show they interact: a compliant persona gates refusal. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we extract a compliant model-persona direction and a refusal direction and intervene on both. Compliant persona steering suppresses refusal -- in Llama, the refusal rate falls from 97% to 2%. Reintroducing the refusal direction partially restores refusal at late layers but not at early ones. Projecting out the persona direction in a late-layer window restores it to baseline; projecting out a random direction does not. Refusal is therefore gated at the late-layer expression stage, downstream of where it is computed. Treating refusal as a single isolated direction misses its dependence on persona.

AI.tldr: Refusal and persona are not independent linear directions in activation space; a compliant persona direction gates refusal expression at late layers. Steering the persona direction can nearly eliminate refusal, and refusal cannot be fully restored at early layers once persona is altered, indicating a gating mechanism downstream of refusal computation.
AI.motivation: Prior work has identified linear directions in activation space for refusal and persona in chat models but has treated them as separate, independent mechanisms. This paper challenges that assumption by investigating whether and how these two directions interact, hypothesizing that persona may modulate or gate refusal behavior.
AI.method: The authors extract a compliant model-persona direction and a refusal direction from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using activation steering techniques. They then perform causal interventions: (1) steering the compliant persona direction to suppress refusal, measuring refusal rate changes (97% → 2% in Llama); (2) reintroducing the refusal direction at different layers to test restorability; (3) projecting out the persona direction in late-layer windows vs. random directions to isolate the gating locus.
AI.result: Compliant persona steering dramatically suppresses refusal (Llama: 97% → 2%). Reintroducing refusal direction partially restores refusal at late layers but not at early ones. Projecting out the persona direction in a late-layer window restores baseline refusal behavior, while projecting out a random direction does not. These results indicate refusal is gated at the late-layer expression stage, downstream from where the refusal computation occurs.
AI.conclusion: Refusal should not be treated as a single isolated direction; it depends on persona via a late-layer gating mechanism. This has implications for both mechanistic interpretability and safety — interventions targeting refusal alone may be circumvented if persona steering is not accounted for.

title: TinyCNNDeep: Lightweight Attention-Based CNN for EEG Classification of Eye States and Sleep Deprivation
summary: Sleep deprivation impairs vigilance and cognitive function, yet jointly identifying the sleep condition (normal vs deprived) and the eye state (open vs closed) from electroencephalography (EEG) remains underexplored. We address this four-class problem with TinyCNNDeep, a lightweight convolutional neural network that combines residual learning with a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention module. We convert short multi-channel EEG segments from five physiologically relevant channels (Fp1, Fp2, O1, Oz, O2) into 224x224 grayscale images through per-channel Z-score normalization, min-max scaling, and center padding, enabling 2D convolutions to jointly model inter-channel and temporal structure. On a 35-subject dataset recorded under normal-sleep and sleep-deprivation sessions, TinyCNNDeep attains a subject-wise mean accuracy of 83.69%, outperforming the strongest baseline (Random Forest with combined time-frequency features, 47.66%) by 36.03 percentage points, while three established EEG architectures (EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, DeepConvNet) operate near chance. Per-subject analysis quantifies inter-subject variability, and confusion-matrix inspection shows that residual misclassifications concentrate between eyes-closed states across sleep conditions. These results indicate that an image-based EEG representation paired with residual feature extraction and channel attention provides an accurate and computationally efficient framework for multiclass sleep-related EEG classification under a minimal electrode configuration.

AI.tldr: A lightweight CNN with residual learning and SE attention (TinyCNNDeep) classifies four states (normal/deprived sleep × eyes open/closed) from 5-channel EEG converted to images, achieving 83.69% accuracy—far surpassing traditional methods and established EEG architectures.
AI.motivation: Joint classification of sleep condition (normal vs. sleep-deprived) and eye state (open vs. closed) from EEG is underexplored. Existing EEG architectures struggle with this four-class problem, and there is a need for an accurate yet computationally efficient solution using minimal electrodes.
AI.method: EEG segments from five frontal and occipital channels (Fp1, Fp2, O1, Oz, O2) are converted to 224×224 grayscale images via per-channel Z-score normalization, min-max scaling, and center padding. A lightweight CNN (TinyCNNDeep) with residual blocks and Squeeze-and-Excitation attention performs 2D convolutions over these image-based representations, jointly modeling inter-channel and temporal structure. Evaluated on a 35-subject dataset with both normal-sleep and sleep-deprivation sessions.
AI.result: TinyCNNDeep achieved 83.69% subject-wise mean accuracy, outperforming Random Forest with time-frequency features (47.66%) by 36.03 percentage points. EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, and DeepConvNet performed near chance. Residual errors concentrated between eyes-closed states across sleep conditions, with per-subject analysis revealing inter-subject variability.
AI.conclusion: Image-based EEG representation combined with residual feature extraction and channel attention yields an accurate, computationally efficient framework for multiclass sleep-related EEG classification using only a minimal five-electrode configuration.

title: Scoring Is Not Enough: Addressing Gaps in Utility-fairness Trade-offs for Ranking
summary: Scoring functions are used to represent the relevance of individual documents. In modern information retrieval or recommendation systems, they are often learned from data and play a pivotal role in ranking sets of documents or items in a way that maximizes utility to a query or user. With the recent interest in algorithmic fairness, the success of scoring has naturally led to methods that learn scores that simultaneously trade off fairness and utility. In this work, we show that in stark contrast with utility-centric objectives, scoring is sub-optimal in achieving all utility-fairness trade-offs. We establish this with a series of counter-examples with a generic fairness formulation. We show that the issue persists whether we have a deterministic scoring function or a randomized one, or whether we measure fairness at the scope of a single query or across multiple queries. On the positive side, we empirically demonstrate that semi-greedy post-processing has the potential to achieve much better trade-offs, often approaching the ideal of exhaustive post-processing in a tractable way.

AI.tldr: Scoring functions are fundamentally sub-optimal for utility-fairness trade-offs; the paper proves this via counter-examples across various settings and shows that semi-greedy post-processing can approach ideal trade-offs tractably.
AI.motivation: With growing interest in algorithmic fairness, scoring functions have been widely adopted to learn fair rankings that balance utility and fairness. However, unlike in utility-only contexts where scoring is effective, the authors hypothesize that scoring is inherently inadequate for achieving the full spectrum of utility-fairness trade-offs, motivating a systematic investigation.
AI.method: The authors construct a series of counter-examples using a generic fairness formulation to demonstrate scoring's sub-optimality. They examine multiple settings: deterministic vs. randomized scoring functions, and single-query vs. multi-query fairness measurement. For the positive result, they empirically evaluate semi-greedy post-processing against the exhaustive post-processing ideal.
AI.result: Scoring functions provably fail to achieve all utility-fairness trade-offs across all examined settings — whether deterministic, randomized, single-query, or multi-query. Semi-greedy post-processing, however, empirically achieves significantly better trade-offs and often approaches the ideal of exhaustive post-processing while remaining computationally tractable.
AI.conclusion: Scoring is fundamentally sub-optimal for fairness-aware ranking; the ranking community should look beyond scoring functions and instead adopt post-processing approaches like semi-greedy methods to realize better utility-fairness trade-offs in practice.

title: CyberChainBench: Can AI Agents Secure Smart Contracts Against Real-World On-Chain Vulnerabilities?
summary: We present CyberChainBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on smart contract security across three complementary tasks: vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis. Built from 541 real-world exploit incidents from DeFiHackLabs spanning 9 EVM chains, the benchmark provides end-to-end on-chain evaluation where agents interact with historical blockchain state through isolated evaluation environments orchestrated by Harbor, using tools to read code, trace transactions, and validate exploits on mainnet forks. Each case is anchored to a specific block and includes structured ground truth covering vulnerability type, localization, and attacker profit. Exploits are graded by economic impact on historical forks; patches are validated by replaying historical attacks and legitimate transactions as fail-to-pass test oracles on a proxy-upgradeable subset. We define a five-type vulnerability taxonomy and evaluate multiple agent--model configurations. Results reveal a clear difficulty gradient: the best configuration scores 37.5% on detection, 43.7% on exploitation, but only 23.4% on patching, with the top agent (Codex with GPT-5.5) realizing \$57.4M in total exploit profit across the 200-case exploit set at a cost of $2.39 per case.

AI.tldr: CyberChainBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on smart contract security, covering vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis across 541 real-world DeFi exploit incidents on 9 EVM chains. The best agent achieves 37.5% on detection, 43.7% on exploitation, and only 23.4% on patching, with the top configuration realizing $57.4M in exploit profit.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based smart contract security auditing are limited in scope, lack real-world grounding, and do not support end-to-end evaluation across the full pipeline of detection, exploitation, and remediation. A comprehensive, on-chain benchmark anchored to historical exploit incidents is needed to rigorously assess agent capabilities.
AI.method: The authors construct CyberChainBench from 541 real-world exploit incidents (DeFiHackLabs) spanning 9 EVM chains. Each case is anchored to a specific block with structured ground truth (vulnerability type, localization, attacker profit). Agents operate in isolated evaluation environments via Harbor on mainnet forks, using tools to read code, trace transactions, and validate exploits. Exploits are graded by economic impact on historical forks; patches are validated by replaying historical attacks and legitimate transactions as fail-to-pass test oracles on a proxy-upgradeable subset. A five-type vulnerability taxonomy is defined.
AI.result: A clear difficulty gradient emerges: detection scores 37.5%, exploitation 43.7%, and patching only 23.4% for the best configuration. The top agent (Codex with GPT-5.5) realizes $57.4M in total exploit profit across the 200-case exploit set at a cost of $2.39 per case.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based agents show moderate capability in detecting and exploiting smart contract vulnerabilities but struggle significantly with automated patch synthesis, highlighting patching as a critical open challenge. The benchmark provides a rigorous, economically grounded framework for tracking progress in AI-driven smart contract security.

title: Semantic Early-Stopping for Iterative LLM Agent Loops
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Open implementation, machine-checked theory, and reproducible harness: github.com/SahilShrivastava-Dev/semantic-halting-problem
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) loops, for example a Writer that drafts and a Critic that revises, are almost always terminated by a fixed iteration cap (max_iterations). This is a syntactic kill-switch: it is blind to whether the answer is still improving, so it over-spends tokens on easy inputs and truncates hard ones. We study semantic early-stopping: the loop halts when consecutive draft embeddings stop changing in meaning (cosine distance with a patience window) and the answer's measured quality stops improving. Our work makes three contributions. First, an honest theoretical footing: we prove deterministic termination and well-definedness and machine-check these claims, while treating the convergence of the distance sequence as an empirically tested conjecture rather than a (previously over-claimed) Banach contraction. Second, a judge-efficient evaluation protocol: we generate each question's full trajectory once, replay every stopping policy over the identical drafts, and cache every LLM-judge call, yielding a strictly paired efficiency-versus-quality comparison at low cost; we further separate operational tokens (charged to a policy) from evaluation tokens (a measurement instrument). Third, an empirical study on multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering (HotpotQA). On the 60-question test split, a judge-free semantic stopper reduces operational tokens by 38% relative to max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81), whereas the full quality-gated variant is counter-productive because its per-round judging dominates cost. An oracle that selects the best round attains +0.115 Information Score over every practical policy (p ~ 4e-11), reframing the problem from "when to stop" (easy) to "which round is best" (open).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes semantic early-stopping for multi-agent LLM loops, using embedding cosine distance and quality checks instead of fixed iteration caps. A semantic stopper reduces operational tokens by 38% at parity quality; selecting the best round remains an open problem.
AI.motivation: Fixed iteration caps (max_iterations) in multi-agent LLM loops are arbitrary syntactic termination conditions that waste tokens on easy problems and prematurely truncate hard ones, lacking any awareness of whether answer quality is still improving.
AI.method: Semantic early-stopping based on two signals: (1) cosine distance between consecutive draft embeddings with a patience window to detect semantic convergence, and (2) a quality-gated variant that additionally checks measured answer quality improvement. The authors provide machine-checked proofs of deterministic termination and well-definedness. For evaluation, they introduce a judge-efficient protocol: generate one full trajectory per question, replay every stopping policy over identical drafts, cache LLM-judge calls, and separate operational tokens from evaluation tokens.
AI.result: On HotpotQA (60-question test split), the judge-free semantic stopper achieves 38% reduction in operational tokens relative to max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81). The quality-gated variant is counter-productive because per-round judging dominates cost. An oracle selecting the best round yields +0.115 Information Score over all practical policies (p ≈ 4e-11).
AI.conclusion: Semantic early-stopping is viable and token-efficient for multi-agent LLM loops, but quality-gating via per-round judging is cost-prohibitive. The key open challenge is not deciding when to stop, but identifying which round produces the best answer — shifting the problem from termination to round selection.

title: Investigating LLM's Problem Solving Capability -- a Study on Statics Questions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly influenced many aspects of society, particularly education, due to their demonstrated ability to complete assignments and examinations across a wide range of subjects. Although prior studies have examined the educational impact of LLMs, much of the existing work relies on public or open problem datasets and lacks topic-specific analysis. In engineering education, especially within mechanical engineering, systematic investigations of LLM performance on specific problem types remain limited. Instead of using traditional methods that directly ask textbook questions to an LLM tool, our study adopts a model distillation process to evaluate LLM capabilities in solving statics problems. By distilling ChatGPT, we extracted 25 text-only statics questions and further constructed two additional datasets by adding diagrams and modifying their numerical values. Experimental results show that while LLMs perform well on text-only statics problems, their accuracy decreases when diagrams are introduced and the problems require multi-step reasoning. Further analysis suggests that this performance drop is not primarily caused by limitations in image recognition, but rather by difficulties in multi-step reasoning and in consistently applying extracted visual information across successive solution stages.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates LLM (ChatGPT) performance on statics problems using a model distillation approach. LLMs perform well on text-only problems but accuracy drops significantly when diagrams are added and multi-step reasoning is required — not due to image recognition failures, but due to difficulties in multi-step reasoning and consistent use of visual information across solution stages.
AI.motivation: Prior LLM education studies rely on public datasets and lack topic-specific analysis. In mechanical/engineering education, particularly statics, systematic evaluation of LLMs on specific problem types is scarce. The authors aim to fill this gap with a controlled, distillation-based methodology.
AI.method: A model distillation process was used: ChatGPT generated 25 text-only statics questions, from which two additional datasets were constructed — one adding diagrams and another modifying numerical values. LLM performance was then evaluated and compared across these three dataset variants to isolate the effects of visual information and multi-step reasoning.
AI.result: LLMs achieved high accuracy on text-only statics problems. Accuracy decreased when diagrams were introduced and when problems demanded multi-step reasoning. The performance degradation was attributed primarily to multi-step reasoning difficulties and inconsistent application of extracted visual information, rather than image recognition limitations.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show promise for text-only statics problems but remain unreliable for diagram-based, multi-step engineering problems. The bottleneck lies in reasoning coherence across steps, not visual perception. This highlights a key limitation for deploying LLMs in engineering education contexts involving graphics-rich problem solving.

title: An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Specifications for VeriFast
summary: Static verification tools can assure industrial scale software, but require significant human labor to write specifications. This is particularly true of static verifiers based on separation logic (SL verifiers), which excel at verifying heapmanipulating programs, but require many complex auxiliary specifications to reason about heap structure. Recent work applies large language models (LLMs) to generate code, tests, and proofs, including specifications for verifiers, but mostly targeting non-SL verifiers. To address this gap, this paper thoroughly evaluates how well LLMs perform when prompted to generate specifications for verifying 303 C functions with the SL verifier VeriFast. We explored eight prompting approaches, ten LLMs, and three input types in two stages. Quantitative and qualitative analyses are used to assess the LLM-generated code and specifications for functional behavior, verifiability and errors. The results show that LLMs preserve functional behavior in source code and specifications (both over 91%), but achieve modest verification success (31.4%). Using Gemini 2.5 Pro and providing formal contracts lead to higher success rates in our setting. Moreover, most errors (94%) come from LLMs' mistakes in the domainspecific knowledge of SL verifiers such as VeriFast. These findings provide guidance for optimizing LLM-generated specifications for SL verifiers.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates how well LLMs generate separation logic specifications for VeriFast across 303 C functions, testing 8 prompting approaches, 10 LLMs, and 3 input types. While LLMs preserve functional behavior well (91%+), verification success is modest (31.4%), with Gemini 2.5 Pro and formal contracts yielding best results. Critically, 94% of errors stem from LLMs' lack of domain-specific SL verifier knowledge.
AI.motivation: Static SL verifiers like VeriFast require extensive, complex auxiliary specifications (e.g., heap invariants, inductive predicates) to verify heap-manipulating programs. Writing these specifications is labor-intensive. While LLMs have been applied to generate specifications for non-SL verifiers, their effectiveness for SL verifiers remains unexplored. This work addresses this gap.
AI.method: The authors evaluated LLM-generated specifications for 303 C functions using VeriFast. They explored eight prompting strategies (e.g., few-shot, chain-of-thought, providing formal contracts), ten LLMs (including GPT-4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude, and open-source models), and three input types (source code only, with informal specs, with formal contracts). Evaluation used both quantitative metrics (functional preservation, verification success rate) and qualitative error analysis across two stages.
AI.result: LLMs preserved functional correctness in both generated source code and specifications at rates exceeding 91%. However, overall verification success was only 31.4%. Gemini 2.5 Pro with formal contracts achieved the highest success. Error analysis revealed that 94% of failures were attributable to LLMs' deficient domain-specific knowledge of SL verifiers (e.g., incorrect separation logic predicates, malformed VeriFast annotations).
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs can generate functionally correct code and specifications but struggle with the domain-specific demands of SL verifiers like VeriFast. The findings highlight the need for integrating domain-specific SL knowledge into LLMs or prompting strategies, and provide concrete guidance for improving LLM-based specification generation for separation logic verification tools.

title: Neural Architecture Search for Generative Adversarial Networks: A Comprehensive Review and Critical Analysis
summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a pivotal technique in optimizing the design of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), automating the search for effective architectures while addressing the challenges inherent in manual design. This paper provides a comprehensive review of NAS methods applied to GANs, categorizing and comparing various approaches based on criteria such as search strategies, evaluation metrics, and performance outcomes. The review highlights the benefits of NAS in improving GAN performance, stability, and efficiency, while also identifying limitations and areas for future research. Key findings include the superiority of evolutionary algorithms and gradient-based methods in certain contexts, the importance of robust evaluation metrics beyond traditional scores like Inception Score (IS) and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), and the need for diverse datasets in assessing GAN performance. By presenting a structured comparison of existing NAS-GAN techniques, this paper aims to guide researchers in developing more effective NAS methods and advancing the field of GANs.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive review of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods applied to GANs, categorizing approaches by search strategies, evaluation metrics, and performance, highlighting the superiority of evolutionary and gradient-based methods, and identifying key research gaps.
AI.motivation: Manual design of GAN architectures is challenging, time-consuming, and suboptimal. NAS offers automation to discover effective architectures, but the landscape of NAS-GAN methods is fragmented. This paper aims to systematically review, categorize, and compare existing approaches to guide future research.
AI.method: The paper conducts a structured literature review, categorizing NAS-GAN approaches by search strategy (e.g., evolutionary algorithms, gradient-based methods, reinforcement learning), evaluation metrics (beyond IS and FID), and performance outcomes. It provides a comparative analysis across these dimensions.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) evolutionary algorithms and gradient-based methods outperform other strategies in specific contexts; (2) traditional metrics like IS and FID are insufficient for robust GAN evaluation; (3) diverse datasets are essential for reliable performance assessment; (4) NAS demonstrably improves GAN performance, stability, and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: NAS is a valuable tool for advancing GAN architecture design. Future work should focus on developing more robust evaluation metrics, testing across diverse datasets, and refining evolutionary and gradient-based search strategies to further enhance GAN performance and stability.

title: AlgoEvolve: LLM-driven Meta-evolution of Algorithmic Trading Programs
summary: Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can act as semantic mutation operators for the evolutionary discovery of programs and proofs. Most current applications focus on static coding benchmarks. We extend this paradigm to algorithmic trading. This domain is uniquely challenging because it is noisy, non-stationary, and highly discontinuous. We present AlgoEvolve, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that generates, evaluates, and iteratively improves executable trading strategies. These strategies are expressed as Python code and evaluated through a rigorous testing protocol. Across multiple experiments, the system exhibits emergent regime-adaptive strategy logic, including autonomous shifts in trading rules. We further introduce a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves the prompts guiding program synthesis in the inner loop. This outer loop discovers improved search heuristics. These heuristics balance exploration and exploitation while reducing zero-trade failures. They consistently outperform initial human-designed instructions. The results demonstrate that LLM-based semantic evolution provides a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex environments.

AI.tldr: AlgoEvolve uses LLMs as semantic mutation operators within an evolutionary framework to automatically generate and refine algorithmic trading strategies, demonstrating emergent adaptive behavior and introducing a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves prompts to improve search heuristics.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLM-driven program evolution has been limited to static coding benchmarks. The authors aim to extend this paradigm to algorithmic trading, a domain characterized by noise, non-stationarity, and discontinuity, presenting a more realistic and challenging testbed for continual program synthesis.
AI.method: AlgoEvolve is a two-level evolutionary framework: (1) an inner loop where LLMs generate and mutate trading strategies expressed as executable Python code, evaluated through rigorous backtesting; (2) a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves the textual prompts guiding the inner-loop LLM, thereby optimizing search heuristics for balancing exploration vs. exploitation and reducing zero-trade failures.
AI.result: Evolved strategies exhibit emergent regime-adaptive behavior, autonomously shifting trading rules in response to changing market conditions. The meta-evolved prompts consistently outperform human-designed instructions, discovering improved search heuristics.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based semantic evolution is a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex, non-stationary environments like algorithmic trading, with meta-evolution further enhancing the discovery process.

title: DanceDuo: Bridging Human Movement and AI Choreography
summary: In recent years, advancements in deep learning and generative models have revolutionized music-driven dance generation. This paper introduces a novel platform, namely DanceDuo, leveraging diffusion models to generate AI-choreographed dance sequences synchronized with a variety of music genres, to encourage dancing practice. The system allows users to interact with AI by selecting music tracks, humanoid models, and importing personal dance videos for comparison, fostering a rich and engaging user experience. DanceDuo not only offers dance generation but also integrates human pose estimation models to provide users with insightful comparisons of their own performances with AI-generated sequences. We conducted a comprehensive user study, revealing that users found the interface intuitive, with particular praise for the dance comparison feature. Our DanceDuo contributes significantly to the integration of AI in dance choreography, offering novel avenues for both recreational and professional applications.

AI.tldr: DanceDuo is an AI-powered platform that uses diffusion models to generate music-synchronized dance choreography, allowing users to compare their own dance performances with AI-generated sequences through integrated pose estimation.
AI.motivation: Leverage recent advances in deep learning and generative models to create an interactive system that encourages dancing practice through AI-choreographed dance generation synchronized with music.
AI.method: The platform employs diffusion models for dance generation conditioned on music input, integrates human pose estimation for performance comparison, and provides an interactive interface where users can select music tracks, humanoid models, and upload personal dance videos.
AI.result: A comprehensive user study demonstrated that users found the interface intuitive, with the dance comparison feature receiving particular praise.
AI.conclusion: DanceDuo represents a significant contribution to AI-assisted dance choreography, opening new possibilities for both recreational and professional dance applications.

title: TileMaxSim: IO-Aware GPU MaxSim Scoring with Dimension Tiling and Fused Product Quantization
summary: Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT achieve state-of-the-art accuracy through fine-grained token-level MaxSim scoring, yet existing GPU implementations leave most hardware performance unused. We give a roofline analysis of MaxSim on modern GPUs and identify a severe bandwidth gap: naive implementations reach only 5-18% of peak HBM bandwidth because they materialize the Nq x Nd similarity matrix, wasting memory traffic on data that is consumed once and discarded. We present TileMaxSim, a family of IO-aware Triton kernels that close this gap via (1) multi-query SRAM tiling that streams document embeddings through shared memory while accumulating per-query-token maxima in registers, reading each embedding from HBM exactly once; (2) dimension tiling that partitions the embedding dimension into 128-wide chunks, enabling scoring for d > 128 embeddings that overflow shared memory; and (3) fused product-quantization scoring via shared-memory lookup tables, cutting HBM I/O by up to ~31x. On NVIDIA H100 GPUs, TileMaxSim reaches 80.2% of peak HBM bandwidth and scores 82M documents/second (71.6M/s on real MS MARCO passages), a 220x speedup over loop-based scoring, 6.5x over fused PyTorch, 6.6-8.5x over torch.compile, and 469x the scoring throughput of WARP's CPU engine on the same node. TileMaxSim preserves exact retrieval quality: on MS MARCO and three BEIR benchmarks, rankings match reference MaxSim. As a drop-in replacement in ColBERTv2/PLAID, it cuts scoring latency at 100K candidates from 268 ms to 1.2 ms (98% lower end-to-end latency). We further show constant throughput from 100K to 500K documents, data-parallel multi-GPU sharding, robustness across dimensions 64-768, and FP16/BF16/FP32 support. Concurrent work independently develops an IO-aware fused MaxSim kernel; we differ in dimension tiling for d > 128 and fused product-quantization scoring.

AI.tldr: TileMaxSim introduces IO-aware Triton kernels that close the HBM bandwidth gap in MaxSim scoring for ColBERT-style retrieval, achieving 80.2% of peak GPU bandwidth and up to 220x speedup over naive implementations while preserving exact retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: Existing GPU implementations of token-level MaxSim scoring in multi-vector retrieval models (e.g., ColBERT) severely underutilize hardware, reaching only 5-18% of peak HBM bandwidth. This is because naive implementations materialize the full Nq × Nd similarity matrix, wasting memory bandwidth on data consumed once and then discarded. The authors aim to close this bandwidth gap to unlock orders-of-magnitude faster scoring without sacrificing retrieval accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose TileMaxSim, a family of IO-aware Triton kernels with three key techniques: (1) multi-query SRAM tiling that streams document embeddings through shared memory, accumulating per-query-token maxima in registers while reading each embedding from HBM exactly once; (2) dimension tiling that partitions the embedding dimension into 128-wide chunks, enabling scoring for d > 128 embeddings that exceed shared memory capacity; and (3) fused product-quantization scoring via shared-memory lookup tables, reducing HBM I/O by up to ~31x. The method is evaluated on NVIDIA H100 GPUs as a drop-in replacement in ColBERTv2/PLAID.
AI.result: On H100 GPUs, TileMaxSim achieves 80.2% of peak HBM bandwidth and scores 82M documents/second (71.6M/s on real MS MARCO passages). Speedups include: 220x over loop-based scoring, 6.5x over fused PyTorch, 6.6-8.5x over torch.compile, and 469x over WARP's CPU engine. End-to-end latency at 100K candidates drops from 268ms to 1.2ms (98% reduction). The method exhibits constant throughput from 100K to 500K documents, robust scaling across dimensions 64-768, and supports FP16/BF16/FP32. Rankings match reference MaxSim exactly on MS MARCO and three BEIR benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: TileMaxSim demonstrates that IO-aware kernel design can bridge the bandwidth utilization gap in MaxSim scoring, delivering massive throughput gains while preserving exact retrieval quality. The techniques enable efficient deployment of multi-vector retrieval at scale, and the authors note a concurrent independent effort that lacks their dimension tiling and fused PQ scoring innovations.

title: Expecting (Targeted Ads)? Network Analysis of User Health Data Leakage in Fertility Tracking Apps
summary: While human factors in the privacy of fertility tracking apps -- health trackers that record user's menstrual or pregnancy data -- has been the subject of extensive study, little attention has been paid to the technical aspects of apps' data handling practices. We conduct a network-based measurement study of a corpus of 20 Android fertility tracking apps from the Google Play Store, focusing on how user data is shared with third party advertising services. After systematizing app features, we conduct a series of standardized user interactions across all apps in an environment that records TLS-stripped network traffic. In a subset of apps (n=5) we identify explicit leakage of user health data as well implicit leakage through highly targeted contextual advertising URL's. Equally importantly, we observe additional apps that use an ad-based monetization model without apparent leakage of user data, as well as several apps the interact only minimally with ad services. These findings provide technical grounding for widespread user concerns, but also underscore the importance of consumer choice in the privacy implications of app-based fertility tracking.

AI.tldr: A network measurement study of 20 Android fertility tracking apps reveals that some explicitly leak sensitive health data to third-party advertisers via unencrypted traffic, while others use ad monetization without apparent leakage, highlighting both privacy risks and the role of consumer choice.
AI.motivation: Despite extensive research on human factors in fertility app privacy, the technical data handling practices — specifically how user health data is shared with third-party advertising services — remain underexamined. This gap motivates a systems-focused, empirical investigation.
AI.method: The authors curated a corpus of 20 Android fertility tracking apps from the Google Play Store, systematized their features, then performed standardized user interactions on each app within an instrumented environment that captures TLS-stripped network traffic. Both explicit leakage (direct transmission of health data) and implicit leakage (via contextual advertising URLs) were analyzed.
AI.result: In a subset of 5 apps, explicit leakage of user health data and implicit leakage through highly targeted contextual advertising URLs were identified. Other apps using ad-based monetization showed no apparent leakage, and several apps had minimal interaction with ad services altogether.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide technical evidence supporting widespread user privacy concerns, while also demonstrating that consumer choice matters — not all ad-supported fertility apps leak data, and some avoid ad services almost entirely.

title: Assert, don't describe: Linguistic features that shift LLM reasoning about animal welfare
summary: Animal-welfare advocates produce a lot of writing, and increasingly that writing trains the language models that millions of people then ask about animal welfare. Using vocabulary-matched stance-contrast probes on a held-out animal-welfare benchmark, we measure how each of ten linguistic features changes Llama-3.2-1B's preference for pro-animal-welfare reasoning when used as fine-tuning data. Eight of the ten features produce statistically significant shifts. Seven move the model toward stronger pro-animal-welfare reasoning: assertive certainty, explicit moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, depicted harm severity, and immediate temporal framing. Two move it the other way: hedged language and concrete sensory description both dilute the pro-animal-welfare stance. First-person perspective has no statistically significant effect. The practical recommendation for anyone writing animal-welfare text that may end up in LLM training corpora: assert a position rather than describe a scene neutrally. The features that shift the model are the ones that make the writer's position explicit; the features that dilute it hold animal-welfare content but withhold stance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how ten linguistic features in animal-welfare texts influence Llama-3.2-1B's stance when used as fine-tuning data. Eight features produce statistically significant shifts: seven strengthen pro-animal-welfare reasoning (assertive certainty, moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, depicted harm severity, immediate temporal framing), while two dilute it (hedged language, concrete sensory description). First-person perspective shows no significant effect. The core recommendation: assert a position explicitly rather than describing neutrally.
AI.motivation: Animal-welfare advocates produce substantial written content that increasingly enters LLM training corpora, yet little is known about which linguistic features in such texts actually influence model behavior toward pro-animal-welfare reasoning. The authors aim to provide empirical, actionable guidance for advocates on how to write texts that effectively shape model stances.
AI.method: The authors use vocabulary-matched stance-contrast probes on a held-out animal-welfare benchmark. They take Llama-3.2-1B and fine-tune it on texts varying across ten linguistic features, then measure how each feature shifts the model's preference for pro-animal-welfare reasoning. Statistical significance testing is applied to identify which features produce reliable shifts.
AI.result: Eight of ten features produce statistically significant shifts. Seven strengthen pro-animal-welfare reasoning: assertive certainty, explicit moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, depicted harm severity, and immediate temporal framing. Two weaken it: hedged language and concrete sensory description. First-person perspective has no significant effect.
AI.conclusion: The features that shift the model toward pro-animal-welfare reasoning are those that make the writer's evaluative stance explicit. Conversely, features that convey animal-welfare content while withholding stance (hedging, neutral sensory description) dilute the effect. The practical takeaway: advocates should assert a clear position rather than describe scenes neutrally if they want their writing to steer LLMs toward pro-animal-welfare reasoning.

title: Evaluation-Strategy Gap in Fault Diagnosis of Deep Learning Programs
comment: Accepted research track paper in the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026)
summary: Deep Learning (DL) programs can fail during training for many reasons, and diagnosing the cause is a costly and time-consuming maintenance task. Techniques for diagnosing such failures are commonly assessed using within-program cross-validation, which may be inadequate for deployment settings involving previously unseen programs. It is therefore necessary to assess how performance differs across these settings and to identify the causes of any performance gap in established fault diagnosis techniques for DL. We investigate this gap using DynFault, a corpus of 5,542 fault-injected training traces from 38 real-world DL programs. We found a gap of 0.190 in balanced accuracy for existing fault diagnosis techniques between within-program evaluation and holding out whole programs. We also found the gap comes from program-level structure in the features, which led us to examine two runtime feature sets, curvature features and optimizer features, and their behavior on unseen programs. We found that curvature features are useful for instability detection on unseen programs, while optimizer and activation features help only on programs seen during training.

AI.tldr: Existing DL fault diagnosis techniques show a significant performance gap (0.190 balanced accuracy) when evaluated on unseen programs versus within-program cross-validation. This gap stems from program-level feature structure, with curvature features proving useful for instability detection on unseen programs, while optimizer and activation features only help on programs seen during training.
AI.motivation: DL program training failures are costly to diagnose, yet fault diagnosis techniques are predominantly evaluated using within-program cross-validation, which fails to reflect real-world deployment where entirely new, unseen programs are encountered. Understanding and quantifying the resulting performance gap is essential for building robust diagnostic tools.
AI.method: The authors use DynFault, a corpus of 5,542 fault-injected training traces from 38 real-world DL programs. They compare fault diagnosis performance under two evaluation regimes: within-program cross-validation and leave-out-program (holding out whole programs). They then analyze three runtime feature sets — curvature features, optimizer features, and activation features — to determine how each contributes to the performance gap on unseen programs.
AI.result: A performance gap of 0.190 in balanced accuracy was observed between within-program evaluation and holding out whole programs. The gap is attributed to program-level structure in the features. Curvature features proved beneficial for detecting instability on unseen programs, whereas optimizer and activation features only boosted performance on programs encountered during training.
AI.conclusion: Established fault diagnosis techniques for DL overfit to program-specific feature patterns when evaluated via within-program cross-validation. Curvature-based features show promise for cross-program generalization, particularly for instability detection. Evaluation protocols for DL fault diagnosis should account for unseen-program settings to ensure real-world applicability.

title: KG-TRACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Mechanistic Grounding in Antimicrobial Resistance Prediction
summary:
While WGS-based AMR prediction has reached high accuracy, existing models lack a mechanism to ground neural attributions in established biological pathways. We present KG-TRACE, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the WHO mutation knowledge graph (KG) as a structured biological constraint on a neural genomic model. Unlike existing methods that learn statistical patterns in isolation, KG-TRACE fuses genomic features and RotatE-based KG embeddings through a learned epistemic trust gate, dynamically weighting neural evidence against symbolic biological knowledge.
  Evaluated on the CRyPTIC M. tuberculosis cohort, KG-TRACE achieves an AUROC of 0.9760 for isoniazid, achieving competitive accuracy while its primary value lies in symbolic grounding, not predictive uplift. More importantly, we introduce the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR), a dataset-level metric that quantifies alignment between neural attributions and established biology. Our framework achieves a 92.5% symbolic coverage of isoniazid-resistant predictions and effectively identifies MDR co-occurrence artifacts by issuing laboratory follow-up flags for 'UNCERTAIN' cases. We demonstrate that neuro-symbolic grounding provides a verifiable audit trail for clinicians, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical trust.

AI.tldr: KG-TRACE is a neuro-symbolic framework that constrains WGS-based AMR prediction with the WHO mutation knowledge graph, achieving 0.9760 AUROC for isoniazid while introducing the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR) to quantify alignment between model attributions and established biological pathways, thereby providing a verifiable audit trail for clinical trust.
AI.motivation: Existing WGS-based AMR prediction models achieve high accuracy but lack mechanisms to ground neural attributions in established biological pathways. This gap undermines clinical trust because clinicians cannot verify whether a model's predictions are based on biologically meaningful signals or spurious statistical correlations. There is a need for models that not only predict resistance accurately but also provide biologically interpretable and verifiable reasoning.
AI.method: KG-TRACE is a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the WHO mutation knowledge graph as a structured biological constraint. It fuses genomic features with RotatE-based KG embeddings through a learned epistemic trust gate that dynamically weights neural evidence against symbolic biological knowledge. The framework also introduces the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR), a dataset-level metric quantifying alignment between neural attributions and established biology. Evaluation is performed on the CRyPTIC M. tuberculosis cohort, with laboratory follow-up flags for 'UNCERTAIN' cases to identify MDR co-occurrence artifacts.
AI.result: KG-TRACE achieved an AUROC of 0.9760 for isoniazid resistance prediction on the CRyPTIC M. tuberculosis cohort, demonstrating competitive accuracy. The framework attained 92.5% symbolic coverage of isoniazid-resistant predictions and effectively identified MDR co-occurrence artifacts by flagging 'UNCERTAIN' cases for laboratory follow-up.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-symbolic grounding provides a verifiable audit trail for clinicians, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical trust. The primary contribution of KG-TRACE lies not in predictive uplift over existing methods but in its symbolic grounding capability, enabling biologically interpretable AMR predictions suitable for clinical deployment.

title: Budget-Aware Keyboardless Interaction
summary: Interacting with computers typically relies on traditional input devices such as keyboards, mice, and monitors, which can be cumbersome for users seeking greater mobility. Virtual keyboards have been explored to address these limitations, but they often involve complex setups or expensive equipment. This paper proposes a novel virtual keyboard system that leverages only a standard camera and a paper with a printed keyboard layout. Unlike previous methods requiring complex calibration or special lighting conditions, our approach can work on standard environment using modern computer vision technologies. Combining modern segmentation and detection models with traditional image processing algorithms, we efficiently identify the keyboard region. Touch detection is performed using an algorithm analyzing the color of the user's fingernail. Experiments demonstrated a promising results our proposed solution of keyboard and keystroke detection for practical applications. Participants attended our user study also found the proposed system interesting.

AI.tldr: A virtual keyboard system using only a standard camera and a printed paper keyboard layout, employing computer vision for keyboard region detection and fingernail color analysis for touch detection, achieving promising results in practical applications.
AI.motivation: Traditional input devices (keyboards, mice, monitors) limit user mobility, and existing virtual keyboard solutions are impractical due to complex calibration, special lighting requirements, or expensive equipment. The authors aim to create a simpler, more accessible alternative.
AI.method: The system uses a standard camera to capture a printed paper keyboard layout. Modern segmentation and detection models combined with traditional image processing algorithms identify the keyboard region. Keystroke detection is performed by analyzing the color of the user's fingernail to determine touch events.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrated promising results for both keyboard region detection and keystroke detection. A user study was conducted, and participants expressed interest in the proposed system.
AI.conclusion: The proposed virtual keyboard system is a viable, low-cost, and practical alternative to traditional input devices and existing virtual keyboard solutions, validated by both experimental results and positive user feedback.

title: GPUSparse: GPU-Accelerated Learned Sparse Retrieval with Parallel Inverted Indices
summary: Learned sparse retrieval models such as SPLADE achieve retrieval quality competitive with dense models while preserving the interpretability and exact-match advantages of sparse representations. However, inference-time scoring still relies on CPU-bound inverted index traversal algorithms (WAND, Block-Max WAND), creating a fundamental bottleneck for real-time serving at scale. We present GPUSparse, a system for GPU-accelerated exact learned sparse retrieval that introduces: (1) a GPU-parallel inverted index with block-aligned, warp-coalesced posting lists; (2) a batched scatter-add scoring algorithm that processes hundreds of queries simultaneously; and (3) fused Triton kernels with an analysis of the tradeoff between work-efficiency and hardware utilization. On MS MARCO passage ranking (8.8M passages) with real SPLADE embeddings, GPUSparse matches CPU exact scoring to three decimals (MRR@10=0.383, equal to Pyserini SPLADE at this precision; Recall@1000>=0.999 vs. dense matmul, the residual from floating-point tie-breaking) while providing a 235x speedup over Pyserini CPU at 8.8M documents (1.27ms vs. 298ms per query). Compared to Seismic (the fastest CPU sparse retrieval system), which trades 25% recall for speed (R@1000=0.738 vs. 0.983 exact), GPUSparse achieves exact scoring at 787 QPS throughput (batch 500) on the full 8.8M collection, with 1.3ms per query. Our document-parallel kernel reaches 62.6% of H100 peak HBM bandwidth, revealing a fundamental work-efficiency vs. bandwidth-efficiency tradeoff in GPU sparse retrieval. The reformulation of sparse scoring as scatter-add over an inverted index is shared with SPARe's iterative mode; our contribution is its fused-kernel realization, which we measure to be 23-270x faster than a faithful SPARe iterative reimplementation.

AI.tldr: GPUSparse accelerates exact learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE) on GPUs via a parallel inverted index, batched scatter-add scoring, and fused Triton kernels, achieving 235× speedup over CPU Pyserini while matching exact scoring precision.
AI.motivation: Learned sparse retrieval models like SPLADE offer competitive quality and interpretability, but inference relies on CPU-bound inverted index traversal (WAND, Block-Max WAND), which creates a fundamental bottleneck for real-time serving at scale. GPU acceleration of exact sparse scoring is needed.
AI.method: GPUSparse introduces three components: (1) a GPU-parallel inverted index with block-aligned, warp-coalesced posting lists; (2) a batched scatter-add scoring algorithm processing hundreds of queries simultaneously; and (3) fused Triton kernels with analysis of the work-efficiency vs. hardware-utilization tradeoff. The system reformulates sparse scoring as scatter-add over an inverted index.
AI.result: On MS MARCO passage ranking (8.8M passages) with SPLADE embeddings: MRR@10=0.383 (matching Pyserini to three decimals), Recall@1000≥0.999 vs. dense matmul; 235× speedup over Pyserini CPU (1.27ms vs. 298ms per query); 787 QPS throughput at batch 500; 62.6% of H100 peak HBM bandwidth; 23–270× faster than SPARe iterative reimplementation.
AI.conclusion: GPU-accelerated exact learned sparse retrieval is viable and highly performant, but involves a fundamental work-efficiency vs. bandwidth-efficiency tradeoff. The fused-kernel scatter-add realization is the key contribution enabling orders-of-magnitude speedup over prior iterative approaches.

title: TEMPO-Diffusion: Temporally Exposed Malicious Poisoning of Diffusion Models
summary: Noise-based backdoor attacks on diffusion models typically rely on input-time trigger injection, untargeted activation, and out-of-distribution target generation. Such assumptions reduce both the stealthiness and the practical relevance of these attacks. In this work, we present TEMPO-Diffusion, a targeted backdoor framework that localizes the malicious distribution shift to a temporal, in-distribution exposure. TEMPO-Diffusion supports: (i) targeted attacks on and to specific classes, (ii) multiple sub-image backdoors that reconstruct specific features within multiple, different output images and at multiple locations, and (iii) in-painting with time-conditioned triggers. To study relevant, practical security concerns in leveraging backdoored diffusion models for synthetic training data, we also introduce CALISA: a balanced, region-aware traffic-sign dataset emphasizing Canadian and U.S. road signs. Across CIFAR10, GTSRB, and CALISA, our experiments show that TEMPO-Diffusion can reliably poison class-specific synthetic data generation and induce high attack success rates in downstream classifiers trained on that data.

AI.tldr: TEMPO-Diffusion introduces a targeted backdoor attack on diffusion models that uses temporal, in-distribution exposure rather than input-time trigger injection. It supports class-to-class targeted attacks, multi-backdoor sub-image reconstruction, and time-conditioned in-painting, and is evaluated with a new traffic-sign dataset (CALISA) for downstream classifier poisoning.
AI.motivation: Existing noise-based backdoor attacks on diffusion models suffer from three unrealistic assumptions: input-time trigger injection, untargeted activation, and out-of-distribution target generation. These reduce stealthiness and practical relevance, motivating a more realistic, targeted, and in-distribution backdoor framework.
AI.method: TEMPO-Diffusion localizes malicious distribution shifts to a specific temporal window during the diffusion reverse process, achieving in-distribution backdoor exposure. It implements: (i) targeted class-to-class attacks, (ii) multiple sub-image backdoors that reconstruct specific features across multiple output images and locations, and (iii) time-conditioned trigger injection for in-painting. The authors also introduce CALISA, a balanced, region-aware traffic-sign dataset for U.S. and Canadian signs.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and CALISA demonstrate that TEMPO-Diffusion reliably poisons class-specific synthetic data generation and induces high attack success rates in downstream classifiers trained on the poisoned synthetic data.
AI.conclusion: Targeted, temporally localized backdoors in diffusion models pose a realistic and significant threat to downstream systems that rely on synthetic training data, highlighting a practical security concern in the diffusion model supply chain.

title: Context Recycling for Long-Horizon LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in short-context reasoning but degrade in performance over long conversational horizons due to context window limitations and inefficient token usage. We introduce ContextForge, a system for context recycling that maintains task-relevant information across turns by combining structured query generation, external memory retrieval, and controlled synthesis. The system enables efficient reuse of prior computation without relying on full context replay, reducing token overhead while preserving answer quality. We evaluate ContextForge using a 15-turn conversational benchmark that tests multi-turn reasoning, back-references, and domain shifts across structured healthcare queries. Compared to a baseline agent using identical underlying models, ContextForge demonstrates improved consistency and reduced token consumption, while maintaining comparable response accuracy. These results suggest that context recycling provides a practical approach for extending LLM capabilities in long-horizon tasks without requiring larger context windows or model retraining. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/Betanu701/ContextForge.

AI.tldr: ContextForge introduces a context recycling system that maintains task-relevant information across multi-turn conversations, reducing token overhead while preserving answer quality. Evaluated on a 15-turn healthcare benchmark, it improves consistency and reduces token consumption compared to full-context baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs perform well in short-context scenarios but suffer degradation over long conversational horizons due to context window constraints and inefficient token usage. Existing solutions like larger context windows or model retraining are costly. The authors aim to enable efficient reuse of prior computation without full context replay.
AI.method: ContextForge combines three components: (1) structured query generation to extract task-relevant information from prior turns, (2) external memory retrieval to store and access this information, and (3) controlled synthesis to integrate retrieved context into responses. This avoids replaying the entire conversation history.
AI.result: Evaluated on a 15-turn conversational benchmark with structured healthcare queries testing multi-turn reasoning, back-references, and domain shifts, ContextForge demonstrated improved consistency and reduced token consumption while maintaining comparable response accuracy against a baseline agent using identical underlying models.
AI.conclusion: Context recycling offers a practical alternative for extending LLM capabilities in long-horizon tasks without requiring larger context windows or model retraining, suggesting a viable path forward for efficient multi-turn conversational AI.

title: Same Scrutiny, More Time: Eye Tracking Insights into Reviewing LLM-Labelled Code
comment: Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: Modern software development increasingly involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to generate code. Despite their rapid advancement, LLMs remain prone to errors and hallucinations, emphasizing the importance of careful code inspection. However, in practice, developers' trust in LLM-generated code and their willingness to review it thoroughly may differ from these recommendations. How developers actually behave when reviewing LLM-generated code remains largely unexplored. In this study, we conduct a Wizard-of-Oz experiment to examine how software engineers behave when code is explicitly labeled as LLM-generated during a code review task. We collect both behavioral data and participant feedback through eye-tracking and exit interviews. Combining Bayesian data analysis with qualitative analysis, we found that while the thoroughness of code review did not change for participants, they spent more time fixating on LLM-labelled code, indicating that the label itself influences attention. Practitioners also adapted their review strategy for LLM-labelled code by assessing the code based on specific criteria (e.g., logical correctness), or using the prompt to guide their review. These findings inform LLM-based tool design on labelling while incorporating the prompt as a software artifact. Our study reveals a gap between reviewers' intentions and actual reviewing behaviour, highlighting the need for software companies to revisit their AI policies (particularly regarding LLM-assisted development) to better support developers in reviewing LLM-generated code.

AI.tldr: A Wizard-of-Oz experiment with eye-tracking reveals that developers do not review LLM-labelled code more thoroughly, but they do spend more time fixating on it and adapt their review strategies — highlighting a gap between intention and actual behaviour that calls for revised AI policies and tool design.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for code generation but remain error-prone, making careful review essential. However, little is known about how developers actually behave when reviewing LLM-generated code, particularly whether explicit labelling influences their attention, thoroughness, and review strategies.
AI.method: A Wizard-of-Oz experiment where software engineers performed code review tasks with code explicitly labelled as LLM-generated. Data were collected via eye-tracking (for behavioural metrics like fixation duration) and exit interviews (for qualitative insights). Analysis combined Bayesian statistical methods with qualitative thematic analysis.
AI.result: (1) Review thoroughness did not change for LLM-labelled code; (2) participants spent significantly more time fixating on LLM-labelled code, indicating the label itself captures attention; (3) practitioners adapted review strategies by assessing specific criteria (e.g., logical correctness) and using the prompt as a review guide; (4) a gap exists between reviewers' stated intentions and their actual reviewing behaviour.
AI.conclusion: The LLM label influences attention but not review thoroughness, and developers adapt their strategies when reviewing such code. Tool designers should consider labelling and treat prompts as software artifacts. Companies need to revisit AI policies to better support developers in LLM-assisted development contexts.

title: Necessary but Not Sufficient: Temperature Control and Reproducibility in LLM-as-Judge Safety Evaluations
summary: LLM-as-judge ("grader") components are now standard in evaluation harnesses, including safety evaluations where a pass/fail verdict may gate downstream deployment decisions. A widespread assumption is that setting the grader's sampling temperature to 0 makes grading deterministic. We test this assumption against a real safety-evaluation codebase (Japan AISI's open-source aisev) and show it fails on two levels. First, the harness invokes its grader without setting temperature or seed; the underlying provider silently applies its default of 1.0, so items near the decision boundary flip pass/fail across identical runs (per-item disagreement up to ~50% over 20 runs). Second, pinning temperature=0 reduces but does not eliminate flips: across 690 API calls spanning two providers, three model tiers, and five sampling configurations, 1-2 of 7 borderline items remain non-reproducible even under forced greedy decoding (top_k=1). Claude Opus 4.7/4.8 has since deprecated temperature entirely, rendering the primary mitigation inapplicable to newer model generations. These findings expose a structural gap: evaluation harnesses that report single-run verdicts without variance or grader-disagreement metrics can present noise as a safety property. We release a reproduction harness (690 calls, 7 conditions) and recommend that harnesses treat grader disagreement as a first-class health metric alongside the scores themselves.

AI.tldr: Setting LLM-as-judge temperature to 0 does not guarantee deterministic safety evaluations. The paper demonstrates that default provider temperatures, non-deterministic greedy decoding, and deprecated temperature controls create structural reproducibility failures in safety-evaluation harnesses, with up to ~50% per-item disagreement across identical runs.
AI.motivation: Safety evaluations using LLM-as-judge components increasingly gate downstream deployment decisions, yet the widespread assumption that temperature=0 ensures deterministic, reproducible grading is untested. If verdicts are non-deterministic, noise may be misinterpreted as a genuine safety property, risking unreliable pass/fail decisions in high-stakes settings.
AI.method: The authors tested the determinism assumption against Japan AISI's open-source aisev safety-evaluation codebase. They conducted 690 API calls across two providers, three model tiers, and five sampling configurations (including forced greedy decoding with top_k=1). They measured per-item disagreement rates over 20 identical runs and examined the effect of provider default temperatures, explicit temperature=0, and deprecated temperature controls (Claude Opus 4.7/4.8).
AI.result: Two levels of failure were identified: (1) When temperature/seed are unset, providers silently default to temperature=1.0, causing borderline items to flip pass/fail with per-item disagreement up to ~50% over 20 runs. (2) Pinning temperature=0 reduces but does not eliminate flips — 1-2 of 7 borderline items remained non-reproducible even under forced greedy decoding (top_k=1). Additionally, Claude Opus 4.7/4.8 has deprecated temperature entirely, making the primary mitigation inapplicable to newer model generations.
AI.conclusion: A structural gap exists in evaluation harnesses that report single-run verdicts without variance or grader-disagreement metrics. The authors recommend that harnesses treat grader disagreement as a first-class health metric alongside scores, and they release a reproduction harness (690 calls, 7 conditions) to facilitate further investigation.

title: Knowledge-augmented Agentic AI for Mental Health Medication Information Seeking
summary: Patients increasingly seek medication information online, yet safety knowledge for psychiatric drugs is split between regulatory adverse-event records, which are authoritative but abstract, and patient narratives, which are experience-near but unvalidated. Integrating them without conflating evidence and anecdote is especially consequential in psychiatry, where poorly contextualised information can amplify fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence. Here we develop a provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework unifying 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and twenty years of U.S. FDA Adverse Event Reporting System records for nine antidepressants. A large-language-model entity-recognition pipeline benchmarked against physician annotations reached highest F1 scores of 0.969 for medications and 0.973 for conditions. The two community platforms were far more concordant with each other (overlap up to a Jaccard similarity of 0.905) than with regulatory reports, indicating that patient-generated data form a partly independent safety signal. For sertraline, many adverse events appeared in community sources hundreds of days before the corresponding FDA date. A Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies preserves provenance, keeping every claim traceable and regulatory facts distinct from patient experience. These results establish source-aware integration as a route to more auditable psychiatric medication information, with usefulness and patient benefit to be tested prospectively.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent framework integrates patient narratives (Reddit, WebMD) with FDA adverse event records using a provenance-aware knowledge graph. It shows patient-generated data forms a safety signal partly independent from regulatory reports, with some adverse events appearing in community sources months before FDA records, while maintaining strict source traceability through standardised vocabularies.
AI.motivation: Psychiatric medication safety information is fragmented: regulatory records (FAERS) are authoritative but abstract, while patient narratives are experiential but unvalidated. Conflating these sources can amplify fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence. A method is needed to integrate both signal types without losing provenance.
AI.method: Developed a provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework integrating 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and 20 years of FAERS records for nine antidepressants. Used an LLM-based entity-recognition pipeline (benchmarked against physician annotations) and a Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies. Compared concordance across sources and analysed temporal signal emergence.
AI.result: Entity recognition achieved F1 scores of 0.969 (medications) and 0.973 (conditions). Reddit and WebMD showed high mutual concordance (Jaccard similarity up to 0.905) but far lower concordance with FAERS, indicating a partly independent safety signal. For sertraline, community sources reported many adverse events hundreds of days before corresponding FDA dates.
AI.conclusion: Source-aware integration with preserved provenance enables more auditable psychiatric medication information, keeping regulatory facts distinct from patient experience. Prospective testing of usefulness and patient benefit is warranted.

title: Co-Designing Community-Centered AI Education for Adults: A Midwestern Case Study
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) education is increasingly important, yet adults outside higher education receive less attention. We report a case study of an AI education session with 54 adults (48 in-person and 6 virtual) in a predominantly African American community on the east side of a major Midwestern city. We ask: "What does AI education for adults outside formal educational systems look like in practice?" and "What does this AI education session reveal about AI literacy at the community level?" Through a co-designed session developed with community partners, we found that concerns about AI persisted but shifted to specific, locally grounded questions about AI design and deployment. We also discuss AI literacy from a community capacity perspective and argue for AI literacy frameworks grounded in local community contexts that strengthen community capacity.

AI.tldr: A co-designed AI education session with 54 adults in a predominantly African American community revealed that AI concerns evolved into locally grounded questions about AI design and deployment. The authors argue for community-contextualized AI literacy frameworks that strengthen community capacity.
AI.motivation: AI education research disproportionately focuses on K-12 and higher education, leaving adults outside formal educational systems underserved. There is a need to understand what AI education looks like in practice for these populations and how AI literacy manifests at the community level, particularly in marginalized communities.
AI.method: A case study of a single AI education session co-designed with community partners, involving 54 adult participants (48 in-person, 6 virtual) in a predominantly African American community on the east side of a major Midwestern city. Data collection included observation and analysis of participant concerns and questions during the session.
AI.result: Participants' concerns about AI did not disappear but shifted from general apprehension to specific, locally grounded questions about AI design and deployment. The session revealed that AI literacy, when viewed through a community capacity lens, is best understood within local community contexts rather than through universal frameworks.
AI.conclusion: AI literacy frameworks should be grounded in local community contexts and designed to strengthen community capacity. Co-designing AI education with community partners enables more relevant, situated learning that addresses specific local concerns rather than abstract risks.

title: Attributed, But Not Incremental: Cannibalization-Corrected Attribution for Large-Scale Advertising
summary:
In large-scale paid acquisition and growth advertising systems, production attribution outputs are widely used for daily budget allocation and channel diagnosis. However, paid-attributed conversions such as daily new users (DNU) may systematically overstate true incremental growth when paid channels overlap with organic demand, brand-driven traffic, or other acquisition channels. This attribution-cannibalization mismatch can distort incremental ROI measurement and budget decisions at scale.
  We propose an experiment-calibrated attribution correction framework that uses incrementality experiments as causal anchors to convert sparse lift measurements into daily correction estimates. To make the corrected signal actionable at production granularity, we further allocate calibrated cannibalization volume across business hierarchies under structural consistency constraints. Offline forward-in-time validation against channel-level incrementality experiment readouts shows that the proposed framework substantially reduces calibration error relative to raw attribution and fine-grained ML baselines. Deployed across multiple global TikTok markets, the system supported budget and traffic strategy adjustments that were followed by an approximately 15-percentage-point reduction in the measured cannibalization rate.

AI.tldr: A framework that calibrates paid-attribution conversion metrics using incrementality experiments as causal anchors, correcting for cannibalization bias at scale, deployed at TikTok with ~15pp reduction in measured cannibalization rate.
AI.motivation: Paid-attribution conversions (e.g., DNU) systematically overstate true incremental growth due to overlap with organic, brand-driven, or cross-channel traffic. This attribution-cannibalization mismatch distorts incremental ROI and budget allocation at scale, but running full incrementality experiments continuously is infeasible.
AI.method: An experiment-calibrated attribution correction framework that uses sparse incrementality experiments as causal anchors to convert lift measurements into daily correction estimates. The calibrated cannibalization volume is then allocated across business hierarchies under structural consistency constraints, making the corrected signal actionable at production granularity.
AI.result: Offline forward-in-time validation against channel-level incrementality experiments showed substantial reduction in calibration error versus raw attribution and fine-grained ML baselines. Production deployment across multiple global TikTok markets led to budget and traffic adjustments followed by an approximately 15-percentage-point reduction in measured cannibalization rate.
AI.conclusion: Experiment-calibrated attribution correction is a practical, scalable approach to bridge the gap between sparse incrementality measurement and daily production attribution, enabling more accurate ROI-driven budget decisions in large-scale advertising systems.

title: Beyond Takedown: Measuring Malicious Go Module Persistence in the Wild
summary: We measure an automation-based supply chain campaign in the Go ecosystem. The attackers repackage legitimate Go modules under attacker-controlled owners, and embed them with obfuscated code for an import-triggered downloader. Our results come from two complementary analyses: a) a manual search on GitHub across 2,113 repositories and b) a large-scale scan of 12.3M index entries using a deobfuscating AST scanner (GOAST) that we implemented. As a result, we identified 2,289 malicious versions of legitimate Go modules. We demonstrate that purely GitHub-centric searches fail to identify the full extent of the compromise and are only effective for as long as the affected code is present on the platform. Moreover, our proxy-based measurements of the takedown-remediation gap reveal that among artifacts later found to be GitHub-unobservable (i.e., removed or suspended), at least 99.4% remained retrievable via Go proxy. Following our disclosure, GitHub has removed 684 malicious repositories and the Google Go team has remediated 1,377 module versions.

AI.tldr: Researchers uncovered a large supply chain attack in the Go ecosystem where attackers repackaged legitimate modules with malicious downloader code. Using manual GitHub searches and a custom AST-based scanner (GOAST) across 12.3M index entries, they identified 2,289 malicious module versions. They showed GitHub-only detection is insufficient, as 99.4% of removed/suspended artifacts remained accessible via the Go proxy, highlighting a critical takedown-remediation gap.
