AI.motivation: To measure the scope and persistence of an automation-based supply chain campaign in the Go ecosystem, assess the effectiveness of GitHub-centric detection versus proxy-based scanning, and quantify the takedown-remediation gap — the window during which malicious artifacts remain retrievable via the Go module proxy even after GitHub removal.
AI.method: A two-pronged approach: (a) manual search across 2,113 GitHub repositories to identify repackaged malicious Go modules, and (b) a large-scale automated scan of 12.3 million Go module proxy index entries using GOAST, a custom deobfuscating AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) scanner capable of detecting obfuscated import-triggered downloader code.
AI.result: Identified 2,289 malicious versions of legitimate Go modules. Purely GitHub-centric searches failed to capture the full compromise and were only effective while malicious code remained on the platform. Among GitHub-unobservable artifacts (removed/suspended), at least 99.4% remained retrievable via the Go proxy. Following disclosure, GitHub removed 684 malicious repositories and the Google Go team remediated 1,377 module versions.
AI.conclusion: Reliance solely on GitHub for detecting supply chain attacks in the Go ecosystem is inadequate due to the persistence of malicious modules on the Go proxy. Proxy-side scanning and remediation are essential complements to repository takedowns. Coordinated disclosure can drive meaningful cleanup, as evidenced by the large-scale remediation actions taken by GitHub and the Go team.

title: Reducing Conversational Escalation in Large Language Model Dialogue with Nonviolent Communication Constraints
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in emotionally charged situations involving interpersonal conflict, frustration, and distress. While prior safety research has focused on preventing explicit harms such as toxic or policy-violating content, less attention has been paid to conversational behaviors that may unintentionally escalate conflict. In this paper, we investigate whether LLMs can be guided toward more de-escalating dialogue behavior through lightweight prompt-level constraints derived from Nonviolent Communication (NVC). We reformulate NVC principles as process-oriented guidelines that discourage blame attribution, emphasize attention to users' emotional experiences, and encourage clarification before advice. Using a dual-agent simulation framework across multiple instruction-tuned models and user resistance levels, we show that NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation and stabilizes interactions with highly resistant users. These results suggest that simple communication constraints can meaningfully improve the trustworthiness of LLM dialogue in conflict-prone settings.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using Nonviolent Communication (NVC) principles as prompt-level constraints to guide LLMs toward de-escalating dialogue in emotionally charged situations. Using dual-agent simulation across multiple models, the authors find NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation, especially with resistant users.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in emotionally charged contexts involving interpersonal conflict, yet prior safety research has focused mainly on preventing explicit harms (toxicity, policy violations) rather than unintentional conflict escalation. There is a gap in understanding how lightweight conversational constraints can promote de-escalation.
AI.method: The authors reformulate NVC principles into process-oriented guidelines that (1) discourage blame attribution, (2) emphasize attending to users' emotional experiences, and (3) encourage clarification before offering advice. These constraints are applied at the prompt level. Evaluation uses a dual-agent simulation framework across multiple instruction-tuned models under varying user resistance levels.
AI.result: NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation and stabilizes interactions, particularly with highly resistant users, across all tested instruction-tuned models.
AI.conclusion: Simple communication constraints derived from NVC can meaningfully improve LLM trustworthiness in conflict-prone settings, suggesting that lightweight, process-oriented prompting strategies are a viable approach to de-escalation beyond traditional safety filters.

title: ConcoLixir: Reactive LLM Discovery Oracles for Python Concolic Testing
summary: Concolic testing combines concrete execution with symbolic constraint solving, but Python programs expose recurring limits. Library calls can cause symbolic variables to downgrade to concrete values. Regular expressions, checksums, parsers, and other semantic operations can be hard to solve, and exploration can plateau on already covered paths. We present ConcoLixir, a reactive LLM extension for Python concolic execution. The LLM acts as a discovery oracle, not a replacement for the solver or a correctness oracle. It generates initial seeds, proposes concrete inputs after solver failures, and targets uncovered code when coverage stalls. Each candidate is executed concolically, and only observed coverage and collected path constraints guide later exploration. Across synthetic, real-world, and library targets, ConcoLixir improves mean line coverage over the baseline concolic tester without an LLM oracle by 8.6, 15.1, and 17.0 percentage points. The gains are strongest near semantic barriers and library boundaries, and the full evaluation costs \$1.63 in API charges. These results show that bounded LLM discovery can complement symbolic reasoning without replacing it.

AI.tldr: ConcoLixir augments Python concolic testing with an LLM acting as a discovery oracle — generating seeds, proposing inputs when the solver fails, and targeting uncovered code — yielding significant coverage gains (8–17 pp) at minimal cost ($1.63), especially near semantic barriers.
AI.motivation: Python concolic execution faces hard limits: library calls concretize symbolic variables, semantic operations (regex, checksums, parsers) are solver-unfriendly, and exploration stalls on already-covered paths. Existing solvers cannot reason across these semantic barriers.
AI.method: ConcoLixir integrates an LLM as a reactive, bounded discovery oracle (not a solver replacement or correctness oracle). The LLM performs three targeted interventions: (1) generating initial seed inputs, (2) proposing concrete inputs after solver failures on hard constraints, and (3) suggesting inputs targeting uncovered code when coverage plateaus. All candidates are executed concolically; only observed coverage and collected path constraints guide subsequent exploration, preventing hallucination from corrupting the symbolic state.
AI.result: Across synthetic, real-world, and library benchmarks, ConcoLixir improved mean line coverage over the baseline concolic tester by 8.6, 15.1, and 17.0 percentage points respectively. Gains concentrated near semantic barriers and library boundaries. Total API cost for the full evaluation was $1.63.
AI.conclusion: Bounded LLM discovery can effectively complement symbolic reasoning without replacing it. The LLM's role as a targeted oracle — filling gaps where solvers are fundamentally limited — proves both cost-effective and impactful for improving concolic testing coverage.

title: Clue-Guided Money Laundering Group Discovery
summary: Money Laundering Group Discovery (MLGD) aims to identify hidden criminal groups and recover their complete structures in large-scale financial networks. Existing graph anomaly detection methods mainly produce node-level risk alerts, while global group discovery methods passively search for suspicious groups over the whole network. Both are mismatched with real Anti-money-laundering (AML) investigations, where analysts usually start from a concrete clue and gradually expand the investigation to recover the responsible group. To address this gap, we propose Clue-Guided Group Discovery (CGGD), where a laundering group is progressively recovered from an initial clue set through analyst interaction. We further propose Clue2Group, a framework that first constructs a compact local investigation context to reduce noise and preserve chain-like and cycle-like laundering structures. It then estimates a clue-conditioned local risk field with a multi-semantic local-temporal GNN, and finally integrates risk, structural, and prior-pattern evidence to recover a coherent laundering group. Experiments on two large-scale AML benchmarks show that Clue2Group provides a practical clue-driven analysis framework for AML investigations, offering a feasible step toward bridging the gap between graph-based AML research and real investigation workflows.

AI.tldr: Proposes Clue-Guided Group Discovery (CGGD), a paradigm where laundering groups are progressively recovered from initial clues via analyst interaction, and Clue2Group, a framework using local investigation context, multi-semantic local-temporal GNN, and evidence integration to reconstruct coherent criminal groups from financial networks.
AI.motivation: Existing graph anomaly detection produces only node-level risk alerts, while global group discovery passively searches the entire network. Neither matches real AML investigations, where analysts start from concrete clues and expand outward to recover the full responsible group. This operational mismatch motivates a clue-driven, interactive discovery paradigm.
AI.method: Clue2Group framework: (1) constructs a compact local investigation context to reduce noise while preserving chain-like and cycle-like laundering structures; (2) estimates a clue-conditioned local risk field using a multi-semantic local-temporal GNN; (3) integrates risk, structural, and prior-pattern evidence to recover a coherent laundering group. Operates within the CGGD paradigm of progressive group recovery from an initial clue set.
AI.result: Experiments on two large-scale AML benchmarks demonstrate that Clue2Group provides a practical clue-driven analysis framework, showing feasibility in bridging graph-based AML research with real investigation workflows.
AI.conclusion: Clue2Group offers a viable step toward aligning graph-based AML techniques with how investigations are actually conducted — starting from clues rather than scanning entire networks — enabling more practical and effective money laundering group discovery.

title: Accelerating Skill Assessment in Chess: A Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System
comment: Accepted at the IEEE Conference on Games (IEEE CoG) 2026
summary: Rating systems such as Elo serve as the gold standard for matchmaking in competitive chess. However, they inherently suffer from response lag due to their exclusive reliance on match outcomes, neglecting the granular quality of gameplay. Nevertheless, incorporating move-by-move information into rating adjustments presents a significant challenge given the substantial noise and the vastness of the game-state space. To address this, we propose the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System (DD-Elo), a novel skill assessment framework inspired by the drift diffusion model (DDM) from cognitive neuroscience. By modeling skill expression as a decision-making process, our model integrates move-level data to capture rapid skill fluctuations. We provide a rigorous mathematical derivation proving that DD-Elo maintains a bounded deviation from the traditional Elo system, ensuring theoretical alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes faster than Elo. Our findings suggest that DD-Elo offers an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible solution for chess rating ecosystems. The implementation code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aquila-zhou1/DD-Elo .

AI.tldr: DD-Elo enhances the traditional Elo rating system by incorporating move-level gameplay quality using a drift-diffusion model from cognitive neuroscience, enabling faster adaptation to skill changes while maintaining theoretical alignment with classical Elo.
AI.motivation: Traditional Elo rating systems suffer from response lag because they rely solely on binary match outcomes, ignoring the rich, granular information contained in individual moves. Incorporating move-by-move data is challenging due to noise and the vast game-state space. The authors aim to bridge this gap by developing a rating system that leverages within-game decision-making signals for more responsive skill tracking.
AI.method: The authors propose the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo (DD-Elo) system, which models skill expression as a decision-making process using the drift-diffusion model (DDM) from cognitive neuroscience. Move-level data is integrated to capture rapid skill fluctuations. A rigorous mathematical derivation proves that DD-Elo maintains bounded deviation from traditional Elo, ensuring theoretical consistency and backward compatibility.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes significantly faster than the traditional Elo system, demonstrating improved responsiveness while remaining explainable and backward-compatible.
AI.conclusion: DD-Elo provides an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible solution for chess rating ecosystems, offering a principled way to incorporate within-game performance data into established rating infrastructures. Code is publicly available.

title: An exploratory behavioral and electroencephalographic study of artificial intelligence-assisted learning modes in high school students
summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly integrating into education, concerns have emerged regarding its potential implications on cognitive engagement and problem-solving behavior. However, existing research largely treats AI exposure as a binary condition (AI vs. no-AI), with limited differentiation between interaction modalities and post-exposure effects. This study investigates whether distinct AI interaction modes (Tutor, Collaborator, Solver) influence frontal EEG spectral activity. Electroencephalography (EEG) data and quantified behavioral metrics were recorded from 48 study participants (24 males, 24 females; ages 14-18) across two counterbalanced quizzes in a within-subject design. Statistical analyses included Friedman tests, repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t-tests, and effect size calculations. Behavioral changes were mathematically analyzed in an observation matrix of three characteristics -Initiation, Processing, and Stress-measured on an ordinal scale. Each mode showed significant differences in all three behavioral measures. Descriptive EEG patterns in AI interaction mode were observed, and the possibility of short-term carryover effects of AI was explored. Although the EEG data did not reach statistical significance, the patterns observed across the three AI interaction modes warrant further investigation. This study provides preliminary behavioral evidence and investigative electrophysiological observations, exploring possible AI-interaction-mode-based differences in neural activity and behavior, while establishing a replicable framework for future human-AI interaction studies.

AI.tldr: This study examines how three distinct AI interaction modes (Tutor, Collaborator, Solver) differentially affect frontal EEG spectral activity and problem-solving behavior in 48 adolescents. While EEG patterns did not reach statistical significance, significant behavioral differences were found across all three modes in Initiation, Processing, and Stress measures. The study also explores short-term carryover effects and establishes a replicable framework for future human-AI interaction research.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-in-education research predominantly treats AI exposure as a binary condition (AI vs. no-AI), failing to differentiate how specific interaction modalities may distinctly influence cognitive engagement and problem-solving behavior. Additionally, post-exposure carryover effects remain underexplored. This gap motivates a more granular, modality-specific investigation using both neural and behavioral metrics.
AI.method: A within-subject design with 48 participants (24 male, 24 female; ages 14–18) completed two counterbalanced quizzes across three AI interaction modes: Tutor, Collaborator, and Solver. Frontal EEG spectral activity was recorded, and behavioral metrics were quantified across three ordinal-scale characteristics—Initiation, Processing, and Stress—using an observation matrix. Statistical analyses included Friedman tests, repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t-tests, and effect size calculations.
AI.result: Each AI interaction mode produced significant differences in all three behavioral measures (Initiation, Processing, Stress). Descriptive EEG patterns were observed across modes, though these did not reach statistical significance. Preliminary evidence of short-term carryover effects from AI interaction was also noted.
AI.conclusion: The study provides preliminary behavioral evidence and descriptive electrophysiological observations suggesting AI-interaction-mode-based differences in neural activity and behavior. It establishes a replicable experimental framework for future human-AI interaction studies and recommends further investigation into the observed EEG patterns with larger samples or more sensitive paradigms.

title: A Shared IPTC Topic Space for Cross-Source Topic Modelling
summary: Comparing topic attention across different media is hindered by a fundamental modelling problem: topic models fitted separately to each corpus produce corpus-specific topic spaces that cannot be aligned directly. This paper presents a reproducible framework that places corpora in a single shared topic space defined by a taxonomy. Discovered topics are obtained with guided BERTopic, scored against the ninety-four IPTC Media Topics' taxonomy topics (level-1) through weighted keyword and target centroids, and then collapsed upward to seventeen IPTC parent topics by a maximum-similarity rule. The framework was developed and selected on a controlled New York Times 2011 corpus through a narrowing sequence: a broad model screen, a focused mapping refinement, a strict finalist comparison, a target-construction ablation, and a threshold calibration. In this corpus, the guided family retained substantially stronger mapped coverage than a zero-shot benchmark under stricter assignment thresholds, a parent-enriched target construction improved both coverage and parent consistency, and coverage declined gradually rather than collapsing as the assignment threshold was tightened. The contribution is an externally anchored method for constructing a shared topic space that enables reproducible cross-source topic comparison.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reproducible framework using guided BERTopic and the IPTC Media Topics taxonomy to project corpora into a single shared topic space, enabling cross-media topic comparison. Evaluated on NYT 2011 data, the guided approach outperforms zero-shot baselines in coverage and consistency under strict thresholds.
AI.motivation: Comparing topic attention across different media is hindered by the incomparability of corpus-specific topic spaces generated by standard topic models. There is a need for a method that maps disparate corpora into a common, externally anchored topic space to enable reproducible cross-source comparison.
AI.method: The framework uses guided BERTopic to discover topics, then scores them against the 94 IPTC Media Topics (level-1) using weighted keyword and target centroids. Topics are collapsed upward to 17 IPTC parent topics via a maximum-similarity rule. Development involved a controlled NYT 2011 corpus evaluated through: broad model screening, focused mapping refinement, strict finalist comparison, target-construction ablation, and threshold calibration.
AI.result: The guided family retained substantially stronger mapped coverage than a zero-shot benchmark under stricter assignment thresholds. A parent-enriched target construction improved both coverage and parent consistency. Coverage declined gradually rather than collapsing as the assignment threshold was tightened.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an externally anchored method for constructing a shared topic space, enabling reproducible cross-source topic comparison that overcomes the fundamental incompatibility of corpus-specific topic models.

title: Hybrid privacy-aware semantic search: SVD-truncated document geometry and CKKS-encrypted query reranking under a restricted threat model
summary:
Dense embeddings power semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embedding-inversion attacks can reconstruct source text from a vector: when a vector database leaks, the documents behind it leak too. The textbook defences are extremes - encrypting the whole search homomorphically is sound but too slow at million-document scale, while privacy noise degrades ranking long before it protects. We study a middle path exploiting the asymmetry between the static collection and the dynamic query. The collection is protected geometrically: each vector is truncated onto a lower-dimensional SVD subspace and rotated by a secret orthogonal transform known only to the owner. The query is protected cryptographically: it is reranked under CKKS homomorphic encryption, so an honest-but-curious server never sees the query or the scores. CKKS parameters come from a small offline benchmark.
  We prove a tight lower bound on the reconstruction error of any attacker confined to the protected subspace. On one million documents and five encoders the scheme preserves ranking quality (slightly improving it on strong encoders, as a linear denoiser) at sub-second latency, and an off-the-shelf inversion attack on the protected space collapses to the noise floor. We then test stronger adversaries: a known-plaintext attacker recovers the rotation by orthogonal Procrustes from about as many leaked pairs as the retained dimension; the public product-quantization codes preserve most nearest-neighbour structure; and random-projection, calibrated-noise and BEIR baselines show the truncation is an encoder-dependent accuracy cost, not a free denoiser. We state the limits: query confidentiality is cryptographic, but document protection is an empirical obfuscation layer (SVD truncation plus a secret rotation), not a cryptographic primitive, and we delimit the threat model for each claim.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid privacy-preserving semantic search scheme: document vectors are protected geometrically via SVD truncation and secret rotation, while queries are protected cryptographically via CKKS homomorphic encryption. The approach balances efficiency and privacy, preserving ranking quality at sub-second latency on million-document scales while empirically defending against embedding-inversion attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses against embedding-inversion attacks are polar extremes: fully homomorphic encryption is sound but impractically slow at scale, while differential privacy noise degrades ranking quality before achieving meaningful protection. The authors seek a practical middle ground that exploits the asymmetry between static document collections and dynamic queries.
AI.method: The collection is protected geometrically: each document vector is projected onto a lower-dimensional SVD subspace and rotated by a secret orthogonal matrix known only to the data owner. The query is protected cryptographically: reranking is performed under CKKS homomorphic encryption, so the server never sees plaintext queries or relevance scores. CKKS parameters are determined via a small offline benchmark. Security is analyzed via lower bounds on reconstruction error for subspace-confined attackers, and tested against known-plaintext attacks using orthogonal Procrustes, product quantization leakage, and various baselines (random projection, calibrated noise, BEIR).
AI.result: On one million documents across five encoders, the scheme preserves ranking quality (slightly improving it on strong encoders, acting as a linear denoiser) with sub-second latency. Off-the-shelf inversion attacks on the protected space collapse to the noise floor. However, a known-plaintext attacker can recover the secret rotation via orthogonal Procrustes given roughly as many leaked document-vector pairs as the retained dimension. Product-quantization codes preserve most nearest-neighbor structure. Truncation incurs an encoder-dependent accuracy cost, not a free denoising gain.
AI.conclusion: Query confidentiality is cryptographically grounded via CKKS, but document protection is an empirical obfuscation layer (SVD truncation plus secret rotation), not a cryptographic primitive. The authors explicitly delimit the threat model: geometric protection raises the bar against inversion but is breakable given sufficient leaked pairs. The scheme offers a practical performance-security tradeoff for large-scale semantic search.

title: Low Resource Multimodal Translation of Nepali Spoken Words into Emotion-Conditioned Sign Language Avatars
summary: Sign language communication systems, that integrate emotional expression remain underexplored, particularly for low-resource languages. This pilot study presents NEST-V1 (Nepali Emotion and Speech Transformer - Version 1), a proof-of-concept multimodal framework that demonstrates the feasibility of generating emotion-conditioned Nepali Sign Language avatars from spoken input. As a preliminary investigation, we focus on four common Nepali words ("thank you", "hello", "house", "me") across three emotional states (happy, neutral, sad) to validate our core technical approach. Our lightweight architecture employs a shared acoustic encoder for simultaneous Automatic Speech Recognition and emotion classification, achieving 81.1% ASR accuracy and 79.21% emotion recognition accuracy on a dataset of 600 labeled audio samples from 50 speakers. The system demonstrates 37% parameter efficiency compared to separate model architectures while maintaining a lightweight footprint with only 22.1M parameters suitable for edge deployment. This pilot work establishes the technical foundation for emotion-aware sign language translation in low-resource settings and provides a scalable framework for future expansion to larger vocabularies and more diverse emotional expressions. Our preliminary results indicate the viability of real-time, emotionally expressive sign language communication systems for the hearing-impaired community, with clear pathways for enhancement in subsequent development phases.

AI.tldr: NEST-V1 is a proof-of-concept multimodal framework that generates emotion-conditioned Nepali Sign Language avatars from speech, achieving 81.1% ASR accuracy and 79.21% emotion recognition using a shared acoustic encoder with only 22.1M parameters.
AI.motivation: Emotionally expressive sign language communication systems are underexplored, especially for low-resource languages like Nepali. Existing systems lack integration of emotional expression with sign language generation, creating a gap in natural communication for hearing-impaired communities.
AI.method: A lightweight multimodal architecture with a shared acoustic encoder performs simultaneous Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and emotion classification. The system was trained and evaluated on 600 labeled audio samples from 50 speakers, covering four Nepali words across three emotional states (happy, neutral, sad), and generates emotion-conditioned sign language avatars from spoken input.
AI.result: The shared encoder achieved 81.1% ASR accuracy and 79.21% emotion recognition accuracy. The architecture demonstrates 37% parameter efficiency over separate models, with a compact 22.1M parameter footprint suitable for edge deployment.
AI.conclusion: The pilot study establishes technical feasibility for emotion-aware sign language translation in low-resource settings. Results indicate viability for real-time, emotionally expressive communication systems, with clear pathways for scaling to larger vocabularies and broader emotional ranges in future work.

title: Quantum Mutant Equivalence via Transpilation
summary: Mutation testing evaluates test suite quality by introducing artificial faults (mutants) and checking whether tests detect (kill) them. A central challenge is the equivalent mutant problem: some mutants are syntactically different from the original program but semantically identical to it and therefore cannot be killed by any test. If left unidentified, such mutants waste testing effort and distort mutation scores. In quantum software, mutation testing is increasingly used, but the equivalent mutant problem remains unsolved. A recent study generated more than 700,000 quantum circuit mutants and found that roughly half survived the available tests, making it unclear whether these survivors reflect weak tests or semantic equivalence. We propose Transpiler-Based Equivalence (TBE), a lightweight approach that identifies equivalent quantum mutants by transpiling original and mutated circuits under the same configuration and comparing their resulting OpenQASM code. We evaluate TBE on 348,299 surviving mutants, 92,011 of which are equivalent; TBE identifies 29,536 of them (32.1%) as equivalent while achieving 100% precision and 82% accuracy.

AI.tldr: TBE identifies equivalent quantum mutants by comparing transpiled circuit outputs, achieving 100% precision on 348K surviving mutants.
AI.motivation: Quantum software mutation testing faces an unsolved equivalent mutant problem: up to half of mutants survive testing, but it is unclear whether survival indicates weak tests or semantic equivalence. This wastes effort and distorts mutation scores.
AI.method: Transpiler-Based Equivalence (TBE): transpile original and mutated quantum circuits under identical configuration, then compare the resulting OpenQASM code; identical transpiled outputs indicate semantic equivalence.
AI.result: Evaluated on 348,299 surviving mutants (92,011 ground-truth equivalent). TBE identified 29,536 equivalent mutants (32.1% recall) with 100% precision and 82% overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: TBE is a lightweight, precise method for detecting equivalent quantum mutants, though its 32.1% recall suggests many equivalents require more sophisticated analysis beyond transpiler comparison.

title: Federated Hash Projected Latent Factor Learning
summary: Hash Learning (HL) is an efficient representation learning approach that maps real-valued data into compact binary representations. Traditional HL methods typically require users to upload personal data to a central server, which is incompatible with increasingly stringent data security regulations. Federated Learning (FL) provides a decentralized paradigm for learning globally optimal models without centralizing private data. However, most FL methods rely on transmitting large-scale real-valued gradient information, leading to high communication overhead and potential privacy risks. Integrating HL into FL is a promising solution. Nevertheless, existing HL methods suffer from limited representational capacity of binary codes, which may degrade model accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a Federated Hash Projected Latent Factor (FHPLF) model. FHPLF introduces three key innovations: (a) replacing real-valued gradient matrices with binary gradient-like matrices, significantly reducing computation, storage, and communication costs while enhancing privacy protection; (b) leveraging Projected Hamming Distance for similarity modeling, which captures the importance of individual binary bits to improve representation capability; and (c) proposing a Secure Binary Gradient Reassembly and Privacy-Enhanced Upload (SBG-PEU) strategy to further reduce the risk of user interaction leakage during transmission. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that FHPLF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art HL and FL methods, achieving a favorable trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and privacy preservation.

AI.tldr: FHPLF integrates hash learning into federated learning by replacing real-valued gradients with binary gradient-like matrices, using Projected Hamming Distance for similarity modeling, and employing a Secure Binary Gradient Reassembly strategy — achieving superior accuracy-efficiency-privacy trade-offs over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional HL requires centralized data upload (violating privacy regulations), while standard FL transmits large real-valued gradients (high communication overhead, privacy risks). Integrating HL into FL is promising but limited by binary codes' weak representational capacity, motivating a method that balances accuracy, efficiency, and privacy.
AI.method: FHPLF proposes three innovations: (1) binary gradient-like matrices replace real-valued gradients to reduce computation/storage/communication costs and enhance privacy; (2) Projected Hamming Distance models similarity while capturing per-bit importance for improved representation; (3) a Secure Binary Gradient Reassembly and Privacy-Enhanced Upload (SBG-PEU) strategy mitigates user interaction leakage during transmission.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show FHPLF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art HL and FL methods, achieving a favorable trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and privacy preservation.
AI.conclusion: FHPLF effectively addresses the limitations of integrating HL into FL through binary gradient compression, enhanced similarity modeling with Projected Hamming Distance, and secure transmission strategies, yielding a practical solution that balances model accuracy, communication efficiency, and privacy protection.

title: Governing Actions, Not Agents: Institutional Attestation as a Governance Model for Autonomous AI Systems
summary: Autonomous AI agents may begin to perform consequential, irreversible actions such as clinical prescribing and production software deployment. This paper observes that human institutions have governed powerful autonomous actors not by monitoring their reasoning but by requiring independently attested evidence at the point of consequential action. We formalise this institutional pattern as a computational governance model for AI agent systems. Under the proposed model, an agent retains full autonomy over planning and reasoning but holds no execution authority over designated high-risk actions. Execution is conditional on preconditions that are each independently attested by a separate authoritative source, cryptographically bound to a declared intent, and evaluated by a deterministic policy. Decisions are recorded in a tamper-evident log amenable to independent re-verification. We present a proof-of-concept implementation and illustrate the model with examples from software deployment and clinical prescribing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a computational governance model for autonomous AI agents where high-risk actions (e.g., clinical prescribing, software deployment) require independently attested evidence from separate authoritative sources before execution, rather than monitoring the agent's internal reasoning. Execution authority is separated from planning autonomy and gated by cryptographically bound preconditions evaluated by deterministic policy.
AI.motivation: As autonomous AI agents begin performing consequential, irreversible actions in domains like healthcare and software deployment, relying on monitoring an agent's internal reasoning is insufficient for governance. The authors observe that human institutions have long governed powerful actors (e.g., notaries, auditors) through independently attested evidence at the point of action, not by scrutinizing their thought processes. This institutional pattern needs formalization for AI governance.
AI.method: The authors formalize an institutional governance pattern into a computational model with the following components: (1) the agent retains full autonomy over planning and reasoning but holds no execution authority over designated high-risk actions; (2) execution is conditional on preconditions independently attested by separate authoritative sources; (3) attestations are cryptographically bound to a declared intent; (4) a deterministic policy evaluates whether conditions are met; (5) all decisions are recorded in a tamper-evident log for independent re-verification. A proof-of-concept implementation is provided.
AI.result: The paper presents a proof-of-concept implementation of the governance model and illustrates its application through examples in software deployment and clinical prescribing contexts, demonstrating how the model separates planning autonomy from execution authority for high-risk actions.
AI.conclusion: Effective governance of autonomous AI agents should follow the institutional pattern of requiring independently attested evidence at the point of consequential action, rather than attempting to monitor or constrain the agent's internal reasoning. This model enables agents to retain autonomy over planning while ensuring appropriate checks on irreversible high-stakes decisions.

title: HiLSVA: Design and Evaluation of a Human-in-the-Loop Agentic System for Scientific Visualization
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents enable natural language interaction for scientific visualization (SciVis). Still, prior systems have essentially prioritized autonomy over human analytical control, thereby limiting transparency and human oversight. We present HiLSVA, a human-in-the-loop agentic system that supports mixed-initiative SciVis workflows. HiLSVA integrates a plan-first multi-agent architecture with explicit human oversight, stepwise provenance tracking, and learn-at-test-time adaptation from user feedback. The system supports fluid handoff between humans and agents through both natural language and direct manipulation of visualizations, while sandboxed execution ensures safe, reproducible workflows. In doing so, HiLSVA reframes agentic SciVis as a collaborative process that augments, rather than replaces, human analytical reasoning. We evaluate HiLSVA through representative case studies and a controlled user study with twelve participants of varying expertise across multiple autonomy settings. Results show that mixed-initiative interaction improves task completion, user control, and workflow transparency across different levels of user expertise, while revealing a tradeoff between execution efficiency and human oversight. These findings highlight the importance of human-centered design in agentic SciVis and guide the development of future collaborative visualization systems. We encourage readers to explore our demo video, case studies, and source code at https://hilsva.github.io/.

AI.tldr: HiLSVA is a human-in-the-loop agentic system for scientific visualization that combines a plan-first multi-agent architecture with explicit human oversight, provenance tracking, and user-feedback-driven adaptation, reframing agentic SciVis as a collaborative rather than autonomous process.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent systems for scientific visualization prioritize full autonomy over human control, resulting in limited transparency and insufficient human oversight. There is a need for systems that augment rather than replace human analytical reasoning.
AI.method: HiLSVA employs a plan-first multi-agent architecture with several key components: (1) explicit human oversight and stepwise provenance tracking, (2) learn-at-test-time adaptation from user feedback, (3) fluid handoff via natural language and direct manipulation, (4) sandboxed execution for safe, reproducible workflows. The system is evaluated through case studies and a controlled user study (N=12, varied expertise) across multiple autonomy settings.
AI.result: Mixed-initiative interaction improved task completion, user control, and workflow transparency across expertise levels. A tradeoff emerged between execution efficiency and human oversight—greater human involvement improved transparency but reduced raw speed.
AI.conclusion: Human-centered design is critical for agentic SciVis systems. HiLSVA demonstrates that collaborative, mixed-initiative workflows yield better outcomes than fully autonomous approaches, providing guidance for future collaborative visualization system development.

title: TriPAH: Imbalance-Aware Tri-Prompt Affinity Hashing for Cross-Modal Medical Retrieval
summary: In the era of big medical data, efficient cross-modal retrieval is pivotal for evidence-based diagnosis and large-scale case management. Cross-modal medical hashing retrieval aims to enable efficient image-text search and support downstream tasks such as case-based reasoning and decision support by learning compact, semantically aligned binary codes. However, current methods suffer from semantic fragmentation due to noisy clinical language, long-tailed labels, and brittle quantization that weakens alignment. We propose TriPAH, a Tri-Prompt Affinity Hashing framework. TriPAH synthesizes ontology-grounded, patient-level prompts conditioned on normalized clinical cues to yield low-noise textual representations for initial alignment. A lightweight prompt-token mixer performs hierarchical, multi-granularity alignment and produces quantization-ready features under an asymmetric multi-task objective coupling multi-positive contrastive alignment, imbalance-aware classification, and progressive quantization regularization. A patient-level consistency module further stabilizes codes across complementary views. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that TriPAH significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: TriPAH is a cross-modal medical hashing framework that uses ontology-grounded prompts, hierarchical alignment, and patient-level consistency to generate robust binary codes for image-text retrieval, outperforming existing methods on three public datasets.
AI.motivation: Current cross-modal medical hashing methods suffer from semantic fragmentation caused by noisy clinical language, long-tailed label distributions, and brittle quantization, which degrade semantic alignment between images and text.
AI.method: TriPAH introduces three components: (1) ontology-grounded patient-level prompts conditioned on normalized clinical cues for low-noise textual representations; (2) a lightweight prompt-token mixer performing hierarchical multi-granularity alignment with an asymmetric multi-task objective combining multi-positive contrastive alignment, imbalance-aware classification, and progressive quantization regularization; (3) a patient-level consistency module that stabilizes hash codes across complementary views.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three public datasets show TriPAH significantly outperforms state-of-the-art cross-modal hashing methods.
AI.conclusion: TriPAH effectively addresses semantic fragmentation in medical cross-modal hashing through prompt-based noise reduction, hierarchical alignment, and consistency regularization, achieving superior retrieval performance.

title: Verifying Intent and Harm: A Unified Defense Against LLM-Generated Threats
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive applications, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial interactions that induce harmful, deceptive, or policy-violating outputs. Existing defenses typically analyze either user prompts or generated outputs, but not both. However, many real-world attacks exploit a separation between adversarial intent expressed in the prompt and actionable harm manifested only in the response. As a result, prompt-only and response-only defenses frequently miss unsafe interactions that appear benign when viewed from either side in isolation. We present a verification-centric defense framework that jointly evaluates prompt intent and response harm before an LLM response is delivered to a user. The framework employs specialized analysts for intent and harm assessment together with a Judge for conflict resolution. We formalize a threat model for prompt-response attacks and evaluate the framework across five threat categories: jailbreaks, prompt injection, phishing, cyber abuse, and harmful content. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that jointly verifying prompt intent and response harm consistently outperforms single-sided defenses and single-agent reasoning baselines. Across threat categories, the framework improves average F1 from 0.90 for the strongest applicable baselines to 0.95 while reducing the average attack success rate to 4.1 percent. Compared with a Single-Agent+CoT baseline, it improves average F1 from 0.87 to 0.95 and reduces the false positive rate on benign-sensitive requests from 0.12 to 0.06. We further evaluate architecture-aware adaptive attacks in which the attacker knows the verifier structure and attempts to bypass individual verification components. Our results suggest that prompt-response verification provides a practical foundation for securing LLM applications against evolving adversarial threats.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a verification-centric defense framework that jointly evaluates both prompt intent and response harm before delivering LLM outputs, using specialized intent/harm analysts and a Judge for conflict resolution. Tested across five threat categories, it achieves F1 of 0.95 and reduces attack success rate to 4.1%, outperforming single-sided defenses and single-agent baselines, even against architecture-aware adaptive attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM defenses analyze either user prompts or generated outputs in isolation, but real-world attacks exploit the gap between adversarial intent in the prompt and harmful content in the response — appearing benign when viewed from only one side. This fundamental limitation causes prompt-only and response-only defenses to miss unsafe interactions.
AI.method: A verification-centric defense framework with three components: (1) an intent analyst that assesses whether the prompt contains adversarial intent, (2) a harm analyst that evaluates the generated response for harmful content, and (3) a Judge that resolves conflicts between the two assessments. The framework is formalized under a threat model for prompt-response attacks and evaluated across five threat categories: jailbreaks, prompt injection, phishing, cyber abuse, and harmful content. The paper also tests against architecture-aware adaptive attacks where the attacker knows the verifier structure.
AI.result: The framework improves average F1 from 0.90 (strongest single-sided baselines) to 0.95 and from 0.87 (Single-Agent+CoT) to 0.95. Average attack success rate drops to 4.1%. False positive rate on benign-sensitive requests is reduced from 0.12 to 0.06. The framework also demonstrates robustness against adaptive attacks targeting individual verification components.
AI.conclusion: Joint prompt-response verification provides a practical and effective foundation for securing LLM applications against diverse and evolving adversarial threats, consistently outperforming single-sided and single-agent approaches.

title: Where Larger Models Excel: The Primacy of Constraint-Guided Reasoning
summary: Larger language models consistently outperform smaller ones on reasoning benchmarks, yet the reasoning differences underlying this gap remain underexplored. Across benchmarks in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and programming, we observe stable performance gaps: averaged over datasets, Qwen3-32B outperforms Qwen3-8B by 6.43%, while GPT-OSS-120B exceeds GPT-OSS-20B by 7.38%. To study the reasoning differences behind these gains, we develop AdvCluster, an automated framework that identifies questions where the larger model shows a stable advantage, extracts fine-grained advantage descriptions from paired reasoning traces produced by larger and smaller models, and organizes them through semantic clustering with quantitative evaluation and selection guided by a reviewer model. Our analysis yields a systematic taxonomy of larger model reasoning advantages, spanning both common advantages that recur across domains and specialized advantages associated with particular domains. Across these patterns, a recurring theme is Constraint-Guided Reasoning: larger models are better at identifying explicit and implicit constraints, organizing them into structured reasoning, and using them to rule out infeasible paths and verify intermediate steps.

AI.tldr: Larger language models outperform smaller ones on reasoning benchmarks by 6-7% on average. Using AdvCluster, an automated framework for analyzing paired reasoning traces, the authors identify a systematic taxonomy of reasoning advantages, with "Constraint-Guided Reasoning" emerging as a core theme: larger models better identify, structure, and leverage constraints to prune infeasible paths and verify intermediate steps.
AI.motivation: While performance gaps between larger and smaller language models on reasoning benchmarks are well-documented, the specific reasoning differences that underlie these gains remain underexplored. The authors aim to move beyond aggregate metrics to produce a fine-grained, systematic understanding of *how* larger models reason differently.
AI.method: The authors propose AdvCluster, an automated framework with three stages: (1) identifying questions where the larger model holds a stable advantage using repeated sampling, (2) extracting fine-grained advantage descriptions from paired reasoning traces (larger vs. smaller model) via LLM-based analysis, and (3) organizing these descriptions through semantic clustering, with quantitative evaluation and selection guided by a reviewer model to produce a systematic taxonomy. The study spans benchmarks in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and programming, using model pairs: Qwen3-32B vs. Qwen3-8B and GPT-OSS-120B vs. GPT-OSS-20B.
AI.result: Stable performance gaps were observed across domains: Qwen3-32B outperforms Qwen3-8B by 6.43% and GPT-OSS-120B exceeds GPT-OSS-20B by 7.38% on average. AdvCluster produced a systematic taxonomy revealing both domain-general advantages (recurring across subjects) and domain-specific advantages. The dominant overarching pattern is Constraint-Guided Reasoning: larger models more effectively identify explicit and implicit constraints, organize them into structured reasoning chains, and employ them to rule out infeasible solution paths and verify intermediate steps.
AI.conclusion: The reasoning superiority of larger LMs is not merely a matter of scale but is characterized by identifiable, systematic reasoning patterns—most notably Constraint-Guided Reasoning. The AdvCluster framework provides a general methodology for auditing and understanding model reasoning differences beyond simple accuracy comparisons.

title: Knowledge-Based Pull Requests: A Trusted Workflow for Agent-Mediated Knowledge Collaboration
summary: AI coding agents are changing the bottleneck in software collaboration: code is increasingly cheap, while understanding intent, negotiating scope, and governing long-term project responsibility remain costly. This paper proposes \emph{Knowledge-Based Pull Requests} (KPR), a trusted workflow for agent-mediated software collaboration across trust boundaries, including open source, enterprise, vendor, contractor, and customer-driven settings. In KPR, an external collaborator's local code, tests, and cleaned agent interaction trace are treated as knowledge sources rather than as the default merge candidate. Agents distill these sources into a human-confirmed knowledge package and render it into reviewer-facing forms such as design memos, risk checklists, test plans, or implementation briefs. A project-owned inner trusted coding agent then regenerates candidate code inside the receiving project's environment under repository context, engineering conventions, tests, and security policy. KPR therefore separates two decisions that traditional pull requests often collapse: whether the knowledge should enter the project, and whether a particular implementation should be merged. We contribute the KPR workflow, a candidate artifact schema, a cost-accounting view, a collaboration gateway architecture, a minimal controlled simulation pilot over seven merged public pull requests, and an evaluation agenda. The pilot shows that KPR packages can be instantiated from real PR material and stress-tested under description ablation, diff ablation, and synthetic poisoned-patch conditions. We position KPR as an empirically testable workflow: its value depends on whether auditable extraction, transformation, and project-side regeneration reduce the cost of understanding and reworking high-context external changes.

AI.tldr: KPR proposes a workflow where external code contributions are treated as knowledge sources rather than direct merge candidates. Agents distill these into human-confirmed knowledge packages, and a project-owned trusted agent regenerates the code internally under project conventions, separating the "accept knowledge" decision from the "merge implementation" decision.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents make code generation cheap, but the real costs in software collaboration have shifted to understanding intent, negotiating scope, and governing long-term responsibility—especially across trust boundaries (open source, enterprise, vendor, contractor settings). Traditional pull requests collapse the decision of whether knowledge should enter a project with whether a specific implementation should be merged.
AI.method: The KPR workflow treats external collaborator code, tests, and cleaned agent interaction traces as knowledge sources. Agents distill these into a human-confirmed knowledge package (design memos, risk checklists, test plans, implementation briefs). A project-internal trusted coding agent then regenerates candidate code under the receiving project's environment, conventions, tests, and security policies. The paper contributes a workflow definition, artifact schema, cost-accounting view, collaboration gateway architecture, and a minimal controlled simulation pilot over seven merged public PRs, stress-tested under description ablation, diff ablation, and synthetic poisoned-patch conditions.
AI.result: The pilot demonstrates that KPR packages can be instantiated from real PR material and remain robust under ablation and adversarial conditions (poisoned patches). This provides initial empirical feasibility evidence for the approach.
AI.conclusion: KPR is positioned as an empirically testable workflow whose value hinges on whether auditable extraction, transformation, and project-side regeneration demonstrably reduce the cost of understanding and reworking high-context external changes across trust boundaries.

title: Statistical and Structural Approaches to Algorithmic Fairness
summary: Modern machine learning systems have outgrown their origins as isolated predictive constructs, evolving into complex socio-technical architectures that actively mediate human opportunity. As algorithms increasingly determine access to economic and social opportunities, it has become widely recognized that these systems are deeply embedded with the structural inequalities and prejudices of their environments. The field of algorithmic fairness emerged in response to the growing recognition that models optimized for predictive accuracy can systematically disadvantage marginalized groups. Early mitigation strategies, however, rested on fragile simplifications that limited their effectiveness in complex socio-technical environments. This thesis identifies and addresses two fundamental limitations of contemporary fairness paradigms: the reliance on deterministic point estimates for auditing and the treatment of individuals as isolated entities devoid of structural context.

AI.tldr: This thesis critiques two core limitations in algorithmic fairness research — reliance on deterministic point estimates for auditing and treating individuals as decontextualized entities — arguing that these simplifications undermine fairness interventions in complex socio-technical systems.
AI.motivation: Modern machine learning systems now mediate access to economic and social opportunities, yet they are embedded with structural inequalities. While algorithmic fairness emerged to address discrimination against marginalized groups, early mitigation strategies relied on fragile simplifications that fail in real-world socio-technical environments. The work is motivated by the need to move beyond these inadequate paradigms.
AI.method: The thesis identifies and interrogates two foundational limitations: (1) the use of deterministic point estimates for fairness auditing, which ignores uncertainty and variability in model behavior across populations; and (2) the atomistic treatment of individuals as isolated entities, stripping them of structural context, social networks, and systemic factors that shape outcomes.
AI.result: The abstract does not specify empirical results; it frames the thesis as identifying and addressing these two paradigmatic limitations, implying that subsequent chapters develop and validate alternative approaches that incorporate uncertainty quantification and structural-relational context into fairness frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Contemporary fairness paradigms are undermined by oversimplified assumptions — point-estimate auditing and individualistic framing. Addressing these limitations is necessary for developing fairness interventions robust enough to operate effectively within the complex socio-technical architectures that characterize real-world machine learning deployments.

title: COrigami: An AI Pipeline for Co-Designing Flat-Foldable Visually Recognisable Origami
summary: While generative AI has achieved remarkable success in solving problems with verifiable solutions, generating physical art that satisfies both strict geometric constraints and subjective visual aesthetics remains a challenge. This paper presents an approach to tackle these difficulties in the domain of computational origami, a mathematically rigid environment that grounds artistic design within the equations of flat foldability. We present COrigami, an end-to-end AI-driven pipeline that assists the design cycle by generating crease patterns from natural language. Our pipeline involves generating a semantic stick figure, computing a base packing, solving for a flat-foldable crease pattern, shaping the flat-folded crease pattern, and refining the generated model using reinforcement learning driven by an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop. Our system acts as a highly effective collaborative assistant, generating structural starting points that human artists can further expand and shape. By integrating algorithmic optimisation with autonomous aesthetic critique, this work demonstrates how AI systems can satisfy multi-objective physical constraints to enable reliable, mathematically grounded co-creativity.

AI.tldr: COrigami is an end-to-end AI pipeline that generates flat-foldable origami crease patterns from natural language descriptions, combining geometric constraint solving with reinforcement learning-based aesthetic refinement to serve as a collaborative tool for human artists.
AI.motivation: Current generative AI excels at tasks with verifiable solutions but struggles with domains requiring satisfaction of both strict physical/geometric constraints (e.g., flat foldability in origami) and subjective visual aesthetics. The paper aims to bridge this gap in computational origami, a mathematically rigorous domain where artistic design is grounded in precise equations.
AI.method: The COrigami pipeline consists of five stages: (1) generating a semantic stick figure from natural language input, (2) computing a base circle packing representing the crease topology, (3) solving for a flat-foldable crease pattern using mathematical constraints, (4) shaping the flat-folded form, and (5) refining the output via reinforcement learning with an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop that provides reward signals for visual quality.
AI.result: The system acts as an effective collaborative assistant, producing structurally valid origami crease patterns that serve as starting points for human artists to expand upon. The integration of algorithmic optimization with autonomous aesthetic critique enables reliable, mathematically grounded co-creativity.
AI.conclusion: AI systems can successfully satisfy multi-objective physical constraints to enable co-creativity in domains requiring both mathematical rigor and artistic judgment. COrigami demonstrates that bridging algorithmic optimization with autonomous aesthetic evaluation allows generative AI to contribute meaningfully to constrained artistic workflows like computational origami.

title: Reviving Reflection-in-Action: Instilling Designerly Thinking in AI-Supported Ideation through Multimodal Prompting
summary: Current AI-powered creativity support tools (AI-CSTs) primarily use text prompting to generate solution-oriented outputs. However, the potential value of multimodal prompting in designer-AI interaction, specifically the introduction of productive friction to encourage iteration and reflection, has not been fully explored. To address this, we developed SketchifAI, a prototype AI-CST, and evaluated it with design students. In a mixed-methods, within-participants study, we examined how different input modalities (text, sketch, and sketch-plus-tags) affected design students' perceived ability to express their intent, their perception of creativity support, and their divergent thinking performance. Our preliminary findings suggest that the sketch modality tended to enhance fluency, with inconclusive evidence for differences in variety, originality, or quality compared to text modality. Yet, paradoxically, participants showed a strong preference for text prompting. We discuss how AI tools might be designed to reintroduce reflection-through-sketching, ensuring that designer-AI interaction supports, rather than erodes, essential design skills in students.

AI.tldr: A study comparing text, sketch, and sketch-plus-tags input modalities in an AI creativity support tool (SketchifAI) found that sketching enhanced fluency but users paradoxically preferred text prompting, raising questions about how to design AI tools that preserve reflective design skills.
AI.motivation: Current AI-powered creativity support tools rely predominantly on text prompting for solution-oriented outputs, neglecting the potential of multimodal interaction — particularly how "productive friction" through sketching might foster iteration and reflection in the design process. The authors aimed to explore whether alternative input modalities could better support designer-AI collaboration without eroding essential design competencies.
AI.method: The authors developed SketchifAI, a prototype AI-CST, and conducted a mixed-methods, within-participants study with design students. Three input modalities were compared: text prompting, sketch, and sketch-plus-tags. Outcomes measured included perceived ability to express intent, perception of creativity support, and divergent thinking performance (fluency, variety, originality, and quality).
AI.result: Preliminary findings showed that the sketch modality tended to enhance fluency compared to text. However, evidence was inconclusive regarding differences in variety, originality, or quality. Paradoxically, despite sketching's cognitive benefits, participants expressed a strong preference for text prompting.
AI.conclusion: AI creativity support tools should be intentionally designed to reintroduce reflection-through-sketching, balancing usability preferences with the pedagogical need to preserve and cultivate essential design skills in students, rather than allowing convenient text-based interaction to erode them.

title: UniFormer: Efficient and Unified Model-Centric Scaling for Industrial Recommendation
summary: Recently, substantial progress has been made in industrial recommendation through component-centric model scaling, where individual components such as behavior modeling, feature interaction, or task modeling are independently scaled to improve model capacity. Although recent methods such as HyFormer and OneTrans further explore cross-module co-scaling by jointly modeling behavior and interaction, their designs are still confined to the feature space and lack a unified model-centric scaling framework over the overall modeling space. In this paper, we propose UniFormer, an efficient and unified model-centric scaling framework for industrial recommender systems. To improve efficiency, UniFormer decomposes the overall modeling space into feature and task spaces, which are modeled by stacked Feature-space Interaction Modules and Task-space Interaction Modules, respectively. Moreover, UniFormer introduces semantic-based tokenization scheme to enable user-item decoupling, thereby achieving request-level inference acceleration. To prevent preference collapse, UniFormer employs multi-sequence cross-attention to separately capture heterogeneous behavior patterns, followed by the self-attention to enhance interaction modeling. Besides, dedicated multi-view FFNs are introduced to support flexible and scalable parameter scaling across different modeling components. Extensive online A/B testing in two production scenarios, Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite, shows that UniFormer consistently improves user engagement and interaction metrics, achieving gains of +0.101%/+0.260% in App Stay Time and +0.729%/+1.113% in Watch Time, respectively.

AI.tldr: UniFormer is a unified model-centric scaling framework for industrial recommender systems that decomposes the modeling space into feature and task spaces, uses semantic tokenization for user-item decoupling and inference acceleration, and employs multi-sequence cross-attention with multi-view FFNs to prevent preference collapse while enabling flexible parameter scaling. It achieved significant gains in online A/B tests at Kuaishou.
AI.motivation: Existing industrial recommendation models scale individual components independently (component-centric) or explore limited cross-module co-scaling confined to feature space (e.g., HyFormer, OneTrans). There is no unified model-centric scaling framework that holistically covers the entire modeling space — both feature and task dimensions — in an efficient and scalable manner.
AI.method: UniFormer decomposes the overall modeling space into feature-space and task-space interaction modules, stacked to form a unified architecture. Key technical contributions include: (1) a semantic-based tokenization scheme that decouples user and item representations, enabling request-level inference acceleration; (2) multi-sequence cross-attention to separately capture heterogeneous behavior patterns, followed by self-attention for enhanced interaction modeling; and (3) multi-view FFNs that support flexible, scalable parameter scaling across different modeling components.
AI.result: Online A/B testing in two production scenarios — Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite — demonstrated consistent improvements: +0.101% and +0.260% in App Stay Time, and +0.729% and +1.113% in Watch Time, respectively.
AI.conclusion: UniFormer provides an effective, unified model-centric scaling paradigm that outperforms component-centric and feature-space-limited co-scaling approaches. By jointly modeling feature and task spaces with efficient tokenization and attention mechanisms, it achieves both improved recommendation quality and inference efficiency at production scale.

title: Lessons from the Adoption and Deprecation of the Privacy Sandbox Web APIs
summary: While several web actors have been trying to reduce web tracking for years, it remains unclear how to achieve both desirable levels of utility and privacy. In 2019, Google launched the Privacy Sandbox initiative to balance that trade-off and find privacy alternatives to common use cases such as advertising. Yet, in late 2025, Google canceled the project and deprecated most of the newly introduced APIs. Despite its end, the Privacy Sandbox represents a unique opportunity to learn about how the ecosystem reacted to the proposed changes and make observations about why and how it failed. In this paper, we present a longitudinal measurement and analysis study of the Privacy Sandbox APIs to characterize their adoption and deprecation over the past seven years by different web actors. Leveraging historical HTTP Archive crawls and public Chrome telemetry data, we offer the largest study of its kind into the prevalence of each Privacy Sandbox feature, during their entire respective lifetime (5+ years for some), on popular websites (CrUX top 100k), and as experienced by Chrome users during their browsing journey. Our results showcase an adoption that remained limited and uneven across the years; only few web actors implemented very specific APIs, and in disparate manners. We motivate our interpretation of these results by considering the incentives (interest, resources, timeline, etc.) and risks (potential trade-offs, privacy violations, and legal exposure, etc.) for these actors. Finally, our analysis also yields actionable recommendations for the next generation of web privacy proposals. More broadly, the Privacy Sandbox illustrates the limitations and disparities across browsers of ``fix it in the browser'' remedies: today, tracking and third-party cookies limitations in Chrome still remain largely opt-in, while they have been enabled by default on other browsers like Brave, Firefox, or Safari.

AI.tldr: A seven-year longitudinal measurement study of Google's Privacy Sandbox APIs reveals limited, uneven adoption by web actors, culminating in the project's 2025 cancellation. The authors analyze HTTP Archive and Chrome telemetry data to characterize adoption patterns, interpret failures through incentive/risk analysis, and offer recommendations for future web privacy proposals.
AI.motivation: Google's Privacy Sandbox initiative (2019–2025) represented a major attempt to balance web utility (advertising) with privacy by replacing third-party cookies. Its cancellation provides a unique learning opportunity: understanding why it failed and how the web ecosystem reacted to privacy-preserving API proposals is critical for designing the next generation of web privacy mechanisms.
AI.method: Longitudinal measurement study spanning ~7 years using two primary data sources: (1) historical HTTP Archive crawls to measure Privacy Sandbox API adoption on CrUX top 100k websites, and (2) public Chrome telemetry data to capture real user exposure. Each API is tracked across its entire lifetime (5+ years for some). Results are interpreted through an incentive/risk framework considering interest, resources, timeline, trade-offs, privacy violations, and legal exposure.
AI.result: Adoption of Privacy Sandbox APIs remained limited and uneven across the study period. Only a small number of web actors implemented specific APIs, often in disparate and inconsistent ways. Third-party cookie limitations in Chrome remain largely opt-in, contrasting with default-enabled protections in Brave, Firefox, and Safari.
AI.conclusion: The Privacy Sandbox's failure illustrates fundamental limitations of browser-centric ("fix it in the browser") privacy remedies. The study yields actionable recommendations for future web privacy proposals and highlights significant disparities across browsers in default privacy protections.

title: From Lexicon to AI: A Structured-Data Pipeline for Specialized Conversational Systems in Low-Resource Languages
summary: Low-resource languages face a critical challenge in AI development: creating specialized conversational systems without access to massive training corpora. We present a systematic methodology for transforming structured linguistic resources into specialized AI systems, demonstrating that expert-curated lexical databases can serve as effective foundations for conversational AI development. Our approach converts Hindi WordNet into 1.25 million diverse instruction-response pairs, fine-tunes a 12B-parameter language model using resource-efficient LoRA with 4-bit quantization. Evaluation through a Hindi language learning chatbot demonstrates that structured-knowledge-based systems achieve superior pedagogical effectiveness (91.0 vs. 79.4-83.6 for general-purpose models) while maintaining competitive semantic performance and exceptional consistency. The complete pipeline demonstrates a proof-of-concept methodology using Hindi for developing specialized AI systems for any languages with WordNet resources. This work addresses the critical gap in AI accessibility for low-resource languages, offering a practical alternative to corpus-intensive approaches and potentially enabling specialized AI development for the hundreds of languages with existing WordNet resources.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a methodology for converting structured lexical databases (specifically Hindi WordNet) into training data for specialized conversational AI, using LoRA fine-tuning with 4-bit quantization on a 12B-parameter model, achieving superior pedagogical performance over general-purpose models while enabling AI development for low-resource languages.
AI.motivation: Low-resource languages lack the massive training corpora needed for developing specialized conversational AI systems, creating an accessibility gap. The authors aim to demonstrate that existing expert-curated structured linguistic resources (WordNets) can serve as effective alternatives to corpus-intensive approaches, enabling specialized AI development without requiring large-scale parallel corpora.
AI.method: The methodology involves: (1) transforming Hindi WordNet—a structured lexical database—into 1.25 million diverse instruction-response pairs through systematic conversion; (2) fine-tuning a 12B-parameter language model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique, combined with 4-bit quantization to minimize computational resource requirements; (3) evaluating the resulting system via a Hindi language learning chatbot application.
AI.result: The structured-knowledge-based system achieved 91.0 on pedagogical effectiveness metrics compared to 79.4–83.6 for general-purpose models, demonstrating superior teaching capability. The system also maintained competitive semantic performance and exhibited exceptional consistency relative to baselines.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline serves as a proof-of-concept that WordNet resources can be leveraged for specialized AI development across hundreds of languages, offering a practical, resource-efficient alternative to corpus-intensive approaches for low-resource language AI accessibility.

title: A Deterministic Control Plane for LLM Coding Agents
comment: 45 pages, 9 figures, 13 tables. Dataset and reproduction scripts: Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20780913. Ancillary files include report.json, organizations.txt, and figure-reproduction scripts
summary:
LLM coding harnesses grant agents broad file and shell access, yet the configuration layer that steers them -- rules files, agent definitions, IDE-specific markdown -- is largely unmanaged. A prevalence study of 10,008 public GitHub repositories (n=6,145 agent config files) finds that agent configurations propagate as undeclared shared components: 10.1% of tracked paths are SHA-256 exact duplicates across independent repositories (fork-adjusted, threshold-independent), with 75.5% of clone pairs crossing organisational boundaries. Two further patterns are indicative: configurations are rarely revised (58% single-commit; 0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month age-normalised against CI/CD workflows), and rarely declare permission boundaries (<1% of agent configs vs 33% of Actions workflows, n=31 true positives).
  We propose a deterministic control plane above the harness that maps one-to-one to these gaps. Rel(AI)Build treats agent definitions as a managed supply chain (SHA-256 content addressing, HMAC-stamped lockfiles, hash-chained audit logs); enforces tiered permissions and attack-derived blocklists before LLM invocation; gates feature work through a phase state machine with requirement-to-file-to-test traceability; compiles a single canonical definition to seven IDE targets; and detects prompt drift via Jaccard similarity. Conformance tests on injected violations confirm each mechanism enforces its stated invariant; developer outcomes remain future work. Governance of this layer must be deterministic and tool-agnostic -- not delegated to further LLM orchestration.

AI.tldr: A study of 10,008 GitHub repos reveals that LLM coding agent configurations are largely unmanaged: they suffer from widespread unchecked duplication across orgs, are rarely revised, and almost never declare permission boundaries. The authors propose Rel(AI)Build, a deterministic control plane that treats agent definitions as a managed supply chain with content addressing, lockfiles, audit logs, tiered permissions, blocklists, a phase state machine, multi-target compilation, and prompt drift detection.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents are granted broad file and shell access, but the configuration layer steering them (rules files, agent definitions, IDE markdown) is largely ungoverned. Without systematic management, configurations are duplicated without audit, permissions go undeclared, and changes are untracked — creating security, reproducibility, and maintenance risks.
AI.method: First, an empirical prevalence study on 10,008 public GitHub repositories (6,145 agent config files), measuring SHA-256 exact duplication rates (fork-adjusted, threshold-independent), cross-organizational clone pairs, commit frequency (age-normalized against CI/CD workflows), and permission boundary declaration rates (compared to GitHub Actions workflows). Second, the design and implementation of Rel(AI)Build: a deterministic control plane featuring SHA-256 content addressing, HMAC-stamped lockfiles, hash-chained audit logs, tiered permissions with attack-derived blocklists, a phase state machine enforcing requirement-to-file-to-test traceability, canonical definition compilation to seven IDE targets, and Jaccard-similarity-based prompt drift detection. Third, conformance testing with injected violations to verify invariant enforcement.
AI.result: 10.1% of tracked agent config paths are SHA-256 exact duplicates across independent repositories; 75.5% of clone pairs cross organizational boundaries. 58% of configs are single-commit; commit rates are 0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month age-normalized against CI/CD. Permission boundaries are declared in <1% of agent configs versus 33% of Actions workflows (n=31 true positives). Conformance tests confirm each Rel(AI)Build mechanism enforces its stated invariant.
AI.conclusion: Agent configuration governance must be deterministic and tool-agnostic — not delegated to further LLM orchestration. Rel(AI)Build demonstrates that a supply-chain-style control plane can systematically address the identified gaps, though developer outcome evaluation remains future work.

title: Topology-Informed Neural Networks for Flood Detection in Optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar Imagery
summary: Floods frequently impact regions around the world. Rapid and accurate flood detection is crucial for emergency response and timely mitigation of human and economic loss.
