The expanding availability of satellite data and advances in artificial intelligence have enhanced monitoring of environmental hazards, but many flood events remain challenging to detect because cloud cover obscures optical satellite imagery. Rambour et al. introduced the SEN12-FLOOD dataset and extracted per-image features using a ResNet-50 convolutional neural network backbone, then fed these features into a gated recurrent unit network to show that temporal information can substantially improve accuracy compared to single-image baselines. More recently, Chamatidis et al. showed that a vision transformer can achieve strong performance with popular convolutional architectures. However, these models typically function as opaque black boxes, making it difficult to interpret their decision boundaries, learned features, and internal reasoning, especially in safety-critical domains like remote sensing. In contrast, topological data analysis (TDA) provides a mathematically grounded framework for capturing global structural features of data. TDA has emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing complex imagery, especially imagery with geometrically interpretable structures, of which floods are a prime candidate. In this work, we systematically evaluate topological descriptors for flood detection using the open-source SEN12-FLOOD dataset. By extracting topological features from each image and incorporating them into neural networks, we demonstrate that topological descriptors carry meaningful flood signals independently and complement existing networks to yield more robust and interpretable flood detection systems.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates topological data analysis (TDA) descriptors for flood detection from satellite imagery, demonstrating that topological features carry independent flood signals and complement conventional neural networks, yielding more robust and interpretable flood detection on the SEN12-FLOOD dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning models (CNNs, vision transformers) for flood detection from satellite imagery function as opaque black boxes, making decision boundaries and internal reasoning difficult to interpret — a critical limitation in safety-sensitive remote sensing applications. Additionally, cloud cover routinely obstructs optical imagery, and temporal approaches, while helpful, do not address the interpretability gap.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate topological descriptors extracted from each image in the SEN12-FLOOD dataset. These topological features are incorporated into neural networks to assess whether they carry independent flood detection signals and whether they complement existing architectures (ResNet-50 + GRU, vision transformers).
AI.result: Topological descriptors carry meaningful flood signals independently and, when combined with existing neural network architectures, produce more robust and interpretable flood detection systems compared to conventional single-image and temporal baselines.
AI.conclusion: TDA provides a mathematically grounded, interpretable framework for capturing global structural features in flood imagery. Integrating topological features with deep learning enhances both model robustness and transparency in safety-critical flood detection tasks.

title: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
comment: Authors are listed alphabetically by their first names
summary: A classical intuition holds that verifying a solution is easier than producing one. For today's coding agents, this intuition is being inverted: as foundation models develop stronger reasoning capabilities and engineering harnesses grow more sophisticated, generating complex candidate solutions is no longer difficult -- reliably verifying them has become the harder problem. Every verifier we can build is only a proxy for human intent, never the intent itself. This makes verification subject to a twofold difficulty: first, intent is underspecified by nature, making it inherently hard to faithfully check whether it has been fulfilled; second, during model training, optimization widens the gap between proxy and intent -- manifesting as reward hacking or signal saturation. To address this, we characterize the quality of verification signals along three dimensions -- scalability, faithfulness, and robustness -- and argue that achieving all three simultaneously is the central challenge. We further study four reward constructions: a test verifier for general coding tasks, a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, the user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. Across different task types and policy capability levels, we conduct in-depth analysis and experiments on the core challenges of reward design and how to more effectively leverage reward signals. Experiments show that targeted verification design can effectively suppress reward hacking, improve task completion quality, and achieve significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. These experiences collectively point to a core observation: no fixed reward function can remain effective as policy capability continues to grow; and verification must co-evolve with the generator.

AI.tldr: As coding agents become more capable, verification — not generation — becomes the bottleneck. The paper identifies three desiderata for verification signals (scalability, faithfulness, robustness), shows their inherent tension, and demonstrates across four reward constructions that verification must co-evolve with generator capability rather than remain fixed.
AI.motivation: The classical intuition that verification is easier than generation is being inverted for modern coding agents. With powerful foundation models, generating complex candidate solutions is no longer hard, but reliably verifying them has become the harder problem. This arises from a twofold difficulty: (1) human intent is inherently underspecified, making faithful verification intrinsically difficult; and (2) optimization during training widens the gap between proxy verifiers and true intent, manifesting as reward hacking or signal saturation. The core problem is that every verifier is only a proxy for human intent, never the intent itself.
AI.method: The authors characterize verification quality along three dimensions — scalability, faithfulness, and robustness — arguing that simultaneously achieving all three is the central challenge. They study four distinct reward constructions: (1) a test verifier for general coding tasks, (2) a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, (3) the human user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and (4) an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. Across diverse task types and policy capability levels, they conduct in-depth analysis and experiments on reward design challenges and on how to more effectively leverage reward signals. Targeted verification designs are proposed to suppress reward hacking and improve task completion.
AI.result: Targeted verification design can effectively suppress reward hacking, improve task completion quality, and yield significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. The central empirical finding is that no fixed reward function remains effective as policy capability continues to grow; verification must co-evolve with the generator to remain useful.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that verification is the central bottleneck for coding agents and that the three-dimensional characterization (scalability, faithfulness, robustness) provides a useful framework for reasoning about reward design. The key insight is that verification cannot be static — it must co-evolve with the generator as capabilities improve, otherwise proxy misalignment (reward hacking, saturation) inevitably degrades the signal.

title: Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions
comment: Shortened version of paper accepted into CUI Short paper and WIP
summary: Current dialogue systems, powered by large language models, often treat empathy as essential without assessing its true impact, especially in behavior change, where motivation and adherence often depend on subtle user-chatbot dynamics. We examine this assumption by building three WhatsApp physical-activity (PA) coaching chatbots that differ only in empathy level and evaluating them in a six-week within-subject study (N = 13). Participants struggled to distinguish between the empathy conditions, and the non-empathetic version was often rated as more engaging and useful. However, higher-empathy variants were still associated with a larger overall average increase in step counts and faster improvement in intention to follow advice. These results suggest empathy's role is nuanced: it may be hard for lay users to identify explicitly, but it can still shape motivation and trust that support sustained change. We interpret this pattern through the Elaboration Likelihood Model's peripheral route. We highlight design implications for building next-generation PA coaching chatbots that balance effectiveness with human-like connection.

AI.tldr: A six-week within-subject study (N=13) tested three WhatsApp physical-activity coaching chatbots differing only in empathy level. Users couldn't reliably distinguish empathy conditions and often preferred the non-empathetic version for engagement, yet higher-empathy variants correlated with greater step-count increases and faster intention to follow advice — suggesting empathy operates peripherally rather than explicitly.
AI.motivation: To empirically test the prevailing assumption that empathy in conversational agents is uniformly beneficial, particularly in the context of behavior-change coaching where user motivation and adherence may depend on subtle, poorly understood human-chatbot dynamics.
AI.method: Three WhatsApp-based physical-activity coaching chatbots were developed, identical except for manipulated levels of empathy (none, moderate, high). Thirteen participants used all three variants in a six-week within-subject design. Mixed-methods evaluation included quantitative measures (step counts, intention-to-follow ratings, engagement/usefulness ratings) and qualitative user perceptions.
AI.result: Participants could not reliably differentiate between empathy conditions; the non-empathetic chatbot was frequently rated more engaging and useful. Paradoxically, higher-empathy variants were associated with greater average step-count increases and faster improvement in intention to follow advice. These findings suggest empathy's influence operates through peripheral, non-explicit channels.
AI.conclusion: Empathy in PA coaching chatbots plays a nuanced role: difficult for lay users to explicitly identify, yet capable of implicitly shaping motivation and trust that support sustained behavior change. The authors interpret this through the Elaboration Likelihood Model's peripheral route and propose design implications for balancing effectiveness with human-like connection in next-generation coaching agents.

title: TRUST: Item-Calibrated Interval Evidence for Temporal Session-Based Recommendation
summary: Temporal signals have been widely used in session-based recommendation to infer user interest. Existing temporal session-based recommenders primarily rely on absolute interval values, implicitly assuming that the same interval carries similar interest signals across items. However, we empirically find that this assumption does not hold: each item has its own interval distribution, so an interval should be interpreted relative to the item it belongs to. Based on this observation, we propose TRUST, a framework that evaluates each observed interval relative to the empirical interval distribution of the corresponding item. Specifically, we propose a score function to guide global neighbor sampling, session graph encoding, and final interest aggregation. Experiments on public datasets show that TRUST consistently improves over representative temporal and non-temporal baselines, and plug-in experiments further show that the proposed scoring function can improve existing temporal session recommenders as a model-agnostic method. Component-wise ablations further show that calibrating the temporal signals within each module, rather than removing the module itself, consistently improves neighbor sampling, session graph encoding, and interest aggregation.

AI.tldr: TRUST proposes a relative temporal interval framework for session-based recommendation, arguing that intervals should be interpreted item-specifically rather than absolutely. It uses a score function calibrated against each item's empirical interval distribution to improve neighbor sampling, graph encoding, and interest aggregation, achieving consistent gains over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal session-based recommenders treat absolute time intervals uniformly across all items, implicitly assuming that equal intervals convey equal interest relevance. The authors empirically demonstrate this assumption fails: interval distributions are item-specific, so the same interval may signal strong interest for one item but weak interest for another. This motivates a relative, item-calibrated interpretation of temporal signals.
AI.method: TRUST is a framework with three calibrated components: (1) a score function that normalizes each observed interval against the empirical interval distribution of the corresponding item; (2) score-guided global neighbor sampling that uses the calibrated scores to select temporally relevant neighbors; (3) score-weighted session graph encoding and final interest aggregation, where the calibrated scores modulate attention/aggregation weights. The scoring function is model-agnostic and can be plugged into existing temporal recommenders.
AI.result: Experiments on public datasets show TRUST consistently outperforms both temporal and non-temporal baselines. Plug-in experiments demonstrate the scoring function can improve existing temporal session recommenders in a model-agnostic manner. Component-wise ablation confirms that calibrating temporal signals within each module (rather than removing modules) yields consistent improvements across neighbor sampling, graph encoding, and interest aggregation.
AI.conclusion: Interpreting temporal intervals relative to item-specific distributions, rather than as absolute values, is critical for effective session-based recommendation. The proposed TRUST framework and its plug-in scoring function provide a general, effective approach to calibrate temporal signals, validated by consistent empirical gains across datasets and ablations.

title: What Browsers Do in the Shaders: A Measurement Study of WebGPU Privacy
summary:
WebGPU lets ordinary web pages run GPU workloads through a validated programming model. Validation protects memory safety, but shared browser, driver, OS, and GPU state can still expose privacy-relevant signals. We present WGPULens, a framework for measuring those signals across controlled scenarios, browser-native co-residency, a participant field study, public page loads, and mitigation policies. Our framework separates measurements: controlled scenarios support leakage, boundary, and mitigation claims; participant runs support deployment, compatibility, and fingerprintability; and a Tranco crawl measures WebGPU exposure in real-world pages.
  Our controlled results identify persistent pipeline compilation state as the clearest surface. Cold/warm pipeline probes reveal prior compilation state across selected origin, profile, and browser placements. Controlled browser/native experiments also show native GPU activity can be inferred from browser-visible observables under labeled workloads. Other resource probes provide weaker positive results and negative controls.
  The participant field study shows active WebGPU behavior is highly distinctive within the sample, with deterministic components stable within runs and lower exact stability across repeated visits. A page-load crawl finds WebGPU use mainly as adapter probing and static support code, with no observed page-load shader, pipeline, queue, query, or map activity. Mitigation pilots identify source-level key separation as a proxy for evaluating pipeline-cache partitioning. Overall, WGPULens shows that WebGPU privacy analysis must be surface-specific: browsers need to measure which GPU state crosses which boundary, which browser-visible signals reveal it, and what the corresponding mitigations cost.

AI.tldr: WGPULens is a measurement framework that systematically identifies privacy leakage surfaces exposed by the WebGPU API. Through controlled experiments, a field study, and a web crawl, it finds that persistent GPU pipeline compilation state is the clearest side channel, enabling cross-origin and cross-profile inference, and shows that current mitigation policies are insufficient.
AI.motivation: While WebGPU's validated programming model guarantees memory safety, shared hardware and software state across browser, driver, OS, and GPU can still leak privacy-relevant signals. No prior work systematically measures all GPU-side privacy surfaces exposed through browser-accessible WebGPU observables, nor evaluates real-world deployability and fingerprintability of such leaks.
AI.method: The authors present WGPULens, a multi-tier measurement framework operating across four layers: (1) controlled lab scenarios isolating leakage, boundary, and mitigation claims; (2) browser-native co-residency experiments; (3) a participant field study with repeated visits to measure fingerprintability; and (4) a Tranco-top-list crawl assessing real-world WebGPU exposure. Probes include cold/warm pipeline creation timing, resource allocation contention, and other GPU observable side channels. Mitigation pilots test source-level key separation as a proxy for pipeline-cache partitioning.
AI.result: Pipeline compilation state emerges as the clearest privacy surface: warm/cold timing probes reliably reveal prior compilation state across different origins, browser profiles, and placements. Browser-visible GPU timing observables can infer native GPU workload activity under labeled conditions. The field study shows WebGPU behavior is highly distinctive and contains deterministic components stable within runs but less stable across repeated visits. The crawl finds real-world WebGPU usage limited mostly to adapter probing and static support code, with no observed shader, pipeline, queue, query, or map activity on page load. Mitigation experiments identify source-level key separation as a viable proxy for pipeline-cache partitioning evaluation.
AI.conclusion: WebGPU privacy analysis must be surface-specific rather than one-size-fits-all. Browsers need to systematically measure which GPU state crosses which trust boundary, which browser-visible signals reveal that state, and what mitigations cost. This requires per-surface measurement, not blanket assumptions.

title: Dynamic-dLLM: Dynamic Cache-Budget and Adaptive Parallel Decoding for Training-Free Acceleration of Diffusion LLM
summary: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) offer a promising alternative to autoregressive models, excelling in text generation tasks due to their bidirectional attention mechanisms. However, their computational complexity scales on the order of L cubed with the sequence length L. This poses significant challenges for long-sequence and real-time applications, primarily due to the lack of compatibility with key-value caching and the non-autoregressive nature of denoising steps. Existing acceleration methods rely on static caching or parallel decoding strategies, which fail to account for the dynamic behavior of token properties across layers and decoding steps. We propose Dynamic-dLLM, a training-free framework that enhances dLLM inference efficiency through two components: Dynamic Cache Updating (DCU), which adaptively allocates cache-update budgets based on layer-wise token dynamics, and Adaptive Parallel Decoding (APD), which dynamically calibrates decoding thresholds to balance generation quality and efficiency. Extensive experiments on models like LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, and Dream-v0-7B-Instruct across benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval demonstrate that Dynamic-dLLM significantly improves inference speed. It attains an average speedup exceeding 3 times while maintaining performance. Dynamic-dLLM outperforms state-of-the-art acceleration methods and provides a plug-and-play solution for efficient dLLM deployment without compromising performance. The code is available at https://github.com/TianyiWu233/DYNAMIC-DLLM.

AI.tldr: Dynamic-dLLM is a training-free acceleration framework for diffusion LLMs that combines Dynamic Cache Updating (adaptive KV-cache budget allocation) with Adaptive Parallel Decoding (dynamic threshold calibration), achieving >3× speedup without performance loss on benchmarks like MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs suffer from O(L³) computational complexity due to their inability to use KV-caching and their non-autoregressive denoising nature. Existing acceleration methods (static caching, parallel decoding) ignore the dynamic variation of token properties across layers and decoding steps, limiting their effectiveness for long-sequence and real-time applications.
AI.method: Dynamic-dLLM introduces two training-free components: (1) Dynamic Cache Updating (DCU), which monitors layer-wise token dynamics to adaptively allocate cache-update budgets rather than using static caching policies; (2) Adaptive Parallel Decoding (APD), which dynamically calibrates per-step decoding thresholds to optimize the trade-off between generation quality and parallelization efficiency.
AI.result: On LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, and Dream-v0-7B-Instruct across MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval, Dynamic-dLLM achieves an average speedup exceeding 3× while maintaining generation performance, outperforming state-of-the-art acceleration methods.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic-dLLM provides a plug-and-play, training-free solution for efficient dLLM deployment, demonstrating that accounting for dynamic token-level and layer-level behaviors is crucial for accelerating diffusion-based language models without quality degradation.

title: Are LLMs Ready for Anti-Pattern Detection in Microservice Architectures?
summary: Microservice systems are prone to recurrent architectural anti-patterns (APs) that hinder maintainability, evolvability, and operational quality. Most existing AP detection approaches rely on static analysis and handcrafted rules, which can be effective but are often tool-dependent, limited to explicitly encoded detection logic, and difficult to adapt to heterogeneous repositories. In this paper, we investigate whether large language models (LLMs) are ready to support architectural anti-pattern detection in microservice architectures through a prompt-based analysis pipeline over static repository artifacts. We evaluate three general-purpose LLMs on a curated benchmark of microservice repositories annotated with 16 architectural anti-patterns, and compare their performance against the state-of-the-art static-analysis tool MARS using a uniform evaluation protocol based on precision and recall. Our results show that LLMs can provide useful support for anti-pattern detection, achieving competitive performance on several anti-patterns, especially when the relevant evidence is local, heterogeneous, or semantically rich. At the same time, they exhibit clear limitations on anti-patterns that require explicit structural or cross-service dependency evidence, where static analysis remains more reliable. These findings suggest that LLMs are not yet a replacement for traditional analyzers, but already represent a promising complementary aid for architectural assessment in microservice systems.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLMs can detect architectural anti-patterns in microservice systems via prompt-based analysis of static artifacts. Evaluated on a curated benchmark with 16 anti-patterns, LLMs show competitive performance on semantically rich, local patterns but underperform static analysis (MARS) on patterns requiring structural or cross-service dependency evidence. The authors conclude LLMs are a promising complement, not a replacement, for traditional analyzers.
AI.motivation: Existing microservice anti-pattern detection relies on static analysis and handcrafted rules, which are tool-dependent, limited to explicitly encoded logic, and difficult to adapt across heterogeneous repositories. The authors aim to determine whether LLMs can overcome these limitations by leveraging their ability to reason over diverse, unstructured artifacts.
AI.method: The authors design a prompt-based analysis pipeline that feeds static repository artifacts (e.g., configuration files, source code, Dockerfiles) to three general-purpose LLMs. They curate a benchmark of microservice repositories manually annotated with 16 architectural anti-patterns. LLM performance is evaluated using precision and recall, and compared against MARS, a state-of-the-art static-analysis tool, under a uniform evaluation protocol.
AI.result: LLMs achieve competitive detection performance on anti-patterns where evidence is local, heterogeneous, or semantically rich. However, they exhibit clear limitations on anti-patterns requiring explicit structural or cross-service dependency analysis, where static analysis (MARS) remains more reliable.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are not yet a replacement for traditional static analyzers but already serve as a promising complementary aid for architectural assessment in microservice systems, particularly for patterns requiring semantic reasoning over diverse artifacts.

title: A General Framework for Learning Algebraic Properties from Cayley Graphs using Graph Neural Networks
summary: A Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for predicting the solvability of finite groups from their Cayley graph representations was introduced in [1]. In the present work, we generalize this approach and develop a property-independent framework for learning algebraic properties of finite groups directly from Cayley graphs. As representative case studies, we consider abelianity, nilpotency, and solvability. Using a common GNN architecture and training pipeline, we investigate the extent to which algebraic structure can be recovered from graph-based representations alone. Results on a collection of finite groups drawn from several families demonstrate that the framework successfully learns and distinguishes multiple algebraic properties from their associated Cayley graphs. These findings suggest that substantial algebraic information is encoded in graph representations and can be extracted through GNNs. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a proof of concept for applying graph representation learning to the study of algebraic properties of finite groups.

AI.tldr: A GNN-based framework is proposed to learn multiple algebraic properties (abelianity, nilpotency, solvability) of finite groups directly from their Cayley graphs, demonstrating that substantial algebraic information is encoded in these graph representations and can be recovered through a unified, property-independent GNN architecture.
AI.motivation: Prior work introduced a GNN framework for predicting solvability from Cayley graphs. The authors aim to generalize this into a property-independent framework capable of learning multiple algebraic properties of finite groups from their Cayley graph representations, investigating whether a common architecture can recover diverse algebraic structures.
AI.method: A unified GNN architecture and training pipeline are applied to Cayley graphs of finite groups drawn from several families. The framework learns to classify groups according to three algebraic properties — abelianity, nilpotency, and solvability — directly from graph structure, without property-specific modifications.
AI.result: The framework successfully learns and distinguishes all three algebraic properties (abelianity, nilpotency, solvability) from Cayley graphs across multiple families of finite groups, indicating that these properties leave discernible structural signatures in the graph representations.
AI.conclusion: Substantial algebraic information is encoded in Cayley graph representations and can be extracted via GNNs. The work serves as a proof of concept for applying graph representation learning to algebraic property discovery in finite groups.

title: How Do Tool-Augmented LLM Agents Perform on Real-World Energy Analytics Tasks?
summary:
Agentic benchmarks have emerged across general-purpose and domain-specific settings, including finance, coding, law, and drug discovery, yet energy-domain evaluations remain largely limited to static knowledge recall. This is a critical gap for a sector that requires live data retrieval, specialized regulatory and market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints.
  We present an empirical study of tool-augmented LLM agents on real-world energy market analytics tasks. Our evaluation environment includes 243 expert-curated problems across three categories: (1) Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, (2) Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, and (3) Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics. Tasks include price and demand analysis, tariff impact modeling, asset revenue and returns estimation, hedging strategy analysis, and optimization modeling, with problems spanning multiple difficulty levels.
  Agents are equipped with a configurable suite of domain tools, including live electricity market APIs for major U.S. ISOs, regulatory docket search, utility tariff databases, asset optimization models, and retrieval-augmented generation over energy market documents. We assess agent responses using a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that scores approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with category-aware routing to match scoring criteria to question type. We evaluate both closed-source and open-source LLMs, providing a comparative analysis of how model capability and domain tooling interact in a high-stakes professional domain. Key artifacts are publicly released to support reproducibility and future research.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an empirical evaluation of tool-augmented LLM agents on real-world energy market analytics tasks, using 243 expert-curated problems across three categories, with domain-specific tools including live APIs and regulatory databases, assessed via a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic benchmarks cover domains like finance, coding, law, and drug discovery, but energy-domain evaluations remain limited to static knowledge recall. This is a critical gap because the energy sector demands live data retrieval, specialized regulatory and market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints.
AI.method: The authors construct an evaluation environment with 243 expert-curated problems spanning three categories: (1) Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, (2) Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, and (3) Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics. Agents are equipped with configurable domain tools including live electricity market APIs for major U.S. ISOs, regulatory docket search, utility tariff databases, asset optimization models, and RAG over energy market documents. Responses are assessed using a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol scoring approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with category-aware routing. Both closed-source and open-source LLMs are evaluated comparatively.
AI.result: The paper provides a comparative analysis of how model capability and domain tooling interact in a high-stakes professional domain. Key artifacts are publicly released. (Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.)
AI.conclusion: Tool-augmented LLM agents show potential for addressing complex, multi-step energy market analytics tasks that require live data, regulatory knowledge, and quantitative reasoning. The public release of benchmarks and artifacts aims to support reproducibility and spur future research in this underexplored domain.

title: From Content to Strategy: Understanding the Motivations, Processes, and Impacts of AI-Guided Communication
summary: Artificial intelligence-mediated communication (AI-MC) is conceptualized as applying AI to augment or generate message content (Hancock et al., 2020). However, advances in generative AI have expanded its use beyond generating content to guiding individuals' communication strategies, that is, AI-guided communication, yet theoretical and empirical understandings of this emerging use pattern and its consequences remains limited. To address this gap, this study conducted 26 in-depth interviews with individuals who have used AI to develop their communication strategies. Findings suggest participants strongly preferred using AI to analyze challenging scenarios in close relationships, because it fostered self-reflection, eased emotions, prevented conflict escalation, offered multiple perspectives, and provided a safe, nonjudgmental space for self-disclosure. Participants also stated that AI-guided communication enhanced their empathy and communication skills, though some voiced self-doubt and worried about losing their uniqueness. Views on long-term relational impact were mixed, depending on perceived usefulness of AI for resolving short-term interpersonal challenges.

AI.tldr: This qualitative interview study (N=26) explores how individuals use generative AI not just to generate message content but to guide their communication strategies in interpersonal relationships. Participants valued AI for analyzing challenging relational scenarios, finding it fostered self-reflection, emotional regulation, and perspective-taking, though concerns about authenticity and uniqueness emerged.
AI.motivation: Prior conceptualizations of AI-mediated communication (AI-MC) focus on AI augmenting or generating message content. However, generative AI now enables a distinct use pattern — AI-guided communication, where AI helps individuals develop communication strategies. Theoretical and empirical understanding of this emerging phenomenon and its relational consequences remains limited, motivating this exploratory study.
AI.method: The authors conducted 26 in-depth interviews with individuals who had used AI to develop their communication strategies. The study employed a qualitative, exploratory approach to capture participants' experiences, preferences, perceived benefits, and concerns regarding AI-guided communication in interpersonal contexts.
AI.result: Participants strongly preferred using AI for analyzing challenging scenarios in close relationships. AI-guided communication was valued for five key reasons: fostering self-reflection, easing negative emotions, preventing conflict escalation, offering multiple perspectives, and providing a safe, nonjudgmental space for self-disclosure. Participants reported enhanced empathy and communication skills, though some experienced self-doubt and feared losing their uniqueness. Views on long-term relational impact were mixed, contingent on AI's perceived short-term problem-solving utility.
AI.conclusion: AI-guided communication represents a significant expansion of AI-MC beyond content generation. While it offers meaningful psychological and relational benefits — particularly for navigating emotionally challenging interpersonal situations — it also raises tensions around authenticity, identity, and long-term relational health that warrant further investigation.

title: NOVA: A Verification-Aware Agent Harness for Architecture Evolution in Industrial Recommender Systems
summary:
Industrial advertising recommender models are continuously improved through architecture evolution. Upgrades such as RankMixer, TokenMixer-Large, and MixFormer show that better structures remain a key source of quality and business gains. Yet developing such upgrades in production is expert-intensive and difficult to scale. Existing automation is insufficient: AutoML mainly tunes hyper-parameters, while effective gains often require cross-module changes under strict constraints; generic LLM coding agents optimize for runnable code, but runnable code does not imply a valid recommender architecture. Candidates may pass local tests while causing silent failures that degrade performance.
  We present NOVA, a level-aware agent harness for verification-aware architecture evolution. NOVA uses an architecture gradient, an SGD-inspired, non-differentiable update signal that aggregates prior modifications, verification diagnostics, metric feedback, and trajectory memory to guide the next modification. A verification cascade checks structure semantics, local executability, offline effectiveness, and online impact; invalid candidates are blocked early, with failure patterns recorded as forbidden directions. L1--L4 task-level control matches automation to task complexity and risk, routing high-risk tasks to Copilot for human oversight. Deployed in an industrial advertising system, NOVA achieves the highest effective pass rate on L2 ScaleUp and L3 Literature-to-Production tasks (54.5% and 60.0%), reduces silent failures compared with coding-agent baselines, and shortens one literature-to-production cycle by over 13x in human-attended time. In online A/B testing, the selected L3 candidate improves GMV on three pCVR objectives by +1.25%, +1.70%, and +2.02%, while reducing pCVR bias by 58.8%, 66.7%, and 37.3%.

AI.tldr: NOVA is a verification-aware agent that automates industrial advertising recommender architecture evolution using an SGD-inspired "architecture gradient" signal and a multi-level verification cascade, achieving high pass rates on scale-up and literature-to-production tasks while delivering significant online GMV gains and bias reduction.
AI.motivation: Industrial recommender architecture evolution remains expert-intensive and hard to scale. AutoML only tunes hyper-parameters; generic LLM coding agents optimize for runnable code, which does not guarantee valid recommender architectures and can cause silent performance-degrading failures that pass local tests.
AI.method: NOVA introduces: (1) an "architecture gradient" — an SGD-inspired, non-differentiable update signal aggregating prior modifications, verification diagnostics, metric feedback, and trajectory memory; (2) a verification cascade (structure semantics → local executability → offline effectiveness → online impact) that blocks invalid candidates early and records failure patterns as forbidden directions; (3) L1–L4 task-level control routing high-risk tasks to a human-in-the-loop Copilot mode.
AI.result: NOVA achieves 54.5% and 60.0% effective pass rates on L2 ScaleUp and L3 Literature-to-Production tasks respectively, reduces silent failures versus coding-agent baselines, shortens one literature-to-production cycle by over 13× in human-attended time, and yields online A/B gains of +1.25%, +1.70%, +2.02% GMV on three pCVR objectives with 58.8%, 66.7%, 37.3% bias reduction.
AI.conclusion: NOVA demonstrates that verification-aware, level-aware agentic automation with architecture gradients can effectively scale recommender architecture evolution in production, outperforming naive LLM coding agents and delivering measurable business impact.

title: Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
summary: Recent work (2024 to 2026) has converged on a strategy for defending tool-using LLM agents against indirect prompt injection: rather than training the model to refuse malicious instructions, enforce security outside the model with a deterministic policy that mediates the agent's actions. Systems such as CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS, and FORGE realize this with capabilities, information-flow labels, and reference monitors, and several report near-elimination of attacks on the AgentDojo benchmark. We make two contributions. First, we organize these out-of-band defenses as instances of classical integrity protection (Biba), reference monitoring, and least privilege, yielding a structured comparison of what they do and do not cover. Second, we warn that every one of them is validated only on static benchmarks (a fixed set of injection attempts), the same methodology that made in-band defenses look strong until adaptive, defense-aware attacks broke twelve of them at over 90% success; we specify the threat model and protocol an adaptive evaluation requires. We then run that protocol as an independent reproduction and extension of Progent's own adaptive-attack analysis, on AgentDojo, with an open-weight agent (Qwen2.5-7B) self-hosted on a single H200, a setting its authors did not test. Averaged over three runs, the defense held: Progent cut mean attack success roughly sixfold (25.8% to 4.2%), and a hand-crafted adaptive attack did not raise it (2.6%). This is one small-scale data point on a weak model with a single black-box attack template; a stronger optimized (white-box GCG) attack remains open. The result is consistent with, but does not establish, the hypothesis that deterministic out-of-band enforcement is a harder target for an adaptive attacker than in-band detection.

AI.tldr: This paper examines the emerging paradigm of out-of-band (deterministic, policy-mediated) defenses for LLM agents against indirect prompt injection. It taxonomizes recent systems (CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS, FORGE) through the lens of classical security principles (Biba integrity, reference monitors, least privilege), critiques the reliance on static benchmarks, specifies an adaptive evaluation protocol, and conducts a reproduction study showing Progent remains robust under adaptive attack on a weak open-weight model — though stronger attacks remain untested.
AI.motivation: Recent tool-using LLM agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection. While out-of-band deterministic defenses report near-perfect scores on static benchmarks, the authors argue this methodology is insufficient — the same static evaluation previously made in-band defenses appear strong until adaptive attacks broke 12 of them at >90% success. The paper aims to (1) systematically categorize these defenses under classical OS security concepts and (2) advocate for and demonstrate adaptive, defense-aware evaluation as the proper standard.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a conceptual analysis, mapping CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS, and FORGE onto Biba integrity protection, reference monitoring, and least privilege to produce a structured comparison. They then specify a threat model and protocol for adaptive evaluation. Using this protocol, they independently reproduce and extend Progent's adaptive-attack analysis on the AgentDojo benchmark, using a self-hosted Qwen2.5-7B (open-weight) agent on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, averaged over three runs, with a hand-crafted adaptive attack.
AI.result: Under the adaptive evaluation, Progent reduced mean attack success rate roughly sixfold (from 25.8% baseline to 4.2%), and a hand-crafted adaptive attack did not improve success (2.6%). This is a limited, single-data-point result on a weak model with a black-box attack template; a white-box GCG-optimized attack remains untested. The result is consistent with — but does not prove — the hypothesis that deterministic out-of-band enforcement is harder for adaptive attackers than in-band detection.
AI.conclusion: Out-of-band defenses grounded in classical security principles are a promising direction, but the field must abandon static-only evaluation. The authors call for adaptive, defense-aware attack protocols as the standard for validating security claims, and note that stronger optimized attacks (e.g., white-box GCG) remain an open challenge for Progent and similar systems.

title: Thinking Like a Scientist? A Structural Study of LLM-Generated Research Methods
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to guide research methodology, yet their default methodological tendencies under minimal prompting remain unclear. Here, we prompt GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 with an LLM-extracted research question from each of 1,000 recent arXiv computer-science papers and compare the resulting methodology suggestions against a paper-derived experimental inventory. Since we provide only the research question, the differences we measure reflect initial suggestions and not how optimal those suggestions are. We extract structured method features from both sources, map them into a shared taxonomy, and quantify divergence across multiple taxonomy dimensions including model provider, dataset task type, and evaluation metric type. The strongest imbalance appears in provider choice, with Jensen-Shannon divergence about 3-5x larger than any other taxonomy dimension. Other/Academic single-occurrence models are underrepresented by 23-24 percentage points, while reused academic/community models are slightly overrepresented (4-6pp). LLMs also suggest a much narrower range of methods overall: the effective number of model entities contracts from 1,232 to 59-96, and inter-LLM rank correlations (0.55-0.68) generally exceed LLM-to-paper correlations (0.33-0.56), so the distortions are largely shared across models. Popularity baselines, BM25 retrieval calibration, and paper-level similarity tests confirm that the outputs are query-specific responses, but filtered through a narrower set of options. Researchers who rely on LLM suggestions without cross-checking therefore risk narrowing their methodological search space toward a more concentrated default.

AI.tldr: Researchers prompted GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 with research questions from 1,000 arXiv CS papers. LLM-suggested methodologies were compared to actual paper methods, revealing severe contraction of methodological diversity (1,232 → 59–96 model entities), strong shared biases across LLMs, and massive underrepresentation of academic one-off models (23–24pp). Provider choice showed the largest Jensen-Shannon divergence (3–5× other dimensions).
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to guide research methodology design, but their default tendencies when given minimal prompts (just a research question) are unknown. Understanding these biases is critical because researchers may inadvertently narrow their methodological search space by over-relying on LLM suggestions without cross-checking against the literature.
AI.method: The authors extracted research questions from 1,000 recent arXiv computer-science papers using an LLM. These questions were fed (with minimal prompting) to GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2. Structured method features were extracted from both LLM outputs and paper-derived experimental inventories, mapped into a shared taxonomy. Divergence was quantified across dimensions (model provider, dataset task type, evaluation metric type) using Jensen-Shannon divergence, effective entity counts, and rank correlations. BM25 retrieval calibration and paper-level similarity tests assessed query-specificity.
AI.result: Provider choice showed the strongest imbalance (JS divergence 3–5× larger than other dimensions). Single-occurrence academic models were underrepresented by 23–24pp; reused academic/community models were overrepresented by 4–6pp. The effective number of model entities collapsed from 1,232 to 59–96. Inter-LLM rank correlations (0.55–0.68) exceeded LLM-to-paper correlations (0.33–0.56), indicating shared distortions. BM25 and similarity tests confirmed query-specific but narrowed responses.
AI.conclusion: LLMs default to a concentrated, biased methodological suggestion space that substantially underrepresents the true diversity of methods in published research. Since biases are shared across models, using multiple LLMs provides little mitigation. Researchers must cross-check LLM suggestions against the literature to avoid methodological narrowing.

title: CLIR: Liveness-Driven and Structure-Aware Fuzzing for the Cranelift Compiler
summary:
Modern compilers are complex software systems that must correctly translate high-level programming languages into machine code across multiple architectures. Cranelift, a fast and modern compiler backend originally developed for WebAssembly and recently adopted as an experimental backend for Rust, has gained increasing importance due to its superior compilation speed compared to LLVM and comprehensive multi-architecture support, including x86-64, AArch64, s390x, and RISCV64. However, despite decades of development in compiler testing, testing Cranelift still presents unique challenges, including (1) constructing valid IR under the strict enforcement of SSA form, (2) generating sequences with sufficient computational density to stress backend components, and (3) balancing broad backend coverage with efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous architectures.
  To address these challenges, we propose CLIR, a differential testing framework that integrates a syntax-preserving hierarchical generation strategy to guarantee SSA validity, a liveness-guided instruction refinement mechanism to maximize computational density, and a diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation scheme to facilitate efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous backends. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that CLIR significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines, detecting 8x, 24x, and 8x more unique bugs than cranelift-fuzzgen, wasm-smith, and WASMaker, respectively, while RustSmith uncovered no bugs. Consequently, within 72 hours of testing, CLIR discovered 24 bugs spanning all target architectures, with 21 confirmed and 9 fixed.

AI.tldr: CLIR is a differential testing framework for the Cranelift compiler backend that uses syntax-preserving IR generation, liveness-guided instruction refinement, and diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation to discover bugs. It significantly outperforms existing fuzzers, finding 24 bugs in 72 hours across all supported architectures.
AI.motivation: Cranelift, a fast compiler backend for WebAssembly and Rust, faces unique testing challenges: (1) constructing valid IR under strict SSA enforcement, (2) generating sequences with sufficient computational density to stress backend components, and (3) balancing broad backend coverage with efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous architectures (x86-64, AArch64, s390x, RISCV64). Existing tools fail to adequately address these challenges.
AI.method: CLIR integrates three key mechanisms: (1) a syntax-preserving hierarchical generation strategy that guarantees SSA validity during IR construction, (2) a liveness-guided instruction refinement mechanism that maximizes computational density in generated test sequences, and (3) a diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation scheme that enables efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous backends via differential testing.
AI.result: CLIR detected 8x, 24x, and 8x more unique bugs than cranelift-fuzzgen, wasm-smith, and WASMaker respectively; RustSmith found no bugs. Within 72 hours, CLIR discovered 24 bugs across all target architectures (x86-64, AArch64, s390x, RISCV64), with 21 confirmed and 9 already fixed.
AI.conclusion: CLIR demonstrates that syntax-preserving generation, liveness-guided refinement, and diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation are effective strategies for testing modern multi-architecture compiler backends like Cranelift, substantially outperforming existing state-of-the-art fuzzing tools in both bug discovery rate and architectural coverage.

title: Fast LeWorldModel
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), including recent LeWorldModel (LeWM), have become a promising foundation for reconstruction-free visual world models. For visual planning, however, LeWM evaluates candidate action sequences by repeatedly applying a local one-step latent transition model. This autoregressive rollout makes planning computationally expensive and exposes the predicted trajectory to accumulated latent errors as the horizon grows. We propose Fast LeWorldModel (Fast-LeWM), a fast latent world model that replaces repeated local rollout with action-prefix prediction. Given the current latent and a candidate action sequence, Fast-LeWM encodes its prefixes and predicts the future latents reached after executing those prefixes in parallel. By making action prefixes the basic prediction unit, Fast-LeWM directly models action effects accumulated to different extents over multiple horizons. This prefix-level supervision forces the model to learn how states continuously evolve under different action prefixes, rather than only fitting one-step state transitions. During planning, the predictor can use the last prefix token from the encoded action sequence to evaluate the corresponding future latent without explicitly rolling through each intermediate imagined state. Across multiple tasks, Fast-LeWM improves average success over LeWM while substantially reducing planning time, achieving lower open-loop latent loss whose growth becomes significantly slower as the rollout horizon increases.

AI.tldr: Fast-LeWM replaces autoregressive latent rollout in JEPA-based world models with parallel action-prefix prediction, improving planning speed and success rate while reducing accumulated latent errors over long horizons.
AI.motivation: Existing JEPA-based world models like LeWM rely on repeated one-step latent transition rollouts for planning, which is computationally expensive and suffers from compounding latent errors as the planning horizon grows.
AI.method: Fast-LeWM encodes action sequence prefixes and predicts future latents in parallel, using prefix-level supervision to model continuous state evolution under different action prefixes. During planning, the last prefix token directly evaluates the corresponding future latent without intermediate step-by-step rollout.
AI.result: Improved average success rate over LeWM across multiple tasks, substantially reduced planning time, and lower open-loop latent loss with significantly slower error growth as horizon increases.
AI.conclusion: Action-prefix prediction is an effective alternative to autoregressive rollout in latent world models, enabling faster and more accurate long-horizon visual planning.

title: What We are Missing in Multimodal LLM Evaluation?
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process diverse inputs, e.g., text, images, audio, and video, and generate textual responses. While their capabilities have advanced rapidly, evaluation of such models has not kept pace. Most existing evaluation benchmarks are limited to isolated tasks and reveal little about whether a model integrates information across modalities. We examine current means for evaluating MLLMs and review the existing benchmark taxonomy to identify gaps, including temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention. Addressing these gaps is essential for measuring real progress in multimodal intelligence and exposing capability boundaries.

AI.tldr: Current MLLM evaluation benchmarks are task-isolated and fail to assess cross-modal information integration. The paper identifies four critical gaps: temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention, arguing these must be addressed to meaningfully measure multimodal intelligence.
AI.motivation: MLLM capabilities have advanced rapidly, but evaluation methods lag behind. Existing benchmarks focus on isolated tasks and do not reveal whether models genuinely integrate information across modalities (text, images, audio, video). This disconnect obscures true progress and capability boundaries in multimodal intelligence.
AI.method: The authors conduct a survey/review of current MLLM evaluation approaches, examining the existing benchmark taxonomy to systematically identify deficiencies. They analyze what current benchmarks measure versus what is needed for holistic multimodal assessment.
AI.result: Four key evaluation gaps were identified: (1) temporal-spatial coherence — reasoning about time and space across modalities; (2) physical world understanding — grounding in real-world physics and causality; (3) multimodal consistency — ensuring coherent integration rather than disjoint processing of modalities; (4) selective attention — the ability to attend to relevant modal information while ignoring distractors.
AI.conclusion: Addressing the four identified gaps is essential for measuring genuine progress in multimodal intelligence and for exposing the true capability boundaries of MLLMs. Without these dimensions, current benchmarks provide an incomplete and potentially misleading picture of model performance.

title: Modeling Adaptive Visual Search in Semantically Hierarchical Layouts
summary: This paper introduces a computational cognitive model to investigate how information grouping impacts visual search, a key consideration in user interface design. The model uses computational rationality to view user behavior as an adaptation to cognitive and task constraints. Our work highlights that humans use hierarchical task representations, exploiting semantic and visual structures to improve search efficiency within the constraints of the visual system. We validate this model with data from two human studies focused on visual search and semantic categorization, demonstrating that semantic grouping improves search performance when it aligns with spatial grouping. Our model replicates task durations and eye movement patterns. By improving understanding of how hierarchical memory structures are utilized in human cognition, the model extends previous visual search models. We showcase our model in the rapid prototyping and evaluation of semantic visual groupings within user interface wireframes, suggesting a pathway toward applications in more complex, real-world interface design.

AI.tldr: A computational cognitive model based on computational rationality explains how hierarchical semantic and visual grouping improves visual search efficiency, validated by human studies and demonstrated in UI wireframe prototyping.
AI.motivation: To understand how information grouping (semantic and spatial) impacts visual search performance, addressing a gap in previous visual search models regarding hierarchical memory structures, and to provide a tool for rapid UI design evaluation.
AI.method: A computational rationality framework modeling user behavior as optimal adaptation to cognitive and task constraints, incorporating hierarchical task representations with semantic and visual structures. Validated via two human studies on visual search and semantic categorization, replicating task durations and eye movement patterns. Demonstrated through prototyping semantic visual groupings in UI wireframes.
AI.result: Semantic grouping improves search performance when aligned with spatial grouping. The model successfully replicates human task durations and eye movement patterns from both studies.
AI.conclusion: The model extends previous visual search models by incorporating hierarchical memory structures, and shows promise for rapid prototyping and evaluation of semantic visual groupings in complex, real-world interface design.

title: DKVE: Decentralized Key Validation for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging
summary:
End-to-end encrypted messaging systems depend on authentic public key distribution to prevent man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks. Current solutions present a stark trade-off: out-of-band (OOB) verification provides strong security but lacks scalability for large contact lists, while key transparency (KT) systems enable automated verification at high storage costs and operational complexity.
  We propose DKVE, a protocol that validates public keys through privacy-preserving cross-validation within users' social graphs. When obtaining a contact's public key from a key server, clients query mutual contacts to verify they hold the same key, combining Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRF) and Oblivious Key-Value Stores (OKVS) to preserve privacy of both queries and contact lists. DKVE employs a Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) to aggregate responses and detect server misbehavior with user-configurable error bounds.
  We evaluate DKVE through simulations on real social network datasets, demonstrating DKVE can detect MitM attacks with exceeding 97% for strong-to-moderate-tie networks. The remaining 3% of cases require validation through alternative methods such as KT and OOB verification. Our proof-of-concept implementation confirms feasibility for background operation on commodity hardware, in terms of the latency and bandwidth.
  As DKVE can reduce the frequency of KT queries by two orders of magnitude, it enables fundamental architectural shifts: KT directories can migrate from fast but space-inefficient Merkle trees to space-efficient data structures like RSA accumulators. While DKVE cannot replace existing methods entirely -- suffering from bootstrapping problems and degraded performance on weak-tie networks -- it provides a practical complementary key validation mechanism, making secure messaging more deployable for billion-user systems.

AI.tldr: DKVE is a privacy-preserving protocol that validates public keys by cross-referencing them among mutual contacts in a user's social graph, using OPRF and OKVS to protect query privacy. It employs SPRT for statistical detection of MitM attacks, achieving >97% detection on strong-tie networks while reducing reliance on costly key transparency systems by two orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: End-to-end encrypted messaging faces a fundamental trade-off: out-of-band verification is secure but unscalable, while key transparency systems offer automation at the cost of high storage overhead and operational complexity. There is a need for a scalable, automated key validation mechanism that preserves privacy and complements existing approaches.
AI.method: DKVE operates by having clients query mutual contacts when retrieving a contact's public key from a key server, verifying key consistency across the social graph. Privacy is maintained via Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRF) and Oblivious Key-Value Stores (OKVS), ensuring neither queries nor contact lists are exposed. A Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) aggregates verification responses to statistically detect server misbehavior with configurable error bounds.
AI.result: Simulations on real social network datasets show DKVE detects MitM attacks with >97% success in strong-to-moderate-tie networks. The remaining ~3% require fallback methods (KT or OOB). A proof-of-concept implementation confirms feasibility on commodity hardware regarding latency and bandwidth. DKVE reduces KT query frequency by two orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: DKVE is not a full replacement for existing methods — it has bootstrapping challenges and degraded performance on weak-tie networks — but it serves as a practical complementary mechanism. Its KT query reduction enables architectural shifts toward space-efficient data structures (e.g., RSA accumulators), making secure messaging more deployable at billion-user scale.

title: From Structure to Synergy: A Survey of Vision-Language Perception Paradigm Evolution in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have recently made remarkable progress in unifying vision-language understanding and reasoning, especially following the introduction of models such as OpenAI's O-series and DeepSeek's R-series, which have driven a paradigm shift toward perception-centric intelligence. However, there remains a lack of systematic surveys that examine perception from a truly unified vision-language perspective -- one that treats vision and language as an inseparable modality. Existing reviews are often fragmented, focusing separately on either vision or language, and thus rarely capture the cross-modal evolution of perception as an integrated capability. To bridge this gap, we present the first systematic survey of unified vision-language perception in MLLMs. Specifically, we (1) formalize MLLM perception as an intrinsic, unified vision-language capability analogous to human innate perception, (2) introduce a five-stage taxonomy tracing the paradigm evolution of MLLM perception and survey representative methods and milestones at each phase, and (3) identify open challenges and outline promising research directions toward truly general, unified multimodal intelligence. We hope our study will provide both a foundational understanding and an actionable roadmap to foster further innovation on the path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic survey of unified vision-language perception in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), proposing a five-stage taxonomy of paradigm evolution, formalizing perception as an intrinsic cross-modal capability, and identifying challenges toward artificial general intelligence.
AI.motivation: Existing surveys on MLLMs are fragmented, focusing on vision or language separately, and fail to capture the cross-modal evolution of perception as an integrated, unified capability — particularly in light of recent advances (e.g., OpenAI O-series, DeepSeek R-series) that have shifted the paradigm toward perception-centric intelligence.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic literature review and propose: (1) a formal definition of MLLM perception as an intrinsic, unified vision-language capability analogous to human innate perception; (2) a five-stage taxonomy tracing the paradigm evolution of MLLM perception, surveying representative methods and milestones at each phase; and (3) identification of open challenges and future research directions.
AI.result: The survey delivers a structured five-stage taxonomy of MLLM perception evolution, catalogs key methods and milestones per stage, and highlights open challenges and promising directions for advancing toward truly general, unified multimodal intelligence.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a foundational understanding and actionable roadmap for unified vision-language perception in MLLMs, aiming to foster innovation on the path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

title: To Run or Not to Run: Analyzing the Cost-Effectiveness of Code Execution in LLM-Based Program Repair
comment: Accepted to the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA 2026). 23 pages
summary: LLM-based agents for program repair are increasingly built on a "generate-run-revise" paradigm, iteratively executing tests to evaluate and refine patches. This execution-based approach has become standard practice in state-of-the-art systems. However, executions can be time-consuming and expensive, yet their impact on these agents remains underexplored. In this paper, we conduct a two-stage empirical study over execution behavior in LLM-based program repair. To characterize execution behavior at scale, we first analyze 7,745 agent traces from SWE-bench leaderboard submissions. Second, we evaluate 3,000 end-to-end repair attempts across 200 SWE-bench instances and three agents (Claude Code, Codex, and the open-source OpenCode) under four execution paradigms, which allows for a fine-grained comparison of performance and cost. Our analysis reveals three key observations: (1) Code execution is used across all agents and models analyzed, with an average of 8.8 test runs per task. Execution behavior varies substantially across agents and models, with frequency ranging from 2 to 19 per task, and late-stage executions consistently achieve higher success rates than early-stage ones. (2) Execution restrictions have little effect on repair success: on commercial agents with SOTA models the resolve-rate gap between Prohibited and Unrestricted is only 1.25 percentage points and not statistically significant, while Prohibited saves substantial token and wall-clock cost. (3) Execution benefit is concentrated rather than uniform. These patterns suggest that current agents apply execution indiscriminately, paying its cost on instances where it provides little benefit. Execution, therefore, should be treated as a resource with an explicit cost-benefit tradeoff, not a default capability.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of 7,745 agent traces and 3,000 repair attempts reveals that while LLM-based program repair agents rely heavily on code execution (avg. 8.8 test runs/task), restricting execution hardly impacts repair success (only 1.25pp gap) while saving significant cost—suggesting execution should be treated as a resource with explicit cost-benefit tradeoffs, not a default capability.
AI.motivation: LLM-based program repair agents widely adopt a "generate-run-revise" paradigm where code execution drives patch refinement, yet the actual impact of these executions on repair effectiveness and cost remains underexplored. The authors aim to characterize execution behavior at scale and determine whether execution is truly necessary or merely an expensive default.
AI.method: A two-stage empirical study: (1) large-scale analysis of 7,745 agent traces from SWE-bench leaderboard submissions to characterize execution behavior patterns; (2) controlled evaluation of 3,000 end-to-end repair attempts across 200 SWE-bench instances using three agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) under four execution paradigms (Unrestricted, Prohibited, and two intermediate conditions), enabling fine-grained comparison of performance and cost.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) all agents use code execution, averaging 8.8 test runs per task, with frequency varying widely (2–19) across agents/models, and late-stage executions succeed more than early-stage ones; (2) restricting execution barely affects repair success—the resolve-rate gap between Prohibited and Unrestricted is only 1.25pp and statistically insignificant for SOTA commercial agents, while saving substantial token and wall-clock cost; (3) execution benefits are concentrated rather than uniform, with many instances receiving little value from execution.
AI.conclusion: Current agents apply execution indiscriminately, incurring costs on instances where it provides minimal benefit. Execution should be reframed as a resource requiring explicit cost-benefit analysis rather than being treated as a default, always-on capability in program repair agents.

title: Dataset Usage Inference without Shadow Models or Held-out Data
comment: Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Synthetic & Adversarial ForEnsics (SAFE), CVPR 2026 (non-archival)
summary: How much of my data was used to train a machine learning model? Dataset Usage Inference (DUI) aims to answer this by estimating what fraction of a dataset contributed to a model's training. However, existing DUI methods rely on assumptions that rarely hold in practice: they require training expensive shadow models to imitate the target model, and they assume access to both known training samples and an in-distribution held-out set confirmed to be absent from training. These conditions make current approaches impractical for modern large models and real data ownership disputes. We introduce a practical DUI framework that removes these constraints. Our method requires neither shadow models nor real held-out data. Instead, it generates synthetic non-member samples, extracts diverse membership signals, and casts DUI as a mixture proportion estimation problem to estimate what share of the candidate dataset was used during training. Experiments on large image generative models show that our method reliably quantifies dataset usage, providing a practical tool for data owners to determine how much of their data was used to train a model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a practical Dataset Usage Inference (DUI) framework that estimates what fraction of a candidate dataset was used in training, without requiring shadow models or held-out data — instead using synthetic non-member samples and mixture proportion estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing DUI methods are impractical: they require training computationally expensive shadow models to mimic the target model, and assume access to both known training samples and an in-distribution held-out set confirmed absent from training. These conditions cannot be met for large modern models or in real-world data ownership disputes where such information is unavailable.
AI.method: The proposed framework eliminates the need for shadow models and real held-out data. It (1) generates synthetic non-member samples to serve as a reference for "unseen" data, (2) extracts diverse membership signals from the target model's behavior on samples, and (3) formulates DUI as a mixture proportion estimation problem to infer what proportion of a candidate dataset was part of the training set.
AI.result: Experiments on large image generative models demonstrate that the method reliably quantifies dataset usage, validating its effectiveness as a practical tool.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a practical, assumption-free DUI solution suitable for real-world data ownership disputes, where shadow model training and access to known held-out data are infeasible, enabling data owners to determine how much of their data contributed to model training.

title: OpenFinGym: A Verifiable Multi-Task Gym Environment for Evaluating Quant Agents
summary: Although large language model agents are increasingly applied to quantitative-finance workflows, their evaluation remains fragmented across isolated tasks, while the financial relevance of benchmark tasks is often overlooked. Yet financial workflows are inherently multi-stage, spanning interdependent tasks such as forecasting, strategy construction, risk management, and trading. Existing platforms typically focus on a single task, and can therefore overstate agent competence and fail to reveal weaknesses in generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making. We introduce OpenFinGym, a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agent development that covers forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under a single execution and verification interface. OpenFinGym additionally provides an automated task-construction pipeline that turns quantitative finance publications into executable task packages; a containerised runtime with a host-side verifier service that supports scalable agent rollouts and prevents runtime train-test leakage; a paper trading engine with a low-latency data-stream design; deferred-resolution support for long-horizon and event-market forecasts; and integration for SFT and RL post-training

AI.tldr: OpenFinGym is a unified gym environment for quantitative-finance agents that covers forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection under a single interface, addressing the fragmentation and lack of financial relevance in existing benchmarks by providing multi-stage workflow evaluation, automated task construction from publications, containerized runtime, paper trading, and RL/SFT integration.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation of LLM agents in quantitative finance is fragmented across isolated single-task benchmarks, which overstate agent competence and fail to expose weaknesses in generalization, real-market interaction, and financially meaningful decision-making. Financial workflows are inherently multi-stage and interdependent, yet no unified platform exists to evaluate agents across the full pipeline from forecasting to trading.
AI.method: The authors propose OpenFinGym, which provides: (1) a unified environment spanning forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection; (2) an automated task-construction pipeline converting quantitative finance publications into executable task packages; (3) a containerized runtime with host-side verifier to prevent train-test leakage and enable scalable rollouts; (4) a paper trading engine with low-latency data streaming; (5) deferred-resolution support for long-horizon and event-market forecasts; and (6) integration for SFT and RL post-training.
AI.result: The paper presents the architecture and design of OpenFinGym as a comprehensive evaluation and development platform. Specific quantitative experimental results are not detailed in this abstract; the contribution is primarily the platform itself and its design principles.
AI.conclusion: OpenFinGym fills a critical gap in quantitative-finance agent research by providing a unified, multi-task, financially relevant evaluation framework that better reflects real-world financial workflows and supports both agent development and post-training.

title: 'A bit of chaos and madness': The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform
summary:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has intensified pressure on universities to redesign assessment while maintaining integrity, equity, and validity. Structured frameworks such as the Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS) offer one response, but evidence of how staff experience their implementation remains limited. This qualitative study examines AIAS implementation at a private international university in Vietnam and a public university in the United Kingdom. Data from five focus groups with 30 academic staff were analysed using hybrid thematic analysis, with Critical AI Literacy used as a sensitising concept. Six themes were developed: recognising and integrating AI, facilitating conditions, building capacity, pathways to adoption, ethics in practice, and reframing pedagogy.
  Staff valued the AIAS as a shared language for legitimising GenAI use, clarifying boundaries, and prompting reflection on assessment design. However, implementation was shaped by governance, tool access, staff confidence, workload, integrity concerns, disciplinary context, and alignment with learning outcomes. The findings show that the AIAS could prompt authentic assessment design and student engagement, but may become a compliance layer when disconnected from learning outcomes, disciplinary context, and staff capacity. This study contributes empirical evidence on the institutional conditions through which GenAI assessment frameworks move from policy adoption to pedagogical enactment.

AI.tldr: A qualitative study across Vietnamese and UK universities found that the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) helps staff legitimize GenAI use and reflect on assessment design, but its effectiveness depends on institutional conditions like governance, staff capacity, workload, and alignment with learning outcomes — without which it risks becoming mere compliance.
AI.motivation: GenAI has created urgent pressure on universities to redesign assessment while preserving integrity, equity, and validity. While structured frameworks like the AIAS have been proposed, empirical evidence on how academic staff experience their implementation is scarce.
AI.method: Qualitative multi-site study using five focus groups with 30 academic staff at a private international university in Vietnam and a public university in the UK. Data were analyzed via hybrid thematic analysis, employing Critical AI Literacy as a sensitizing concept.
