AI.result: Six themes emerged: (1) recognizing and integrating AI, (2) facilitating conditions, (3) building capacity, (4) pathways to adoption, (5) ethics in practice, and (6) reframing pedagogy. Staff valued the AIAS as a shared language for legitimizing GenAI, clarifying boundaries, and prompting assessment redesign. However, implementation was heavily mediated by governance structures, tool accessibility, staff confidence, workload, integrity concerns, disciplinary context, and learning outcome alignment.
AI.conclusion: The AIAS can catalyze authentic assessment design and student engagement, but without integration with learning outcomes, disciplinary context, and adequate staff capacity, it risks devolving into a superficial compliance layer. The study provides empirical evidence on the institutional conditions necessary for GenAI assessment frameworks to transition from policy adoption to genuine pedagogical enactment.

title: VIGIL: Runtime Enforcement of Behavioral Specifications in AI Agent Skills
summary:
Agentic systems increasingly act through third-party skills, allowing model-generated decisions to affect files, communication channels, and cyber-physical devices. These skills often include natural-language specifications that define access permissions, disclosure limits, execution privileges, and required preconditions. Although such specifications describe the intended boundaries of skill behavior, they do not by themselves provide executable runtime enforcement. Enforcing them raises a contextual granularity challenge: even when a policy is written for a particular task context, a monitor must still decide which events to observe, what state to retain, how far across the execution to reason, and where to intervene. Choosing the wrong granularity can either block benign executions or miss violations that emerge only across multiple actions. Most existing enforcement mechanisms, however, assume a fixed event model or enforcement point.
  In this work, we present VIGIL, an end-to-end runtime enforcement framework for agentic systems. VIGIL checks an agent's actual execution trace against behavioral policies from skill specifications, operator-defined constraints, and global rules spanning multiple skills. To make such policies executable, VIGIL introduces a policy language that captures context-specific enforcement requirements over agent-tool events, including temporal dependencies, argument constraints, and value-flow conditions. The language is paired with symbolic evaluation rules that translate policies into SMT constraints over finite traces, allowing VIGIL to detect violations that depend on event order, argument relationships, or cross-call value flow rather than relying on fixed single-call filters. On real LLM-agent runs spanning office-document, operational, and engineering tasks, VIGIL detects policy violations with over 95% recall and a false-positive rate below 10%.

AI.tldr: VIGIL is a runtime enforcement framework for agentic systems that translates behavioral policies (from skill specs, operator constraints, and global rules) into SMT constraints over finite traces, enabling detection of violations involving temporal dependencies, argument relationships, and cross-call value flow with >95% recall and <10% false-positive rate.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems increasingly use third-party skills with natural-language specifications defining access, disclosure, and execution boundaries, but these specifications lack executable runtime enforcement. The core challenge is contextual granularity: monitors must decide what events to observe, what state to retain, how far to reason across execution, and where to intervene. Wrong granularity causes false positives (blocking benign actions) or false negatives (missing cross-action violations). Existing mechanisms assume fixed event models or enforcement points and cannot adapt to varying policy contexts.
AI.method: VIGIL is an end-to-end framework with three key components: (1) a policy language that captures context-specific enforcement requirements including temporal dependencies, argument constraints, and value-flow conditions over agent-tool events; (2) symbolic evaluation rules that translate policies into SMT constraints over finite execution traces, enabling reasoning about event order, argument relationships, and cross-call value flow; (3) a runtime monitor that checks actual agent execution traces against policies synthesized from skill specifications, operator-defined constraints, and global cross-skill rules.
AI.result: Evaluated on real LLM-agent runs across office-document, operational, and engineering task domains, VIGIL achieved over 95% recall in detecting policy violations with a false-positive rate below 10%.
AI.conclusion: VIGIL demonstrates that context-sensitive, SMT-based runtime enforcement is feasible and effective for agentic systems, overcoming the granularity limitations of fixed-filter approaches by enabling precise reasoning over event order, argument relationships, and cross-call value flow.

title: Phonetic and semantic analyses of spoken corpora of Beijing and Taiwan Mandarin indicate that the neutral tone is a lexical tone
summary: The neutral, or floating, tone of Mandarin Chinese is a tone with an enigmatic set of properties. It has been described as a reduced tone, or as a tone that sometimes is lexically fixed but that can also be toneless. In two-syllable words, it is found only on the second syllable, but single-syllable words can also have the neutral tone. We present a corpus-based study of the phonetic realization of the neutral tone in spontaneous conversational speech corpora of Beijing Mandarin and Taiwan Mandarin. We show that the neutral tone has its own tonal target, just as the four lexical tones of Mandarin. We also show that disyllabic words with a neutral tone have pitch contours that have a pitch component that depends on the tone on the first syllable, just as has been observed for two-syllable words with a lexical tone on the second syllable (Chuang et al., 2026). Furthermore, words with a floating tone have word-specific pitch signatures, which have also been documented for single-syllable words (Jin et al., 2026) as well as two-syllable words (Lu et al., 2026b). These word-specific pitch signatures are shown to be predictable to some extent from words' contextualized embeddings, as previously reported for lexical tones (Chuang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b). As there is also considerable variability in the realization of lexical tones, we propose that the neutral tone is, in fact, a lexical tone in both Taiwan Mandarin and Beijing Mandarin. We document both similarities and differences in the realization of the floating tone in these two varieties and provide evidence, using contextualized embeddings, that some of the observed differences may arise from differences in the meanings of the words as used in the two corpora.

AI.tldr: A corpus-based phonetic study of Mandarin's neutral tone in Beijing and Taiwan Mandarin reveals it has its own tonal target and word-specific pitch signatures predictable from contextualized embeddings, leading the authors to argue the neutral tone is in fact a lexical tone.
AI.motivation: The neutral (floating) tone of Mandarin Chinese has long been regarded as enigmatic — sometimes described as reduced, toneless, or lexically fixed. The authors aim to resolve this ambiguity by empirically investigating whether the neutral tone possesses phonetic properties consistent with it being a genuine lexical tone, rather than merely a reduced or toneless element.
AI.method: Corpus-based acoustic-phonetic analysis of spontaneous conversational speech from two corpora: Beijing Mandarin and Taiwan Mandarin. The study examines pitch contours of disyllabic words with neutral tones, comparing them to words with lexical tones. It also employs contextualized word embeddings to predict word-specific pitch signatures, following methodologies from prior work (Chuang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026b).
AI.result: The neutral tone exhibits its own tonal target, similar to the four lexical tones. Disyllabic words with neutral tone show pitch components dependent on the first syllable's tone — paralleling patterns in words with lexical second-syllable tones. Words with floating tone display word-specific pitch signatures, predictable from contextualized embeddings. Differences between Beijing and Taiwan Mandarin realizations partially stem from semantic usage differences between the two corpora.
AI.conclusion: The neutral tone is, in fact, a lexical tone in both Taiwan Mandarin and Beijing Mandarin. Variability in its realization mirrors that of lexical tones, and cross-variety differences are attributable in part to differences in word meanings as captured by contextualized embeddings.

title: How Much Static Structure Do Code Agents Need? A Study of Deterministic Anchoring
comment: Accepted to the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA 2026). 21 pages
summary: LLM-based code agents navigate repositories through keyword search but miss the structural relationships, such as call graphs, inheritance hierarchies, and configuration dependencies, that define how software actually works. This makes agent navigation stochastic and difficult to reproduce across runs. We investigate whether lightweight static analysis can provide deterministic anchors for these agents: stable structural facts injected as plain-text comments that constrain probabilistic exploration and make navigation more predictable. Starting from a strong baseline, Codex from OpenAI, we systematically inject varying granularities of structural annotations and measure their effects on localization, trajectory behavior, and run-to-run stability. Our study identifies what we call the deterministic anchoring effect: static structure helps less by making agents "smarter" and more by making their navigation disciplined and reproducible. Three observations support this finding: (1) Anchoring works: lightweight call/inheritance topology improves function-level localization (+2.2pp Func@5) and shortens trajectories (-1.6 interaction rounds); (2) Anchoring is scale-sensitive: the optimal granularity and directionality depend on repository characteristics, where denser semantics show diminishing returns and hub-heavy projects benefit from inverse-only links that expose "who-calls-me" without forward edges; (3) Anchoring stabilizes: tags raise link-following rate from 0.15-0.18 to 0.21-0.24, roughly halve run-to-run variance, and improve single-run reliability (Pass@1 +3.4 pp) on medium-scale repositories, at the cost of roughly 10% more input tokens. These observations suggest practical guidelines: default to lightweight topology on medium projects, prune forward edges in large repositories, and reserve dense tags for implicit-dependency cases.

AI.tldr: Injecting lightweight static analysis annotations (call graphs, inheritance) as comments into code stabilizes LLM-based code agent navigation, improving localization accuracy, shortening trajectories, and reducing run-to-run variance, with the primary benefit being disciplined reproducibility rather than increased intelligence.
AI.motivation: LLM-based code agents rely on stochastic keyword search for repository navigation, missing structural relationships (call graphs, inheritance, configuration dependencies) that define software behavior. This makes navigation non-deterministic and hard to reproduce. The authors investigate whether lightweight static analysis can provide deterministic anchors to constrain and stabilize agent exploration.
AI.method: Using OpenAI Codex as a strong baseline, the authors systematically inject structural annotations at varying granularities (call/inheritance topology, forward/reverse edges, dense semantic tags) as plain-text comments into code. They then measure effects on function-level localization (Func@5), trajectory length (interaction rounds), link-following rates, run-to-run variance, and Pass@1 reliability across repositories with different characteristics.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Anchoring improves Func@5 by +2.2pp and reduces trajectory length by 1.6 rounds; (2) Optimal annotation granularity is scale-sensitive — dense semantics show diminishing returns, and hub-heavy projects benefit from inverse-only links; (3) Anchoring raises link-following rates from 0.15–0.18 to 0.21–0.24, halves run-to-run variance, improves Pass@1 by +3.4pp on medium repos, at ~10% token overhead.
AI.conclusion: The "deterministic anchoring effect" shows static structure helps more by making agent navigation disciplined and reproducible than by making agents smarter. Practical guidelines: use lightweight topology on medium projects, prune forward edges in large repos, and reserve dense tags for implicit-dependency cases.

title: Equivariance and Augmentation for Bayesian Neural Networks
summary: Symmetries are important for many deep learning tasks, ranging from applications in the sciences to medical imaging. However, there is an ongoing debate about whether to impose symmetry constraints on the neural network architecture (yielding equivariant neural networks) or learn them from augmented training data. Although equivariant networks are well-studied theoretically, much less is known about data augmentation, since analyzing augmentation requires control over the training dynamics. Inspired by recent results that show that augmented infinite deep ensembles are exactly equivariant, we study data augmentation for Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) trained with variational inference. We focus on variational distributions in the exponential family and derive conditions under which exact equivariance is reached. We furthermore obtain bounds on the equivariance error and introduce three novel symmetrization techniques which boost the effect of data augmentation in this setting. We conduct extensive numerical experiments which show that one of our symmetrization methods (orbit expansion) outperforms the baseline in both equivariance and overall performance. Our code is available at github.com/dmw1998/augment-BNNs

AI.tldr: This paper studies data augmentation in Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) trained with variational inference. It derives conditions for achieving exact equivariance, provides bounds on equivariance error, and introduces three symmetrization techniques, with orbit expansion outperforming baselines in both equivariance and performance.
AI.motivation: There is an ongoing debate on whether to impose symmetry constraints via equivariant architectures or learn symmetries through data augmentation. While equivariant networks are well-understood theoretically, data augmentation's effect on symmetry is poorly understood due to the complexity of training dynamics. The authors aim to bridge this gap by analyzing augmentation in the context of variational inference for BNNs.
AI.method: The authors analyze data augmentation for BNNs under variational inference with exponential family distributions. They derive theoretical conditions for exact equivariance, establish bounds on equivariance error, and propose three symmetrization techniques: orbit expansion, posterior symmetrization, and an ensemble-based method. Extensive numerical experiments validate the approaches.
AI.result: The paper provides conditions under which variational BNNs achieve exact equivariance through augmentation. Three symmetrization methods are introduced. Orbit expansion consistently outperforms the baseline in both equivariance error and overall predictive performance across experiments.
AI.conclusion: Data augmentation, when properly symmetrized, can effectively induce equivariance in BNNs without requiring architectural constraints. Orbit expansion is a particularly effective technique, and the code is publicly available to facilitate further research.

title: MedSWFlow: An Open-Source LLM Workflow for Drafting Medical Social Work Case Plans
summary: We present MedSWFlow, an open-source, model-agnostic LLM workflow for drafting medical social work case plans. The framework translates professional case-planning tasks into six stages: assessment, problem analysis, goal setting, intervention planning, risk anticipation, and planned effect evaluation. Drawing on established social work and behavioral frameworks, MedSWFlow standardizes case inputs, builds structured case profiles, and generates reviewable assessment forms and service plans through staged prompting. The system is released as an open-source research framework for reproducible case-plan generation across LLM providers. Outputs are intended as practitioner-reviewed drafts rather than final service decisions. Source code: https://github.com/santhiyacw-droid/MedSWFlow/tree/main.

AI.tldr: MedSWFlow is an open-source, model-agnostic LLM workflow that standardizes medical social work case-plan drafting through a six-stage structured prompting pipeline, producing reviewable assessment forms and service plans intended as practitioner-reviewed drafts.
AI.motivation: Medical social work case planning is a complex, multi-stage professional task requiring structured documentation, yet there is a lack of reproducible, open-source, and LLM-agnostic frameworks to support practitioners in drafting case plans efficiently and consistently across different LLM providers.
AI.method: The authors decompose professional case-planning into a six-stage staged prompting workflow: (1) assessment, (2) problem analysis, (3) goal setting, (4) intervention planning, (5) risk anticipation, and (6) planned effect evaluation. The system standardizes case inputs, builds structured case profiles, and generates reviewable assessment forms and service plans. It is designed as model-agnostic and released as an open-source research framework on GitHub.
AI.result: The paper presents MedSWFlow as a completed, open-source framework. The system produces structured, reviewable drafts of assessment forms and service plans. As a framework release paper, the primary result is the availability of a reproducible, standardized case-plan generation pipeline across different LLM providers, with outputs explicitly positioned as practitioner-reviewed drafts rather than final clinical decisions.
AI.conclusion: MedSWFlow demonstrates the feasibility of translating professional medical social work case-planning into a structured, multi-stage LLM-based prompting workflow. By grounding the pipeline in established social work and behavioral frameworks and releasing it as open-source, the work enables reproducible research and practical tool development across LLM providers while maintaining appropriate human-in-the-loop safeguards.

title: ProvenAI: Provenance-Native Traces of Evidence in Generated Answers
summary: Retrieval-augmented systems routinely present citations alongside generated answers, yet a citation does not confirm that the corresponding source meaningfully shaped the output. This paper introduces ProvenAI, a framework that decomposes transparency in multi-hop question answering into three independently measurable layers: answer correctness, citation fidelity against benchmark supporting evidence, and per-document influence under leave-one-resource-out intervention. Targeting the HotpotQA distractor benchmark through a seven-stage pipeline covering data normalisation, retrieval indexing, citation-aware answer generation, attribution auditing, ablation-based influence estimation, batch evaluation, and interactive inspection, ProvenAI evaluates 7,405 validation examples drawn from a canonical corpus of 509,300 passages. The system achieves 53.53% answer accuracy alongside a mean citation-fidelity score of 71.55%, and a worked example surfaces what we call the citation-influence gap: a clean citation audit co-occurring with a profile in which one cited source registers only weak influence while seven uncited sources demonstrably shift the output. We formalise the relationship between the implemented surface proxy and a token-level KL-divergence target through a stated faithfulness condition, ground the framework in causal-mediation analysis and database-provenance theory, and discuss how the three measurement layers compose with cryptographic provenance architectures emerging in autonomous scientific discovery. ProvenAI establishes that meaningful transparency in retrieval-grounded QA requires traceable links across retrieved, cited, and behaviourally influential evidence as three distinct, independently measured layers.

AI.tldr: ProvenAI introduces a three-layer transparency framework for retrieval-augmented QA, measuring answer correctness, citation fidelity, and per-document influence via ablation. Evaluated on HotpotQA across 7,405 examples, it reveals a "citation-influence gap" where cited sources may show weak influence while uncited sources demonstrably shift outputs, establishing that meaningful transparency requires independently measuring retrieved, cited, and behaviorally influential evidence.
AI.motivation: Citations in retrieval-augmented systems are presented as transparency mechanisms, but they do not guarantee that the cited source actually influenced the generated answer. There is no existing framework that decomposes transparency into independently measurable and verifiable layers connecting what is retrieved, what is cited, and what causally shapes the output.
AI.method: A seven-stage pipeline: (1) data normalization, (2) retrieval indexing over 509,300 passages, (3) citation-aware answer generation, (4) attribution auditing for citation fidelity against benchmark supporting evidence, (5) ablation-based influence estimation using leave-one-resource-out intervention, (6) batch evaluation, and (7) interactive inspection. The framework grounds itself in causal-mediation analysis and database-provenance theory, with a formal faithfulness condition linking the surface proxy to a token-level KL-divergence target.
AI.result: On 7,405 HotpotQA validation examples, ProvenAI achieves 53.53% answer accuracy and a mean citation-fidelity score of 71.55%. A key finding is the "citation-influence gap": cases where a clean citation audit co-occurs with one cited source registering weak influence while seven uncited sources demonstrably shift the output.
AI.conclusion: Meaningful transparency in retrieval-grounded QA requires traceable links across three distinct, independently measured layers — retrieved evidence, cited evidence, and behaviorally influential evidence — rather than treating citations alone as sufficient attestations of provenance. The framework also connects to cryptographic provenance architectures relevant to autonomous scientific discovery.

title: TESLA-for-5G: Broadcast Authentication for 5G Networks Using TESLA
summary: 5G base stations broadcast unauthenticated system information (SI) that every user equipment (UE) reads during cell selection. This enables attackers to broadcast forged SI from a fake base station (FBS), deceiving UEs into camping on it. Prior approaches require UEs to authenticate System Information Block 1 (SIB1) using digital signatures. This necessitates computation-heavy verification for every SIB1 reception, imposing a significant burden on resource-constrained UEs. We propose TESLA-for-5G (TF5), a broadcast authentication protocol for 5G SIB1 that combines TESLA with GG09 Schnorr-like identity-based signatures (IBS). In the steady state, TF5 enables UEs to authenticate each SIB1 message using a symmetric MAC and delayed key disclosure, eliminating the need for per-message digital signatures. Initial trust is bootstrapped during cell entry using a lightweight GG09 IBS over the TESLA parameters, avoiding certificate distribution overhead. We formally verify TF5 in Tamarin under a Dolev-Yao adversary and demonstrate its favorable computation, communication, and storage costs through both an implementation on the OpenAirInterface 5G stack and trace-driven analysis.

AI.tldr: TF5 is a broadcast authentication protocol for 5G SIB1 that replaces per-message digital signatures with symmetric MACs and delayed key disclosure (TESLA), bootstrapped by a lightweight identity-based signature, dramatically reducing computational burden on UEs.
AI.motivation: 5G base stations broadcast unauthenticated System Information (SI), allowing attackers to deploy fake base stations (FBS) that broadcast forged SIB1 to trick UEs into camping on them. Existing countermeasures require UEs to verify digital signatures on every SIB1, which is computationally prohibitive for resource-constrained devices.
AI.method: The authors propose TESLA-for-5G (TF5), combining the TESLA broadcast authentication protocol (symmetric MAC with delayed key disclosure for steady-state operation) with GG09 Schnorr-like identity-based signatures (IBS) for initial trust bootstrapping of TESLA parameters during cell entry, avoiding certificate distribution overhead. Formal verification is conducted in Tamarin under a Dolev-Yao adversary model, and a prototype is implemented on the OpenAirInterface 5G stack with trace-driven cost analysis.
AI.result: Tamarin formal verification confirms TF5's security under the Dolev-Yao model. Implementation on OpenAirInterface and trace-driven analysis demonstrate favorable computation, communication, and storage costs compared to per-message digital signature approaches, significantly reducing UE-side overhead.
AI.conclusion: TF5 provides a practical and lightweight broadcast authentication solution for 5G SIB1, enabling resource-constrained UEs to securely authenticate system information without the heavy burden of per-message asymmetric cryptography, while maintaining formal security guarantees.

title: Charting the Growth of Social-Physical HRI (spHRI): A Systematic Review Pipeline Augmented by Small Language Models
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables, Companion Proceedings of the 21st ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction
summary: Social-physical human-robot interaction (spHRI) has grown rapidly across robotics, human-computer interaction, human-robot interaction, and haptics. Yet, fragmented terminology and inconsistent methodologies make systematic synthesis difficult. To support scalable review practices, we evaluated the extent to which small language models (SLMs; < 1.5B parameters) can assist with title and abstract screening for a large spHRI systematic review. While no SLMs matched human reviewers' performance, the models operated locally and screened papers orders of magnitude faster. The combined SLM ensemble identified 39 papers reviewers missed, representing 10.29% of the final relevant dataset. These results demonstrate that SLMs can augment, rather than replace, expert reviewers and make large-scale literature reviews accessible and sustainable.

AI.tldr: Evaluates small language models (<1.5B parameters) for title/abstract screening in a large systematic review on social-physical human-robot interaction. SLMs couldn't match human performance but were orders of magnitude faster, and their ensemble recovered 39 missed papers (10.29% of the final dataset), demonstrating SLMs can augment rather than replace expert reviewers.
AI.motivation: The field of social-physical human-robot interaction (spHRI) suffers from fragmented terminology and inconsistent methodologies, making systematic synthesis difficult. The authors aim to explore whether small language models can assist with scalable, sustainable literature screening to address this challenge.
AI.method: The authors evaluated small language models (SLMs with fewer than 1.5 billion parameters) on the task of title and abstract screening for a large spHRI systematic review. SLMs operated locally and were compared against human reviewer performance. An ensemble approach combining multiple SLMs was also tested.
AI.result: No individual SLM matched human reviewer performance. However, SLMs screened papers orders of magnitude faster. The combined SLM ensemble identified 39 relevant papers that human reviewers missed, constituting 10.29% of the final relevant dataset.
AI.conclusion: SLMs can augment, not replace, expert reviewers in systematic literature reviews. They make large-scale reviews more accessible and sustainable by combining computational speed with complementary coverage that helps catch papers human reviewers may overlook.

title: Cleaning Logs for Downstream Tasks (Registered Report)
comment: This article supersedes arXiv:2004.07194: the tool name has been updated from LogCleaner to LogPurifier; the evaluation plan has been updated
summary: Background: Software systems generate logs during execution to record critical events and runtime information for troubleshooting and monitoring. However, in practice, logs often contain significant amounts of redundant and irrelevant information, which can negatively impact the performance of downstream analysis tasks, such as model inference and anomaly detection. Objective: The objective of this study is to clean log data by identifying and removing free-standing messages -- messages that are not relevant to the execution behaviors of interest and are interleaved with messages capturing the system's functional behavior. Method: To address this objective, we propose LogPurifier, a task-agnostic log-cleaning approach based on dependency relationships between log message templates. The paper presents a plan for an empirical evaluation using a controlled experimental design to assess the impact of LogPurifier on the effectiveness and efficiency of two downstream tasks: model inference and anomaly detection.

AI.tldr: LogPurifier is a task-agnostic log-cleaning method that removes free-standing (irrelevant) log messages by leveraging dependency relationships between log message templates, aiming to improve downstream tasks like model inference and anomaly detection.
AI.motivation: Software logs contain substantial redundant and irrelevant information (free-standing messages) that degrades the performance of downstream analysis tasks such as model inference and anomaly detection. Existing log parsing and cleaning approaches do not adequately filter out these interleaved irrelevant messages.
AI.method: LogPurifier employs a task-agnostic approach based on analyzing dependency relationships between log message templates to identify and remove free-standing messages — those not relevant to the functional execution behaviors of interest.
AI.result: The paper outlines a plan for empirical evaluation using a controlled experimental design to measure the impact of LogPurifier on both the effectiveness and efficiency of model inference and anomaly detection tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes a planned empirical study; definitive conclusions are pending the execution of the controlled experiments assessing LogPurifier's impact on downstream log analysis tasks.

title: SSM Adapters via Hankel Reduced-order Modeling: Injection Site Determines Task Suitability in Long-Context Fine-Tuning
summary: While parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) typically targets attention projectors, its efficacy for tasks requiring sequential state accumulation remains under-explored. We examine if PEFT for such tasks can benefit from state space model (SSMs) adapters, and if MLP blocks are better injection sites. We introduce Hankel Reduced order Model (HRM) adapter, an SSM-based residual module initialized via Balanced Truncation of empirical Hankel Grammians. By leveraging the time-invariance of the system matrix $\bar{A}$, HRM enables an exact FFT-based parallel scan, achieving computational parity with LoRA across all context lengths. In iso-parametric evaluations on Mistral-7B (8.4M trainable parameters), HRM outperforms LoRA variants on LongBench tasks, including QuALITY (+34.8\% relative accuracy) and QMSum (+71.6\% relative ROUGE-1). HRM further demonstrates consistent superiority across 18 configurations of synthetic state-tracking (DFA, Parity) and character-level language modeling (enwik8). Gate analysis reveals that HRM adapters effectively learn to modulate recurrence, providing a robust architectural alternative to low-rank adaptation for long-context sequence modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Hankel Reduced order Model (HRM) adapter, an SSM-based PEFT module initialized via Balanced Truncation of Hankel Gramians. It outperforms LoRA on long-context tasks (LongBench, state-tracking, enwik8) while maintaining FFT-based parallel scan efficiency, and is shown to be more effective when injected into MLP blocks rather than attention projections.
AI.motivation: Existing PEFT methods like LoRA primarily target attention projections and are underexplored for tasks requiring sequential state accumulation (e.g., long-context reasoning, state tracking). The authors investigate whether SSM-based adapters can better serve such tasks and whether MLP blocks are superior injection sites compared to attention modules.
AI.method: HRM adapter: an SSM-based residual module initialized via Balanced Truncation of empirical Hankel Gramians, leveraging the time-invariance of the system matrix Ā to enable exact FFT-based parallel scan. HRM is injected into MLP blocks (rather than attention) and compared iso-parametrically against LoRA variants on Mistral-7B with 8.4M trainable parameters.
AI.result: On LongBench, HRM achieves +34.8% relative accuracy on QuALITY and +71.6% relative ROUGE-1 on QMSum versus LoRA. HRM shows consistent superiority across 18 configurations spanning synthetic state-tracking (DFA, Parity) and character-level LM (enwik8). Gate analysis confirms HRM adapters learn to modulate recurrence effectively.
AI.conclusion: HRM adapters provide a robust architectural alternative to low-rank adaptation for long-context sequence modeling, particularly when injected into MLP blocks. The SSM-based design with Hankel initialization combines strong empirical performance with computational efficiency matching LoRA.

title: Accelerating Returns and the Qualitative Engine for Science
summary: Ray Kurzweil described a thesis of accelerating returns, which is the most influential narratives in discussions of technological progress. Its central claim is that advances in multiple technological fields, especially compute, artificial intelligence, brain science, and biotechnology, interact in such a way that progress becomes self-amplifying and approximately exponential. This paper gives a simple mathematical interpretation of that claim and then argues that, even if such acceleration is real, it does not by itself resolve the central problem of scientific discovery. The reason is that accelerating returns apply most naturally to executional and infrastructural capability, whereas genuine discovery often depends on a different capacity: qualitative reasoning about when a current framework is structurally inadequate and what conceptual move is needed next. Recent ARC-AGI-3 results sharpen this distinction: humans solve the benchmark at ceiling, whereas frontier AI systems remain below 1%, indicating that the gap between current AI and human flexible reasoning is still very large. At the same time, Demis Hassabis has emphasized that humans must retain their sense of meaning and what they choose to focus their lives on, a reminder that the future of AI is not only a technical forecast but also a question of what forms of human understanding are worth preserving and transmitting. This paper positions the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) [3] as a response to that missing capacity. In this view, the Kurzweil theory helps explain why quantitative capability may accelerate, while QES addresses the central problem in scientific discovery that acceleration alone does not solve. Its value does not depend on when AGI arrives, but on the fact that the processes of scientific discovery themselves constitute a form of human wisdom worth preserving, organizing, and making accessible.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques Kurzweil's accelerating returns thesis by arguing that exponential quantitative progress does not solve the core problem of scientific discovery, which requires qualitative conceptual reasoning. ARC-AGI-3 results (humans at ceiling, AI <1%) illustrate this gap. The Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) is proposed as a framework addressing this missing capacity, emphasizing that scientific discovery processes represent human wisdom worth preserving.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing Kurzweilian narrative that self-amplifying exponential progress across compute, AI, and biotechnology will automatically solve scientific discovery. The author argues that accelerating returns primarily enhance executional/infrastructural capability, not the qualitative conceptual reasoning required for genuine breakthroughs.
AI.method: The paper provides a simple mathematical interpretation of Kurzweil's accelerating returns thesis, then employs conceptual argumentation to distinguish between two types of capability: (1) quantitative/executional capability (subject to acceleration) and (2) qualitative reasoning about structural inadequacy in current frameworks (not subject to simple acceleration). ARC-AGI-3 benchmark results serve as empirical evidence for this distinction. The Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) is introduced as a constructive response.
AI.result: The ARC-AGI-3 benchmark reveals a stark gap: humans achieve ceiling performance while frontier AI systems score below 1%, demonstrating that flexible qualitative reasoning remains a major limitation of current AI. This empirically supports the paper's core distinction between accelerate-able quantitative progress and non-accelerate-able qualitative discovery.
AI.conclusion: Kurzweil's theory explains why quantitative capability may accelerate, but the central problem of scientific discovery — recognizing when current frameworks are structurally inadequate — requires qualitative reasoning that acceleration alone cannot provide. QES addresses this gap. The value of preserving scientific discovery processes as human wisdom is independent of AGI timelines, aligning with Hassabis's emphasis on human meaning and focus.

title: Optimizing Human-Machine Interface for Real-Time AI Support in the Operating Room: the CVS Copilot
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for automated Critical View of Safety (CVS) assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy are nearing clinical translation. Beyond algorithmic performance, clinical safety and effectiveness depend on the quality of the human-machine interface (HMI). This work examines how AI-generated predictions should be presented and controlled intraoperatively. Seventeen surgeons, including residents, attending surgeons, and professors, took part in a mixed-methods, user-centered design study to optimize an intraoperative HMI for AI-assisted safe laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Interviews explored interaction modalities, timing of assistance, visualization strategies, and control mechanisms across surgical roles, and were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and human-factors heuristics. Most surgeons (16/17) supported the use of AI for intraoperative decision support while rejecting autonomous decision-making. Attendings preferred minimal AI feedback at decisive moments (13/14), whereas residents favored optional guidance (3/3) with confidence indicators and on-demand anatomical overlays. Across interviews, surgeons consistently prioritized visual, surgeon-controlled, minimally intrusive displays, with the strongest support for a minimal overlay (16/17) and on-demand anatomical segmentation (13/17). Recurrent concerns included persistent overlays, haptic feedback, and numeric confidence displays, although these were not uniformly raised across the cohort. These findings informed the design of CVS Copilot, a surgeon-controlled, role-adaptive HMI that provides AI-based CVS assessment with minimal default visualization and optional overlays.

AI.tldr: A user-centered design study with 17 surgeons identified preferences for AI-assisted CVS assessment in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: minimal, surgeon-controlled visual overlays with role-adaptive feedback — leading to the CVS Copilot HMI design.
AI.motivation: AI systems for automated Critical View of Safety (CVS) assessment are approaching clinical use, but their safety and effectiveness depend critically on the human-machine interface (HMI) design — how predictions are presented and controlled intraoperatively — a gap this study addresses.
AI.method: Mixed-methods, user-centered design study with 17 surgeons (residents, attendings, professors) using interviews exploring interaction modalities, timing, visualization, and control. Data analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis and human-factors heuristics.
AI.result: 16/17 surgeons supported AI for decision support but rejected autonomy. Attendings preferred minimal feedback at decisive moments (13/14); residents favored optional guidance with confidence indicators (3/3). Strongest support was for minimal overlays (16/17) and on-demand anatomical segmentation (13/17). Persistent overlays, haptic feedback, and numeric confidence displays raised concerns.
AI.conclusion: Findings directly informed CVS Copilot: a surgeon-controlled, role-adaptive HMI featuring AI-based CVS assessment with minimal default visualization and optional on-demand overlays, tailored to experience level.

title: Extracting Problem and Method Sentence from Scientific Papers: A Context-enhanced Transformer Using Formulaic Expression Desensitization
summary: Billions of scientific papers lead to the need to identify essential parts from the massive text. Scientific research is an activity from putting forward problems to using methods. To learn the main idea from scientific papers, we focus on extracting problem and method sentences. Annotating sentences within scientific papers is labor-intensive, resulting in small-scale datasets that limit the amount of information models can learn. This limited information leads models to rely heavily on specific forms, which in turn reduces their generalization capabilities. This paper addresses the problems caused by small-scale datasets from three perspectives: increasing dataset scale, reducing dependence on specific forms, and enriching the information within sentences. To implement the first two ideas, we introduce the concept of formulaic expression (FE) desensitization and propose FE desensitization-based data augmenters to generate synthetic data and reduce models' reliance on FEs. For the third idea, we propose a context-enhanced transformer that utilizes context to measure the importance of words in target sentences and to reduce noise in the context. Furthermore, this paper conducts experiments using large language model (LLM) based in-context learning (ICL) methods. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our proposed models achieve a higher macro F1 score compared to the baseline models on two scientific paper datasets, with improvements of 3.71% and 2.67%, respectively. The LLM based ICL methods are found to be not suitable for the task of problem and method extraction.

AI.tldr: To overcome the limitations of small-scale annotated datasets in scientific paper understanding, the authors propose formulaic expression (FE) desensitization for data augmentation, a context-enhanced transformer model, and evaluate LLM-based in-context learning, achieving state-of-the-art macro F1 improvements of 3.71% and 2.67% on two benchmarks for problem and method sentence extraction.
AI.motivation: Manually annotating problem and method sentences in scientific papers is labor-intensive, resulting in small-scale datasets. Models trained on such limited data overfit to specific formulaic expressions (FEs), severely reducing their generalization capability to unseen papers.
AI.method: The paper addresses the small-data problem from three angles: (1) Increasing dataset scale via FE desensitization-based data augmenters that generate synthetic training samples; (2) Reducing model dependence on FEs using the same FE desensitization technique; (3) Enriching sentence-level information with a context-enhanced transformer that leverages surrounding context to weight word importance in target sentences and filter contextual noise. Additionally, LLM-based in-context learning (ICL) is benchmarked for this task.
AI.result: The proposed models outperform baselines by 3.71% and 2.67% in macro F1 score on two scientific paper datasets. LLM-based ICL methods proved unsuitable for problem and method extraction.
AI.conclusion: Combining FE desensitization data augmentation with a context-enhanced transformer effectively mitigates the generalization issues caused by small-scale corpora in scientific paper sentence classification, whereas LLM-based ICL is not a viable alternative for this specific extraction task.

title: Adversarial Diffusion Across Modalities: A Fusion Survey of Attacks, Defenses, and Evaluation for Text, Vision, and Vision-Language Models
summary: Adversarial evaluation of AI systems has matured along four largely disconnected tracks: diffusion-based attacks on text and large language models (LLMs), diffusion-based attacks on image classifiers, jailbreak pipelines against vision-language models, and diffusion-based input purification defenses. Each has developed its own vocabulary, threat models, and benchmarks, with denoising diffusion models emerging as a shared generative mechanism whose recipes are now actively ported between communities. This survey performs an information-fusion exercise at the meta-research level: we integrate these four tracks into a single conceptual framework with a unified taxonomy, evaluation criteria, and research agenda, focusing on the LLM-side slice. We catalog fifty published papers across four scope areas (text/LLM, image classifier, vision-language model, defense), plus four diffusion-LLM-as-victim entries and ten non-diffusion baselines against which any new attack must be compared. We propose a six-class taxonomy of diffusion roles in adversarial pipelines, augmented by a threat-model axis recording attacker knowledge, query budget, and target accessibility, and apply a five-dimension framework (attack success rate, transferability, query budget, perplexity, defense-evasion) uniformly across modalities. The review adopts a dual attacker-defender perspective: alongside the attack catalog we cover four diffusion-based defenses that form the natural evaluation backdrop for new attacks. Our critical analysis identifies five recurring weaknesses of the current LLM-side literature, and we close with a research agenda of open questions and concrete experimental designs. The companion catalog and spreadsheet are released with the paper. We are explicit that this is a narrative review with quality assessment, not a PRISMA-compliant systematic review, and discuss the implications for replication.

AI.tldr: A meta-level survey that unifies four disconnected tracks of adversarial AI evaluation — text/LLM attacks, image classifier attacks, vision-language model jailbreaks, and diffusion-based defenses — into a single conceptual framework with a unified taxonomy, evaluation criteria, and research agenda, cataloging 50+ papers and proposing standardized dimensions for cross-modal comparison.
AI.motivation: The four research tracks on diffusion-based adversarial attacks and defenses have evolved in isolation, each with distinct vocabularies, threat models, and benchmarks, despite sharing denoising diffusion models as a common generative mechanism. This fragmentation impedes cross-pollination of techniques and consistent evaluation, motivating a meta-research integration.
AI.method: The authors conduct a narrative review (not PRISMA-compliant systematic) with quality assessment. They catalog 50 published papers across four scope areas, propose a six-class taxonomy of diffusion roles in adversarial pipelines augmented by a threat-model axis (attacker knowledge, query budget, target accessibility), and apply a five-dimension uniform evaluation framework (attack success rate, transferability, query budget, perplexity, defense-evasion) across modalities. A dual attacker-defender perspective is adopted, covering both attacks and diffusion-based defenses.
AI.result: The survey identifies five recurring weaknesses in the current LLM-side adversarial literature and integrates four previously disconnected tracks into a unified conceptual structure. A companion catalog and spreadsheet with all surveyed papers, baselines, and evaluation dimensions are released alongside the paper.
AI.conclusion: The field would benefit from standardized cross-modal evaluation and taxonomy. The authors outline a research agenda with open questions and concrete experimental designs to guide future work, while transparently acknowledging the narrative (non-systematic) nature of the review and its implications for replication.

title: ProfileFoundry: A Synthetic Person-Object Substrate for Privacy, Memory, and Tool-Use Evaluation in LLM Agent
summary: Foundation-model research increasingly needs data about people: user state, personal histories, relationships, contact-like fields, documents, and longitudinal updates. Real user data is difficult to share, perturb, audit, or redistribute responsibly, while independently generated fake fields rarely preserve the cross-field and temporal consistency needed for controlled evaluation. We present PROFILEFOUNDRY, a deterministic generator and fixed reference release of 100,000 adult synthetic Person Objects across eight locales. Each object combines a typed current snapshot, household, family, and employer links, snapshot-aligned events, normalized relational views, and generation provenance. The release contains 709,228 events, 40,338 households, 52,491 employers, and 518,564 directed relationship edges. We report evidence in separate categories: selected population-marginal comparisons, per-object invariant checks, release-wide referential and temporal closure, and coincidence/provenance screens. PROFILEFOUNDRY is not a population-fidelity model, a rendered-text corpus, or a formal privacy mechanism. Instead, it is a responsible synthetic source layer for constructing downstream foundation-model evaluations involving memory, privacy, document understanding, record linkage, and agent state while keeping the synthetic person behind each artifact inspectable

AI.tldr: PROFILEFOUNDRY is a deterministic synthetic data generator releasing 100,000 adult Person Objects with cross-field consistency, temporal coherence, and relational structure, designed as a responsible evaluation layer for foundation-model research involving personal data.
AI.motivation: Foundation-model research requires realistic personal data (user state, histories, relationships, documents) for controlled evaluation, but real user data poses sharing, privacy, and audit challenges. Independently generated fake fields lack the cross-field and temporal consistency needed for meaningful testing. A responsible, inspectable synthetic data source is needed.
AI.method: The authors developed PROFILEFOUNDRY, a deterministic generator producing 100,000 synthetic Person Objects across eight locales. Each object includes a typed current snapshot, household/family/employer links, snapshot-aligned events, normalized relational views, and generation provenance. The release comprises 709,228 events, 40,338 households, 52,491 employers, and 518,564 directed relationship edges. Evaluation uses population-marginal comparisons, per-object invariant checks, referential/temporal closure, and coincidence/provenance screens.
AI.result: The release achieves cross-field and temporal consistency across all generated entities. Evidence is reported across four categories: selected population-marginal comparisons, per-object invariant checks, release-wide referential and temporal closure, and coincidence/provenance screens. The generator is explicitly not a population-fidelity model, rendered-text corpus, or formal privacy mechanism.
AI.conclusion: PROFILEFOUNDRY serves as a responsible synthetic source layer for downstream foundation-model evaluations involving memory, privacy, document understanding, record linkage, and agent state, while maintaining inspectability of each synthetic person behind every artifact. It addresses a critical gap between unusable real data and inconsistent fake data.

title: The Spec Growth Engine: Spec-Anchored, Code-Coupled, Drift-Enforced Architecture for AI-Assisted Software Development
summary:
AI coding agents dramatically accelerate implementation speed but introduce two structural failure modes that existing spec-driven approaches do not fully solve: (1) context explosion -- the agent must reason over an entire repository at once, degrading output quality as the context window fills; and (2) silent spec-code drift -- code evolves, the specification does not, and the divergence becomes invisible until it is costly to repair.
  We present the Spec Growth Engine, a lightweight framework that addresses both failure modes through a machine-readable spec graph whose nodes carry explicit contract/design separation, a Spine context assembler that scopes agent context to an ownership path, a vertical-slice growth protocol that enforces hardest-first ordering, and a drift gate that makes spec-code divergence a blocking merge condition.
  The design synthesises well-established software engineering principles (Parnas information hiding, C4, ADRs, Walking Skeleton, Reflexion Models, Fitness Functions) into a lean, code-coupled, machine-enforced whole -- without the overhead of heavy-weight frameworks such as RUP or MDA.

AI.tldr: The Spec Growth Engine is a lightweight framework that addresses two key failure modes of AI coding agents — context explosion and silent spec-code drift — by combining a machine-readable spec graph, scoped context assembly, hardest-first vertical-slice growth, and a drift gate that makes divergence a blocking merge condition.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents accelerate implementation but suffer from (1) context explosion, where reasoning over an entire repository degrades output quality as the context window fills, and (2) silent spec-code drift, where code evolves without corresponding specification updates, making divergence costly to repair. Existing spec-driven approaches do not fully solve these problems.
AI.method: The framework consists of four integrated components: (1) a machine-readable spec graph with explicit contract/design separation per node; (2) a Spine context assembler that scopes agent context to an ownership path; (3) a vertical-slice growth protocol enforcing hardest-first ordering; and (4) a drift gate that makes spec-code divergence a blocking merge condition. It synthesizes established principles (Parnas information hiding, C4, ADRs, Walking Skeleton, Reflexion Models, Fitness Functions) into a code-coupled, machine-enforced whole.
AI.result: The paper presents the architectural design of the Spec Growth Engine framework. No empirical evaluation or quantitative results are described in this abstract.
AI.conclusion: The Spec Growth Engine offers a lean alternative to heavyweight frameworks like RUP or MDA, addressing AI coding agent failure modes through principled software engineering practices adapted for agent-driven development.

title: Narration-of-Thought: Inference-Time Scaffolding for Defeasible Ethical Reasoning in Large Language Models
comment: 24 pages, 8 figures, 16 tables. To appear at ACL 2026 (submitted via ARR)
summary: Standard chain-of-thought on moral dilemmas exhibits two failure modes: stakeholder collapse (the trace names at most one party with a stake in the outcome) and uncertainty suppression (no explicit unknowns or hedges before committing to an action). We introduce narration-of-thought (NoT), a system prompt that structures chain-of-thought into five sections: protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, then commitment. NoT adds no training, parameters, or fine-tuning. On 100 DailyDilemmas scenarios across four generators from three vendors, NoT cuts stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1% and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to 1-24% on every model. A matched-budget verbose-CoT control rules out token spend as the active ingredient; NoT retains Cliff's delta advantages of +0.79 to +0.90 on stakeholder count and +0.65 to +0.93 on uncertainty score for three of four generators, and a section ablation attributes each shift to its specific sub-instruction. Textual-gradient descent initialised at NoT improves the scaffold further; a cross-family training judge (different vendor from the generator) dominates an in-family one on every measured axis. Extended to a five-round multi-stakeholder debate protocol, the scaffold converts a 6% standoff into 95% full consensus on a calibration set and 100% combined convergence on a DailyDilemmas replication. The resulting traces externalise the stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainty grounding each commitment, providing an auditable substrate for dependable agentic deployment.

AI.tldr: Chain-of-thought reasoning on moral dilemmas suffers from stakeholder collapse and uncertainty suppression. The authors propose Narration-of-Thought (NoT), a structured prompt scaffold that forces explicit identification of parties, consequences, uncertainty, and commitment. NoT dramatically reduces both failure modes across multiple LLMs without any training, and extends to enabling near-total consensus in multi-stakeholder debates.
AI.motivation: Standard chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning on moral dilemmas exhibits two systematic failure modes: (1) stakeholder collapse — naming at most one affected party, ignoring others with legitimate stakes; and (2) uncertainty suppression — proceeding directly to commitment without acknowledging unknowns or hedging. These failures undermine the auditability and dependability of LLM moral reasoning in agentic deployments.
AI.method: The authors introduce Narration-of-Thought (NoT), a system prompt that structures CoT into five sequential sections: protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences (immediate then downstream), uncertainty, and final commitment. NoT requires no training, fine-tuning, or additional parameters. Evaluation uses 100 DailyDilemmas scenarios across four generators from three vendors. A matched-budget verbose-CoT control isolates token spend from structural effects. Section ablation identifies each sub-instruction's contribution. Textual-gradient descent further refines the NoT scaffold, and the method is extended to a five-round multi-stakeholder debate protocol.
AI.result: NoT reduces stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1%, and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to 1-24% across all models. Cliff's delta effect sizes show advantages of +0.79 to +0.90 on stakeholder count and +0.65 to +0.93 on uncertainty score for three of four generators. The verbose-CoT control confirms that improved performance is not attributable to increased token spend. A cross-family training judge (different vendor from the generator) outperforms an in-family judge. In the multi-stakeholder debate extension, the scaffold converts a 6% standoff into 95% full consensus on a calibration set and achieves 100% combined convergence on the DailyDilemmas replication.
AI.conclusion: NoT provides a lightweight, training-free scaffold that externalizes stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainty, yielding auditable moral reasoning traces suitable for dependable agentic deployment. The structured narration format proves robust across models and vendors, and the multi-stakeholder debate extension demonstrates strong consensus-building capability.

title: Game Changers: Designing and Measuring Dynamic Feedback To Help Users Self-Regulate in a VR Pointing Game
summary: The way games dynamically convey information through feedback is critical to players' ability to perform, learn, and improve. However, it is poorly understood how performance metrics impact player performance and perception in core game tasks like pointing or steering. With a virtual reality pointing task we systematically explored how three performance metrics driving the feedback affected players when rewarding short completion times, straight movements, or high peak speed. across different points in time - continuously, at end-of-action, or at end-of-task. On average the dynamic feedback helped people point more straight and faster, while for others it had small or opposite effect. The study quantitatively compared dynamic feedback across three forms with the metrics driving the form as the intended locus of quantitative comparison. Our work improves game designers basis for crafting dynamic feedback by helping them know when to employ feedback schemes that align with desirable game performance objectives.

AI.tldr: This study systematically investigates how different performance metrics (completion time, straightness, peak speed) and feedback timing (continuous, end-of-action, end-of-task) affect player performance and perception in a VR pointing task. Dynamic feedback generally improved speed and straightness on average, though with individual variability, offering game designers evidence-based guidance on aligning feedback schemes with performance objectives.
AI.motivation: Game designers lack a systematic understanding of how performance metrics driving dynamic feedback influence player performance and perception in fundamental interaction tasks like pointing and steering. Existing knowledge on feedback design is fragmented, with little empirical comparison across different metric types and delivery timings.
AI.method: A controlled experiment using a virtual reality pointing task. Three performance metrics (completion time, movement straightness, peak speed) were each used to drive dynamic visual feedback, presented at three temporal granularities: continuously during action, at the end of each action, or at the end of the entire task. Quantitative comparisons were made across these conditions to isolate the effects of metric type and feedback timing on both objective performance and subjective perception.
AI.result: On average, dynamic feedback led to straighter and faster pointing movements. However, individual differences were notable: some participants showed minimal improvement or even opposite effects. The study provides a quantitative comparison across the three feedback forms, with the metrics driving the form serving as the intended locus of comparison.
AI.conclusion: The findings equip game designers with empirical evidence on when and how to deploy specific dynamic feedback schemes. By aligning feedback metrics with desired performance outcomes (e.g., rewarding straightness to improve accuracy, rewarding speed to reduce completion time), designers can more intentionally craft feedback that supports player learning and performance in interactive tasks.

title: Utilizing Cognitive Signals Generated during Human Reading to Enhance Keyphrase Extraction from Microblogs
summary: Microblogging platforms generate massive amounts of short, noisy, and dispersed user content, making automatic keyphrase extraction (AKE) an important but challenging task. Prior studies have used eye-tracking signals to improve microblog-based AKE because such signals reflect readers' attention to salient words. However, eye tracking alone is limited by physiological, acquisition, and feature-decoding constraints. To address this issue, we investigate whether electroencephalogram (EEG) signals can complement eye-tracking signals for AKE. Using the ZuCo cognitive language processing corpus, we select 8 EEG features and 17 eye-tracking features and incorporate them into microblog-based AKE models. To reduce possible distortion of cognitive signals by model structures, we inject these features into the input of the soft-attention layer and the query vectors of the self-attention layer. We then evaluate different combinations of cognitive signals across AKE models. The results show that cognitive signals produced during reading consistently improve AKE performance, regardless of feature combinations and model architectures. EEG features bring the largest gains, while combining EEG and eye-tracking features yields performance between the two individual signal types, suggesting partial complementarity but also possible redundancy or noise. These findings indicate that EEG signals provide useful cognitive evidence for microblog-based AKE and that multimodal cognitive signals deserve further investigation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether EEG signals can complement eye-tracking signals for automatic keyphrase extraction (AKE) from microblogs. Using the ZuCo corpus, 8 EEG and 17 eye-tracking features are injected into soft-attention and self-attention layers of AKE models. Results show cognitive signals consistently improve AKE, with EEG alone providing the largest gains. Combining both signals yields intermediate performance, suggesting partial complementarity but also redundancy.
AI.motivation: Microblog-based keyphrase extraction is challenging due to short, noisy, dispersed content. Prior work used eye-tracking signals to improve AKE by capturing reader attention to salient words, but eye tracking suffers from physiological, acquisition, and feature-decoding limitations. The authors hypothesize that EEG signals—reflecting neural processing during reading—may provide complementary cognitive evidence that overcomes these constraints.
AI.method: Using the ZuCo cognitive language processing corpus, the authors select 8 EEG features (e.g., band power, event-related potentials) and 17 eye-tracking features (e.g., fixation duration, saccade length). These cognitive features are injected into two positions of AKE models: (1) the input of the soft-attention layer and (2) the query vectors of the self-attention layer—to minimize model-induced distortion of the cognitive signals. Multiple AKE model architectures are evaluated with different combinations of EEG-only, eye-tracking-only, and combined features.
AI.result: Cognitive signals consistently improve AKE performance across all feature combinations and model architectures. EEG features alone produce the largest performance gains. Combining EEG and eye-tracking features yields performance between the two individual signal types, indicating partial complementarity but also possible redundancy or noise when both modalities are used together.
AI.conclusion: EEG signals provide useful cognitive evidence for microblog-based AKE and can complement eye-tracking signals, though simply combining both modalities introduces redundancy. The findings warrant further investigation into multimodal cognitive signal fusion for keyphrase extraction, with more sophisticated integration methods potentially needed to fully exploit their complementarity.

title: Agents That Know Too Much: A Data-Centric Survey of Privacy in LLM Agents
summary: Large language model agents increasingly query databases, search document collections, call external APIs, remember past interactions, and act on a user's behalf. As they move from answering questions to operating over sensitive data, privacy becomes harder to enforce. An agent touches many data sources, runs multi-step workflows, keeps state across sessions, and acts with delegated permissions. Sensitive information can therefore leak not only through its final answer but through the queries it issues, the intermediate results it handles, the memory it writes, and the messages it exchanges with other agents. We survey the privacy of LLM agents from a data-centric view, organizing the field around the data an agent touches rather than by attack type, and we use data agent as shorthand for an LLM agent that works with data. Research on these risks is active but scattered across retrieval-augmented generation, text-to-SQL interfaces, agent memory, prompt injection, access control, and contextual privacy. This survey brings that work together: we taxonomize the data sources an agent touches, the privacy risks each source creates, and the governance mechanisms that address them; we map the benchmarks used to measure these risks and identify what is missing; and we set out the open problems. Two findings recur: among governance mechanisms only information-flow control covers both compositional and cross-session inference leakage, the two least-protected risks; and no benchmark drives an agent across its data surfaces under one privacy policy, the instrument the field most lacks. Our goal is a reference that situates the scattered literature and gives future work a common framing.

AI.tldr: This survey organizes the fragmented research on LLM agent privacy around a data-centric taxonomy: the data sources agents touch (databases, documents, APIs, memory, inter-agent messages), the privacy risks each creates, and the governance mechanisms available. It finds that information-flow control uniquely addresses compositional and cross-session inference leakage, and that no existing benchmark evaluates an agent across all its data surfaces under a single privacy policy.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are evolving from question-answering to operating autonomously over sensitive data across multiple sources, multi-step workflows, persistent memory, and delegated permissions. Privacy leakage can occur not only in final outputs but through queries, intermediate results, stored memory, and inter-agent messages. Existing research on these risks is scattered across disparate subfields (RAG, text-to-SQL, prompt injection, access control, etc.), lacking a unified framing. The authors aim to consolidate this work into a coherent reference for future research.
AI.method: The authors conduct a data-centric survey: (1) they taxonomize the data sources an LLM agent touches (databases, retrieval corpora, API endpoints, persistent memory, and communication channels with other agents); (2) for each source, they categorize the privacy risks (leakage through queries, intermediate handling, stored state, and composition across sources/sessions); (3) they survey governance mechanisms (access control, differential privacy, censorship, information-flow control, etc.) mapped to these risks; (4) they map existing benchmarks to identify measurement gaps.
AI.result: Two key findings: (1) Among all governance mechanisms, only information-flow control addresses both compositional leakage (across multiple data sources in a workflow) and cross-session inference leakage (via persistent memory), which are the two least-protected risk categories. (2) No existing benchmark drives an agent across all its data surfaces while enforcing a single unified privacy policy — this is identified as the most critical missing instrument for the field.
AI.conclusion: The survey provides a structured, data-centric taxonomy that situates scattered literature on LLM agent privacy and offers a common framing for future work. The authors identify open problems, chief among them the need for holistic benchmarks and governance mechanisms that cover compositional and cross-session privacy threats across the full data surface of an agent.

title: ConflictScore: Identifying and Measuring How Language Models Handle Conflicting Evidence
summary: Existing metrics for factuality and faithfulness evaluate whether an answer is supported or contradicted by its grounding documents, but they fail to capture when both supporting and contradicting evidence coexist. We introduce ConflictScore, a novel metric that quantifies how well a model's response acknowledges conflicting evidence in its grounding documents. Our framework decomposes responses into atomic claims, labels each claim against each grounding document, and then aggregates these labels into two complementary measures: ConflictScore-Count (CS-C), the proportion of claims exhibiting conflicts, and ConflictScore-Ratio (CS-R), the balance between supporting and contradicting evidence. We develop ConflictBench, a benchmark covering diverse forms of conflicts such as ambiguity, contradiction, and divergent opinions, to systematically evaluate our metric. Experiments show that ConflictScore effectively detects overconfident claims across domains and can serve as a corrective feedback mechanism that improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA.

AI.tldr: ConflictScore is a new metric that quantifies how well a model acknowledges conflicting evidence (both supporting and contradicting) in its grounding documents, unlike existing metrics that only check for support or contradiction. It decomposes responses into atomic claims, labels each against grounding documents, and produces two scores: CS-C (proportion of conflicting claims) and CS-R (balance of support vs. contradiction). A benchmark called ConflictBench is also introduced.
AI.motivation: Existing factuality and faithfulness metrics only evaluate whether an answer is supported or contradicted by grounding documents, but fail to capture scenarios where both supporting and contradicting evidence coexist. This gap means overconfident or one-sided responses that ignore conflicting evidence go undetected.
AI.method: The ConflictScore framework operates in three stages: (1) decompose responses into atomic claims, (2) label each claim against each grounding document for support/contradiction/neutral, and (3) aggregate labels into two complementary metrics — ConflictScore-Count (CS-C), the proportion of claims exhibiting conflicts, and ConflictScore-Ratio (CS-R), the balance between supporting and contradicting evidence. ConflictBench is also developed, covering conflict types such as ambiguity, contradiction, and divergent opinions.
AI.result: ConflictScore effectively detects overconfident claims across domains. It also serves as a corrective feedback mechanism that improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark.
AI.conclusion: ConflictScore fills a critical gap in faithfulness evaluation by capturing how well models handle conflicting evidence, enabling both better evaluation and feedback-driven improvement of model truthfulness.

title: ATGBuilder: Feature-Assisted Graph Learning for Activity Transition Graph Construction with Seed Supervision
summary: Android applications are organized around activities that provide visual Graphical User Interface (GUI) containers that host the UI and handle user interaction events. Activity Transition Graphs (ATGs) have been widely used to model apps' GUI navigation. However, the construction of high-quality ATGs is challenging: ATGs based on static analysis may miss acceptable transitions and may extract infeasible ones; while dynamically explored ATGs can yield incomplete transitions. Recent learning-based approaches can treat ATG construction as a seed-supervised link-prediction task. However, the use of activity-layout and widget-trigger information for ATG construction remains limited. We propose ATGBuilder, a feature-assisted graph-learning approach for seed-supervised ATG construction. ATGBuilder uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to summarize UI activity metadata from layouts into compact textual functionality summaries. ATGBuilder explicitly models widget-trigger information into the edge attribute: It then uses an auxiliary widget-attribute reconstruction objective on this information during model training. ATGBuilder's performance was evaluated across a series of ablations on the frontmatter corpus, and an experiment on benchmark using manually-checked ground-truth ATGs. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that ATGBuilder significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. We further demonstrate its effectiveness by improving automated GUI exploration tools through better navigation guidance.

AI.tldr: ATGBuilder is a graph-learning approach for constructing Activity Transition Graphs (ATGs) that leverages LLM-generated activity functionality summaries and widget-trigger edge attributes with an auxiliary reconstruction objective, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks and improving automated GUI exploration tools.
AI.motivation: Existing ATG construction methods are limited: static analysis can miss valid transitions or include infeasible ones, dynamic exploration yields incomplete transitions, and recent learning-based approaches underutilize activity-layout and widget-trigger information. This motivates a feature-assisted approach that explicitly incorporates these underexploited signals.
AI.method: ATGBuilder is a seed-supervised, feature-assisted graph-learning method. It (1) uses an LLM to distill UI activity metadata from layouts into compact textual functionality summaries, (2) explicitly encodes widget-trigger information as edge attributes, and (3) introduces an auxiliary widget-attribute reconstruction objective during training. Evaluation includes ablations on the frontmatter corpus and benchmarking against manually-verified ground-truth ATGs.
AI.result: ATGBuilder significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks. Ablation studies on the frontmatter corpus validate the contribution of individual components. Its utility is further demonstrated by enhancing the navigation guidance of automated GUI exploration tools.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling activity-layout semantics via LLM summaries and widget-trigger information via edge attributes with auxiliary reconstruction leads to superior ATG construction. The approach not only advances ATG quality but also translates to practical improvements in downstream GUI exploration tasks.

title: High-Probability PL-SGD with Markovian Noise: Optimal Mixing and Tail Dependence
summary:
We study first-order methods for smooth objectives satisfying the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition when gradient samples are generated by an exogenous Markov chain. In the light-tailed setting, prior uniform-in-time high-probability bounds for ordinary Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) under a standard growth envelope scale as $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}^2/k)$, leaving a gap with the $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}/k)$ expectation bounds. We close this gap using a lag-blocking argument to establish a uniform high-probability guarantee with a leading stochastic term of $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}/(k+K_0))$ under geometric mixing. We prove this linear dependence on the mixing time is optimal via a matching $Ω(σ^2 t_{mix}/k)$ lower bound on a quadratic objective driven by a persistent two-state chain.
  We then extend this framework to heavy-tailed Markovian gradients satisfying a stationary finite-$p$-moment condition, $p \in (1,2]$. We design an all-samples clipped block method that uses every Markov transition while mitigating Markovian bias. Under a transition budget $T$, this algorithm achieves a high-probability stochastic error of $\widetilde{O}(σ_p^2(t_{mix}/T)^{2(p-1)/p})$. We establish a matching lower bound by reducing PL optimization to heavy-tailed mean estimation for a sticky Markov chain. Ultimately, this work tightly characterizes the optimal polynomial dependence on mixing time for light-tailed PL-SGD, and the optimal heavy-tail exponent and effective-sample-size dependence in the robust regime.
