AI.tldr: This paper establishes tight high-probability convergence rates for SGD under the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition when gradients follow a Markov chain, closing the gap between expectation and high-probability bounds in the light-tailed setting and providing matching upper/lower bounds in the heavy-tailed regime.
AI.motivation: Prior high-probability bounds for Markovian SGD under the PL condition scaled as Õ(t_mix²/k), leaving a quadratic gap versus the Õ(t_mix/k) expectation bounds. Furthermore, no tight characterization existed for heavy-tailed Markovian gradients in this setting. The authors aim to close the light-tailed gap and provide optimal rates for the heavy-tailed case.
AI.method: For light tails: a lag-blocking argument establishes uniform high-probability guarantees with Õ(t_mix/(k+K₀)) leading term under geometric mixing, with a matching Ω(σ² t_mix/k) lower bound via a quadratic objective with a persistent two-state chain. For heavy tails (finite p-moment, p∈(1,2]): an all-samples clipped block method uses every Markov transition while controlling Markovian bias, achieving Õ(σ_p²(t_mix/T)^(2(p-1)/p)). A matching lower bound is obtained by reducing PL optimization to heavy-tailed mean estimation for a sticky Markov chain.
AI.result: The light-tailed method achieves Õ(t_mix/(k+K₀)) high-probability error, matching the Ω(σ² t_mix/k) lower bound up to logarithmic factors—establishing linear dependence on mixing time is optimal. The heavy-tailed method achieves Õ(σ_p²(t_mix/T)^(2(p-1)/p)) error with a matching lower bound, tightly characterizing the optimal polynomial mixing-time dependence, heavy-tail exponent, and effective-sample-size dependence in the robust regime.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a tight characterization of optimal convergence rates for PL-conditioned SGD under Markovian gradients in both light- and heavy-tailed settings. The linear mixing-time dependence in the light-tailed case and the exponent (2(p-1)/p) in the heavy-tailed case are both proven optimal via matching lower bounds.

title: Geometry-Aware MCTS for Extremal Problems in Combinatorial Geometry
summary: We study certain extremal problems in combinatorial geometry that ask about configurations of points in an $n \times n$ grid that satisfy strict, global geometric constraints. Classical exact solvers suffer from combinatorial explosion for these types of problems, and standard reinforcement learning and transformer-based models struggle with the sparse reward "validity cliff" and quadratic token-consumption limits. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework. Our approach strictly enforces geometric constraints through incremental updates to the feasible action space. For constraints about collections of collinear points, like those that occur in the classic No-Three-in-Line problem (Max-N3IL), this mechanism reduces the constraint checking complexity from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$. To improve search efficiency, we exploit geometric symmetries in two ways: canonical pruning during node expansion to reduce the branching factor, and symmetric batch transitions to accelerate the discovery of promising configurations. We perform extensive experiments and establish new best-known computational results on five out of six of the problems that we considered. Notably, for Max-N3IL we find configurations of size roughly $1.8 n$ for grids of size $82 \le n \le 119$. For the Smallest Complete Set problem, we find configurations of size roughly $0.95 n$, providing new upper bounds within the tested grids. This work establishes Geometry-Aware MCTS as a highly adaptable framework for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework to solve extremal combinatorial geometry problems involving point configurations on an n×n grid. It introduces incremental feasible action updates (reducing constraint checking from O(n³) to O(n²)) and exploits geometric symmetries via canonical pruning and symmetric batch transitions. The method achieves new best-known results on five of six benchmark problems, including Max-No-Three-in-Line configurations of size ~1.8n for grids 82≤n≤119.
AI.motivation: Classical exact solvers suffer combinatorial explosion on extremal grid configuration problems, while standard RL and transformer-based models face sparse reward "validity cliffs" and quadratic token-consumption limits. There is a need for a framework that efficiently enforces hard geometric constraints during search while scaling to larger grids.
AI.method: The authors propose a Geometry-Aware MCTS framework with three key components: (1) incremental updates to the feasible action space that strictly enforce geometric constraints, reducing collinearity checking from O(n³) to O(n²); (2) canonical pruning during node expansion that leverages geometric symmetries (dihedral group D₄) to reduce branching factor; and (3) symmetric batch transitions that simultaneously evaluate symmetry-equivalent states to accelerate discovery of promising configurations.
AI.result: The method establishes new best-known computational results on five out of six benchmark problems. For Max-No-Three-in-Line (Max-N3IL), it finds configurations of size roughly 1.8n for grids 82≤n≤119. For the Smallest Complete Set problem, it finds configurations of size roughly 0.95n, yielding new upper bounds. The approach consistently outperforms prior exact solvers, RL, and transformer-based methods.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-Aware MCTS is established as a highly adaptable and effective framework for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry. By tightly integrating geometric constraints into the search process and exploiting symmetries, it overcomes key limitations of prior approaches and pushes the frontier of computational results on several open problems.

title: Continuous Behavioral Synthesis for Adaptive Health Dashboards: An LLM-Mediated Architecture Integrating Explicit Preference, Spatial Reorganization, and Attention Allocation Signals
summary: The engineering of adaptive user interfaces has traditionally relied on either rule-based systems encoding designer intuitions about user needs or machine learning approaches requiring substantial historical data before achieving effective personalization. We present a technical architecture that leverages Large Language Models as behavioral synthesis engines to enable immediate adaptation from sparse, heterogeneous user signals. Our system integrates three distinct behavioral channels, i) explicit micro-feedback on individual interface elements, ii) spatial priority inferred from manual widget reorganization through drag-and-drop interaction, iii) and attentional investment measured through dwell time during hover events, within a structured prompt engineering framework that continuously regenerates dashboard layouts while maintaining explanatory coherence. The architecture addresses the technical challenge of translating low-level interaction patterns into high-level design decisions through a layered prompt construction methodology that separates temporal context determination, behavioral signal extraction, explicit preference enforcement, and user profile synthesis. The approach combines manually specified behavioral interpretations and temporal heuristics with LLM-mediated synthesis, enabling the reconciliation of multiple simultaneous signals that would be difficult to encode through explicit rules alone. We demonstrate the system through an instantiation in the personal health monitoring domain, including an analytical evaluation of adaptation behavior across multiple scenarios and a working implementation managing fourteen distinct health metrics across seven widget visualization modalities. The evaluation compares profile-driven initialization, multi-signal behavioral adaptation, and presents the resulting interfaces through representative post-adaptation screenshots.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a technical architecture that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) as behavioral synthesis engines for adaptive user interfaces, enabling immediate personalization from sparse user signals through a structured prompt engineering framework that integrates micro-feedback, spatial reorganization, and dwell-time attention signals.
AI.motivation: Traditional adaptive UI systems are constrained by two limitations: rule-based systems require designers to pre-encode all adaptation logic, while machine learning approaches need extensive historical data before delivering effective personalization. Neither approach handles sparse, heterogeneous, simultaneous user signals well for immediate adaptation.
AI.method: The system integrates three behavioral channels (explicit micro-feedback on UI elements, drag-and-drop spatial reorganization, and hover dwell-time attentional measurement) within a layered prompt construction methodology. This methodology separates temporal context determination, behavioral signal extraction, explicit preference enforcement, and user profile synthesis. LLMs serve as the synthesis engine, combining manually specified behavioral interpretations and temporal heuristics to reconcile multiple simultaneous signals and regenerate dashboard layouts.
AI.result: The system is instantiated in a personal health monitoring domain with a working implementation managing 14 health metrics across 7 widget visualization modalities. An analytical evaluation demonstrates adaptation behavior across multiple scenarios, comparing profile-driven initialization and multi-signal behavioral adaptation, with results shown through representative post-adaptation screenshots.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively serve as behavioral synthesis engines for adaptive UIs, translating low-level interaction patterns into coherent high-level design decisions through structured prompt engineering, thereby overcoming the cold-start and rule-encoding limitations of prior approaches.

title: SocialPersona: Benchmarking Personalized Profiling and Response with Multimodal Social-Media Context
summary: Personalized language-model assistants are often evaluated through a memory lens: can a model recall preferences users have explicitly stated in dialogue? More comprehensive personalization demands a harder capability -- inferring what users care about from the multimodal traces they naturally leave behind. We introduce SocialPersona, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can recover revealed preferences from longitudinal social-media timelines and use them in dialogue. Built from longitudinal timelines of 171 everyday, non-promotional social-media users, SocialPersona contains text, images, timestamps, and 2,597 human-verified preference tags across seven interest domains, separating stable interests from recent interests. It supports two tasks: constructing structured user profiles from multimodal context and generating responses aligned with inferred profiles. Experiments with proprietary and open-weight MLLMs show that models can identify broad interest domains, yet their performance drops on fine-grained and recent interests and degrades further when inferred profiles must be used to personalize dialogue. Together with evidence that text and images provide complementary preference signals, these results indicate that robust cross-modal, long-horizon user modeling remains a key challenge, and that SocialPersona can help measure and advance progress toward assistants that infer and act on revealed preferences.

AI.tldr: SocialPersona is a benchmark that evaluates whether multimodal LLMs can infer users' preferences from longitudinal social-media timelines (text, images, timestamps) and use those inferred preferences to personalize dialogue, revealing that current models struggle with fine-grained and recent interests.
AI.motivation: Existing personalization evaluations focus narrowly on explicit memory recall of stated preferences. The authors argue that true personalization requires a harder capability: inferring "revealed preferences" from the multimodal traces users naturally leave behind (social media activity), without explicit statements.
AI.method: The authors constructed SocialPersona from longitudinal timelines of 171 everyday social-media users, containing text, images, timestamps, and 2,597 human-verified preference tags across seven interest domains (separating stable from recent interests). The benchmark supports two tasks: (1) constructing structured user profiles from multimodal context, and (2) generating dialogue responses aligned with inferred profiles. Both proprietary and open-weight MLLMs were evaluated.
AI.result: Models can identify broad interest domains but perform poorly on fine-grained and recent interests, and performance degrades further when inferred profiles must be used to personalize dialogue. Text and images provide complementary preference signals.
AI.conclusion: Robust cross-modal, long-horizon user modeling remains a key challenge. SocialPersona provides a valuable benchmark for measuring progress toward assistants that can infer and act on revealed preferences rather than merely recalling explicitly stated ones.

title: TGHE: Template-based Graph Homomorphic Encryption for Privacy-Preserving GNN Inference in Edge-Cloud Systems
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at IEEE ICWS 2026
summary: Existing homomorphic encryption (HE)-based GNN systems adopt a graph-centric paradigm that couples per-query cost to global graph size, limiting evaluations to at most ~20k nodes and making them incompatible with dynamic, large-scale financial graphs. We propose TGHE (Template-based Graph Homomorphic Encryption), an ego-centric framework that resolves this by exploiting a template phenomenon: local computation trees in transaction graphs converge into a small set of structural shapes. TGHE canonicalizes ego-graphs at the edge and packs structurally identical trees into shared CKKS ciphertexts for SIMD-parallel encrypted inference, with two long-tail optimizers (Approximate Template Fitting and Topology Collapse) ensuring full SIMD coverage. On DGraphFin (3.7M nodes, 4.3M edges), TGHE-Collapse achieves a 66.9x speedup over the sequential encrypted baseline with less than 0.002 AUC loss.

AI.tldr: TGHE proposes an ego-centric encrypted GNN framework that exploits structural template convergence in transaction graphs, packing isomorphic computation trees into shared CKKS ciphertexts for SIMD-parallel inference. On a 3.7M-node financial graph, it achieves 66.9× speedup over sequential baselines with negligible AUC loss.
AI.motivation: Existing HE-based GNN systems use a graph-centric paradigm where per-query cost scales with global graph size, capping evaluations at ~20k nodes and failing on dynamic, large-scale financial graphs. A scalable, efficient encrypted inference approach is needed.
AI.method: TGHE uses an ego-centric framework with three key components: (1) canonicalization of ego-graphs at the edge level to identify structural templates, (2) packing structurally identical computation trees into shared CKKS ciphertexts for SIMD-parallel encrypted inference, and (3) two long-tail optimizers — Approximate Template Fitting and Topology Collapse — that merge rare/non-conforming topologies into dominant templates to ensure full SIMD coverage.
AI.result: On the DGraphFin dataset (3.7M nodes, 4.3M edges), TGHE-Collapse delivers a 66.9× speedup over the sequential encrypted baseline while incurring less than 0.002 AUC loss.
AI.conclusion: The template-based ego-centric approach decouples encrypted inference cost from global graph size, enabling practical HE-based GNN inference on large-scale dynamic financial graphs for the first time.

title: On the Reproducibility of Quantum Software Defect Datasets: A Case Study of Bugs4Q
comment: 10 pages plus 2 pages of references. Accepted to the Replication and Negative Results (RENE) Track of ICSME 2026
summary: The reproducibility of software defect datasets is essential for obtaining reliable and comparable research results. Zhu et al. have shown that defect datasets such as Defects4J suffer from reproduction failures (i.e., reported bugs become non-reproducible) as time passes since their creation. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize to quantum software defect datasets. We therefore conduct a replication study of the prior work using Bugs4Q, a widely used dataset of real-world bugs in quantum programs. Our analysis includes 77,700 quantum program executions of 37 Bugs4Q artifacts across 21 core-library versions. The experimental results showed that the reproducibility of Bugs4Q dropped from 62.2% on Qiskit v0.20.1 to 16.2% on v2.3.1, the latest version as of April 1, 2026. A manual inspection of the root causes further indicated that 93.6% of the failures were dependency-related. While these findings are consistent with those of the prior work, we also observed differences. In particular, most reproduction failures in Bugs4Q cannot be resolved merely by adjusting dependency versions; instead, they require source-code modifications such as migrating import paths and API invocations. Based on this observation, we curated Bugs4Q-Robust, a patched version of Bugs4Q to restore reproducibility. Bugs4Q-Robust increases reproducibility from 16.2% to 78.4% on Qiskit v2.3.1. Our findings highlight the importance of continuous dataset maintenance in the rapidly evolving quantum software ecosystem.

AI.tldr: A replication study on the Bugs4Q quantum software defect dataset reveals that reproducibility drops from 62.2% to 16.2% across Qiskit versions, primarily due to dependency issues. Unlike prior findings on classical software, fixing these requires source-code modifications rather than just version adjustments. The authors provide Bugs4Q-Robust, restoring reproducibility to 78.4%.
AI.motivation: Prior work by Zhu et al. showed that classical defect datasets like Defects4J suffer from reproduction failures over time. This study investigates whether the same phenomenon generalizes to quantum software defect datasets, specifically Bugs4Q, which had not been empirically validated in this regard.
AI.method: The authors conducted a replication study by executing 77,700 quantum program runs across 37 Bugs4Q artifacts and 21 versions of the Qiskit core library, spanning from v0.20.1 to v2.3.1. They manually inspected root causes of reproduction failures and categorized them. Based on findings, they created Bugs4Q-Robust by patching source-code issues such as import paths and API invocations, then re-evaluated reproducibility.
AI.result: Reproducibility of Bugs4Q declined from 62.2% (Qiskit v0.20.1) to 16.2% (Qiskit v2.3.1). Among failures, 93.6% were dependency-related. Unlike classical datasets, most failures required source-code modifications (e.g., migrating import paths and API calls) rather than mere dependency version pinning. Bugs4Q-Robust restored reproducibility to 78.4% on the latest Qiskit version.
AI.conclusion: The phenomenon of declining reproducibility generalizes from classical to quantum software defect datasets, but the nature of failures differs: quantum datasets require active source-code maintenance beyond version pinning. This underscores the need for continuous dataset curation in the fast-evolving quantum software ecosystem. Bugs4Q-Robust serves as a practical contribution to mitigate this problem.

title: EVOM: Agentic Meta-Evolution of Actor-Critic Architectures for Reinforcement Learning
summary: In actor-critic reinforcement learning, network architectures are typically manually designed. Automating this design is challenging because each candidate must be trained before evaluation, and the design space is open-ended. To address these challenges, we introduce EVOM, an agentic meta-evolution framework for discovering high-performance actor-critic architectures. We frame architecture search as a bi-level optimization: an inner loop trains weights via the low-fidelity proximal policy optimization (PPO), while an outer loop drives meta-evolution by iteratively refining architecture programs. Crucially, this outer loop is powered by an LLM-based design agent that operates purely as an architecture designer, completely decoupled from policy execution and environment control. Experiments reveal that EVOM outperforms the manually designed baseline, an LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES, delivering superior performance on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4. Ablation studies validate that both the meta-evolution loop and the LLM Design Agent are indispensable for final performance.

AI.tldr: EVOM introduces an agentic meta-evolution framework that uses an LLM-based design agent in an outer evolutionary loop to automatically discover high-performance actor-critic architectures, outperforming manually designed baselines and existing automated methods on continuous control tasks.
AI.motivation: Actor-critic network architectures are typically hand-crafted, requiring significant human expertise. Automating this process is challenging because architecture search requires training each candidate before evaluation (computationally expensive) and the design space is open-ended, making exhaustive exploration infeasible.
AI.method: EVOM frames architecture search as bi-level optimization: (1) an inner loop trains network weights using low-fidelity PPO for efficient evaluation; (2) an outer loop performs meta-evolution, iteratively refining architecture programs via an LLM-based design agent that acts solely as an architecture designer, fully decoupled from policy execution and environment interaction.
AI.result: EVOM outperforms manually designed baselines, LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4 tasks. Ablation studies confirm both the meta-evolution loop and the LLM Design Agent are essential for achieving final performance gains.
AI.conclusion: The meta-evolution framework with a decoupled LLM design agent is an effective approach for automated actor-critic architecture discovery, with both components proving indispensable. The framework successfully navigates the open-ended design space without requiring the LLM to interact with the environment.

title: When Agents Meet Electric Bus Fleet Operations: Pricing Behavior, Trade-offs, and Policy Implications in an Aggregator Framework
summary: Agentic systems are changing how complex operational tasks are coordinated, introducing a new paradigm for connecting heterogeneous data sources and automating processes. Electric bus fleets provide a relevant test case. Their operation requires continuous coordination between service reliability, battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) opportunities. This paper proposes an agentic aggregator framework that streamlines this decision environment by coupling an optimization-based electric bus scheduling model with supervisory agents for disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. The optimization core enforces physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges, while the agentic layer interprets changing operating conditions, triggers real-time re-optimization when needed, and defines how flexibility value is allocated between the aggregator and the public transport operator (PTO). A realistic depot case study evaluates day-ahead and real-time operations under profit-based and operation-based coordination modes, considering service delays, route-energy deviations, electricity price shocks, and combined disturbances. The results show that agentic aggregation can support adaptive fleet-grid coordination by maintaining feasible schedules, activating re-optimization selectively, and improving the use of charging and V2G flexibility. However, they also reveal a critical trade-off: the same agentic capability that reduces operational complexity can extract value from the PTO when configured around profit-oriented pricing. These findings suggest that agentic aggregators can become useful for managing electric bus V2G operations, but their deployment in public-fleet contexts requires transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting, and explicit value-sharing rules.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an agentic aggregator framework that couples optimization-based electric bus scheduling with supervisory agents for disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. Tested on a realistic depot case study, the framework demonstrates adaptive fleet-grid coordination but reveals a critical trade-off: profit-oriented agent configurations can extract value from public transport operators, necessitating transparent, auditable value-sharing rules.
AI.motivation: Electric bus fleet operations require continuous coordination across multiple dynamic variables (battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, V2G opportunities). Traditional optimization approaches struggle to handle real-time disturbances and the complexity of connecting heterogeneous data sources. An agentic paradigm is proposed to streamline this decision environment by coupling optimization with intelligent supervisory layers.
AI.method: The authors develop an agentic aggregator framework with two layers: (1) an optimization core that enforces physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges; and (2) a supervisory agentic layer that interprets changing operating conditions, triggers real-time re-optimization, and allocates flexibility value between the aggregator and the public transport operator. The framework is evaluated via a realistic depot case study under both profit-based and operation-based coordination modes, testing disturbances such as service delays, route-energy deviations, electricity price shocks, and combined disruptions in both day-ahead and real-time settings.
AI.result: The agentic aggregator successfully maintains feasible schedules, selectively activates re-optimization, and improves charging and V2G flexibility utilization. However, results expose a critical trade-off: profit-oriented pricing configurations enable the agentic layer to extract value from the public transport operator, even as it reduces operational complexity.
AI.conclusion: Agentic aggregators are promising for managing electric bus V2G operations, but their deployment in public-fleet contexts demands transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting mechanisms, and explicit value-sharing rules to prevent exploitative value extraction from public transport operators.

title: What Holds Back Brain-Computer Interfaces? Uncovering Challenges and Opportunities in BCI-controlled Games for Cerebral Palsy Rehabilitation
summary: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer promising avenues for cerebral palsy (CP) rehabilitation at home and in the clinic, using games that promote engagement and sustained training effort. Nonetheless, the design constraints of BCI-based CP rehabilitation remain unclear, especially how individuals with CP experience a sense of control through BCI, and how they experience computer-mediated game assistance. To address this gap, we present preliminary clinical and user perspectives on BCI-based CP rehabilitation, drawing on in-clinic insights from a CP therapist and experiential accounts from ten individuals with CP engaging with BCI game prototypes. Sporadic help in BCI games eased monotony, but also fostered doubts regarding agency. The therapist saw BCI rehabilitation as complementary to traditional training, facilitating the transition from playful exercises to autonomous, self-managed training. We outline key challenges and opportunities to inform and empower further design and research of BCI training for CP.

AI.tldr: This paper presents preliminary clinical and user perspectives on BCI-based rehabilitation for cerebral palsy, drawing on insights from a therapist and ten individuals with CP who engaged with BCI game prototypes. It explores how users experience agency and computer-mediated assistance, finding that sporadic help eased monotony but raised doubts about control, and that therapists view BCI as complementary to traditional training.
AI.motivation: The design constraints of BCI-based CP rehabilitation remain poorly understood, particularly regarding how individuals with CP experience a sense of control (agency) through BCI and how they perceive computer-mediated game assistance. The authors aimed to address this gap by gathering empirical perspectives from both clinical and user standpoints.
AI.method: The study employed a qualitative, exploratory approach combining two sources: (1) in-clinic insights from a CP therapist, and (2) experiential accounts from ten individuals with CP who interacted with BCI game prototypes. The analysis focused on user experiences of agency, responses to computer-mediated assistance, and clinical perspectives on integrating BCI into rehabilitation practice.
AI.result: Two key findings emerged: (1) Sporadic, computer-mediated help in BCI games reduced monotony but simultaneously fostered doubts about personal agency — users questioned whether successes were theirs or the system's. (2) The therapist viewed BCI rehabilitation as complementary to conventional training, serving as a bridge from playful, engaging exercises toward autonomous, self-managed training regimens.
AI.conclusion: The paper outlines key challenges and opportunities for BCI-based CP rehabilitation design, emphasizing the need to carefully balance computer assistance with preserving user agency, and advocating for BCI as a complementary tool that can scaffold the transition from guided play to independent training.

title: ConvMemory v3: A Validity Context Layer for Conversational Memory via Target-Conditioned Relation Verification
summary: Conversational memory retrieval optimizes relevance, yet a retrieved memory can be relevant and simultaneously outdated: a later turn updates, corrects, or supersedes it. ConvMemory v3 adds a validity context layer that detects and surfaces this update evidence through target-conditioned relation verification, sitting after the v1/v2 retrieval path. The core mechanism is a dual-evidence gate that conditions a relation judgment on the specific target proposition, scoring a (target, source) pair through the product of a MiniLM slot head and a DeBERTa-v3 slot head and gating it by conservative event/operation evidence. On a synthetic multi-hop validity benchmark the gate reaches 90.12% +/- 1.73 accuracy; through a real-data feedback loop that mines failure patterns but trains on synthetic pairs only, the verifier transfers to Memora role binding with zero target-side labels, reaching 98.8% +/- 0.9 group-all-correct. The deployed layer preserves retrieval by default: a context mode attaches structured validity metadata while keeping the candidate set and rank order fixed, and a query-conditioned demote mode is an explicit opt-in for dense current-state workloads, where it raises current-active H@1 from a never-demote baseline of 45.1% to 95.7% +/- 1.2 while protecting non-superseded memories at 99.4% recall. Six machine-verifiable safety contracts pin the layer's behavior. Multi-hop graph propagation is validated as a mechanism; fully automatic construction of strict prerequisite edges is characterized as a boundary, since strict necessity requires counterfactual world knowledge. This report extends ConvMemory v1 (arXiv:2605.28062) and v2 (arXiv:2606.10842).

AI.tldr: ConvMemory v3 introduces a validity context layer that detects outdated or superseded memories using a dual-evidence gate. It achieves high accuracy on synthetic benchmarks, transfers to real data with zero target-side labels, and significantly improves retrieval precision while maintaining recall for non-superseded memories.
AI.motivation: Retrieved conversational memories can be relevant yet outdated — later turns may update, correct, or supersede earlier information. Existing retrieval systems (v1/v2) lack a mechanism to detect and surface this validity evidence, creating a risk that stale information is used in downstream tasks.
AI.method: A dual-evidence gate conditions a relation judgment on a specific target proposition, scoring (target, source) pairs via the product of a MiniLM slot head and a DeBERTa-v3 slot head, gated by conservative event/operation evidence. The layer operates in two modes: (1) a context mode that attaches structured validity metadata while preserving the existing candidate set and rank order, and (2) an explicit opt-in query-conditioned demote mode for dense current-state workloads. Training uses a synthetic multi-hop validity benchmark with a real-data feedback loop that mines failure patterns but trains only on synthetic pairs, enabling zero-shot transfer to Memora role binding.
AI.result: The gate achieves 90.12% ± 1.73 accuracy on the synthetic benchmark. On Memora role binding with zero target-side labels, it reaches 98.8% ± 0.9 group-all-correct. In demote mode, current-active H@1 improves from 45.1% (never-demote baseline) to 95.7% ± 1.2, while protecting non-superseded memories at 99.4% recall. Six machine-verifiable safety contracts verify the layer's behavior. Multi-hop graph propagation is validated as a mechanism, though fully automatic strict prerequisite edge construction is identified as a boundary due to the need for counterfactual world knowledge.
AI.conclusion: The validity context layer successfully augments conversational memory retrieval by detecting outdated information without disrupting the existing retrieval pipeline. The dual-evidence gating approach transfers robustly from synthetic to real data, and the design's conservative defaults (preserving retrieval by default) make it practical for deployment. The work identifies that strict prerequisite inference remains an open challenge requiring counterfactual reasoning capabilities.

title: The Fungible Reserve Standard: A Deterministic Framework for Encoding Carrying Costs in Asset-Backed Tokens
summary: The tokenization of real-world assets (RWAs) has emerged as a transformative application of blockchain technology, with market projections estimating trillions of dollars in tokenized assets within the coming decade. However, a fundamental challenge remains unaddressed: physical assets such as precious metals, stored commodities, and warehoused goods incur structural negative carry -- custody, insurance, and audit costs that accumulate over time. While existing tokenization models have successfully established the market for digital gold and treasuries, they typically manage operational costs at the issuer level. The FRS introduces a framework to bring these economics directly on-chain, avoiding mechanisms such as token rebasing that compromise fungibility and composability with decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols. This paper proposes the Fungible Reserve Standard (FRS), a deterministic token design framework that encodes carrying costs transparently into on-chain logic. The FRS introduces an asset-per-token variable q(t) that decreases according to a predefined annualized carrying cost rate, coupled with a supply reconciliation mechanism that preserves holder balances and ERC-20 composability. While mathematically inspired by the daily expense ratio accrual in traditional asset management -- which often embed centralized profit margins -- the FRS design specifically encodes actual operational carrying costs to provide pure institutional-grade accounting clarity without compromising DeFi compatibility. The framework is asset-agnostic and applicable to any real-world asset with positive, predictable holding costs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Fungible Reserve Standard (FRS), a deterministic on-chain framework that transparently encodes real-world asset carrying costs (custody, insurance, audit) into a decreasing asset-per-token variable q(t), while preserving ERC-20 composability and avoiding token rebasing.
AI.motivation: Existing tokenization models for real-world assets (RWAs) like precious metals and commodities manage operational costs at the issuer level, but fail to bring carrying-cost economics directly on-chain. Current solutions like token rebasing compromise fungibility and DeFi composability. There is a need for an on-chain accounting mechanism that transparently reflects structural negative carry without sacrificing protocol compatibility.
AI.method: The FRS framework introduces a deterministic asset-per-token variable q(t) that decreases over time at a predefined annualized carrying-cost rate. It couples this with a supply reconciliation mechanism that maintains holder balances and ERC-20 composability. The design mathematically parallels daily expense ratio accrual in traditional asset management but encodes only actual operational costs rather than profit margins.
AI.result: The FRS framework achieves transparent on-chain encoding of carrying costs while preserving ERC-20 composability and avoiding token rebasing. It is asset-agnostic and applicable to any RWA with positive, predictable holding costs.
AI.conclusion: FRS provides institutional-grade accounting clarity for tokenized RWAs by embedding carrying costs directly into on-chain logic, bridging the gap between traditional asset management cost structures and DeFi composability requirements.

title: AnySimLite: A Lightweight Few-Shot Similarity Encoder for On-Device Speech-Adjacent Classification
summary: To minimize privacy concerns and inference latency on edge devices like smartphones, lightweight on-device models remain important for end-user applications. Many of these applications involve natural language classification, but deploying multiple specialized models creates a memory footprint challenge. We investigate: Can a single lightweight architecture solve multiple Speech-Adjacent (SA) classification tasks through reduction to a nuanced text similarity formulation? We propose AnySimLite, a lightweight similarity encoder that combines word-level and character-level channels. Together with a dataset transformation strategy, we evaluate AnySimLite across multiple SA classification tasks and show that it consistently achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) or SOTA-competitive performance in few-shot settings while maintaining a low memory footprint. Even in the worst case, the performance drop remains below 7% while using $<\frac{1}{250}^{\mathrm{th}}$ of the model size of the SOTA qLLaMA_LoRA-7B baseline.

AI.tldr: AnySimLite is a lightweight similarity encoder using word-level and character-level channels that solves multiple speech-adjacent classification tasks via text similarity, achieving SOTA-competitive few-shot performance with under 1/250th the model size of a 7B-parameter baseline.
AI.motivation: Deploying multiple specialized models on memory-constrained edge devices for various natural language classification tasks is impractical. The authors aim to determine whether a single lightweight architecture can handle multiple speech-adjacent tasks through a unified text similarity formulation, thereby reducing memory footprint while preserving accuracy.
AI.method: The paper proposes AnySimLite, a lightweight similarity encoder that fuses word-level and character-level channels for nuanced text similarity computation. A dataset transformation strategy converts various speech-adjacent classification tasks into a similarity-based formulation, enabling a single model to handle multiple tasks in few-shot settings.
AI.result: AnySimLite consistently achieves SOTA or SOTA-competitive performance across multiple SA classification tasks in few-shot settings. In the worst case, performance drops less than 7% while using less than 1/250th of the model size of the qLLaMA_LoRA-7B baseline.
AI.conclusion: A single lightweight similarity encoder with dual-granularity channels can effectively replace multiple specialized models for speech-adjacent classification on edge devices, offering an excellent accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

title: Smaller Models, Unexpected Costs: Trade-offs in LLM Quantization for Automated Program Repair
comment: Accepted for publication in the Research Papers Track of the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026), 14-18 September 2026, Benevento, Italy
summary:
Language Models (LLMs) are powerful toolsand have been increasingly adopted for complex software engineering tasks. As the number of parameters increases, results can often be improved, but this also imposes substantialmemory requirements. While quantization effectively reduces thememory footprint, its overall impact is often summarized onlyby benchmark scores, which mask changes in model behaviorand non-functional overheads. In this work, we conduct anempirical evaluation of LLM quantization using AutomatedProgram Repair (APR), a complex task in software engineering.We analyze 13 quantization configurations spanning differentbit-widths, methods, and target components (weights and KVcache) across six representative LLMs, evaluated on two APRbenchmarks (HumanEval-Java and Defects4J).
  Our findings reveal that base and quantized models can provide different sets of repaired problems with little overlap, whileretaining a comparable number of repaired problems. Althoughquantization successfully reduces memory footprints by up to85%, it increases both inference time and energy consumption,which we attribute to suboptimal hardware utilization. OurPareto trade-off analysis shows that 48% of the configurationsevaluated are strictly dominated by alternatives. Rather thanidentifying a superior quantization method, our findings highlightthat the trade-offs between effectiveness, memory footprint,and energy efficiency are sensitive to the underlying modelarchitecture and the complexity of the task.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically evaluates how quantization affects LLMs on Automated Program Repair (APR), analyzing 13 configurations across 6 models on two benchmarks. Findings show quantized models repair different (not fewer) bugs, reduce memory by up to 85%, but increase inference time and energy due to poor hardware utilization. Trade-offs are highly sensitive to model architecture and task complexity, with 48% of configurations Pareto-dominated.
AI.motivation: While quantization is widely used to reduce LLM memory footprint, its evaluation is typically limited to benchmark scores that obscure changes in model behavior and non-functional costs (latency, energy). The authors aim to provide a holistic, multidimensional assessment of quantization's impact on a complex, real-world software engineering task—Automated Program Repair—rather than relying solely on accuracy metrics.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical study evaluating 13 quantization configurations (varying bit-widths, quantization methods, and target components: weights and KV-cache) across six representative LLMs. Evaluation uses two APR benchmarks: HumanEval-Java and Defects4J. Analysis spans multiple dimensions: repair effectiveness, overlap in repaired problems between base and quantized models, memory footprint reduction, inference time, and energy consumption. A Pareto trade-off analysis identifies dominated configurations.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Base and quantized models repair comparable numbers of problems but with limited overlap—they fix different bugs. (2) Quantization reduces memory by up to 85%. (3) Paradoxically, quantization increases inference time and energy consumption due to suboptimal hardware utilization. (4) Pareto analysis shows 48% of configurations are strictly dominated by alternatives. (5) Trade-offs between effectiveness, memory, and energy are sensitive to model architecture and task complexity, meaning no single quantization method is universally superior.
AI.conclusion: There is no one-size-fits-all quantization strategy for APR tasks. Practitioners must consider the interplay of model architecture, task complexity, and deployment constraints when selecting quantization configurations. The authors call for moving beyond accuracy-only evaluations toward multidimensional assessments that capture behavioral shifts and non-functional overheads.

title: Mesh-RL: Coupled subgrid reinforcement learning
summary: Reinforcement learning in large or sparse-reward environments suffers from slow temporal-difference reward propagation, as value information spreads only locally across the state space. We propose Mesh-RL, a spatial domain-decomposition framework inspired by the finite element method and domain decomposition theory, which partitions the environment into overlapping subgrids and enforces boundary-consistent temporal-difference updates. Such an approach enables localized learning while ensuring globally coherent value propagation. Unlike hierarchical or model-based approaches, Mesh-RL accelerates long-range credit assignment without modifying the reward function, Bellman operator, or introducing explicit planning mechanisms. We evaluate Mesh-RL on hazard-dense grid-world environments with varying geometries and mesh resolutions. Across Q-learning, SARSA, and Dyna-Q, Mesh-RL consistently improves convergence speed, cumulative reward, and learning stability. Higher mesh resolutions sustain exploration, prevent premature convergence, and substantially accelerate value propagation to distant states. While Dyna-Q already benefits from internal planning, it still achieves additional gains under structured decomposition. Overall, Mesh-RL introduces a principled spatial domain-decomposition mechanism for accelerating temporal-difference learning. Our framework bridges finite element method-inspired boundary-consistency techniques from scientific computing with reinforcement learning to improve sample efficiency in sparse-reward environments. We will release source code of the study.

AI.tldr: Mesh-RL applies finite element method-inspired spatial domain decomposition to RL, partitioning environments into overlapping subgrids with boundary-consistent TD updates, accelerating value propagation in sparse-reward settings without modifying rewards or the Bellman operator.
AI.motivation: Temporal-difference learning in large or sparse-reward environments suffers from slow reward propagation because value information spreads only locally. Existing solutions either modify the reward function, alter the Bellman operator, or introduce planning mechanisms. The authors seek a principled spatial decomposition approach that accelerates long-range credit assignment without these modifications.
AI.method: Mesh-RL partitions the environment into overlapping subgrids (spatial domain decomposition inspired by FEM) and enforces boundary-consistent temporal-difference updates across subdomain interfaces. This enables localized learning within each subgrid while maintaining globally coherent value propagation through boundary conditions, without altering the reward function, Bellman operator, or adding planning.
AI.result: Evaluated on hazard-dense grid-worlds with varying geometries and mesh resolutions, Mesh-RL consistently improved convergence speed, cumulative reward, and learning stability across Q-learning, SARSA, and Dyna-Q. Higher mesh resolutions sustained exploration, prevented premature convergence, and accelerated value propagation to distant states. Even Dyna-Q, which already uses internal planning, gained additional benefits.
AI.conclusion: Mesh-RL provides a principled spatial domain-decomposition mechanism for accelerating TD learning, bridging FEM-inspired boundary-consistency techniques from scientific computing with RL to improve sample efficiency in sparse-reward environments. The authors commit to releasing source code.

title: Unbiased Canonical Set-Valued Oracles Via Lattice Theory
summary: A non-agentic "oracle" AI that estimates probabilities of future events faces a self-reference problem: once its answer is learned and acted upon, it can change the very probability it was asked to report. One response, advocated for the Scientist AI programme, is to ask only counterfactual questions, evaluated as if the answer had no influence. We observe that such answers tend to become irrelevant the moment they are learned, precisely because their premise is then false. We therefore explore a self-referential alternative in which the oracle reports not a single probability but a credal set that is simultaneously unbiased and self-consistent with the consequences of being learned. The naive self-consistency requirement is satisfied by too many sets (including the useless answer $[0,1]$), so the problem is to single out a canonical, nontrivial member. We do so with the Knaster--Tarski fixed-point theorem on the complete lattice of closed credal sets, taking the least fixed point of a suitably defined isotone operator; a variant instead reports the least fixed point that contains every self-consistent point estimate. We prove existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness, show that the construction collapses to the classical point answer for non-performative questions, and that for a binary event the canonical answer is, under a natural hull-factoring assumption, an interval. The development is purely lattice-theoretic and extends unchanged from a binary event $B$ to an arbitrary random variable $X$, with $P(B\mid A,C)$ replaced by the conditional law $\mathcal{L}(X\mid A,C)$. We close with open questions, including whether the interval characterization itself survives that generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the self-reference problem in oracle AI by proposing a lattice-theoretic framework where the oracle outputs a credal set (rather than a single probability) that is both unbiased and self-consistent with the consequences of being learned, using the Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem to select a canonical least fixed point.
AI.motivation: When an oracle AI's probability estimates are learned and acted upon, the act of learning changes the very probabilities being estimated—a self-reference problem. The Scientist AI counterfactual approach asks "what would the probability be if this answer had no influence," but such answers become irrelevant once learned because their counterfactual premise is then false. This motivates a self-referential alternative that embraces rather than avoids the performative feedback loop.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem on a complete lattice of closed credal sets (sets of probability measures). They define an isotone (monotone) operator whose fixed points represent self-consistent answers. Using the Knaster–Tarski fixed-point theorem, the canonical answer is the least fixed point of this operator. A variant takes the least fixed point containing all self-consistent point estimates. The framework is developed purely lattice-theoretically and generalizes from binary events to arbitrary random variables using conditional laws.
AI.result: The construction provably exists, is self-consistent, and nonempty. For non-performative questions (where the answer does not affect the outcome), the canonical answer collapses to the classical Bayesian point estimate. For binary events, under a natural "hull-factoring" assumption, the canonical answer is an interval. The generalization to arbitrary random variables is shown to extend unchanged.
AI.conclusion: A self-referential oracle reporting a canonical credal set resolves the self-reference problem while remaining unbiased and non-trivial. The least-fixed-point construction provides a principled selection mechanism. Open questions remain, including whether the interval characterization survives generalization beyond binary events.

title: Floor Raiser or Ceiling Limiter? Differential Storytelling Outcomes with a Child-Centric GenAI System Across Individual Differences
summary: Generative AI (GenAI) holds promise for democratizing creative literacy, yet whether it benefits all children equally remains unclear. Using a child-centric GenAI storytelling system for children aged 7-12, we conducted a mixed-methods within-subjects experiment (N = 40, Grades 2-6) comparing GenAI-assisted and traditional storyboard conditions. Three findings emerged. First, the GenAI-assisted condition was associated with a floor-raising convergence pattern, with the quality gap narrowing by 83.5%, driven by lower-end support and upper-end constraint mechanisms. This convergence was dimension-selective, improving creativity and richness while leaving coherence and narrative structure tied to baseline performance. Second, younger children more often selected semantically distant keywords while older children preferred semantically closer ones, although engagement orientation varied across individuals regardless of age. Third, image regeneration was positively associated with structural quality dimensions, though this association was attenuated after baseline control. We propose mechanism-contingent scaffolding as a design principle for adaptive GenAI storytelling systems serving diverse children.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods experiment (N=40, ages 7–12) found that GenAI-assisted storytelling produced a floor-raising convergence effect, narrowing quality gaps by 83.5% through lower-end support and upper-end constraint. Improvements were dimension-selective (creativity/richness improved; coherence/narrative structure remained baseline-dependent). Younger children chose semantically distant keywords; older children preferred semantically closer ones. Image regeneration correlated with structural quality, attenuated after baseline control. The authors propose mechanism-contingent scaffolding for adaptive GenAI storytelling.
AI.motivation: Generative AI holds potential for democratizing creative literacy, but it is unclear whether its benefits are equitably distributed across children of different ages and ability levels. The study investigates differential effects of GenAI support on children's storyboarding to determine whether it narrows or widens performance gaps.
AI.method: A within-subjects, mixed-methods experiment with 40 children in Grades 2–6 (ages 7–12) using a child-centric GenAI storytelling system. Each participant completed both a GenAI-assisted storyboard condition and a traditional (non-AI) storyboard condition. Measures included storyboard quality dimensions (creativity, richness, coherence, narrative structure), keyword semantic distance, image regeneration behavior, and baseline performance.
AI.result: (1) The GenAI condition produced an 83.5% narrowing of the quality gap — a floor-raising convergence pattern driven by support for lower-performing children and constraint on higher performers. (2) Convergence was dimension-selective: creativity and richness improved across the board, while coherence and narrative structure remained tied to baseline ability. (3) Younger children selected more semantically distant keywords; older children chose semantically closer ones; engagement orientation varied individually regardless of age. (4) Image regeneration frequency was positively associated with structural quality dimensions, but this association weakened after controlling for baseline performance.
AI.conclusion: GenAI-assisted storytelling can reduce performance disparities among children, but its effects are not uniform across quality dimensions. The authors introduce "mechanism-contingent scaffolding" as a design principle — adaptive support that adjusts based on the specific mechanisms (floor-raising vs. ceiling-constraining) operating for different children and different skill dimensions.

title: From Vajrayana Tara to Bengali Baul: A Computational Study of Lexical Transmission Across Buddhist, Shakta, and Vaishnava Traditions in Bengal
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Code and corpus: https://github.com/joyboseroy/bengal-dharma-corpus Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/joyboseroy/bengal-dharma-corpus
summary: We present a computational corpus study of vocabulary relationships across eight tradition layers of Bengali and Sanskrit devotional literature spanning the 8th to 19th centuries, encompassing Buddhist Vajrayana, Shakta Tantra, Vaishnava, and Baul traditions. Using a corpus of 75 texts and TF-IDF character n-gram vectorization with cosine similarity analysis, we address the historically argued but previously unquantified claim that Buddhist Vajrayana vocabulary survived the collapse of the Pala monasteries and was absorbed into the Shakta Tantra tradition of Bengal. The central finding is a specificity result: the Gitagovinda (Vaishnava Sanskrit, 12th century) has zero cosine similarity to Shakta Kali texts, while Bridge Tara texts (Buddhist-Shakta transitional, same century, same language) have cosine similarity 0.54 to Shakta Kali. This 8.5-fold contrast between two Sanskrit traditions from the same century demonstrates that the Buddhist-Shakta vocabulary overlap is not a generic property of Sanskrit devotional literature but is specific to the Buddhist-Shakta transmission chain. Three Brihannilatantra Tara texts show Shakta-to-Buddhist vocabulary ratios of 2.0 to 4.0, constituting measurable evidence of lexical transition within that chain. Ramprasad Sen's 18th-century Bengali Kali songs preserve Buddhist vocabulary residue including 56 occurrences of Tara alongside 103 occurrences of Kali. The Vaishnava Bengali tradition contributes a parallel chain to modern Baul vocabulary (similarity 0.29), slightly weaker than the Buddhist Sahajiya chain via Charyapada (0.31). These results provide the first quantitative multi-tradition corroboration of historically argued Buddhist-Shakta syncretism in Bengal.

AI.tldr: A computational corpus study of 75 Bengali and Sanskrit devotional texts (8th–19th c.) uses TF-IDF character n-grams and cosine similarity to quantitatively demonstrate that Buddhist Vajrayana vocabulary survived and was absorbed into the Shakta Tantra tradition, with a key finding that the Buddhist-Shakta vocabulary overlap is specific to that transmission chain rather than a generic feature of Sanskrit devotional literature.
AI.motivation: To provide the first quantitative, multi-tradition computational evidence for the historically argued but previously unquantified claim that Buddhist Vajrayana vocabulary persisted after the collapse of the Pala monasteries and was absorbed into Bengal's Shakta Tantra tradition.
AI.method: A corpus of 75 texts spanning eight tradition layers (8th–19th centuries) was analyzed using TF-IDF character n-gram vectorization combined with cosine similarity analysis to measure inter-textual vocabulary relationships across Buddhist Vajrayana, Shakta Tantra, Vaishnava, and Baul traditions.
AI.result: The Gitagovinda (Vaishnava Sanskrit) has zero cosine similarity to Shakta Kali texts, while Bridge Tara texts (Buddhist-Shakta transitional) show 0.54 similarity—an 8.5-fold contrast, demonstrating transmission specificity. Three Brihannilatantra Tara texts exhibit Shakta-to-Buddhist vocabulary ratios of 2.0–4.0. Ramprasad Sen's 18th-century Bengali Kali songs contain Buddhist vocabulary residue (56 Tara occurrences alongside 103 Kali). The Buddhist Sahajiya–Charyapada chain to Baul (0.31) marginally outperforms the Vaishnava-Baul chain (0.29).
AI.conclusion: The study provides the first quantitative multi-tradition corroboration of Buddhist-Shakta syncretism in Bengal, showing that the vocabulary overlap is specific to the Buddhist-Shakta transmission chain and not a generic property of Sanskrit devotional literature.

title: DroidBreaker: Practical and Functional Problem-Space Attacks on Machine-Learning Android Malware Detectors
summary: Adversarial APKs are Android applications modified in the problem space to evade machine-learning malware detectors. In this work, we first show that, despite claims, existing problem-space attacks remain largely impractical. Most techniques leverage software transplantation to inject entire benign modules, introducing many side-effect features and often causing build-time failures. Fine-grained methods that inject only a narrow subset of components exhibit limited effectiveness, while those that also use obfuscation rely on brittle bytecode rewriting, producing APKs that are syntactically valid but semantically unusable. Prior work further overestimates attack success rates by running smoke tests that only validate installation and basic execution, without assessing whether the modified APK still preserves its intended behavior. To overcome these limitations, we present DROIDBREAKER, a practical (build-safe) and functional (semantics-preserving) problem-space attack framework that provides: (i) query-efficient white- and black-box attacks by manipulating only the APK components most influential to the target model; (ii) a set of fine-grained, build-safe manipulations (including injection and obfuscation of API calls, app modules, permissions, and URLs) with minimal side effects; and (iii) a semantics-preserving functionality test that enforces runtime equivalence by comparing execution logs and API-level traces between the initial and the modified APK. Evaluated on a recent corpus of Android applications, DROIDBREAKER achieves high evasion rates with few queries and minimal side effects in both white-box and black-box settings, and drastically reduces detections by commercial malware scanners hosted on VirusTotal.

AI.tldr: DROIDBREAKER is a practical, semantics-preserving adversarial attack framework for Android malware detection that overcomes limitations of prior problem-space attacks — which were build-unsafe or functionally broken — by using fine-grained, low-side-effect manipulations and enforcing runtime equivalence through execution log comparison, achieving high evasion rates against both ML detectors and commercial scanners like VirusTotal.
AI.motivation: Prior problem-space adversarial attacks on Android malware detectors are largely impractical: transplantation-based methods cause build failures and excessive side effects; fine-grained methods are ineffective; obfuscation-based approaches produce syntactically valid but semantically broken APKs. Moreover, existing evaluations overestimate success by only smoke-testing basic installation and execution, without verifying semantic preservation of the original malicious behavior.
AI.method: DROIDBREAKER provides three key components: (1) query-efficient white-box and black-box attacks that target only the most influential APK components for the victim model; (2) a suite of fine-grained, build-safe manipulations (injection and obfuscation of API calls, app modules, permissions, and URLs) designed to minimize side-effect features; and (3) a semantics-preserving functionality test that enforces runtime equivalence by comparing execution logs and API-level traces between the original and modified APK.
AI.result: Evaluated on a recent Android application corpus, DROIDBREAKER achieves high evasion rates with few queries and minimal side effects in both white-box and black-box settings, and drastically reduces detections by commercial malware scanners on VirusTotal.
AI.conclusion: DROIDBREAKER demonstrates that practical, build-safe, and semantics-preserving problem-space attacks are feasible, overcoming the key shortcomings of prior work and posing a more realistic threat to both machine-learning-based and commercial Android malware detectors.

title: Soft Token Alignment for Cross-Lingual Reasoning
summary: Multilingual large language models often produce inconsistent reasoning and answers for semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. Prior work suggests that intermediate representations can be relatively language-agnostic, but generation becomes increasingly language-specific as models commit to discrete output tokens. This is problematic because language-specific lexical choices can cause semantically equivalent reasoning paths to diverge across languages. These divergences motivate searching for a cross-lingual alignment signal that is less tied to any single vocabulary item or script. We propose SOLAR, an auxiliary objective for supervised fine-tuning that aligns soft-token representations across languages, using English as a pivot. Soft tokens are probability-weighted mixtures over the vocabulary embeddings, yielding continuous representations that can aggregate information from semantically related tokens across languages. We then align each non-English soft-token summary to its English counterpart in the shared embedding space. Across four multilingual reasoning benchmarks, SOLAR improves accuracy by up to +17.7 points over the base model and +3.8 over standard supervised fine-tuning, with the largest gains on low-resource languages. SOLAR also strengthens final-layer cross-lingual similarity and substantially reduces language-cluster separability, suggesting that aligning soft-token representations helps preserve shared semantic structure during multilingual reasoning.

AI.tldr: SOLAR aligns soft-token representations across languages using English as a pivot during supervised fine-tuning, improving multilingual reasoning accuracy by up to +17.7 points, with largest gains on low-resource languages.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLMs produce inconsistent reasoning for semantically equivalent prompts across languages because language-specific lexical choices cause reasoning paths to diverge. An alignment signal that is less tied to any single vocabulary item is needed to preserve shared semantic structure.
AI.method: SOLAR introduces an auxiliary objective for supervised fine-tuning that aligns soft-token representations (probability-weighted mixtures over vocabulary embeddings) across languages, using English as a pivot. Each non-English soft-token summary is aligned to its English counterpart in the shared embedding space.
AI.result: Across four multilingual reasoning benchmarks, SOLAR improves accuracy by up to +17.7 points over the base model and +3.8 over standard supervised fine-tuning. It strengthens final-layer cross-lingual similarity and reduces language-cluster separability, with the largest gains on low-resource languages.
AI.conclusion: Aligning soft-token representations helps preserve shared semantic structure during multilingual reasoning, effectively mitigating cross-lingual inconsistency in LLM generation.

title: Beyond Objects
summary: A core principle of object orientation -- that the functionality of a system can be partitioned amongst objects that correspond to individuals in the problem domain -- has influenced how software has been specified, designed and implemented for more than fifty years. Later developments in software engineering sought to build on this principle. But in fact this partitioning is neither natural nor straightforward, and the problems that these later developments sought to mitigate -- the fragmentation and conflation of functionality -- were often, in fact, the inevitable consequences of this founding principle. An easier path to addressing these problems therefore starts by going back, abandoning object orientation, and replacing it with an alternative approach that decouples the individuals of the problem domain from the modules that partition functionality.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that object orientation's foundational principle of partitioning functionality by domain individuals is fundamentally flawed, as it inevitably leads to functionality fragmentation and conflation. The proposed solution is to abandon OO entirely and adopt an alternative that decouples domain individuals from functional modules.
AI.motivation: To challenge the long-standing assumption that organizing software around domain entities (the core of OO) is natural or desirable, and to demonstrate that later software engineering remedies (e.g., aspect-oriented programming, design patterns) merely address symptoms of a deeper, inherent problem with the object-oriented paradigm itself.
AI.method: Conceptual and historical analysis: the paper critically examines the 50+ year legacy of object orientation, traces how its founding principle causes fragmentation (scattered functionality) and conflation (tangled concerns), and argues that subsequent mitigations fail because they leave the root cause intact.
AI.result: The analysis concludes that functionality fragmentation and conflation are not accidental side-effects but inevitable consequences of partitioning by domain individuals. Attempts to patch OO are therefore inherently limited; only a paradigm shift away from OO can resolve these issues.
AI.conclusion: The paper advocates retroactively abandoning object orientation in favor of an alternative modularization approach that separates problem-domain individuals from functional partitioning, offering a simpler path to resolving long-standing software design problems.

title: EMA-FS: Accelerating GBDT Training via Gain-Informed Feature Screening
summary:
Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT), exemplified by LightGBM, spend a dominant fraction of training time -- typically 65-70% -- constructing per-feature histograms. Existing approaches such as random feature subsampling (feature_fraction) discard features without regard for their predictive utility. We propose EMA-based Feature Screening (EMA-FS), an algorithm-level optimization that maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) of per-feature split gains across boosting iterations and, after a short warmup, restricts histogram construction to the top-K features ranked by historical gain. Unlike random subsampling, EMA-FS is informed: it retains high-gain features while screening out low-gain ones. Operating at the per-tree level, it preserves full compatibility with LightGBM's histogram subtraction trick, requiring no changes to core routines.
  We evaluate EMA-FS on datasets spanning financial fraud detection, advertising click-through prediction, industrial quality control, and synthetic benchmarks, with feature dimensionalities from 29 to 968. On dense, moderate-to-high-dimensional data it achieves significant speedups: 2.61x on a 500-feature synthetic benchmark and 1.45x on the 432-feature IEEE-CIS Fraud dataset at 30% retention. At 70% retention it improves AUC by 0.11 points while delivering a 1.34x speedup. On extremely sparse data (Bosch, >90% missing) it yields no speedup, as LightGBM's sparse bin optimization already bypasses empty values.
  We further introduce Stochastic EMA-FS (S-EMA-FS), which replaces deterministic top-K selection with gain-weighted random sampling controlled by a concentration parameter beta, unifying deterministic EMA-FS (beta -> infinity) and random subsampling (beta = 0) in one framework. Both are implemented in ~120 lines of C++ across all six LightGBM tree learners and are fully backward-compatible.

AI.tldr: EMA-FS accelerates GBDT training by using historical split gains to selectively build histograms only for high-utility features, achieving up to 2.61x speedup on dense data while maintaining or improving AUC. A stochastic variant (S-EMA-FS) unifies deterministic selection and random subsampling under one framework.
AI.motivation: GBDT training (e.g., LightGBM) spends 65–70% of time constructing per-feature histograms. Existing feature subsampling (feature_fraction) discards features uniformly at random, ignoring their predictive value. This wastes computation on low-gain features and risks discarding important ones.
AI.method: EMA-FS tracks an exponential moving average of per-feature split gains across boosting iterations. After a warmup period, only the top-K features (ranked by historical gain) have histograms built. This operates per-tree, preserving compatibility with LightGBM's histogram subtraction trick. S-EMA-FS extends this by replacing deterministic top-K with gain-weighted random sampling governed by a concentration parameter β, where β→∞ yields deterministic selection and β=0 yields uniform random subsampling. Implementation requires ~120 lines of C++ across all six LightGBM tree learners.
AI.result: On a 500-feature synthetic benchmark, EMA-FS achieves 2.61x speedup at 30% retention. On the 432-feature IEEE-CIS Fraud dataset, it achieves 1.45x speedup at 30% retention and improves AUC by 0.11 points with a 1.34x speedup at 70% retention. On extremely sparse data (Bosch, >90% missing), no speedup is observed since LightGBM's sparse bin optimization already bypasses empty values.
AI.conclusion: EMA-FS provides an informed, gain-based alternative to random feature subsampling, delivering significant training speedups on dense, moderate-to-high-dimensional data with negligible AUC degradation or even improvements. Its stochastic variant offers a tunable spectrum between exploration and exploitation. The method is lightweight, backward-compatible, and ineffective only where existing sparse optimizations already dominate.

title: Estimating Uncertainty in Classifier Performance with Applications to Large Language Models and Nested Data
summary: Researchers increasingly use text classification--supervised models or large language models--to measure constructs from natural language, providing metrics such as recall and precision as evidence of their validity. Yet, though these metrics are point estimates subject to sampling variation, measures of uncertainty are inconsistently reported alongside them. Further, when they are reported, they are often estimated with methods that are not appropriate when relevant labelled datasets are small or performance is high. To increase and improve confidence interval reporting in the field, this paper evaluates confidence interval methods for performance metrics under conditions typical of social science text classification: small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals. Across simulations, default methods such as the Wald interval and the basic percentile bootstrap are the least accurate, with coverage sometimes far below the nominal 95% level. Accuracy is improved with the use of Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap (which is particularly relevant to the calculation of F1). When texts are nested within individuals, we demonstrate that adjustment for both effective N and the appropriate degrees of freedom is necessary for producing accurate analytic intervals. Among bootstrap intervals, the hierarchical bootstrap is more accurate than the cluster bootstrap when individuals produce a moderate number of texts but overly conservative when individuals produce only a few. By providing guidance to the field on appropriate interval estimation, we aim to improve the transparency of machine learning applications, and to encourage greater attention to the validation sample size at the design stage.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates confidence interval methods for text classification performance metrics (precision, recall, F1) under conditions typical of social science: small samples, rare constructs, and nested data. It finds default methods (Wald, basic bootstrap) unreliable, recommends alternatives (Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, pseudo-count regularized bootstrap), and provides guidance on handling hierarchical data structures.
AI.motivation: In social science text classification, researchers report point estimates like recall and precision as validity evidence but inconsistently report uncertainty measures. When confidence intervals are reported, they often use methods inappropriate for small labeled datasets or high-performance settings. The paper aims to improve interval estimation practices and encourage greater attention to validation sample size at the design stage.
AI.method: The authors conduct simulation studies evaluating confidence interval methods across conditions: small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals. They compare analytic intervals (Wald, Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson) and bootstrap methods (basic percentile, cluster, hierarchical, pseudo-count regularized bootstrap), assessing coverage relative to the nominal 95% level. They also examine adjustments for effective sample size and degrees of freedom in clustered data.
AI.result: Default methods (Wald interval, basic percentile bootstrap) are least accurate, with coverage often far below 95%. Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap improve accuracy, with the latter particularly relevant for F1. For nested data, adjusting for both effective N and appropriate degrees of freedom is necessary for accurate analytic intervals. The hierarchical bootstrap outperforms the cluster bootstrap when individuals produce moderate texts but becomes overly conservative with few texts per individual.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides practical guidance for selecting confidence interval methods in text classification validation, recommending specific alternatives to default approaches. It calls for improved transparency in machine learning applications within social science, emphasizing that appropriate uncertainty quantification and adequate validation sample sizes should be priorities at the research design stage.

title: Urban Context and Travel Experience Events: An Exploratory Comparison of Two German Cities
summary: The presented study investigates events influencing public transportation experience in both urban (Hamburg) and rural (Tuttlingen) areas in Germany, with the aim of identifying events that affect travel experience and as a result travel behavior. Using a mobile application, 21 participants in Tuttlingen and 70 participants in Hamburg tracked everyday trips, providing real-time evaluations of travel experiences along with situational data. Multi-level regression analyses were applied to assess the impact of events such as punctuality, capacity offer, information about public transportation and others on the ontrip experience. Results indicate that a sufficient public transportation capacity offer has the strongest positive effect in Tuttlingen, whereas a lack of punctuality and low personal well-being have the strongest negative effects. In Hamburg, a lack of punctuality and a negative information event have the largest impacts. These identified effects provide a foundation for decision-making and measures to improve local public transportation.

AI.tldr: A mobile app-based study in Hamburg (urban) and Tuttlingen (rural), Germany, used multi-level regression to identify key events affecting public transportation experience: capacity offer matters most positively in rural areas, while punctuality deficits and poor information dominate negative impacts in urban settings.
AI.motivation: To identify specific events during public transportation journeys that influence travel experience and, consequently, travel behavior, comparing urban versus rural contexts to inform targeted improvement measures.
AI.method: 21 participants in Tuttlingen (rural) and 70 in Hamburg (urban) used a mobile app to track everyday trips, providing real-time evaluations of on-trip experiences and situational data. Multi-level regression analyses assessed the impact of events (punctuality, capacity offer, information, personal well-being, etc.) on travel experience.
