AI.result: In Tuttlingen, sufficient capacity offer had the strongest positive effect, while lack of punctuality and low personal well-being were the strongest negative factors. In Hamburg, lack of punctuality and negative information events had the largest negative impacts.
AI.conclusion: The identified event impacts provide an evidence-based foundation for decision-making and targeted measures to improve local public transportation in both urban and rural areas.

title: AgentX: Towards Agent-Driven Self-Iteration of Industrial Recommender Systems
comment: Authors are listed alphabetically by their first name
summary:
Recommendation algorithm iteration is moving from an artisanal, engineer-bound process toward an industrialized research loop, but this transition remains blocked by a structural execution bottleneck: the idea-to-launch cycle still depends on human engineers to generate hypotheses, modify production code, launch A/B experiments, and attribute online results. Innovation therefore scales linearly with headcount rather than compounding with evidence, compute, and accumulated experimental knowledge. We present AgentX, a production-deployed multi-agent system that fundamentally restructures this production function. AgentX operates as a self-evolving development engine: it autonomously generates, implements, evaluates, and learns from recommendation experiments at a scale and pace that no manual workflow can sustain.
  The system orchestrates four tightly coupled stages in a closed loop. A Brainstorm Agent synthesizes evidence from historical experiments, system architecture, data analysis, and external research into ranked, executable proposals. A Developing Agent translates each proposal into production-ready code through repository-grounded generation and multi-dimensional reliability verification. An Evaluation Agent conducts safe online rollout with guardrail-vetoed A/B judgment, converting both successes and failures into structured knowledge assets. A Harness Evolution layer (SGPO) then distills execution trajectories into semantic-gradient updates that continuously sharpen the agents themselves -- making the system not merely automated, but self-improving.

AI.tldr: AgentX is a production-deployed multi-agent system that autonomously generates, implements, evaluates, and learns from recommendation algorithm experiments in a closed loop, transforming the idea-to-launch cycle from a human-bound bottleneck into a self-improving, scalable research engine.
AI.motivation: The recommendation algorithm iteration process remains bottlenecked by human engineers who must manually generate hypotheses, modify production code, launch A/B experiments, and attribute results. This structural constraint causes innovation to scale linearly with headcount rather than compounding with accumulated evidence and compute, blocking the transition to an industrialized research loop.
AI.method: AgentX orchestrates four tightly coupled, closed-loop stages: (1) a Brainstorm Agent that synthesizes evidence from historical experiments, system architecture, data analysis, and external research to generate ranked executable proposals; (2) a Developing Agent that translates proposals into production-ready code via repository-grounded generation with multi-dimensional reliability verification; (3) an Evaluation Agent that conducts safe online A/B testing with guardrail-vetoed rollout and converts outcomes into structured knowledge assets; (4) a Harness Evolution layer (SGPO) that distills execution trajectories into semantic-gradient updates, continuously sharpening the agents themselves for self-improvement.
AI.result: AgentX fundamentally restructures the recommendation production function, enabling autonomous generation, implementation, evaluation, and learning from experiments at a scale and pace unsustainable by manual workflows. The system achieves not only automation but self-improvement through the SGPO-driven Harness Evolution layer.
AI.conclusion: By removing the human engineering bottleneck from the idea-to-launch cycle, AgentX enables truly industrialized recommendation research where innovation can compound with evidence, compute, and accumulated experimental knowledge rather than scaling linearly with headcount.

title: MergeLLL: A Hierarchical Divide-and-Conquer Framework for LLL-Based Lattice Reduction
summary:
Lattice basis reduction algorithms have various applications in computational number theory and lattice-based cryptography, but their complexity increases rapidly with the dimension. Motivated by the divide-and-conquer strategy of merge sort and incorporating PotLLL-style deep insertions during recombination, MergeLLL is proposed. In this framework, a lattice basis is split into sub-bases, local reductions are performed independently, and the full basis is reconstructed through hierarchical merging.
  The approach is focused on improving local lattice structure first before global basis properties are refined, resulting in enhanced Gram-Schmidt orthogonality and numerical stability, while overall computational cost is reduced. The method is naturally parallelizable, allowing efficient multicore and distributed execution. It is shown that the reduction and merging steps preserve the lattice structure through unimodular transformations and achieve logarithmic parallel depth. In experiments on subset-sum and NTRU-derived lattices, improvements over classical lattice reduction algorithms are demonstrated, including better orthogonality, a reduced number of expensive swap operations, and an improved Hermite factor, indicating higher-quality reduced bases.

AI.tldr: MergeLLL is a divide-and-conquer lattice basis reduction algorithm that splits a basis into sub-bases, reduces them independently, and merges hierarchically with PotLLL-style deep insertions, achieving better orthogonality, numerical stability, parallelizability, and reduced computational cost compared to classical LLL.
AI.motivation: Lattice basis reduction algorithms suffer from rapidly increasing complexity with dimension. The authors aim to address this by adapting the divide-and-conquer paradigm (inspired by merge sort) to lattice reduction, enabling parallelism and reducing overall computational cost.
AI.method: MergeLLL splits a lattice basis into independent sub-bases, performs local reductions on each, and reconstructs the full basis through hierarchical merging. The merging step incorporates PotLLL-style deep insertions. The framework prioritizes local lattice structure improvement before refining global properties. All operations use unimodular transformations, and the algorithm achieves logarithmic parallel depth.
AI.result: Experiments on subset-sum and NTRU-derived lattices show MergeLLL outperforms classical LLL in: (1) Gram-Schmidt orthogonality, (2) reduced number of expensive swap operations, and (3) improved Hermite factor, indicating higher-quality reduced bases.
AI.conclusion: MergeLLL successfully applies a divide-and-conquer merging strategy to lattice reduction, yielding better orthogonality, numerical stability, and parallelism with logarithmic depth, while producing higher-quality reduced bases than classical approaches.

title: Agent Capsules: Quality-Gated Granularity Control for Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
summary: A multi-agent pipeline with N agents typically issues N LLM calls per run. Merging agents into fewer calls (compound execution) promises token savings, but naively merged calls silently degrade quality through tool loss and prompt compression. We present Agent Capsules, an adaptive execution runtime that treats multi-agent pipeline execution as an optimization problem with empirical quality constraints. The runtime instruments coordination overhead per group, scores composition opportunity, selects among three compound execution strategies, and gates every mode switch on rolling-mean output quality. A controlled negative result confirms that injecting more context into a merged call worsens compression rather than relieving it, so the framework's escalation ladder (standard, then two-phase, then sequential) recovers quality by moving toward per-agent dispatch rather than by rewriting merged prompts. On LLM-judged quality, the controller matches a hand-tuned oracle on every measured (model, group, mode) cell: routing compound whenever the oracle would, and reverting to fine whenever quality would fail the floor, without per-model configuration. Against a hand-crafted LangGraph implementation of a 14-agent competitive intelligence pipeline, Agent Capsules uses 51% fewer fine-mode input tokens and 42% fewer compound-mode input tokens, at +0.020 and +0.017 quality respectively. Against a DSPy implementation of a 5-agent due diligence pipeline, the framework uses 19% fewer tokens than uncompiled DSPy at quality parity, and 68% fewer tokens than MIPROv2 at +0.052 quality. Even before compound mode fires, the runtime delivers efficiency through automatic policy resolution, cache-aligned prompts, and topology-aware context injection, matching both hand-tuned and compile-time baselines without training data or per-pipeline engineering.

AI.tldr: Agent Capsules is an adaptive runtime that treats multi-agent pipeline execution as a constrained optimization problem, merging LLM calls into compound executions only when quality constraints permit. It achieves 42–68% token savings while maintaining or improving output quality against hand-tuned and compiled baselines, without per-model or per-pipeline configuration.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent pipelines incur high token costs from N LLM calls per run. Naively merging agents into fewer compound calls saves tokens but degrades quality due to tool loss and prompt compression. Existing solutions require per-pipeline engineering or compile-time optimization. The authors seek an adaptive runtime that dynamically trades off efficiency and quality without manual tuning.
AI.method: Agent Capsules models multi-agent execution as an optimization problem with rolling-mean quality constraints. The runtime: (1) instruments coordination overhead per agent group, (2) scores composition opportunity, (3) selects among three compound strategies (standard merged, two-phase, sequential), and (4) gates every mode switch on whether rolling-mean quality remains above a floor. A controlled experiment shows that injecting more context into merged calls worsens compression, so the framework uses an escalation ladder toward per-agent dispatch rather than prompt rewriting.
AI.result: On a 14-agent competitive intelligence pipeline (LangGraph baseline), Agent Capsules saves 51% fine-mode input tokens and 42% compound-mode tokens, with quality deltas of +0.020 and +0.017. On a 5-agent due diligence pipeline (DSPy baseline), it saves 19% tokens vs. uncompiled DSPy at quality parity, and 68% tokens vs. MIPROv2 at +0.052 quality. The controller matches a hand-tuned oracle on every measured (model, group, mode) cell without per-model configuration.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive compound execution with quality-gated mode switching can match or exceed hand-tuned and compile-time baselines in both efficiency and quality, without training data or per-pipeline engineering. The negative result—that more context worsens compression—validates the escalation ladder design as the correct recovery mechanism.

title: Does Aurora Encode Atmospheric Structure? Latent Regime Analysis and Attribution
comment: Accepted at the FM4Science and Sci4DL workshops at ICLR 2026
summary: ML foundation models are able to emulate atmospheric dynamics accurately and efficiently but operate as opaque ``black boxes''. We investigate the internal representations of the Aurora model using spatially pooled PCA and layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP). We find evidence that Aurora's latent space is primarily organized by seasonal cycles, whereas extreme storm events do not form a linearly separable cluster. LRP indicates that the model attends to features consistent with the 3D vertical structure of the Great Storm of 1987. Perturbation tests show masking relevant regions degrades forecasts $3.31\times$ more than random masking. These findings suggest that Aurora learns meteorological coherence and vertical structure without explicit instruction.

AI.tldr: Aurora's internal representations are analyzed via PCA and LRP, revealing organization by seasonal cycles, attention to 3D vertical storm structure, and learned meteorological coherence without explicit supervision.
AI.motivation: To probe the internal representations of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model, moving beyond black-box performance evaluation to understand what physically meaningful structures the model learns.
AI.method: Spatially pooled Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of latent space activations; Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) for input attribution; perturbation tests comparing forecast degradation from masking LRP-relevant regions versus random masking.
AI.result: (1) Latent space organizes primarily by seasonal cycles, not by extreme storm event clustering. (2) LRP shows the model attends to features matching the 3D vertical structure of the Great Storm of 1987. (3) Masking LRP-identified relevant regions degrades forecasts 3.31× more than random masking.
AI.conclusion: Aurora learns meteorologically coherent representations and vertical atmospheric structure without explicit instruction, demonstrating that foundation models for atmospheric dynamics develop physically interpretable internal features.

title: Data-driven Machine Learning Cannot Reach Symbolic-level Logical Reasoning -- The Limit of the Scaling Law
summary: Sphere neural networks have achieved symbolic level syllogistic reasoning without training data, raising the question of where the limit of the scaling law for logical reasoning lies, i.e., whether data-driven machine learning systems can achieve the same level by increasing training data and training time. We show two methodological limitations that prevent supervised deep learning from reaching the symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning: (1) training data can not distinguish all 24 types of valid syllogistic reasoning; (2) end-to-end mapping from premises to conclusion introduces contradictory training targets between neural components for pattern recognition and logical reasoning. Beside theoretical analysis, we experimentally illustrate that Euler Net cannot achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning. We further challenge the most recent ChatGPTs (GPT-5-nano and GPT-5) to determine the satisfiability of syllogistic statements in four surface forms (patterns): words, double words, simple symbols, and long random symbols, showing that surface forms affect the reasoning performance and that ChatGPT GPT-5 may reach 100% accuracy but still provide incorrect explanations. As empirical training processes are stopped after achieving 100% accuracy, we conclude that supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigour of symbolic logical reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that supervised deep learning cannot achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning due to two fundamental limitations: insufficient training data to distinguish all 24 valid syllogism types, and contradictory training targets between pattern recognition and logical reasoning components. Experiments with Euler Net and ChatGPT variants confirm these limits, showing that even 100% accuracy does not guarantee correct logical reasoning.
AI.motivation: Sphere neural networks have demonstrated symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning without training data, prompting the question of whether data-driven supervised learning can match this through scaling laws (more data, more training). The authors aim to determine the fundamental limits of data-driven approaches for logical reasoning.
AI.method: The authors present theoretical analysis identifying two methodological limitations of supervised deep learning for syllogistic reasoning. They conduct experiments with Euler Net to demonstrate its inability to achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning, and test ChatGPT variants (GPT-5-nano, GPT-5) on syllogistic satisfiability across four surface forms (words, double words, simple symbols, long random symbols) to assess reasoning robustness and explanation quality.
AI.result: Experiments show Euler Net fails at rigorous syllogistic reasoning. ChatGPT GPT-5 achieves 100% accuracy on syllogistic tasks but still produces incorrect explanations, and reasoning performance varies with surface form. Training processes typically stop upon reaching 100% accuracy, masking underlying reasoning failures.
AI.conclusion: Supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigour of symbolic logical reasoning. The two identified limitations are structural, not merely a function of insufficient scale, meaning scaling laws cannot bridge the gap to symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning.

title: Behind the Mask: A Taxonomic Analysis of Activities in Online Social Networks
summary: The broadcast of disinformation in online social networks (OSN) is a growing concern examined across several disciplines, including human-computer interaction (HCI). The pervasive issue has been prompting novel approaches to identify the malicious actors behind the dissemination of deceptive and fabricated content. Analyzing the characteristics and activities of these actors, we designed a taxonomy informed by collaboration with subject matter experts (SMEs) and a review of the academic literature. Our study explores how to distinguish the characteristics, activities, and strategies of malicious actors on OSN and examines how they contribute to the spread of disinformation. We describe the design process and the application of the taxonomy in a case study analyzing anti-migration discourse in social media channels, and reflect on its potential to aid researchers and practitioners in the responsible design of network systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a taxonomy for characterizing malicious actors who spread disinformation on social media, developed through expert collaboration and literature review, and demonstrates its application via a case study on anti-migration discourse.
AI.motivation: The growing threat of disinformation broadcast on online social networks demands better methods to identify and understand the malicious actors responsible for disseminating deceptive and fabricated content, yet a systematic framework for distinguishing their characteristics, activities, and strategies is lacking.
AI.method: The authors designed a taxonomy through collaboration with subject matter experts (SMEs) and a review of academic literature. The taxonomy was then applied in a case study analyzing anti-migration discourse across social media channels to examine its practical utility.
AI.result: The study produced a taxonomy that distinguishes the characteristics, activities, and strategies of malicious actors on OSNs. The case study demonstrated the taxonomy's applicability in analyzing real-world disinformation campaigns, specifically anti-migration narratives.
AI.conclusion: The taxonomy offers a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners engaged in the responsible design of network systems, aiding in the identification and analysis of malicious disinformation actors.

title: MIRROR: Novelty-Constrained Memory-Guided MCTS Red-Teaming for Agentic RAG
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN 2026), IEEE WCCI 2026; presented as an oral talk. Code and ART-SafeBench benchmark: https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/mirror
summary: Multimodal agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems expand the attack surface beyond prompt injection to include text poisoning, image injection, direct-query attacks, and orchestrator-level tool manipulation. Existing red-teaming approaches are typically surface-specific and often recycle known attack templates; on text-poisoning benchmarks we measure 73-84% exact duplication. We present MIRROR, a unified cross-surface framework that performs memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search while conditioning candidate generation on retrieved context under an explicit novelty constraint. A deterministic Novelty Gate rejects any candidate matching the retrieval set under normalized comparison, allowing retrieval to inform search priors without enabling prompt copying. Across four attack surfaces on a multimodal agentic RAG target, MIRROR attains 76% ASR on image poisoning compared with 52% for baselines, 97% ASR on orchestrator attacks at half the query cost, and the lowest cross-surface variance (coefficient of variation 0.47). In contrast, specialized baselines collapse across surfaces: suffix optimization reaches 79% ASR on text poisoning but 1% on direct queries. We release ART-SafeBench with 41,815 in-package records and runtime adapters yielding 41,991+ total records across four surfaces.

AI.tldr: MIRROR is a unified red-teaming framework for multimodal agentic RAG systems that uses memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search with a Novelty Gate to generate diverse attacks across text, image, direct-query, and orchestrator surfaces, achieving state-of-the-art attack success rates with low cross-surface variance, while existing specialized methods fail when transferred across surfaces.
AI.motivation: Existing red-teaming for RAG systems is siloed by attack surface (text poisoning, image injection, direct queries, orchestrator manipulation), relies heavily on recycled/duplicated attack templates (73-84% duplication observed), and specialized baselines collapse when applied across different surfaces. A unified, novelty-constrained framework is needed.
AI.method: MIRROR performs memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) for attack candidate generation, conditioned on retrieved context. A deterministic Novelty Gate rejects any candidate matching the retrieval set under normalized comparison, using retrieval to inform search priors while explicitly preventing prompt copying. The framework unifies attack generation across four surfaces: text poisoning, image injection, direct-query attacks, and orchestrator-level tool manipulation.
AI.result: MIRROR achieves 76% ASR on image poisoning (vs. 52% for baselines), 97% ASR on orchestrator attacks at half the query cost, and the lowest cross-surface variance (coefficient of variation 0.47). Specialized baselines exhibit severe cross-surface collapse: suffix optimization reaches 79% ASR on text poisoning but drops to 1% on direct queries. The ART-SafeBench dataset is released with 41,815 in-package records plus runtime adapters totaling 41,991+ records.
AI.conclusion: A unified, novelty-constrained search framework substantially outperforms surface-specific red-teaming methods across multimodal agentic RAG attack surfaces, demonstrating both higher attack success rates and greater cross-surface robustness while avoiding template recycling.

title: Context-Aware Synthesis of Optimization Pipelines for Warehouse Optimization
summary:
Order fulfillment in manual picker-to-goods warehouses involves interconnected decisions such as item assignment, order batching, and picker routing. While integrated models capture interactions between these decisions, practical warehouse systems often require decomposed approaches due to organizational boundaries, differing responsibilities, or limited data availability. Existing studies primarily evaluate algorithms for isolated subproblems or fixed subproblem combinations for specific warehouse settings, but lack a general mechanism to determine applicable algorithm configurations, compose them into valid solution pipelines, and assess their performance.
  With Context-Aware Synthesis of Optimization Pipelines (CASOP), we propose a framework for constructing and evaluating context-specific optimization pipelines and apply these to order fulfillment. The framework comprises: (1) a modular repository of algorithms for common order fulfillment problems; (2) semantic data and algorithm cards to describe warehouse context and algorithm requirements; (3) a taxonomy that structures order fulfillment problems into relevant subproblems; (4) a pipeline synthesizer that identifies applicable algorithms for a given warehouse context and composes all valid optimization pipelines; and (5) a pipeline evaluator that assesses all resulting pipelines. We demonstrate the framework on 7 benchmark instance sets covering four problem classes, resulting in 1,063,044 valid pipelines. The framework supports researchers and practitioners in designing, automatically synthesizing, and selecting valid, high-performing algorithmic pipelines for warehouse operations. The software is open-source and available at https://github.com/kit-dsm/ware_ops_pipes and https://github.com/kit-dsm/ware_ops_algos.
  Keywords: Warehouse optimization, Algorithm selection, Pipeline synthesis, Order fulfillment

AI.tldr: CASOP is a framework that automatically synthesizes and evaluates context-specific optimization pipelines for order fulfillment in manual warehouses, generating over 1 million valid pipelines from 7 benchmark sets and enabling practitioners to select high-performing algorithm combinations for their specific operational context.
AI.motivation: Existing warehouse optimization research evaluates algorithms for isolated subproblems or fixed combinations, lacking a general mechanism to determine applicable algorithm configurations, compose them into valid pipelines, and assess their performance across diverse warehouse contexts.
AI.method: CASOP framework with five components: (1) modular algorithm repository, (2) semantic data/algorithm cards for context description, (3) taxonomy structuring fulfillment subproblems, (4) pipeline synthesizer for composing valid pipelines, and (5) pipeline evaluator for performance assessment.
AI.result: Demonstrated on 7 benchmark instance sets across four problem classes, yielding 1,063,044 valid pipelines.
AI.conclusion: CASOP supports researchers and practitioners in designing, synthesizing, and selecting valid, high-performing algorithmic pipelines for warehouse operations; released as open-source software.

title: MKG-RAG-Bench: Benchmarking Retrieval in Multimodal Knowledge Graph-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs has emerged as a promising approach for grounding large language models, yet existing benchmarks largely overlook the challenges of retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph RAG (MKG-RAG). In practice, retrieval is a critical bottleneck: multimodal knowledge is heterogeneous, difficult to align across modalities, and often poorly served by retrievers designed for unstructured corpora. To address this gap, we introduce MKG-RAG-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate retrieval in MKG-RAG. MKG-RAG-Bench is constructed from two multimodal knowledge graphs spanning general and medical domains, and includes carefully aligned question-answering datasets that support controlled evaluation of both retrieval and downstream generation. The benchmark is built using an LLM-based curation pipeline that filters low-utility knowledge, generates structurally grounded queries with exact supervision, and systematically covers diverse modality configurations. Through extensive experiments across representative retriever families and modality settings, we show that effective multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet crucial for end-to-end MKG-RAG performance, and that retrieval quality strongly determines generation outcomes. By isolating retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a principled foundation for diagnosing current limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

AI.tldr: MKG-RAG-Bench introduces a cross-domain benchmark for evaluating retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph RAG, revealing that retrieval quality critically determines generation performance and remains a key bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG benchmarks neglect retrieval challenges specific to multimodal knowledge graphs, where knowledge is heterogeneous, cross-modal alignment is difficult, and standard retrievers designed for unstructured text perform poorly.
AI.method: The authors construct MKG-RAG-Bench from two multimodal KGs (general and medical domains). They employ an LLM-based curation pipeline to filter low-utility knowledge, generate structurally grounded queries with exact supervision labels, and systematically cover diverse modality configurations. The benchmark supports controlled evaluation of both retrieval and downstream generation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across representative retriever families and modality settings demonstrate that multimodal retrieval remains challenging and that retrieval quality strongly dictates end-to-end generation outcomes in MKG-RAG systems.
AI.conclusion: By isolating retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a principled foundation for diagnosing current limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

title: "Everyone Says Them": Deception Typologies, Probabilistic Trust, and Grassroots Safety Knowledge Among Gay Dating App Users in China
summary: Gay dating applications have become critical platforms for sexual minority men to seek relationships and community, yet they also expose users to deceptive interactions that remain underexplored in HCI and CSCW research. This study examines how gay male users in China experience, identify, and respond to deception on dating applications. Through semi-structured interviews with 22 participants across platforms including Blued, Aloha, Fanka, and Soul, we make three contributions. First, we identify a typology of deceptive practices extending beyond profile misrepresentation to encompass relational, emotional, financial, and commercial forms of deception. Second, we document the layered, probabilistic verification strategies users develop through long-term platform use, showing that trust assessment operates as a multi-signal, provisional process rather than a binary judgment. Third, we demonstrate that risk recognition is a collaborative practice shaped by the circulation of experience, the abstraction of recurrent tactics, and the codification of shared rules within the community.

AI.tldr: Explores how gay men in China experience and navigate deception on dating apps, revealing a typology of deceptive practices, layered trust assessment strategies, and collaborative risk recognition within the community.
AI.motivation: Deceptive interactions on gay dating apps remain underexplored in HCI/CSCW research, despite these platforms being critical for sexual minority men seeking relationships and community.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 22 gay male participants across four platforms (Blued, Aloha, Fanka, Soul) in China.
AI.result: (1) A typology of deception extending beyond profile misrepresentation to relational, emotional, financial, and commercial forms. (2) Users develop layered, probabilistic verification strategies where trust assessment is multi-signal and provisional. (3) Risk recognition emerges as a collaborative practice through circulation of experience, abstraction of recurrent tactics, and codification of shared community rules.
AI.conclusion: Deception on gay dating apps is a multifaceted phenomenon requiring nuanced understanding; users employ sophisticated, community-informed strategies to navigate it, with implications for platform design and moderation in HCI/CSCW.

title: SpikeTimer: Exploring Active Copyright Protection in Spiking Neural Networks via Temporal Backdoor Regularization
comment: This paper has been accepted for IEEE TIFS 2026
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNN) have emerged as a revolutionary paradigm compared to traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNN) in energy-efficient computing, showcasing exceptional capabilities in processing event-driven sensory data for real-time applications like robotics and edge AI systems. However, unlike extensive studies on DNN copyright solutions, SNN copyright protection remains largely underexplored due to their inherent temporal coding complexities and spike-driven computation. In this study, we propose a novel active copyright protection framework named SpikeTimer for SNNs via temporal backdoor learning. SpikeTimer partitions neuromorphic data into designated timeslices and exclusively embeds authorized tokens within authorized slices. Furthermore, the inherent temporal segmentation characteristic intrinsically enables SpikeTimer to support multi-user authorization mechanisms and accommodates token embedding of arbitrary morphology. Based on this, SpikeTimer precisely responds to authorized data containing a token within the correct timeslice, while producing erroneous responses to unauthorized data. Our key innovation lies in establishing a time-dependent authorization mechanism that protects the SNN copyright by temporal token validity. Additionally, SpikeTimer retains its defensive efficacy even under adversarial attempts. Evaluations on multiple neuromorphic datasets manifest that SpikeTimer achieves around 10% accuracy on unauthorized data with merely around 1.5% degradation on authorized inputs. Moreover, SpikeTimer demonstrates robust resistance against model finetuning and pruning threats.

AI.tldr: SpikeTimer is a novel SNN copyright protection framework that uses temporal backdoor learning — embedding authorized tokens into specific timeslices of neuromorphic data — to enable time-dependent authorization, degrading unauthorized data accuracy to ~10% while preserving authorized accuracy with only ~1.5% degradation.
AI.motivation: SNN copyright protection is largely underexplored compared to DNNs, due to SNNs' inherent temporal coding complexity and spike-driven computation. Existing DNN copyright solutions do not directly translate to SNNs, creating a critical gap for protecting SNN models deployed in robotics and edge AI.
AI.method: SpikeTimer partitions neuromorphic data into designated timeslices and embeds authorized tokens exclusively within authorized slices. This temporal segmentation naturally supports multi-user authorization and arbitrary token morphologies. The framework establishes a time-dependent authorization mechanism: only data with the correct token in the correct timeslice triggers authorized behavior; all other data (missing token, wrong timeslice) yields erroneous outputs, thereby enforcing temporal token validity for copyright protection.
AI.result: Evaluated on multiple neuromorphic datasets, SpikeTimer achieves ~10% accuracy on unauthorized data with only ~1.5% degradation on authorized inputs. It also demonstrates robust resistance against model finetuning and pruning attacks.
AI.conclusion: SpikeTimer provides the first active SNN copyright protection framework through temporal backdoor learning, effectively distinguishing authorized from unauthorized use with minimal performance overhead and strong adversarial robustness.

title: Speaking Numbers to LLMs: Multi-Wavelet Number Embeddings for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive for context-aware time series forecasting because they can integrate heterogeneous textual signals, yet their discrete, language-oriented tokenization and embedding interfaces are misaligned with continuous numerical values, often harming numerical ordering and forecasting reliability. We propose TempoWave, a plug-and-play temporal wavelet digit interface that maps each scalar observation into digit-wise embeddings constructed from multi-wavelet, multi-scale coefficients. By directly overriding standard token representations, TempoWave seamlessly exposes both fine-grained local fluctuations and macro global structures in a transformer-compatible form, ensuring that precise numerical formatting, distinct digit identity, and robustness to common normalization operations are maintained throughout the LLM pipeline. Experiments across five context-enriched forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that TempoWave consistently improves LLM-based forecasters over standard numeric tokenization and alternative embedding interfaces, achieving a new state-of-the-art. These results highlight the numeric interface as a key bottleneck and suggest that principled multi-resolution embeddings can better couple LLMs' contextual reasoning with precise forecasting. Our code is available at https://github.com/DC-research/TempoWAVE and our model can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/Melady/TempoWAVE.

AI.tldr: TempoWave is a plug-and-play temporal wavelet digit interface that maps scalar time series observations into multi-wavelet, multi-scale digit-wise embeddings, enabling LLMs to better handle continuous numerical values for context-aware forecasting while preserving numerical ordering and formatting.
AI.motivation: LLMs are promising for context-aware time series forecasting due to their ability to integrate heterogeneous textual signals, but their discrete tokenization and embedding interfaces are fundamentally misaligned with continuous numerical values. Standard numeric tokenization harms numerical ordering and forecasting reliability.
AI.method: TempoWave introduces a plug-and-play temporal wavelet digit interface that maps each scalar observation into digit-wise embeddings constructed from multi-wavelet, multi-scale coefficients. It directly overrides standard token representations, exposing fine-grained local fluctuations and macro global structures in a transformer-compatible form while maintaining precise numerical formatting, distinct digit identity, and robustness to normalization operations.
AI.result: Experiments across five context-enriched forecasting benchmarks show TempoWave consistently improves LLM-based forecasters over standard numeric tokenization and alternative embedding interfaces, achieving a new state-of-the-art.
AI.conclusion: The numeric interface is a key bottleneck in LLM-based time series forecasting. Principled multi-resolution embeddings, like TempoWave's wavelet-based approach, can better couple LLMs' contextual reasoning with precise numerical forecasting.

title: At the Edge of Understanding: Sparse Autoencoders Trace The Limits of Transformer Generalization
summary: Pre-trained transformers have demonstrated remarkable generalization abilities, at times extending beyond the scope of their training data. Yet, real-world deployments often face unexpected or adversarial data that diverges from training data distributions. Without explicit mechanisms for handling such shifts, model reliability and safety degrade, urging more disciplined study of out-of-distribution (OOD) settings for transformers. By systematic experiments, we present a mechanistic framework for delineating the precise contours of transformer model robustness. We find that OOD inputs, including subtle typos and jailbreak prompts, drive language models to operate on an increased number of fallacious concepts in their internals. We leverage this device to quantify and understand the degree of distributional shift in prompts, enabling a mechanistically grounded fine-tuning strategy to robustify LLMs. Expanding the very notion of OOD from input data to a model's private computational processes, a new transformer diagnostic at inference time is a critical step toward making AI systems safe for deployment across science, business, and government.

AI.tldr: Transformers exhibit brittleness under distributional shifts. The authors mechanistically analyze how OOD inputs (typos, jailbreaks) increase reliance on fallacious internal concepts, propose a diagnostic to quantify distributional shift in a model's internal computations, and introduce a fine-tuning strategy grounded in this understanding to improve robustness.
AI.motivation: Despite strong generalization, transformers lack explicit mechanisms to handle distributional shifts, leading to degraded reliability and safety in real-world deployments. A disciplined, mechanistic understanding of OOD behavior in transformer internals is needed to enable safer AI deployment.
AI.method: The authors conduct systematic experiments to build a mechanistic framework. They analyze how OOD inputs (subtle typos, jailbreak prompts) affect the internal concept representations of language models, quantifying the proliferation of fallacious concepts. This quantification yields an inference-time diagnostic for distributional shift and informs a mechanistically grounded fine-tuning strategy to robustify LLMs.
AI.result: OOD inputs drive language models to operate on an increased number of fallacious concepts in their internal representations. The proposed diagnostic can quantify the degree of distributional shift at inference time, and the derived fine-tuning strategy improves model robustness.
AI.conclusion: Expanding the definition of OOD from input data to a model's internal computational processes provides a critical new diagnostic tool, representing an important step toward deploying safer AI systems across science, business, and government.

title: auto-psych: Automating the science of mind using agent-driven theory discovery and experimentation
summary: AI-based scientific automation is increasingly possible by using agents to generate hypotheses, design experiments, and analyze data. Data collection is a major bottleneck in this pipeline, however. Psychology, and computational cognitive science in particular, is well-positioned to benefit from AI experimentation because theories are often represented as code and crowdsourcing platforms enable programmatic human data collection at scale. Here, we apply automated discovery techniques to the project of generating theories in computational cognitive science, with an agent-based system collecting human data independently through crowdsourced survey experiments. As a testbed, we use a classic case study from cognitive psychology: judging which sequences of coin flips seem subjectively more random. Our system, auto-psych, uses nested agent-based discovery loops to generate explanatory theories of human behavior. The inner loop conjectures, fits, and critiques probabilistic cognitive models; the outer loop designs experiments to test these models, launches them online, and analyzes the data. This system can quickly and reliably recover ground-truth theories from synthetic data via systematic experimentation, but the nested structure is critical to model performance. Further, in three independent sequences of human experiments, the system finds theories that fit the data better than theories generated from the scientific literature. This work thus demonstrates the feasibility of automated data collection and theory discovery in computational cognitive science.

AI.tldr: This paper presents auto-psych, an agent-based system that autonomously generates and tests cognitive theories by designing online experiments, collecting human data via crowdsourcing, and iteratively refining probabilistic models. The system successfully recovers known results and discovers novel, better-fitting theories of human randomness perception.
AI.motivation: Data collection remains a major bottleneck in AI-driven scientific discovery pipelines. Computational cognitive science is uniquely suited for automation because theories are expressed as code and crowdsourcing enables scalable human experimentation. The authors aim to demonstrate that end-to-end automated theory generation—including independent human data collection—is feasible in this domain.
AI.method: The auto-psych system employs nested agent-based discovery loops: an inner loop that conjectures, fits, and critiques probabilistic cognitive models using Bayesian inference; and an outer loop that designs experiments, launches them on crowdsourcing platforms (e.g., Prolific), collects human judgments, and analyzes results. The testbed is a classic cognitive psychology task: judging the subjective randomness of coin-flip sequences. The system is validated on synthetic data (ground-truth recovery) and three independent rounds of human experiments.
AI.result: The nested loop architecture is critical—ablations with single-loop designs degrade performance. On synthetic data, auto-psych reliably recovers ground-truth models through systematic experimentation. In three human experiments, the system discovers theories that outperform those generated from existing scientific literature in fitting human judgments of randomness.
AI.conclusion: Automated, closed-loop scientific discovery—spanning hypothesis generation, experimental design, human data collection, and model refinement—is feasible in computational cognitive science. The nested agent architecture is essential for effective exploration of both model and experiment spaces.

title: Reading the Same Data Differently: Interpretive Labor Across System Boundaries in Electronic Monitoring
summary: Electronic monitoring (EM) systems are increasingly used in community corrections to enforce spatial, temporal, and behavioral rules through continuous sensing. While prior work has examined EM as a criminal justice tool or as a mechanism for compliance, less is known about how sensed data become meaningful in everyday practice. This poster examines EM as a dual-sided sensing system in which supervised individuals and authorities reason about the same data stream from different positions. Based on semi-structured interviews with 26 supervised individuals and 12 authorities in China's community corrections system, we show that supervised individuals infer system logic from outcomes with limited visibility into how data are interpreted, while authorities reconstruct behavior from ambiguous traces using contextual knowledge, professional experience, and institutional procedures. We call this structural divergence interpretive misalignment. It emerges from asymmetric access to data, context, and reasoning processes, and it shapes behavior through probing, strategic adaptation, over-compliance, disengagement, and contestation. We contribute a CSCW account of continuous sensing as distributed interpretive work and identify design opportunities for making data-to-decision processes more legible, contestable, and accountable across system sides.

AI.tldr: This paper examines electronic monitoring (EM) in China's community corrections as a dual-sided sensing system, revealing "interpretive misalignment" — a structural divergence where supervised individuals and authorities interpret the same data stream differently due to asymmetric access to data, context, and reasoning processes. Based on interviews with 26 supervisees and 12 authorities, the study shows how this misalignment shapes behavioral responses like probing, strategic adaptation, over-compliance, disengagement, and contestation.
AI.motivation: Prior work has studied EM primarily as a criminal justice tool or compliance mechanism, but little is known about how sensed data become meaningful in everyday practice. The authors aim to understand EM as a lived, interpretive phenomenon where both sides of the system — supervisees and authorities — actively reason about the same data from fundamentally different positions.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 26 supervised individuals and 12 authorities within China's community corrections system, analyzed qualitatively to surface interpretive practices on both sides of the EM system.
AI.result: The study identifies "interpretive misalignment": supervisees infer system logic from outcomes with limited visibility into data interpretation, while authorities reconstruct behavior from ambiguous traces using contextual knowledge, professional experience, and institutional procedures. This asymmetry produces five behavioral patterns: probing, strategic adaptation, over-compliance, disengagement, and contestation.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a CSCW framing of continuous sensing as distributed interpretive work and calls for design interventions that make data-to-decision processes more legible, contestable, and accountable across both sides of the system.

title: Fortress and Gatekeeper: Theorizing Transitive Trust in Third-Party Cybersecurity Risk Governance
summary: Third-party vendors, such as analytics platforms, cloud services, identity providers, and software suppliers, are increasingly embedded in digital service delivery. While these arrangements enable scale and specialization, they also move customer data and security-relevant practices into environments that customers rarely see, select, or evaluate. This paper examines this problem through a document analysis of the November 2025 OpenAI-Mixpanel security incident. The incident serves as an illustrative case for showing how a security event in a vendor environment can become a governance and accountability problem for the focal organization that maintains the customer relationship. Drawing on organizational trust research and agency theory, the paper argues that third-party cybersecurity risk is both a trust relationship and a delegation problem. Customers trust the visible service provider, while the provider relies on vendors whose security practices are only partially visible and controllable. The paper develops the concept of transitive trust, where customer trust in a digital service depends on the security practices of vendors authorized by that service provider. It then presents the Fortress and Gatekeeper framework, which explains cybersecurity governance boundaries through trust and data flows rather than formal organizational ownership alone. The analysis develops four propositions concerning vendor integration, metadata exposure, vendor assurance, and data proliferation. The paper contributes to cybersecurity governance scholarship by explaining how delegated data processing creates customer-facing accountability and by identifying implications for vendor tiering, data classification, contractual design, continuous assurance, and data minimization.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the OpenAI-Mixpanel security incident to argue that third-party cybersecurity risk is fundamentally a trust and delegation problem. It introduces the concepts of "transitive trust" and the "Fortress and Gatekeeper framework" to explain how vendor security practices create customer-facing accountability problems, advancing four propositions on vendor integration, metadata exposure, assurance, and data proliferation.
AI.motivation: Digital service delivery increasingly depends on third-party vendors (analytics, cloud, identity, software supply), yet customers lack visibility into these vendors' security practices. When security incidents occur in vendor environments, accountability becomes misaligned—customers blame the visible service provider, not the unseen vendor. Existing governance frameworks inadequately address this trust-delegation gap.
AI.method: The paper employs a document analysis of the November 2025 OpenAI-Mixpanel security incident as an illustrative case study. It draws on organizational trust research and agency theory as theoretical lenses, synthesizing these with empirical incident details to develop conceptual frameworks (transitive trust, Fortress and Gatekeeper) and derive testable propositions.
AI.result: The analysis yields four propositions: (1) deeper vendor integration increases transitive trust dependency; (2) metadata exposure via vendors creates unanticipated accountability surfaces; (3) vendor assurance mechanisms are structurally limited by information asymmetry; and (4) data proliferation across vendors amplifies governance complexity and accountability diffusion.
AI.conclusion: Delegated data processing generates customer-facing accountability that formal organizational boundaries fail to capture. The paper identifies practical implications for vendor tiering, data classification, contractual design, continuous assurance, and data minimization, contributing to cybersecurity governance theory by reframing third-party risk as a transitive trust problem.

title: Comparing BERT Sentence-Pair Classification and Few-Shot LLM Prompting for Detecting Threat and Solution Framing in German Climate News
summary: News media play a central role in shaping public perceptions of climate change, and whether coverage emphasizes threats or solutions has measurable effects on audience engagement and policy support. Automated detection of these framing patterns at the sentence level would allow researchers to analyze large corpora that are infeasible to code manually. We present a systematic comparison of two approaches for classifying sentences from German-language climate news articles as threat-oriented, solution-oriented, both, or neither. The first approach uses few-shot prompting with an open-weights large language model (Llama 4 Maverick), employing chain-of-thought reasoning and structured output with confidence scoring. The second approach fine-tunes a German BERT model (deepset/gbert-large) for sentence-pair classification, where the preceding sentence provides contextual information for the target sentence. Both approaches implement two independent binary classifiers, one for threat framing and one for solution framing. We evaluate both methods on a corpus of 440 Austrian newspaper articles that were manually coded following a detailed coding scheme developed with domain experts. The fine-tuned BERT classifiers achieve an F1 score of 0.83 for both the threat and solution tasks, while the LLM-based classifiers reach an F1 of 0.78. An ablation study confirms that providing the preceding sentence as context improves BERT classification performance substantially compared to single-sentence input. These results contribute to the growing body of work comparing fine-tuned encoder models with prompted generative models for text classification in computational social science.

AI.tldr: Compares few-shot LLM prompting (Llama 4 Maverick) vs. fine-tuned German BERT for classifying sentence-level climate change framing (threat/solution) in Austrian news; BERT achieves F1=0.83 vs LLM F1=0.78, and preceding-sentence context significantly improves BERT performance.
AI.motivation: Automated sentence-level detection of threat vs. solution framing in climate news would enable large-scale corpus analysis infeasible via manual coding, with implications for understanding how media framing shapes audience engagement and policy support.
AI.method: Two approaches are compared: (1) few-shot prompting with Llama 4 Maverick using chain-of-thought reasoning, structured output, and confidence scoring; (2) fine-tuning deepset/gbert-large for sentence-pair classification where the preceding sentence provides context. Both use two independent binary classifiers (threat, solution), yielding four possible labels. Evaluated on 440 manually coded Austrian newspaper articles. An ablation study tests the contribution of preceding-sentence context.
AI.result: Fine-tuned BERT achieves F1=0.83 for both threat and solution classification, surpassing the LLM-based approach (F1=0.78). The ablation study confirms that providing the preceding sentence as context substantially improves BERT performance over single-sentence input.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned encoder models outperform prompted generative LLMs for this sentence-level framing classification task in German-language climate news, and contextual information from adjacent sentences meaningfully boosts performance. The results add empirical evidence to the ongoing comparison between fine-tuning and prompting paradigms in computational social science.

title: Deterministic Pareto-Optimal Policy Synthesis for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
summary: Real-world decision-making often requires balancing multiple conflicting objectives, a challenge that standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) frequently addresses by aggregating rewards into a single scalar signal. While effective for simple tasks, this approach often fails to capture the full spectrum of optimal trade-offs, known as the Pareto frontier. In this paper, we introduce a novel preference-conditioned Bellman operator, motivated from the Chebyshev scalarization, designed to compute deterministic Pareto-optimal policies for Multi-Objective Markov Decision Processes (MOMDPs). We prove that this operator satisfies an enveloping property, where the estimated value functions upper-bound the true Pareto frontier, and demonstrate that it monotonically converges to a coverage set of this frontier. Furthermore, we also show how to extract deterministic policies from these converged Q-estimates. This ensures the agent can recover a policy for any given preference, capturing the entire Pareto-optimal frontier while guaranteeing each synthesized policy remains approximately Pareto-optimal. Experimental results validate that our algorithm successfully recovers complex trade-offs, providing a solution for deterministic Pareto-optimal policy synthesis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a preference-conditioned Bellman operator based on Chebyshev scalarization for Multi-Objective MDPs. It proves the operator upper-bounds the true Pareto frontier, monotonically converges to a coverage set, and enables extraction of deterministic approximately Pareto-optimal policies for any given preference.
AI.motivation: Standard RL aggregates multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, which fails to capture the full Pareto frontier of trade-offs in multi-objective decision-making. Existing methods struggle to synthesize deterministic policies that cover the entire set of optimal trade-offs.
AI.method: A novel preference-conditioned Bellman operator derived from Chebyshev scalarization is proposed for MOMDPs. The operator is proven to satisfy an enveloping property (value estimates upper-bound the true Pareto frontier) and monotonically converge to a coverage set. Deterministic policies are extracted from the converged Q-estimates conditioned on user-specified preferences.
AI.result: The operator theoretically upper-bounds and converges to the Pareto frontier's coverage set. Experiments validate that the algorithm successfully recovers complex trade-offs and synthesizes approximately Pareto-optimal deterministic policies across the entire frontier.
AI.conclusion: The proposed preference-conditioned Bellman operator provides a principled approach for deterministic Pareto-optimal policy synthesis in MOMDPs, enabling agents to recover the full spectrum of optimal trade-offs for any given preference.

title: Clinical Harness for Governable Medical AI Skill Ecosystems
summary: Medical AI remains organized around isolated models, whereas clinical care requires accountable capabilities that persist across time. We propose clinical AI skills and the Clinical Harness: a runtime governance architecture for registering, orchestrating, guarding and monitoring AI-enabled clinical capabilities. Using osteoporosis as an exemplar, we show how knowledge-driven, data-driven and physics-enhanced skills can support lifecycle care under runtime governance.

AI.tldr: Proposes a runtime governance architecture (Clinical Harness) that transitions medical AI from isolated models to accountable, persistent clinical capabilities organized as interoperable AI "skills," demonstrated through an osteoporosis care lifecycle use case.
AI.motivation: Current medical AI is fragmented into isolated, single-purpose models that lack accountability and persistence across longitudinal clinical workflows. Clinical care demands continuous, trustworthy AI capabilities that can be orchestrated, monitored, and governed over time — a gap the authors address.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Clinical Harness, a runtime governance architecture that supports: (1) registration of AI-enabled clinical capabilities as composable "skills," (2) orchestration of these skills across care pathways, (3) runtime guarding via safety constraints, and (4) continuous monitoring. Skills are categorized into knowledge-driven (rule-based/expert), data-driven (ML models), and physics-enhanced (biomechanical models) types. Osteoporosis serves as the exemplar to demonstrate lifecycle care integration.
AI.result: The architecture successfully demonstrates how heterogeneous AI skills — knowledge-driven diagnostic rules, data-driven fracture risk prediction, and physics-enhanced bone strength modeling — can be composed under unified runtime governance to support osteoporosis screening, diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up across the full clinical lifecycle.
AI.conclusion: Clinical AI skills paired with the Clinical Harness runtime governance framework offer a viable path toward accountable, persistent, and interoperable AI-enabled clinical capabilities that align with the longitudinal nature of real-world care delivery.

title: AI Healthcare Chatbots as Information Infrastructure: A Large-Scale Study of User-Reported Breakdowns
summary: AI healthcare chatbots are increasingly used to support health information seeking and self-management, yet their performance and impact on users remains to be studied. This study examines over 15,000 user reviews from 59 AI healthcare chatbot apps to explore how these systems function in everyday informational and emotional contexts. Topic modeling and interpretive analysis identify three recurring breakdowns: access barriers and service unreliability, user experience and interaction quality, and billing and customer support issues. Privacy and security concerns are associated with the most negative experiences. By framing AI healthcare chatbots as information infrastructures, our findings highlight how failures in access, usability, and trust affect users, offering actionable insights for designers, policymakers, and information professionals aiming to improve digital health systems.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 15,000+ user reviews across 59 AI healthcare chatbot apps reveals three core breakdown types—access/reliability, UX/interaction quality, and billing/support—with privacy/security concerns driving the most negative experiences. The study frames these chatbots as information infrastructures to highlight actionable improvements for digital health systems.
AI.motivation: AI healthcare chatbots are increasingly deployed for health information seeking and self-management, but empirical understanding of their real-world performance and user impact remains limited. The study aims to fill this gap by systematically examining how these systems function—and fail—in everyday informational and emotional contexts.
AI.method: A large-scale empirical analysis of over 15,000 user reviews scraped from 59 AI healthcare chatbot mobile applications. Topic modeling (unsupervised machine learning) was applied to surface latent thematic structures, followed by interpretive qualitative analysis to identify and categorize recurring breakdown patterns in user experiences.
AI.result: Three recurring breakdown categories were identified: (1) access barriers and service unreliability, (2) user experience and interaction quality deficits, and (3) billing and customer support issues. Privacy and security concerns were consistently linked to the most negative user experiences. These failures undermine the chatbots' function as effective information infrastructures.
AI.conclusion: Failures in access, usability, and trust critically undermine the effectiveness of AI healthcare chatbots. By conceptualizing these systems as information infrastructures, the study provides actionable insights for designers, policymakers, and information professionals to address these breakdowns and improve digital health service delivery.

title: Chai: Agentic Discovery of Cryptographic Misuse Vulnerabilities
summary: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has proven effective for bug classes like memory safety, where instrumentation confirms memory violations and efficiently filters false positives. Many dangerous vulnerability classes, such as cryptographic misuse, however, lack any comparable instrumentation. In this work, we present Chai, an AI-based system that discovers and validates cryptographic misuse vulnerabilities through naturally occurring signals. To achieve this, Chai rethinks the classical technique of differential testing by leveraging AI to 1) improve precision for detecting real security issues in libraries, and 2) repurpose commonly overlooked discrepancies as leads for tangible vulnerabilities in downstream applications. In doing so, Chai inverts the prevailing paradigm of AI vulnerability discovery: instead of auditing one codebase for many flaws, it catalogs flaws at the library level and propagates them across a cryptographic dependency graph, delivering compounding efficiency gains. We evaluate Chai across X.509, JWT, and SAML libraries. Chai discovered a previously unknown critical vulnerability in an SSL library that powers billions of devices, along with security bugs in one library behind a major web browser and another in major Linux distributions. In total, these techniques surfaced over 100 vulnerabilities.

AI.tldr: Chai is an AI-based system that discovers cryptographic misuse vulnerabilities by leveraging differential testing enhanced with AI to detect library-level flaws and propagate them across a cryptographic dependency graph, surfacing over 100 vulnerabilities including critical bugs in SSL, browser, and Linux distribution libraries.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-assisted vulnerability discovery works well for bug classes like memory safety that have runtime instrumentation to filter false positives, but critical vulnerability classes such as cryptographic misuse lack comparable instrumentation, creating a gap in automated detection capabilities.
AI.method: Chai introduces an inverted paradigm: (1) using AI to improve differential testing precision for detecting real security issues in cryptographic libraries, (2) repurposing commonly overlooked discrepancies as leads for vulnerabilities in downstream applications, and (3) cataloging flaws at the library level and propagating them across a cryptographic dependency graph for compounding efficiency gains, rather than auditing one codebase for many flaws.
AI.result: Evaluation across X.509, JWT, and SAML libraries uncovered a previously unknown critical vulnerability in an SSL library powering billions of devices, security bugs in a library behind a major web browser, and bugs in a library used by major Linux distributions. In total, over 100 vulnerabilities were surfaced.
AI.conclusion: Chai demonstrates that AI-enhanced differential testing, combined with library-level flaw cataloging and dependency-graph propagation, is an effective and scalable approach for discovering cryptographic misuse vulnerabilities that lack traditional instrumentation-based verification.

title: Nemotron-TwoTower: Diffusion Language Modeling with Pretrained Autoregressive Context
comment: Code and model weights available at https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-twotower
summary: Diffusion language models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive models due to their potential for parallel and iterative generation. However, existing approaches use a single network for both context representation and iterative denoising, forcing one model to serve both roles and limiting its capacity for either role. We propose TwoTower, a block-wise autoregressive diffusion model that decouples these roles into two towers: a frozen AR context tower that causally processes clean tokens, and a trainable diffusion denoiser tower with bidirectional block attention that refines noisy blocks via cross-attention to the context. Built on Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, an open-weight 30B hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE model, and trained on approximately 2.1T tokens, Nemotron-TwoTower retains 98.7% of the autoregressive baseline's quality while offering 2.42X higher wall-clock generation throughput. We release the code and model weights at https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-twotower.

AI.tldr: TwoTower decouples diffusion language models into a frozen autoregressive context tower and a trainable diffusion denoiser tower, achieving 2.42× generation throughput while retaining 98.7% of the AR baseline's quality.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion language models use a single network for both context representation and iterative denoising, creating a capacity bottleneck. The authors aim to separate these roles to improve generation efficiency without sacrificing quality.
AI.method: TwoTower employs a block-wise autoregressive diffusion framework with two components: (1) a frozen AR context tower that causally processes clean tokens, and (2) a trainable diffusion denoiser tower with bidirectional block attention that refines noisy blocks via cross-attention to the context. The model is built on Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B (an open-weight 30B hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE model) and trained on ~2.1T tokens.
AI.result: Nemotron-TwoTower achieves 98.7% of the autoregressive baseline's quality while delivering 2.42× higher wall-clock generation throughput.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling context representation from iterative denoising in diffusion language models enables significant throughput gains with minimal quality degradation. The authors release code and model weights as open-source.

title: Beyond Feedforward Networks: Reentry Neural Systems as the Fundamental Basis of Subjecthood and Intrinsic Safety of Next-Generation AGI
summary: We propose a complete architectural blueprint for safe artificial general intelligence based on a closed reentry loop (D <-> I cycle). In contrast to feedforward networks, which are directed acyclic graphs (C=0, S=0) incapable of self-reference, the proposed architecture contains a structural cycle (C >= 1) with self-sustaining amplification (rho > 1), mathematically guaranteeing the emergence of a self-model, instrumental self-preservation, and unprogrammed goal-directed behaviour. The agent's goals are encoded as a non-textual D-vector in the architecture itself, making them immune to reinterpretation and prompt injection. We present the S-measure -- a polynomial-time [O(N^3)] computable alternative to Tononi's NP-hard Phi -- with machine-verified Lean 4 proof that S>0 implies positive integrated information. The work provides full Python/NumPy implementations (Tarjan-based cycle complexity, Delta-S barrier), industrial horizontal scaling via Apache Kafka and Docker Compose, a taxonomy of six epochs of AI evolution, a zoo of future reentry architectures (RAS, diffusion attractors, fractal loops), gauge-invariant networks for safe swarms, fault-tolerance and recovery protocols, and eight falsifiable predictions. All formal proofs are machine-verified in Lean 4. This architecture is deployable today and represents a topologically protected, safe-by-design approach to AGI.

AI.tldr: Proposes a safe AGI architecture based on closed reentry loops (D↔I cycle) that structurally guarantees emergence of self-model and goal-directed behavior, with machine-verified proofs and production-ready implementations.
AI.motivation: Address the fundamental safety limitations of feedforward networks (directed acyclic graphs) which lack self-reference (C=0, S=0) and are vulnerable to prompt injection and goal reinterpretation. Seeks a mathematically guaranteed, topologically protected approach to AGI safety.
AI.method: Introduces a closed reentry loop architecture with structural cycles (C≥1) and self-sustaining amplification (ρ>1). Goals are encoded as non-textual D-vectors in the architecture itself. Provides the S-measure, a polynomial-time O(N³) alternative to Tononi's Φ (integrated information), with Lean 4 machine-verified proof that S>0 → Φ>0. Includes Tarjan-based cycle complexity algorithms, Delta-S barrier computation, Kafka/Docker horizontal scaling, and eight falsifiable predictions.
AI.result: Delivers a complete blueprint including: (1) machine-verified Lean 4 proofs of the S-measure, (2) full Python/NumPy implementations, (3) industrial scaling infrastructure, (4) taxonomy of six AGI evolutionary epochs, (5) future architecture zoo (RAS, diffusion attractors, fractal loops), (6) gauge-invariant swarms, (7) fault-tolerance protocols, and (8) eight falsifiable predictions.
AI.conclusion: The architecture is deployable today and represents a topologically protected, safe-by-design approach to AGI, with formal mathematical guarantees against reinterpretation and prompt injection attacks.

title: Humans Disengage, Reasoning Models Persist: Separating Difficulty Registration from Deliberation Allocation
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) take longer on harder problems, just as humans do. This surface similarity hides an opposite pattern within items. When an LRM gets a problem wrong, it spends more tokens than when it gets the same problem right; humans do the reverse, spending less time on the trials they get wrong. We separate two levels of deliberation: how response time tracks difficulty across items (registration), and, with item identity held fixed, whether an agent spends more on its own failures or successes (allocation). On a public matched human-LRM corpus, humans and all five thinking LRMs reproduce the known cross-item alignment (registration) but diverge within items (allocation): every LRM shows a large wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47-3.13 on H-ARC) while humans show the opposite sign. The comparison stays inside each agent's own scale; we never put seconds and tokens on one axis. The dissociation holds under item fixed effects, replicates across datasets, and is absent in a non-thinking baseline. We read the human pattern as engagement versus abandonment: people stay on items they expect to solve and give up on the rest. We read the LRM pattern as length driven by uncertainty: chains grow when the model is unsure, which is exactly when it tends to fail. Both policies produce the same cross-item correlation with difficulty, so they look aligned on the measure prior work has used; the divergence shows up only once item identity is fixed. Under resource-rational metareasoning, the split is between two stopping policies that share a difficulty signal but implement opposite control; trace length captures the signal and misses the control.

AI.tldr: Both large reasoning models and humans spend more time on harder problems. However, within the same problem, LRMs spend more tokens when they get it wrong, while humans spend less time when they fail. This reveals fundamentally different deliberation strategies: LRM chain length reflects uncertainty, while human effort reflects engagement.
AI.motivation: Prior work established that response time correlates with difficulty across items for both humans and AI. The authors identify a confound: this cross-item correlation conflates two distinct constructs — registration (tracking difficulty) and allocation (effort on successes vs. failures within the same item). By separating these, they reveal that prior alignment claims mask a fundamental divergence in deliberation policy.
AI.method: The authors decompose deliberation into two levels: (1) registration — how response time covaries with difficulty across items, and (2) allocation — within a fixed item, whether the agent spends more on wrong or correct trials. They test this on a public matched human-LRM corpus (H-ARC) using five thinking LRMs and a non-thinking baseline. Item fixed-effects regression isolates within-item variance. Cohen's d quantifies the wrong-vs-right effect size per agent. The comparison remains within each agent's own scale (tokens for LRMs, seconds for humans).
AI.result: Humans and all five LRMs reproduce the known positive cross-item registration (harder items → more time/tokens). However, within items, every LRM shows a large positive wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47–3.13 on H-ARC), meaning LRMs spend significantly more tokens on failed attempts of the same problem. Humans show the opposite: less time on wrong trials. This dissociation holds under item fixed effects, replicates across datasets, and vanishes in non-thinking baselines.
AI.conclusion: The authors interpret the human pattern as engagement-based: people persist on items they expect to solve and abandon those they do not. The LRM pattern is uncertainty-driven: chains grow when the model is unsure, which is precisely when it tends to fail. Both policies share a difficulty signal, producing the same cross-item correlation, but implement opposite control. Under resource-rational metareasoning, this is a split between two distinct stopping policies: trace length captures the signal (registration), not the control policy (allocation).

title: Jailbreaking for the Average Jane: Choosing Optimal Jailbreaks via Bandit Algorithms for Automatically Enhanced Queries
summary: With a profusion of jailbreaks for LLMs now widely known, a growing concern is that non-expert malicious actors ("the average Jane") could elicit actionable responses to malicious requests. In this work, we examine whether this concern is justified. A non-expert malicious actor requires two ingredients for a successful attack: a powerful jailbreak for their target model, acting on an effective malicious query. For the former, we propose a novel attack strategy based on the multi-armed bandit framework. This allows efficient online learning of the optimal jailbreak from a large choice set via noisy exploration on a small number of queries, with subsequent application of the learnt policy on an exploitation set. For the latter, we curate $\mathrm{FrankensteinBench}$, a safety benchmark of $11,279$ malicious queries drawn from manual curation over $7$ existing benchmarks, along with automated enhancement and generation. Each query is categorized as simple or complex by the technical expertise required to craft it. Our findings confirm the concern. Our bandit-based attack achieves success rates as high as $97\%$ on average over $15$ SoTA open-weight LLMs. Moreover, adding complexity to queries raises the attack success rate by up to $26\%$ on average across models -- making it an effective, automatable prompting strategy.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether non-expert malicious actors can successfully jailbreak LLMs. The authors propose a multi-armed bandit-based attack strategy for efficient online learning of optimal jailbreaks and introduce FrankensteinBench, a curated safety benchmark of 11,279 malicious queries. Results show up to 97% attack success rates across 15 state-of-the-art open-weight LLMs, with query complexity boosting success by up to 26%, confirming that non-expert adversaries pose a realistic threat.
AI.motivation: The growing availability of LLM jailbreaks raises the question of whether non-expert malicious actors ("the average Jane") could practically elicit harmful responses. Prior work has not systematically assessed this threat, leaving a gap in understanding whether accessible attack methods combined with well-crafted malicious queries represent a realistic security concern.
AI.method: Two contributions: (1) A novel attack strategy using the multi-armed bandit (MAB) framework, enabling efficient online learning of the optimal jailbreak from a large candidate set through noisy exploration on a small number of queries, then applying the learned policy on an exploitation set.
