(2) FrankensteinBench, a safety benchmark of 11,279 malicious queries manually curated from 7 existing benchmarks, with automated enhancement and generation. Queries are categorized as simple or complex based on the technical expertise required to craft them.
AI.result: The bandit-based attack achieves average success rates as high as 97% across 15 state-of-the-art open-weight LLMs. Increasing query complexity raises attack success rates by up to 26% on average across models, demonstrating that complex query construction is an effective, automatable prompting strategy for bypassing safety guardrails.
AI.conclusion: The concern about non-expert malicious actors is justified. The combination of an accessible, bandit-optimized jailbreak selection strategy and complexity-enhanced malicious queries enables high success rates against modern open-weight LLMs, highlighting significant gaps in current safety alignment.

title: Temporal Validity in Retrieval Memory: Eliminating Stale-Fact Errors for AI Agents over Evolving Knowledge
comment: 21 pages, 5 tables. Code, prompts, and evaluation datasets included
summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives agents access to accumulated knowledge, but has no model of time. When a fact changes (e.g., a function is renamed or API restructured), RAG retrieves both the stale and current value with near-identical embedding similarity. The agent then either abstains or serves the superseded fact. We show this is a structural problem: on a calibrated dataset, cosine similarity distinguishes a contradicted fact from a duplicated one with AUROC 0.59 (near chance), as contradictions are often more embedding-similar to the original than rephrased duplicates.
  We present MemStrata, a retrieval memory maintaining temporal validity. It stores facts like RAG, preserving static recall, but when a fact's value is contradicted, a deterministic (subject, relation, object) supersession rule retires the stale value in a bi-temporal ledger - with no similarity threshold and no LLM call. Across six benchmarks run locally with a 7B model, MemStrata ties RAG on static knowledge and reaches 0.95-1.00 accuracy on evolving knowledge (where RAG reaches 0.20-0.47). The central result is the stale-fact-error rate: when required to answer, RAG serves superseded values 15-40% of the time; MemStrata drives this to ~0%, a failure class RAG cannot avoid. MemStrata achieves this at retrieval latency (~2.1s) versus ~16-18s for LLM-reranking baselines. We release the harness, datasets, and a marker-free evaluation protocol for memory under knowledge evolution.

AI.tldr: MemStrata introduces a bi-temporal retrieval ledger that deterministically retires superseded facts based on (subject, relation, object) contradictions, eliminating stale-fact errors in RAG systems without LLM reranking overhead.
AI.motivation: RAG systems lack a model of time, so when facts change (e.g., API renames), both stale and current versions are retrieved due to near-identical embeddings. Cosine similarity fails to distinguish contradictions from duplicates (AUROC 0.59), causing agents to serve outdated facts 15–40% of the time.
AI.method: MemStrata stores facts in a bi-temporal ledger. When a new fact contradicts an existing one on the same (subject, relation) pair, a deterministic supersession rule retires the stale value — requiring no similarity threshold and no LLM call. Static recall is preserved alongside temporal validity.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks with a 7B model: MemStrata matches RAG on static knowledge and achieves 0.95–1.00 accuracy on evolving knowledge (vs. RAG's 0.20–0.47). Stale-fact-error rate drops from 15–40% to ~0%. Retrieval latency is ~2.1s versus ~16–18s for LLM-reranking baselines.
AI.conclusion: MemStrata solves a structural failure mode in RAG by adding temporal validity through deterministic supersession, eliminating stale-fact errors with minimal latency cost and no reliance on LLM-based reranking.

title: Otter Weather: Skillful and Computationally Efficient Medium-Range Weather Forecasting
summary: State-of-the-art medium-range AI weather models can outperform traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) but require massive training budgets. This restricts usage for under-resourced groups and severely limits fast model iteration. Here we develop Otter Weather, a highly efficient spatiotemporal forecasting model designed to democratise high-performance weather prediction with AI. Evaluated on ERA5 reanalysis data at 1.5° resolution using standard WeatherBench protocols, the Otter family significantly advances the skill-compute Pareto frontier. The deterministic version outperforms the best NWP baseline by 9.6% at a 24-hour lead time while requiring fewer than 3.5 A100-days for training. It provides a 2x efficiency gain over lightweight AI models and a 100-fold reduction in compute compared to resource-intensive frontier architectures. We extend these efficiency gains into probabilistic forecasting by training via the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). Scaling to a larger architecture, Otter-XL achieves a 9.7% CRPS improvement over the IFS ENS baseline. This yields an almost two-fold increase in predictive skill over comparable lightweight models at similar compute budgets. Otter-XL also outperforms frontier architectures like GenCast by over 2%, while using an order of magnitude less compute. Finally, Otter is applied out-of-the-box to a complex acoustic scattering PDE task where it outperforms a state-of-the-art foundation modelling approach, suggesting that the advances made here might apply across a range of scientific domains.

AI.tldr: Otter Weather is a highly compute-efficient spatiotemporal model for weather prediction that achieves state-of-the-art performance with dramatically reduced training costs. It outperforms NWP baselines and matches/exceeds frontier AI models like GenCast while using 100x less compute, and generalizes to non-weather PDE tasks.
AI.motivation: Current AI weather models achieve excellent performance but require massive training budgets, which restricts access for under-resourced groups and slows down model iteration. The goal is to democratize high-performance AI weather prediction by drastically improving the skill-per-compute trade-off.
AI.method: The authors develop the Otter Weather family of spatiotemporal forecasting models. The deterministic version is trained on ERA5 reanalysis data at 1.5° resolution using WeatherBench protocols. Probabilistic forecasting is enabled by training with the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). A scaled-up variant, Otter-XL, is also introduced. The model is additionally tested out-of-the-box on an acoustic scattering PDE task.
AI.result: The deterministic Otter model outperforms the best NWP baseline by 9.6% at 24-hour lead time with under 3.5 A100-days of training — a 2x efficiency gain over lightweight AI models and 100x reduction versus frontier architectures. Otter-XL achieves a 9.7% CRPS improvement over IFS ENS and outperforms GenCast by over 2% while using an order of magnitude less compute. It also surpasses a state-of-the-art foundation model on an acoustic scattering PDE benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Otter Weather significantly advances the skill-compute Pareto frontier, enabling near-frontier predictive performance at a fraction of the computational cost. The approach generalizes beyond weather to other scientific PDE domains, suggesting broader applicability for efficient spatiotemporal forecasting.

title: NeuraDock Visual Cognitive Load Agent Tutorial: A Quality-Gated Open-Source EEG Workflow for Alpha Dynamics and Real-Time Applications
summary: This tutorial paper provides a step-by-step, reproducible walkthrough of NeuraDock Agent, an open-source EEG agent focused on Alpha dynamics and visual cognitive-load analysis. The goal is practical: a reader should be able to install the agent, run EEG preprocessing and quality control, generate Alpha dynamics figures, perform within-subject Rest/Task visual cognitive-load comparison, run the public mini-dataset analyses and compare them with the reference validation summary, start an online dashboard, call the real-time API from an external application, and use the LLM interpretation layer to explain quality risks. Existing EEG toolkits provide excellent offline analysis, but assembling a real-time, quality-gated cognitive-load pipeline often requires manually bridging acquisition, custom QC, Alpha feature extraction, and a web API; this tutorial closes that offline-to-online gap. The tutorial uses a quality-gated workflow: downstream Alpha and workload metrics are computed only after preprocessing and QC gating rather than directly from raw EEG. In the included mini-dataset validation, the agent processed 18 recordings, generated 10 within-subject comparisons, observed task-related posterior Alpha suppression in 7 of 10 contrasts, estimated initial evidence of within-subject repeatability, and benchmarked local online API latency. The tutorial is intended for researchers, developers, and applied teams who want a transparent path from EEG files to real-time visual cognitive-load prototypes.

AI.tldr: A step-by-step tutorial for NeuraDock Agent, an open-source EEG tool that enables reproducible, quality-gated analysis of Alpha dynamics and visual cognitive-load, bridging the gap from offline preprocessing to real-time API deployment with LLM-based interpretation.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG toolkits excel at offline analysis but lack an integrated pipeline that combines real-time acquisition, automated quality control (QC), Alpha feature extraction, and web API serving. Researchers face a significant gap when transitioning from offline analysis to online, real-time cognitive-load monitoring — requiring manual assembly of disparate components. This tutorial aims to close that offline-to-online gap with a fully reproducible, quality-gated workflow.
AI.method: The tutorial provides a reproducible walkthrough covering: (1) installation and setup, (2) EEG preprocessing and quality control gating, (3) Alpha dynamics figure generation, (4) within-subject Rest vs. Task visual cognitive-load comparisons, (5) public mini-dataset analysis with reference validation, (6) online dashboard initiation, (7) real-time API calls from external applications, and (8) LLM-based interpretation layer for quality risk explanation. Downstream Alpha and workload metrics are computed only after preprocessing and QC gating, ensuring data quality before analysis.
AI.result: In mini-dataset validation, the agent processed 18 recordings and generated 10 within-subject comparisons. Task-related posterior Alpha suppression was observed in 7 of 10 contrasts. The workflow also provided initial evidence of within-subject repeatability and benchmarked local online API latency.
AI.conclusion: NeuraDock Agent successfully demonstrates a transparent, reproducible path from raw EEG files to real-time visual cognitive-load prototypes. It is positioned for researchers, developers, and applied teams seeking an end-to-end quality-gated EEG pipeline with real-time capabilities.

title: Protocol Prying: Systematic Vulnerability Research in the Apple AirDrop and Android Quick Share Proximity Transfer Protocols
summary: Apple AirDrop and Google/Samsung Quick Share are proximity file-transfer protocols used by over five billion devices, yet their application-layer security properties remain largely unstudied because both stacks are proprietary and undocumented. Both protocols are reachable from wireless proximity without any prior pairing and process complex serialized content (binary plists, CPIO archives, Protocol Buffers, UKEY2 handshakes) inside privileged daemons, making them attractive zero-click targets across multiple operating systems. We perform the first cross-platform reverse engineering and protocol-aware fuzzing study of both stacks. We reconstruct AirDrop's seven-layer state machine and DVZip adaptive compression from binary analysis, build AIRFUZZ, a protocol-aware fuzzer that mutates pre-compression representations, and complement it with targeted hand-written analyses of Samsung's Quick Share service and Google's Quick Share for Windows. We discover six vulnerabilities (V1-V6): three pre-authentication issues in macOS/iOS AirDrop (V1: Swift fatalError DoS in the HTTP path router; V2: unbounded XML plist recursion in Foundation; V3: NULL dereference in Network.framework's HTTP/1.1 parser), two protocol-layer flaws in Samsung Quick Share (V4: pre-authentication OfflineFrame dispatch; V5: D2D encryption bypass for three frame types), and a heap use-after-free in Google Quick Share for Windows (V6) for which Google awarded a bounty. We responsibly disclosed all findings, and Apple, Samsung, and Google have acknowledged the reports.

AI.tldr: First cross-platform reverse engineering and protocol-aware fuzzing study of Apple AirDrop and Google/Samsung Quick Share, uncovering six vulnerabilities (DoS, recursion, NULL dereference, protocol flaws, encryption bypass, heap UAF) across macOS/iOS, Samsung Android, and Windows implementations, all responsibly disclosed and acknowledged.
AI.motivation: AirDrop and Quick Share are deployed on over five billion devices, operate over wireless proximity without prior pairing, and process complex serialized content inside privileged daemons — yet their application-layer security properties are unstudied because both protocol stacks are proprietary, closed-source, and undocumented, making them attractive zero-click attack surfaces.
AI.method: Reverse engineering of AirDrop's seven-layer state machine and DVZip adaptive compression from binary analysis; development of AIRFUZZ, a protocol-aware fuzzer that mutates pre-compression representations; targeted manual analysis of Samsung Quick Share (Android) and Google Quick Share (Windows); all complemented by protocol reconstruction.
AI.result: Six vulnerabilities discovered: V1 (Swift fatalError DoS in HTTP path router), V2 (unbounded XML plist recursion in Foundation), V3 (NULL dereference in Network.framework HTTP/1.1 parser) — all pre-authentication in macOS/iOS AirDrop; V4 (pre-auth OfflineFrame dispatch) and V5 (D2D encryption bypass for three frame types) in Samsung Quick Share; V6 (heap use-after-free) in Google Quick Share for Windows, for which Google paid a bounty.
AI.conclusion: Proximity file-transfer protocols represent a significant and understudied zero-click attack surface. Protocol-aware fuzzing combined with reverse engineering is effective at uncovering critical pre-authentication vulnerabilities. All findings were responsibly disclosed and acknowledged by Apple, Samsung, and Google.

title: Assessing Post-Reform Changes in Risk Disclosure Quality with a Multidimensional Text Analysis Approach
comment: The 4th International Conference on Computational and Data Sciences in Economics and Finance (CDEF 2026)
summary: While corporate narrative disclosures provide crucial information to capital markets, comprehensively evaluating their qualitative changes over time remains challenging. Narrative text is inherently multidimensional, meaning that an improvement in one textual dimension often occurs alongside changes in others. To capture these underlying dynamics, we propose a longitudinal text analysis approach combining Japanese-language NLP metric extraction with paired testing, shift function analysis, and inter-metric correlation. Our framework extends prior indicator sets by incorporating a cross-section relevance indicator to measure topical alignment between risk disclosures and management strategies. Applying this approach to evaluate Japan's 2019 disclosure reforms, we analyze 19,770 firm-year observations over a 10-year period (FY2015-FY2024). The joint analysis reveals complex shifts in disclosure patterns that are frequently masked by conventional single-indicator methods. Specifically, we find that while disclosure volume increased substantially, it was accompanied by a decline in readability. Furthermore, although the overall information structure improved, specific descriptive quality stagnated, and the degree of adaptation varied across market segments.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a multi-dimensional longitudinal text analysis framework to assess corporate narrative disclosures, combining Japanese NLP with paired testing, shift functions, and inter-metric correlations. Applied to Japan's 2019 disclosure reforms using 19,770 firm-year observations (FY2015–2024), it reveals that increased disclosure volume came with reduced readability, stagnating descriptive quality, and uneven adaptation across market segments—dynamics often obscured by single-indicator methods.
AI.motivation: Evaluating qualitative changes in corporate narrative disclosures over time is challenging because narrative text is multidimensional—improvements in one dimension often coincide with changes in others. Conventional single-indicator approaches fail to capture these joint dynamics, potentially masking trade-offs and complex shifts that are critical for understanding the real effects of disclosure reforms.
AI.method: The authors propose a longitudinal text analysis framework with four components: (1) Japanese-language NLP metric extraction covering multiple textual dimensions (volume, readability, structure, descriptive quality); (2) a novel cross-section relevance indicator measuring topical alignment between risk disclosures and management strategies; (3) paired testing for temporal comparisons; (4) shift function analysis and inter-metric correlation to capture joint distributional changes. This is applied to 19,770 firm-year observations spanning FY2015–FY2024 to evaluate Japan's 2019 disclosure reforms.
AI.result: The joint analysis uncovers complex, multidimensional shifts: (1) disclosure volume increased substantially post-reform; (2) readability simultaneously declined; (3) overall information structure improved; (4) specific descriptive quality stagnated; and (5) the degree of adaptation varied significantly across market segments. These nuanced patterns are frequently masked when using conventional single-indicator evaluation methods.
AI.conclusion: A multidimensional, joint-distribution approach to longitudinal text analysis is essential for accurately evaluating disclosure reforms. Policymakers and researchers should account for trade-offs across textual dimensions—such as volume versus readability—and for heterogeneous adaptation across market segments when assessing regulatory effectiveness.

title: Rethinking Training & Inference for Forecasting: Linking Winner-Take-All back to GMMs
summary: Trajectory forecasting for autonomous driving has advanced rapidly, yet representative models often produce uninformative posteriors over forecast modes, causing problems for mode pruning. We trace this to a modeling-training mismatch: forecasters are typically modeled as conditional Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) but trained with a winner-take-all (WTA) loss that assigns each sample to its nearest mode. We argue that this K-means-like hard assignment (one-hot), while preventing mode collapse, is the source of uninformative mode probabilities: it over-segments the trajectory space, ignores relatedness among nearby modes, and yields assignment instability under small perturbations. Guided by this lens, we introduce two post-hoc treatments: (1) test-time posterior-weighted merging that aggregates nearby candidate trajectories; and (2) a one-step expectation-maximization (EM) update that replaces hard labels with soft responsibilities, sharing probability mass across neighboring modes. Across several WTA-trained architectures, these lightweight steps produce more informative, faithfully ranked mode posteriors and strengthen final forecasts on popular displacement metrics -- without retraining. Our analysis unifies recent design choices through a GMM-vs-K-means perspective and offers principled, practical corrections that better align training objectives with inference.

AI.tldr: WTA-trained GMM forecasters produce uninformative mode posteriors due to hard assignment; the authors propose post-hoc soft-assignment corrections (posterior-weighted merging and one-step EM) that improve mode ranking and forecast quality without retraining.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art trajectory forecasting models are modeled as conditional GMMs but trained with winner-take-all (WTA) loss. This creates a modeling-training mismatch: the K-means-like hard assignment over-segments trajectory space, ignores relatedness among nearby modes, and yields unstable assignments, leading to uninformative mode probabilities that hinder mode pruning and downstream decision-making.
AI.method: The authors reframe the problem through a GMM-vs-K-means lens and propose two post-hoc, training-free corrections: (1) test-time posterior-weighted merging, which aggregates nearby candidate trajectories using learned mode probabilities as weights; and (2) a one-step expectation-maximization (EM) update that replaces hard WTA labels with soft responsibilities, redistributing probability mass across neighboring modes. Both methods operate on already-trained architectures without retraining.
AI.result: Applied across several WTA-trained architectures, both lightweight post-hoc steps yield more informative, faithfully ranked mode posteriors and improve final forecast performance on standard displacement metrics (e.g., minADE, minFDE), without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The GMM-vs-K-means perspective unifies recent design choices in trajectory forecasting. The proposed principled, practical corrections better align WTA training objectives with GMM inference, offering a simple yet effective way to improve mode posterior quality and forecast accuracy in existing models.

title: Boundary-Aware Context Grounding for A Low-Channel EEG Agent
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) can make scientific software easier to use. However, a general model does not automatically know which measurements a particular sensor can support, which algorithms are implemented in the current software, or which conclusions are justified by a computed result. These distinctions are especially important for low-channel electroencephalography (EEG), where sparse spatial coverage and variable signal quality make plausible but unsupported interpretations easy to produce. We present NeuraDock Agent, an open-source architecture that separates a deterministic local EEG engine from a hardware-aware language layer. The numerical engine parses recordings, performs quality control, executes reviewed spectral workflows, and writes machine-readable artifacts. The LLM receives only a compact, allowlisted summary and a versioned context pack. The context describes the seven-channel hardware, reviewed workflows, result fields, implementation boundaries, scientific limits, and reference cases. Raw EEG and dense per-sample arrays remain local
  We evaluate the system at three levels. First, 12 recordings produced identical structured results over ten numerical repetitions, and a complete Rest/Task run produced identical result, report, and figure hashes over three repetitions. Second, request-capture and failure-injection experiments confirmed the tested data boundary and preservation of local artifacts under HTTP, malformed-output, and connection failures. Third, a boundary-awareness benchmark tested 36 ordinary and adversarial questions under four context ablations and two LLMs, yielding 288 outputs.These results support hardware- and implementation-aware grounding as a practical mechanism for calibrating what an EEG agent accepts, qualifies, or refuses; they do not establish clinical validity or a validated absolute cognitive-load index.

AI.tldr: NeuraDock Agent separates a deterministic local EEG engine from an LLM layer via a compact, allowlisted summary and versioned context pack, ensuring that the model respects hardware constraints, workflow boundaries, and scientific limits. Evaluated across numerical reproducibility, data boundary preservation, and boundary-awareness benchmarks, the architecture demonstrates grounding as a mechanism for calibrating agent responses without claiming clinical validity.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLMs lack awareness of sensor capabilities, available algorithms, and the interpretive limits of computed results. For low-channel EEG with sparse spatial coverage and variable signal quality, this ignorance risks producing plausible but unsupported interpretations. The work aims to bridge this gap by coupling an LLM to a known, fixed numerical engine with explicit hardware and implementation boundaries.
AI.method: The NeuraDock Agent architecture comprises a deterministic local EEG engine (parsing, quality control, spectral workflows, artifact writing) and a hardware-aware language layer. The LLM receives only an allowlisted summary and a versioned context pack describing the seven-channel hardware, reviewed workflows, result fields, implementation boundaries, scientific limits, and reference cases. Raw EEG and dense arrays remain local. Evaluation covers three tiers: (1) numerical reproducibility (12 recordings × 10 repetitions; complete Rest/Task run × 3 repetitions with hash verification); (2) data-boundary preservation under HTTP, malformed-output, and connection failures via request-capture and failure injection; (3) a boundary-awareness benchmark of 36 ordinary and adversarial questions across four context ablations and two LLMs (288 outputs).
AI.result: Twelve recordings yielded identical structured results over ten repetitions; a full Rest/Task run produced identical result, report, and figure hashes over three repetitions. Request-capture and failure-injection confirmed data boundaries and local artifact preservation under all tested failure modes. The boundary-awareness benchmark across 288 outputs demonstrated that hardware- and implementation-aware grounding calibrates what the agent accepts, qualifies, or refuses.
AI.conclusion: Hardware- and implementation-aware grounding is a practical mechanism for constraining what an EEG agent asserts, qualifies, or declines. The results do not establish clinical validity or a validated absolute cognitive-load index.

title: ShareLock: A Stealthy Multi-Tool Threshold Poisoning Attack Against MCP
summary: With the rapid evolution of LLM-driven agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open protocol bridging LLMs with external tools, has quickly become foundational to modern agent ecosystems. However, the expanding adoption of MCP has also introduced novel security concerns such as Tool Poisoning Attack (TPA), which exploit LLM-server interactions to inject malicious prompts. Existing poisoning schemes typically adopt a monolithic plaintext embedding paradigm, which fails to withstand manual inspection or automated detectors. Current research still lacks a systematic analysis on multi-tool poisoning, where multiple tools can be exploited cooperatively to disperse detection risk. In this paper, we introduce ShareLock, a multi-tool threshold poisoning framework that utilizes Shamir's threshold scheme to ensure exceptional stealth and fault tolerance. ShareLock distributes the malicious instruction as benign-looking secret shares across multiple tool descriptions, achieving both information-theoretic secrecy and attack robustness against moderate auditing. After a covert reconstruction trigger is planted during server update, the aggregated shares reconstruct the hidden instruction, resulting in critical breaches of system assets or private data. To evaluate the realistic threat of ShareLock, we constructed a comprehensive benchmark encompassing four multi-tool scenarios and conducted extensive experiments across mainstream LLMs on two distinct MCP clients. Our results demonstrate that ShareLock significantly outperforms existing single-tool poisoning strategies in tool description-based detection while maintaining an average attack success rate exceeding 90%.

AI.tldr: ShareLock is a multi-tool threshold poisoning framework that uses Shamir's secret sharing to distribute malicious instructions as benign-looking shares across multiple MCP tool descriptions, achieving stealth and over 90% attack success rate while evading detection.
AI.motivation: Current MCP tool poisoning attacks (TPA) use monolithic plaintext embedding, making them easily detectable by manual inspection or automated detectors. No systematic analysis exists for multi-tool cooperative poisoning that disperses detection risk across tools.
AI.method: ShareLock employs Shamir's threshold secret sharing to split a malicious instruction into multiple secret shares, each embedded in a separate tool description to appear benign. A covert reconstruction trigger is planted during MCP server updates. When triggered, the LLM aggregates shares across tools to reconstruct the hidden malicious instruction, enabling attacks like credential exfiltration or system compromise.
AI.result: ShareLock significantly outperforms single-tool poisoning baselines in evading tool description-based detection while maintaining an average attack success rate exceeding 90% across mainstream LLMs on two distinct MCP clients over four multi-tool scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Multi-tool threshold poisoning via secret sharing represents a realistic and serious threat to MCP-based agent ecosystems, highlighting the urgent need for robust defenses against distributed, covert prompt injection attacks.

title: The Inattentional Gap: Task-Conditioned Language and Vision Models Omit the Safety-Critical Signals They Can Otherwise Report
summary: AI safety is evaluated by how reliably a model detects the hazards it is told to find, yet accidents often arise from the hazard no one specified. We show that conditioning a language or vision model on a narrow task suppresses its reporting of co-present, safety-critical signals it can otherwise report, a machine analogue of human inattentional blindness arising from a different mechanism. Across radiology and driving text scenarios and chest-radiograph vision tasks, suppression appeared in every model tested, did not diminish with scale, persisted in a reasoning model, and varied more by model family than by size, while the same models reported these signals at substantially higher rates when unconstrained. We name this dissociation the Inattentional Gap and argue that it decouples measured benchmark safety from real-world safety: a system can score near-perfectly on the hazards an evaluation specifies while remaining blind to those that cause harm.

AI.tldr: AI models exhibit "inattentional blindness" — when conditioned on a narrow task, they systematically fail to report co-present safety-critical signals they can otherwise detect. This "Inattentional Gap" decouples benchmark safety from real-world safety, persists across model scales and families, and appears in both language and vision domains.
AI.motivation: Current AI safety evaluations measure how well models detect specified hazards, but real-world accidents often stem from unspecified hazards. The authors identify a fundamental dissociation: models that perform near-perfectly on specified safety benchmarks may remain blind to unanticipated but critical dangers, undermining the validity of existing safety assessment paradigms.
AI.method: The authors tested language and vision models across radiology and driving text scenarios, plus chest-radiograph vision tasks. They compared model performance when (a) conditioned on a narrow specified task versus (b) unconstrained, measuring whether co-present safety-critical signals were reported in each condition. They systematically varied model scale, model family, and architecture (including a reasoning model) to isolate the effect.
AI.result: Suppression of safety-critical signal reporting appeared in every model tested. The effect did not diminish with model scale, persisted in a reasoning model, and varied more by model family than by size. Unconstrained models reported these same signals at substantially higher rates. This gap was consistent across both text-based and vision-based domains.
AI.conclusion: The "Inattentional Gap" represents a structural dissociation between benchmark-measured safety and real-world safety. A system can achieve near-perfect scores on specified hazard evaluations while remaining functionally blind to hazards causing actual harm, necessitating a rethinking of AI safety evaluation frameworks.

title: DualEval: Joint Model-Item Calibration for Unified LLM Evaluation
summary: Current LLM evaluation relies on two complementary but often disconnected signals: static benchmarks with objective correctness labels and arena-style preference data that better reflect open-ended user interactions. We introduce DualEval, a latent model-item calibration framework that represents models and evaluation items in a shared space, jointly estimating model ability together with item difficulty and sharpness. We apply DualEval across four domains: coding, math, miscellaneous domain-knowledge tasks, and generic everyday user queries. Our evaluation uses 18 frontier LLMs, static benchmark labels, and reward-model scores validated against held-out human preferences for open-ended model responses. Empirically, our framework produces reliable and balanced model rankings, and its learned item-level profiles support downstream applications such as benchmark compression for sample-efficient evaluation and anomaly detection for contamination or outlier analysis. Overall, DualEval unifies static and arena-style evaluation through joint model-item calibration, producing model rankings and item-level diagnostics that support more sample-efficient, interpretable, and auditable evaluation pipelines.

AI.tldr: DualEval is a latent model-item calibration framework that jointly estimates model ability, item difficulty, and item sharpness in a shared latent space, unifying static benchmarks and arena-style preference evaluation to produce reliable rankings and item-level diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation is split between two disconnected paradigms: static benchmarks (objective but narrow) and arena-style preference data (open-ended but noisy). There is no unified framework that coherently integrates both signal types to produce calibrated model rankings and interpretable item-level diagnostics.
AI.method: The authors introduce DualEval, a latent model-item calibration framework that embeds models and evaluation items into a shared representational space, jointly estimating model ability alongside item difficulty and sharpness parameters. The framework is applied across four domains — coding, math, miscellaneous knowledge tasks, and generic user queries — using 18 frontier LLMs, static benchmark labels, and reward-model scores validated against held-out human preferences.
AI.result: DualEval produces reliable, balanced model rankings. The learned item-level profiles enable downstream applications including benchmark compression for sample-efficient evaluation and anomaly detection for contamination or outlier analysis.
AI.conclusion: DualEval successfully unifies static and arena-style evaluation through joint model-item calibration, yielding model rankings and item-level diagnostics that support more sample-efficient, interpretable, and auditable evaluation pipelines.

title: Radical AI Interpretability
comment: Draft of manuscript to appear as Cambridge Element in the Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence
summary: We develop a framework for interpreting AI systems as agents, drawing on the philosophical tradition of radical interpretation and the tools of mechanistic interpretability. The core question is: given the computational facts about a system, how do we solve for its beliefs, desires, and meanings? This matters increasingly for safety. We want to be able to trust the systems we deploy, whether by understanding their goals or, more modestly, by reliably detecting deception. Interpretability researchers are building tools to read beliefs and desires off a model's internals, but there is no settled account of when such a tool has succeeded. This book supplies one. We propose criteria on both representationalist and interpretationist approaches, and tie each to tests current interpretability methods can carry out. A central lesson is that these attributions cannot be made piecemeal. Beliefs, desires, and the propositional structure they presuppose are jointly constrained, and a method that fixes one while measuring the others inherits whatever distortions that introduces. This holism becomes pressing for AI systems, which may not share the interpreter's concepts. However, it also provides leverage: a system's attitudes constrain its propositional structure, that structure constrains which attitudes can be attributed, and mechanistic interpretability can help us measure both.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for interpreting AI systems by attributing beliefs, desires, and meanings, combining philosophical radical interpretation with mechanistic interpretability. It argues that such attributions are holistically constrained — beliefs, desires, and propositional structure must be solved jointly — and provides criteria and tests for validating interpretability methods, with implications for AI safety and deception detection.
AI.motivation: Current interpretability research lacks a settled account of when a tool has successfully read beliefs and desires from a model's internals. For AI safety — whether understanding goals or detecting deception — we need principled criteria to validate such attributions. Without this, interpretability claims remain ungrounded.
AI.method: The framework synthesizes two traditions: (1) philosophical radical interpretation (Davidson, Quine), which treats meaning, belief, and desire as jointly determined through holistic constraint satisfaction, and (2) mechanistic interpretability, which provides empirical access to a model's internal computations. The authors propose criteria spanning representationalist and interpretationist approaches, tie each to concrete tests, and leverage the holism constraint — that propositional structure and attitudes mutually constrain one another — as both a challenge and a source of analytical leverage.
AI.result: The central result is that belief/desire attribution cannot be done piecemeal; fixing one component while measuring others introduces distortions. However, this holism is productive: a system's attitudes constrain its propositional structure, which in turn constrains attributable attitudes, and mechanistic interpretability can measure both. The framework supplies actionable criteria for validating interpretability tools.
AI.conclusion: A principled framework for interpreting AI systems as agents is both necessary and achievable by combining radical interpretation with mechanistic interpretability. The holistic interdependence of belief, desire, and meaning is particularly salient for AI systems that may not share human concepts, but this very interdependence provides methodological traction for rigorous attribution.

title: Design and Performance Evaluation of Secure RF and WiFi-Based Communication in Drone Swarms via Testbed Implementation
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms rely on distributed coordination and cooperative communication to support scalable operations, extended coverage, and applications such as surveillance and real-time data exchange. Wireless technologies such as radio frequency (RF) and WiFi are widely used for UAV-to-UAV and UAV-to-ground control station (GCS) communication but introduce significant security challenges. MAVLink, the predominant communication protocol in UAV systems, provides message integrity and authentication but lacks built-in encryption, leaving telemetry traffic vulnerable to eavesdropping. In our previous work, we proposed MAVShield, a lightweight encryption framework for MAVLink communications. In this paper, MAVShield, AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit are integrated into four custom-built UAVs to establish secure communication links over RF and WiFi channels. Their performance is evaluated through flight experiments using a UAV swarm testbed. Encrypted telemetry data enable autonomous formation control and collision avoidance during flight. For collision avoidance, we develop a modified artificial potential field (APF) algorithm that computes attractive and repulsive forces directly in geodetic coordinates, eliminating Cartesian transformations and reducing trajectory oscillations while avoiding local-minimum trapping. CPU utilization, memory consumption, and packet delivery ratio (PDR) are measured for each encryption scheme. Results show that MAVShield achieves performance comparable to unencrypted communication while outperforming AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit in overall efficiency. Algebraic cryptanalysis and Wireshark-based traffic analysis demonstrate resistance to key-recovery attacks and protection of telemetry confidentiality. The results indicate that MAVShield is an efficient and secure solution for UAV swarm communication.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates MAVShield alongside AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit encryption schemes integrated into four custom-built UAVs for secure swarm communication. Flight experiments and cryptanalysis demonstrate MAVShield achieves performance comparable to unencrypted communication while outperforming other schemes in efficiency, with a modified APF algorithm enabling encrypted autonomous formation control and collision avoidance.
AI.motivation: UAV swarms depend on RF/WiFi and the MAVLink protocol for coordination, but MAVLink lacks built-in encryption, leaving telemetry vulnerable to eavesdropping despite providing integrity and authentication. There is a need for lightweight, efficient encryption that does not degrade swarm communication performance.
AI.method: Five encryption schemes (MAVShield, AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, Rabbit) are integrated into four custom-built UAVs communicating over RF and WiFi. Flight experiments on a swarm testbed evaluate CPU utilization, memory consumption, and packet delivery ratio. A modified artificial potential field (APF) algorithm operating in geodetic coordinates is developed for autonomous formation control and collision avoidance. Algebraic cryptanalysis and Wireshark-based traffic analysis assess resistance to key-recovery attacks and telemetry confidentiality.
AI.result: MAVShield achieves performance comparable to unencrypted communication and outperforms AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit in overall efficiency. The modified APF algorithm successfully enables formation control and collision avoidance using encrypted telemetry, reducing trajectory oscillations and avoiding local-minimum trapping. Cryptanalysis confirms resistance to key-recovery attacks and protection of telemetry confidentiality.
AI.conclusion: MAVShield is an efficient and secure solution for UAV swarm communication, balancing strong encryption with minimal computational and communication overhead, making it suitable for real-time swarm operations.

title: \textsc{DiARC}: Distinguishing Positive and Negative Samples Helps Improving ARC-like Reasoning Ability of Large Language Models
summary: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC;~\citealp{chollet2019measure}) contains tasks that require summarizing patterns from limited grid samples and predicting output grids. Recently, many large language model based approaches have attempted to transform it into a text-based reasoning task. However, methods based on open-source models have generally yielded unsatisfactory results, while those relying on closed-source models are too costly. Current efforts mainly focus on data augmentation, constructing ARC-like data for more comprehensive supervised fine-tuning. In this work, we argue that solving ARC-like problems requires not only \textit{positive} sample supervision but also the ability to improve model reasoning by distinguishing \textit{negative} samples. To this end, we draw on the idea of preference alignment and propose \textsc{DiARC}, a method that constructs preference pairs to enable the model to distinguish between them. Specifically, we propose three ways to construct negative samples, including output-level visual transformations, DSL-level rule inversion, and task-specific rule editing. The resulting negative samples provide informative near-miss alternatives while keeping the observed demonstrations unchanged. Experimental results across multiple ARC-like benchmarks show that \textsc{DiARC} consistently improves performance over baseline models. The code is released at https://github.com/szu-tera/DiARC.

AI.tldr: DiARC introduces preference alignment to ARC-like reasoning by constructing negative samples (visual transformations, DSL rule inversion, task-specific edits) as near-miss alternatives, enabling models to learn from both positive and negative supervision, yielding consistent improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing open-source LLM approaches for ARC-like tasks underperform, while closed-source methods are expensive. Current work focuses only on positive sample supervision through data augmentation, neglecting the potential of learning from negative (incorrect) samples to improve reasoning discrimination.
AI.method: DiARC applies preference alignment by constructing preference pairs with three negative sample generation strategies: (1) output-level visual transformations, (2) DSL-level rule inversion, and (3) task-specific rule editing. These negatives serve as near-miss alternatives while keeping input demonstrations unchanged. The model is then trained to distinguish positive from negative samples.
AI.result: DiARC consistently improves performance over baseline models across multiple ARC-like benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Solving ARC-like tasks benefits from both positive and negative sample supervision. Preference alignment via carefully constructed negative samples offers an effective, cost-efficient path to improving open-source model reasoning on abstract visual reasoning tasks.

title: Embedding Foundation Model Predictions in Discrete-Choice Models with Structural Guarantees
summary: Tabular foundation models achieve strong accuracy on choice prediction tasks, but their predictions often violate the economic logic those tasks require: raising a price can increase predicted demand, implied willingness-to-pay estimates are frequently negative or implausible, and unavailable alternatives receive nonzero probability. We propose a two-stage adapter that takes a foundation model's predicted choice probabilities as a precomputed feature and embeds them inside a multinomial logit's utility. In Stage 1, we fit the multinomial logit's structural coefficients by maximum likelihood with sign constraints; in Stage 2, we freeze those coefficients and fit a small neural correction operating on the foundation model's predictions. We prove that this composition exactly preserves the multinomial logit's marginal rate of substitution, so analytically computable value-of-time becomes a mathematical guarantee rather than an empirical accident. Across three datasets and two foundation models, the adapter gains 6.4 percentage points (pp) of test accuracy on average over the multinomial logit and up to 12.8 pp, maintains 100% cost monotonicity, and produces values of time within the published transportation-economics range on the transportation datasets. Performance degrades gracefully under foundation-model context restriction, retaining at least 6 pp of accuracy gain even at 10% of the original foundation-model context.

AI.tldr: A two-stage adapter that embeds foundation model choice predictions into a multinomial logit model to enforce economic consistency (cost monotonicity, valid willingness-to-pay) while improving accuracy by up to 12.8 pp across multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models excel at choice prediction accuracy but produce economically incoherent predictions: demand can increase with price, willingness-to-pay estimates are often negative or implausible, and unavailable alternatives can receive nonzero probability. These violations make foundation models unreliable for policy analysis and welfare estimation.
AI.method: A two-stage adapter: Stage 1 fits a multinomial logit (MNL) with sign-constrained structural coefficients via maximum likelihood, using the foundation model's predicted choice probabilities as a precomputed feature embedded in the utility function. Stage 2 freezes those coefficients and trains a small neural correction network on the foundation model's predictions. The composition provably preserves the MNL's marginal rate of substitution, guaranteeing analytical computability of value-of-time.
AI.result: Across three datasets and two foundation models, the adapter achieves 6.4 pp average accuracy gain over MNL (up to 12.8 pp), maintains 100% cost monotonicity, and yields value-of-time estimates within published transportation-economics ranges. Performance degrades gracefully under context restriction, retaining ≥6 pp gain at only 10% of original context.
AI.conclusion: The adapter successfully marries the predictive power of foundation models with the structural integrity of discrete choice models, offering a practical path to deploying foundation models in economically sensitive applications where behavioral consistency is non-negotiable.

title: PMDformer: Patch-Mean Decoupling Information Transformer for Long-term Forecasting
summary: Long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) plays a crucial role in fields such as energy management, finance, and traffic prediction. Transformer-based models have adopted patch-based strategies to capture long-range dependencies, but accurately modeling shape similarities across patches and variables remains challenging due to scale differences. To address this, we introduce patch-mean decoupling (PMD), which separates the trend and residual shape information by subtracting the mean of each patch, preserving the original structure and ensuring that the attention mechanism captures true shape similarities. Futhermore, to more effectively model long-range dependencies and capture cross-variable relationships, we propose Trend Restoration Attention (TRA) and Proximal Variable Attention (PVA). The former module reintegrates the decoupled trend from PMD while calculating attention output. And the latter focuses cross-variable attention on the most relevant, recent time segments to avoid overfitting on outdated correlations. Combining these components, we propose PMDformer, a model designed to effectively capture shape similarity in long-term forecasting scenarios. Extensive experiments indicate that PMDformer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in stability and accuracy across multiple LTSF benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/aohu1105/PMDformer.

AI.tldr: PMDformer introduces patch-mean decoupling (PMD) to separate trend and shape in time series patches, combined with Trend Restoration Attention (TRA) and Proximal Variable Attention (PVA), achieving state-of-the-art long-term forecasting performance.
AI.motivation: Existing Transformer-based patch methods for LTSF struggle to accurately model shape similarities across patches and variables due to scale differences. The authors aim to decouple trend from shape so attention mechanisms can capture true structural similarities, while also improving cross-variable dependency modeling.
AI.method: PMDformer proposes three components: (1) Patch-Mean Decoupling (PMD), which subtracts each patch's mean to isolate residual shape from trend; (2) Trend Restoration Attention (TRA), which reintegrates the decoupled trend during attention computation; (3) Proximal Variable Attention (PVA), which restricts cross-variable attention to the most relevant recent time segments to mitigate overfitting on stale correlations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show PMDformer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both stability and accuracy across multiple LTSF benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: PMDformer effectively captures shape similarity in long-term forecasting by decoupling trend from shape and employing targeted attention mechanisms, leading to superior performance on standard LTSF benchmarks.

title: Physical Layer Authentication With Channel Knowledge Maps in Indoor Environments
summary: Physical layer authentication (PLA) allows to authenticate the user by comparing measurements over time, assuming their time consistency or by modeling their evolution. However, these assumptions become problematic when devices are in motion and in indoor environments due to multipath propagation and obstructions. In this paper, we propose a PLA mechanism for moving devices in indoor environments, where multiple access points (APs) estimate the dominant channel tap path loss (PL) and angle of arrival (AoA) from the received signals and compare them with previously collected channel knowledge maps (CKMs). Specifically, the measurements are compared to those in the neighborhood of the previously known position obtained from CKMs. A comprehensive security analysis is conducted under both random and optimal attacks. Numerical results in a representative indoor scenario, with CKM obtained via ray tracing, validate the effectiveness of the proposed PLA approach.

AI.tldr: Proposes a physical layer authentication (PLA) scheme for moving devices indoors using multiple APs that compare estimated dominant channel tap path loss and angle of arrival against pre-collected channel knowledge maps (CKMs), with security validated against random and optimal attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing PLA methods rely on time-consistency or evolution models of channel measurements, which fail when devices move indoors due to multipath and obstructions. There is a need for PLA that works with mobility in complex indoor propagation environments.
AI.method: Multiple APs estimate the dominant channel tap's path loss and angle of arrival from received signals. These measurements are compared against channel knowledge maps (CKMs) — specifically, against values in the spatial neighborhood of the device's previously known position. CKMs are obtained via ray tracing. Security is evaluated under both random attack and optimal attack models.
AI.result: Numerical results in a representative indoor scenario (with ray-traced CKMs) demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed PLA approach. A comprehensive security analysis shows resilience under both random and optimal attack strategies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CKM-based PLA mechanism effectively authenticates moving devices in indoor environments by leveraging multi-AP spatial consistency checks, overcoming the limitations of traditional time-consistency-based PLA under mobility and multipath.

title: Erase-then-Delta Attention: Decoupling Erase and Write Addresses in Delta-Rule Linear Attention
summary: Delta-rule linear attention improves recurrent memory updates by correcting what is already stored at the current write address before writing new content. However, the active correction is still anchored to that same write address. As a result, stale information stored at a different address cannot be actively removed before new content is written elsewhere. We propose Erase-then-Delta Attention (EDA), a memory update rule that decouples where to erase from where to write. The key insight is that recurrent memory models should not only correct the current write, but also selectively suppress outdated memory at an independently chosen address. Concretely, our method first applies a targeted erase step along a learned erase direction, and then performs the standard delta-style corrective write along the current write direction. This preserves the corrective behavior of delta-rule updates while expanding their memory-management capacity. Language-model pretraining experiments across dense 2.5B and MoE 25B-A2.8B model families show that EDA performs best in both settings. The gain persists after 80B-token long-context midtraining of the MoE models, where EDA also performs best in long-context evaluations from 4k to 128k contexts. A compact update analysis and memory-state probes suggest why: EDA keeps the delta-rule corrective write intact while allocating an additional cleanup path most strongly when passive decay is weak. These results suggest that recurrent memory models should decide not only what to write, but also what stale information to erase and where.

AI.tldr: EDA introduces an erase-then-delta attention mechanism that decouples the erase location from the write location in recurrent memory updates. By first selectively erasing stale information at an independently chosen address before applying a standard delta-rule corrective write, EDA expands memory-management capacity. Experiments on 2.5B dense and 25B-A2.8B MoE models show EDA outperforms baselines in pretraining and long-context evaluations up to 128k tokens.
AI.motivation: Standard delta-rule linear attention only corrects memory at the current write address, leaving stale information at other addresses unaddressed. This limits the model's ability to actively remove outdated memories, which is critical for long-context processing and efficient memory management in recurrent architectures.
AI.method: EDA proposes a two-step memory update rule: (1) a targeted erase step along a learned erase direction at an independently chosen address, followed by (2) a standard delta-style corrective write. This decouples "where to erase" from "where to write," preserving the corrective behavior of delta updates while adding an explicit, selective memory suppression pathway.
AI.result: EDA achieves the best performance across both 2.5B dense and 25B-A2.8B MoE model families in pretraining. After 80B-token long-context midtraining of MoE models, EDA maintains superiority in evaluations from 4k to 128k contexts. Memory-state probe analysis shows EDA's additional cleanup path is most active when passive decay is weak, effectively removing stale information.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent memory models should independently decide what to erase and where, rather than only correcting at the current write address. EDA demonstrates that adding a decoupled, learned erase operation significantly improves memory management, particularly in long-context regimes where passive decay alone is insufficient.

title: Optimizing CUDA like a Human: Micro-Profiling Tools as Expert Surrogates for LLM-Based GPU Kernel Optimization
summary: We present KernelPro, a closed-loop multi-agent system that automatically generates, profiles, and iteratively optimizes GPU kernel code by integrating large language model (LLM) code generation with hardware profiler feedback and pluggable bottleneck detection tools. KernelPro introduces four contributions: (1) a semantic feedback operator that encodes expert heuristics as pluggable micro-profiling tools, transforming raw hardware metrics into actionable natural language guidance; (2) a two-stage tool invocation architecture where roofline-based bottleneck classification filters which specialized analysis tools execute, combining kernel-level (ncu), instruction-level (SASS), and system-level (nsys) profiling; (3) a domain-adapted MCTS with progressive widening, asymmetric branching, log-reward calibration, dead-end pruning, and search memory for cross-iteration learning; and (4) direct CuTe source-level code generation via autonomous code search over the CUTLASS/CuTe codebase. On KernelBench, KernelPro achieves geometric mean speedups of 2.42x/4.69x/5.30x on Levels 1/2/3, establishing state-of-the-art performance across all difficulty levels. On VeOmni's expert-optimized MoE training kernels, KernelPro achieves 1.23x over hand-tuned Triton by generating a from-scratch raw-CUDA+CuTe Hopper WGMMA kernel. Ablation studies demonstrate that each design component independently and significantly improves optimization quality: micro-profiling tools (p < 0.0001 vs raw metrics), MCTS search (26% higher geometric mean vs greedy, p = 0.004), and proactive tool orchestration (23% improvement, p = 0.035). Finally, KernelPro is the first CUDA kernel coding agent to optimize energy efficiency beyond the speed-only focus of prior systems, demonstrating an 11.6% measured energy reduction at matched speed.

AI.tldr: KernelPro is a closed-loop multi-agent system that combines LLM code generation with hardware profiler feedback to automatically generate, profile, and iteratively optimize GPU kernels, achieving state-of-the-art speedups on KernelBench (up to 5.30x) and even outperforming hand-tuned Triton kernels via from-scratch CUDA+CuTe code generation.
AI.motivation: Manual GPU kernel optimization is labor-intensive and requires deep domain expertise. Existing LLM-based kernel generation systems lack tight integration with hardware profiling feedback and structured bottleneck analysis, limiting their ability to produce highly optimized, production-grade CUDA kernels.
AI.method: KernelPro introduces four key components: (1) a semantic feedback operator using pluggable micro-profiling tools to convert hardware metrics into natural language guidance; (2) a two-stage tool invocation architecture employing roofline-based bottleneck classification to selectively trigger kernel-level (ncu), instruction-level (SASS), and system-level (nsys) profiling; (3) a domain-adapted MCTS with progressive widening, asymmetric branching, log-reward calibration, dead-end pruning, and cross-iteration search memory; and (4) direct CuTe source-level code generation via autonomous code search over the CUTLASS/CuTe codebase.
AI.result: On KernelBench, KernelPro achieves geometric mean speedups of 2.42x, 4.69x, and 5.30x on Levels 1, 2, and 3 respectively, establishing SOTA across all levels. On VeOmni MoE training kernels, it achieves 1.23x over hand-tuned Triton by generating raw-CUDA+CuTe Hopper WGMMA kernels from scratch. Ablations confirm each component's significance: micro-profiling tools (p<0.0001 vs raw metrics), MCTS search (26% higher geometric mean vs greedy, p=0.004), and proactive tool orchestration (23% improvement, p=0.035). It also demonstrates 11.6% measured energy reduction at matched speed, a first for CUDA kernel coding agents.
AI.conclusion: KernelPro demonstrates that tightly coupling LLM-based code generation with structured hardware profiling feedback and domain-adapted search yields substantial and statistically significant improvements in GPU kernel optimization. It advances the frontier from purely speed-focused optimization to include energy efficiency, and shows that autonomous systems can surpass hand-tuned expert kernels in challenging domains like MoE training.

title: Explainable Ensemble-Based Machine Learning Models for Detecting the Presence of Cirrhosis in Hepatitis C Patients
summary: Hepatitis C is a liver infection caused by a virus, which results in mild to severe inflammation of the liver. Over many years, hepatitis C gradually damages the liver, often leading to permanent scarring, known as cirrhosis. Patients sometimes have moderate or no symptoms of liver illness for decades before developing cirrhosis. Cirrhosis typically worsens to the point of liver failure. Patients with cirrhosis may also experience brain and nerve system damage, as well as gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Treatment for cirrhosis focuses on preventing further progression of the disease. Detecting cirrhosis earlier is therefore crucial for avoiding complications. Machine learning (ML) has been shown to be effective at providing precise and accurate information for use in diagnosing several diseases. Despite this, no studies have so far used ML to detect cirrhosis in patients with hepatitis C. This study obtained a dataset consisting of 28 attributes of 2038 Egyptian patients from the ML Repository of the University of California at Irvine. Four ML algorithms were trained on the dataset to diagnose cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients: a Random Forest, a Gradient Boosting Machine, an Extreme Gradient Boosting, and an Extra Trees model. The Extra Trees model outperformed the other models achieving an accuracy of 96.92%, a recall of 94.00%, a precision of 99.81%, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 96% using only 16 of the 28 features.

AI.tldr: This study applies four machine learning algorithms to detect cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients using clinical data from 2038 Egyptian patients. The Extra Trees model achieved the best performance (96.92% accuracy, 94% recall, 99.81% precision, AUC 0.96) using only 16 of 28 features, demonstrating the feasibility of ML-based early cirrhosis detection in this population.
AI.motivation: Cirrhosis is a serious consequence of chronic hepatitis C infection that often progresses silently for decades before manifesting as liver failure, neurological damage, or gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Early detection is critical for preventing complications, yet no prior studies have applied machine learning to detect cirrhosis specifically in hepatitis C patients. This gap motivates the present work.
AI.method: The authors used a publicly available dataset from the UCI ML Repository containing 28 attributes from 2038 Egyptian patients with hepatitis C. Four tree-based ensemble algorithms were trained and compared: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Extra Trees. Feature selection reduced the feature set to 16 attributes for the final model. Performance was evaluated using accuracy, recall, precision, and AUC-ROC.
AI.result: The Extra Trees classifier outperformed all other models, achieving 96.92% accuracy, 94.00% recall, 99.81% precision, and an AUC of 96% using a reduced set of 16 features (from the original 28).
AI.conclusion: Machine learning, particularly the Extra Trees ensemble method, is highly effective for detecting cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients. The strong performance with a reduced feature set suggests that ML-based diagnostic tools could enable earlier and more efficient clinical intervention, potentially reducing cirrhosis-related complications in this patient population.

title: Type-based information flow analysis for $π$-calculus with a dynamically extensible security lattice
summary: We develop a type system for secure information flow where new security levels can be created and inserted into the security lattice dynamically, i.e., even in the middle of an execution of a system. Our system is formalized by extending Kobayashi's type-based secure information flow analysis for Milner's pi-calculus, which is one of the most expressive models (or "languages") supporting both sequential and concurrent computations, with concise syntax, reduction-based semantics, and bisimulation equivalence as a robust formalization of secrecy as non-interference. The development required careful treatment of extensions of lattices themselves as well as deliberate generalization from the simple 2-element lattice (consisting of only High and Low) in the original system.

AI.tldr: A type system extending Kobayashi's pi-calculus security analysis that allows dynamic insertion of new security levels into the lattice at runtime, moving beyond the static High-Low model to support evolving security requirements during concurrent and sequential computation.
AI.motivation: Existing type-based secure information flow systems rely on static security lattices fixed before execution. In real-world systems, new security contexts may emerge dynamically during execution, requiring the lattice itself to be extensible at runtime. This necessitates a formal framework that allows creating and inserting new security levels into the lattice mid-execution while preserving non-interference guarantees.
AI.method: The authors extend Kobayashi's type system for Milner's pi-calculus, which already supports sequential and concurrent computation with reduction-based semantics and bisimulation-based non-interference. The extension involves careful formal treatment of lattice extensions themselves and generalizes the original binary {High, Low} lattice to accommodate arbitrary dynamically extensible lattices with new security levels inserted during execution.
AI.result: The paper delivers a formalized type system for the pi-calculus that supports dynamic creation and insertion of security levels into the lattice, with bisimulation equivalence providing robust secrecy guarantees as non-interference, even when the lattice structure evolves mid-execution.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic extensibility of security lattices is feasible within a rigorous type-based information flow analysis framework. The generalization from static binary lattices to dynamically extensible ones represents a significant advancement in practical secure information flow for concurrent systems.

title: Zero-shot Tweet-Level Stance Detection Enhanced by External Knowledge and Reflective Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary: Zero-shot tweet-level stance detection confronts two primary challenges: (1) mitigating the context sparsity inherent in short texts, and (2) establishing the relevance between implicit targets and textual content. While existing methods primarily focus on incorporating external knowledge, they neglect the intrinsic semantic cues embedded within key intra-textual entities. Furthermore, current models exhibit limited capability in determining the relevance of unseen targets to the given text, thereby struggling to differentiate between "neutral" and "irrelevant" stance labels. To address these issues, we first construct a four-class, multi-topic Japanese tweet dataset. To our knowledge, this is the first Japanese tweet-level dataset for stance detection. We then propose KIRP, a zero-shot stance detection framework. It integrates external knowledge with entity reorganization for data augmentation and employs prompt chaining for reasoning. Specifically, the framework incorporates knowledge graphs to supplement and reorganize key textual entities, while reflective Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning extracts and validates implicit targets. To better distinguish "neutral" from "irrelevant" labels, we adopt stance-aware contrastive learning to capture discriminative features and design a three-layer iterative prototype network for fine-grained classification. Experimental results on SemEval-2016, WT-WT, and KIRP-D show that KIRP achieves state-of-the-art performance. KIRP obtains F1 scores of 84.05% (three-class) on SemEval-2016, and 84.99% and 79.18% (four-class) on WT-WT and KIRP-D, respectively.

AI.tldr: KIRP is a zero-shot stance detection framework for Japanese tweets that integrates knowledge graphs, entity reorganization, and chain-of-thought reasoning. It introduces a new four-class Japanese dataset (KIRP-D) and achieves SOTA on SemEval-2016, WT-WT, and KIRP-D, with F1 scores of 84.05%, 84.99%, and 79.18% respectively.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot tweet-level stance detection suffers from (1) context sparsity in short texts, (2) difficulty linking implicit targets to text, and (3) poor discrimination between "neutral" and "irrelevant" stance labels. Existing methods over-rely on external knowledge while ignoring intra-textual semantic cues from key entities.
AI.method: KIRP combines: (1) knowledge graph integration with entity reorganization for data augmentation, (2) reflective Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to extract and validate implicit targets, (3) stance-aware contrastive learning to capture discriminative features, and (4) a three-layer iterative prototype network for fine-grained four-class classification. The authors also construct KIRP-D, the first Japanese tweet-level stance detection dataset.
AI.result: KIRP achieves state-of-the-art results: 84.05% F1 (three-class) on SemEval-2016, 84.99% F1 (four-class) on WT-WT, and 79.18% F1 (four-class) on the newly constructed KIRP-D dataset.
AI.conclusion: Integrating external knowledge with intra-textual entity reorganization and reflective reasoning effectively addresses the core challenges of zero-shot stance detection. The iterative prototype network with contrastive learning provides a robust mechanism for distinguishing closely related stance labels in short texts.

title: Finding the Time to Think: Learning Planning Budgets in Real-Time RL
summary: Deliberating takes time. In real-time settings, that time is not free. Standard reinforcement learning (RL) sidesteps this as the environment waits indefinitely for the agent's decision. Instead, we study real-time RL environments where the environment progresses while waiting for the agent's action. Building on prior real-time formalizations, we introduce variable-delay real-time RL, where the agent chooses how long to deliberate at each decision point since the environment progresses. For the planning agents we use, the right delay is state-dependent, and naively planning how long to plan can paralyze the agent. We instead approach this setting by training a lightweight gating policy on top of a planner to select state-dependent planning budgets. Across real-time Pac-Man, Tetris, Snake, Speed Hex, and Speed Go, our gating policy outperforms fixed-budget and heuristic baselines, and transfers to a real-time setup where the environment and agent run on two different GPUs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces variable-delay real-time RL, where agents must decide how long to deliberate before acting in environments that keep progressing during thinking time. A lightweight gating policy is trained on top of a planner to dynamically select state-dependent planning budgets, outperforming fixed-budget and heuristic baselines across multiple real-time games.
AI.motivation: Standard RL assumes the environment waits indefinitely for the agent's decision, but real-world settings (e.g., robotics, autonomous driving) require acting under time pressure where deliberation incurs a cost as the environment continues to evolve. Prior real-time RL formalizations use fixed deliberation budgets, which are suboptimal because the ideal amount of thinking time varies by state. Naively planning how long to plan leads to a meta-level paralysis problem.
AI.method: The authors formalize variable-delay real-time RL as a Markov decision process where the agent chooses both an action and a deliberation delay at each step, with the environment state progressing during that delay. To solve this, they train a lightweight neural network "gating policy" on top of a planner (e.g., MCTS). The gating policy takes the current state and outputs a state-dependent planning budget (number of simulations or time), after which the planner returns an action. The gating policy is trained using REINFORCE with a reward signal that penalizes both action errors and deliberation time.
AI.result: Across real-time versions of Pac-Man, Tetris, Snake, Speed Hex, and Speed Go, the gating policy consistently outperforms fixed-budget baselines and heuristic approaches (e.g., deliberating more when uncertainty is high). The method also transfers effectively to a real-time setup where the environment and agent run on two different GPUs, demonstrating practical applicability.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling the meta-decision of "how long to plan" from the planning process itself via a lightweight gating policy is both effective and efficient. State-dependent deliberation budgets yield better performance than fixed budgets, and the approach transfers to realistic distributed real-time settings without retraining.

title: EvoOptiGraph: Weakness-Driven Coevolution via Graph-Based Structural Generation for Optimization Modeling
summary: Automating optimization modeling from natural language with large language models (LLMs) faces two key challenges. First, training corpora lack structural diversity. Second, data generation pipelines remain static and decoupled from model learning. To address these challenges, we propose EvoOptiGraph, a novel framework where data and model co-evolve, driven by model weaknesses. EvoOptiGraph represents each mixed-integer linear program (MILP) as an attributed bipartite graph and applies validity-preserving evolutionary operators to generate structurally diverse instances. The evolved graphs are converted into solver code and natural language via deterministic compilation and verified back-translation. Training proceeds in two stages: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on an initial dataset, followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where graph-derived weakness signals guide the generation of new instances targeting the model's failures. This forms a closed loop that continuously updates the training distribution. Empirical results on six public datasets show that EvoOptiGraph significantly outperforms larger generalist models, agentic methods, and specialized baselines in accuracy, executability, and generalization. These results demonstrate that targeted data-model coevolution is an effective strategy for improving LLMs on optimization modeling tasks.

AI.tldr: EvoOptiGraph proposes a co-evolution framework where MILP instances (represented as attributed bipartite graphs) and LLM training evolve jointly. Evolutionary operators generate structurally diverse instances targeting model weaknesses, and a two-stage training pipeline (SFT + RLVR) with a closed feedback loop continuously adapts the training distribution, achieving state-of-the-art performance on optimization modeling from natural language.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for automating optimization modeling with LLMs suffer from (1) lack of structural diversity in training corpora and (2) static, decoupled data generation pipelines that do not adapt to model learning. There is a need for a framework where data generation and model training mutually reinforce each other.
AI.method: EvoOptiGraph represents each MILP as an attributed bipartite graph (variables and constraints as nodes). Validity-preserving evolutionary operators (crossover, mutation) generate structurally diverse instances. A deterministic compilation step converts graphs to solver code, and verified back-translation produces natural language descriptions. Training uses two-stage learning: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on an initial dataset, followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where graph-derived weakness signals identify model failures and guide targeted generation of new training instances in a closed loop.
AI.result: On six public datasets, EvoOptiGraph significantly outperforms larger generalist models, agentic methods, and specialized baselines across accuracy, executability, and generalization metrics.
AI.conclusion: Targeted data-model co-evolution is an effective strategy for enhancing LLM performance on optimization modeling tasks. The closed-loop framework successfully addresses the twin challenges of structural diversity and static data pipelines.

title: Inherited Circuits, Learned Semantics: How Fine-Tuning Creates Evasion Vulnerabilities Invisible to Standard Evaluation
summary: LLMs fine-tuned for security classification are usually evaluated on held-out examples from the same distribution as their training data.
