We show that this can miss vulnerabilities introduced by fine-tuning itself: models can learn token-level indicator semantics that preserve canonical accuracy while failing under behavior-preserving transformations such as PowerShell alias substitution, command reconstruction, string construction, execution indirection, and case mutation. We study Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct and its base model, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, on matched PowerShell classification cohorts. Causal interventions localize the classification circuit to a late-attention route inherited from Llama rather than created by fine-tuning. Fine-tuning concentrates and semantically specializes this inherited structure, improving baseline behavior while creating transformation-sensitive attack surfaces. A three-tier evasion benchmark finds Foundation-Sec misses on iwr substitution, Invoke-Expression reconstruction, and case-mutated Invoke-Expression/IEX variants that Llama does not share. We also derive a pre-deployment monitoring method: a linear probe at the classification boundary and an indicator-token sign test identify command families where canonical indicators change role after fine-tuning. These signals prioritize red-team variant generation using only canonical inputs, showing that security fine-tuning can improve task accuracy while expanding the evasion surface. These results caution against treating small task-specific fine-tunes as straightforwardly safer security classifiers: specialization can convert inherited model structure into brittle indicator rules that preserve held-out accuracy while expanding the evasion surface. Robust AI-enabled security will require specifying the full transformation space of the task and monitoring semantic drift through fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Security fine-tuning of LLMs can introduce brittleness: models learn token-level indicator semantics that preserve in-distribution accuracy but fail under behavior-preserving transformations like alias substitution and case mutation. The paper localizes this vulnerability to inherited late-attention circuits that fine-tuning semantically specializes, and proposes a linear-probe monitoring method to detect such evasion surfaces pre-deployment.
AI.motivation: Standard held-out evaluation of security-tuned LLMs fails to detect vulnerabilities introduced by the fine-tuning process itself, where models overfit to surface-level token indicators rather than robust semantic understanding, creating blind spots exploitable by simple syntactic transformations.
AI.method: The authors study Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct vs. base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using matched PowerShell classification cohorts. They employ (1) causal intervention via activation patching to localize classification circuits to late-attention layers inherited from the base model; (2) a three-tier evasion benchmark (alias substitution, command reconstruction, string construction, execution indirection, case mutation); (3) a pre-deployment monitoring approach using linear probes at the classification boundary combined with an indicator-token sign test to identify commands where canonical indicators shift role post-fine-tuning.
AI.result: Foundation-Sec fails on iwr (Invoke-WebRequest alias) substitution, Invoke-Expression reconstruction, and case-mutated IEX variants that the base Llama model correctly handles. Causal analysis shows the classification circuit is inherited from Llama's late attention, not created de novo by fine-tuning. The linear probe and sign test successfully identify command families prone to indicator-role changes, enabling prioritized red-team variant generation using only canonical inputs.
AI.conclusion: Security fine-tuning can simultaneously improve canonical accuracy and expand the evasion surface by converting inherited model structure into brittle indicator rules. Treating small task-specific fine-tunes as straightforwardly safer is misguided; robust AI security requires specifying the full transformation space and monitoring semantic drift through fine-tuning.

title: Closing the Quality Gap in Low-Resource Text-to-Speech: LoRA Fine-Tuning of VoxCPM2 for Khmer and Korean
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. IEEE conference format (IEEEtran)
summary: Large pretrained text-to-speech (TTS) models sound almost human for well-resourced languages, but much worse for languages that are rare in their training data. We study this quality gap for Khmer and Korean using VoxCPM2, a 2.4B-parameter, tokenizer-free TTS model that joins a MiniCPM-4 language-model backbone with a flow-matching diffusion decoder. We build one shared, language-tagged corpus of about 26 hours and adapt VoxCPM2 with a single Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter, trained on both languages at once and added to both the language model and the decoder. The adapter is zero-initialized, so training starts exactly at the original (zero-shot) model. In native-speaker listening tests, the Khmer Mean Opinion Score (MOS) rises from 3.85 to 4.23 with the best adapter (rank 64), a highly significant gain (paired Wilcoxon test, p<0.001), while training only 0.19 to 3.03 percent of the parameters. The automatic loss and the human ratings, however, disagree on the best rank: validation loss is lowest at rank 128, yet MOS peaks at rank 64. The same adapter brings no gain for Korean, a language the base model already handles well, and at a high rank it even degrades quality. Adaptation therefore helps mainly where the base model is genuinely weak.

AI.tldr: A 2.4B-parameter TTS model (VoxCPM2) is adapted to low-resource languages (Khmer, Korean) using LoRA. The adapter significantly improves Khmer (rare in training data) from MOS 3.85→4.23 at rank 64, but brings no benefit—and even degrades—Korean, which the base model already handles well. Notably, validation loss and human MOS disagree on optimal rank.
AI.motivation: Large pretrained TTS models perform well on well-resourced languages but poorly on languages underrepresented in their training data. The authors aim to quantify and address this quality gap using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, specifically investigating whether LoRA adaptation can close the gap for Khmer and Korean.
AI.method: The study uses VoxCPM2, a 2.4B-parameter tokenizer-free TTS model combining a MiniCPM-4 language-model backbone with a flow-matching diffusion decoder. A single shared LoRA adapter (zero-initialized) is trained on a ~26-hour bilingual (Khmer + Korean) language-tagged corpus, applied to both the LM backbone and decoder. Multiple ranks (including 64 and 128) are evaluated. Native-speaker MOS listening tests with paired Wilcoxon significance testing are conducted.
AI.result: For Khmer: MOS improves from 3.85 (zero-shot) to 4.23 at rank 64 (p<0.001), using only 0.19–3.03% of parameters. For Korean: no improvement; high-rank adaptation degrades quality. Validation loss is lowest at rank 128, but human MOS peaks at rank 64, revealing a mismatch between automatic and human evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: LoRA-based adaptation of large TTS models is effective specifically for languages where the base model is genuinely weak (Khmer), not for already well-handled languages (Korean). Automatic loss metrics do not reliably predict human-perceived quality, underscoring the necessity of human evaluation for TTS adaptation. Zero-initialized adapters provide a safe starting point that preserves original model quality.

title: A Causal Foundation Model for Structure and Outcome Prediction
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, 17 tables, 43rd ICML Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data
summary: We introduce TabPFN-CFM, a causal foundation model that can handle multiple causal problems. TabPFN-CFM predicts both causal structure and outcomes from observational data, supports queries on all three levels of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy and uses known graph structure when available to improve predictions. TabPFN-CFM is trained on synthetic datasets, and generalises to real datasets, demonstrating improved performance over both structural and outcome prediction baselines.

AI.tldr: TabPFN-CFM is a causal foundation model trained on synthetic data that handles multiple causal tasks across Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, outperforming baselines on both structural and outcome predictions on real data.
AI.motivation: Current causal inference methods are typically task-specific and cannot flexibly operate across all three levels of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (association, intervention, counterfactuals). A unified foundation model capable of handling diverse causal problems — from structure learning to outcome prediction — and leveraging known graph structure when available would significantly advance the field.
AI.method: TabPFN-CFM extends the TabPFN architecture to the causal domain. It is trained entirely on synthetically generated datasets encompassing various causal structures and queries. The model accepts observational data as input and predicts both causal structure (graph edges) and causal outcomes. It supports queries across all three levels of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy and can condition on partially known graph structure to improve predictions.
AI.result: TabPFN-CFM generalizes from synthetic training data to real-world datasets, achieving improved performance over baseline methods for both causal structure prediction and outcome prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: A causal foundation model trained purely on synthetic data can effectively generalize to real causal inference problems across all levels of the Causal Hierarchy, offering a flexible, unified alternative to traditional task-specific methods.

title: A Multi-Level Validation and Traceability Framework for AI-Generated Telescope Scheduling Decisions
summary: With the gradual introduction of AI into telescope scheduling, AI-based decision-making has shown advantages in handling complex multi-constraint problems. However, its outputs often suffer from inconsistent data references, reasoning errors, and non-executable decisions, limiting applicability in high-reliability observational tasks. In this work, we propose a multi-level validation and traceable reasoning framework that performs systematic reliability verification of AI-generated decisions prior to execution, and enables explicit representation of the reasoning process to support traceable decision-making. The framework integrates data reference validation, logical consistency checks, and observational and instrumental constraint verification to filter and correct invalid decisions. It also introduces atomic reasoning units and their dependency relationships, representing scheduling decisions as a sequence of interconnected reasoning steps that support error localization and post hoc analysis. Experiments show that the framework improves executability and reliability of AI scheduling and reduces loss of transient opportunities. In particular, feedback correction and structured validation of reasoning steps enhance the ability to repair and block erroneous decisions, especially in complex scenarios. Compared with pure AI methods, the framework-enhanced approach maintains flexibility while substantially improving reliability and executability. These results demonstrate a feasible and verifiable pathway for applying AI to high-reliability astronomical observation scheduling.

AI.tldr: A multi-level validation and traceable reasoning framework is proposed to enhance the reliability of AI-based telescope scheduling by filtering invalid decisions through data reference validation, logical consistency checks, and constraint verification, while enabling error localization via atomic reasoning units.
AI.motivation: AI-based telescope scheduling suffers from inconsistent data references, reasoning errors, and non-executable decisions, which limit its applicability in high-reliability observational tasks that demand dependable and verifiable decision-making.
AI.method: The framework integrates three validation layers — data reference validation, logical consistency checks, and observational/instrumental constraint verification — to filter and correct invalid AI-generated decisions. It also introduces atomic reasoning units with explicit dependency relationships, structuring scheduling decisions as interconnected reasoning steps for error localization and post hoc analysis.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate improved executability and reliability of AI scheduling, reduced loss of transient observation opportunities, and enhanced error repair and blocking capabilities, particularly in complex scenarios, while maintaining the flexibility of pure AI methods.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a feasible and verifiable pathway for deploying AI in high-reliability astronomical observation scheduling, substantially improving reliability and executability without sacrificing flexibility.

title: zQR: A Verifiable QR-Driven zkSNARK Proof Verification Framework for Mobile Platforms
summary: Privacy is one of the fundamental rights of individuals in modern societies. Yet, the practical adoption of privacy-preserving technologies in daily interactions remains limited. Zero-knowledge proofs offer strong privacy guarantees but are often hindered by their technical complexity. In this paper, we advance the idea of verifiable QR codes that enable off-line verifiers to verify proofs encoded in QR codes. Based on this core idea, we build a novel QR-driven zkSNARK proof verification framework (i.e., zQR) for mobile platforms. The framework integrates blockchain for auditability, non-repudiation and logging; and large-language models for automatic circuit generation. We perform a security discussion of the framework by considering multiple attack surfaces. Furthermore, we present an experimental evaluation measuring temporal costs (proof generation and verification latency, QR code encoding and decoding latency) and financial costs (blockchain gas consumption). Our results demonstrate the feasibility of zQR as a proof-of-concept framework for privacy-preserving verification on mobile platform where proofs are compactly represented with QR code symbol version of 19 with low error correction level. Finally, we discuss potential applications, current limitations and future directions for the broader adoption of privacy-preserving technologies in daily interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes zQR, a framework that combines zero-knowledge proofs (zkSNARKs) with QR codes to enable offline, privacy-preserving verification on mobile platforms, integrating blockchain for auditability and LLMs for automatic circuit generation.
AI.motivation: Despite privacy being a fundamental right, practical adoption of privacy-preserving technologies remains low due to technical complexity. Zero-knowledge proofs offer strong privacy guarantees but are cumbersome for everyday use. The authors aim to bridge this gap by making ZKP verification accessible via ubiquitous QR code scanning on mobile devices.
AI.method: The authors design zQR, a framework encoding zkSNARK proofs into verifiable QR codes for offline verification. It integrates: (1) blockchain for auditability, non-repudiation, and immutable logging; (2) large language models (LLMs) for automated circuit generation, lowering the barrier to ZKP creation. Security analysis covers multiple attack surfaces. Experimental evaluation measures temporal costs (proof generation/verification latency, QR encoding/decoding) and financial costs (blockchain gas fees), using QR code symbol version 19 with low error correction.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate feasibility: proofs can be compactly encoded in QR codes (version 19, low error correction) and verified offline on mobile platforms. Both temporal and financial cost measurements support the framework's practicality as a proof-of-concept.
AI.conclusion: zQR is a viable proof-of-concept for enabling privacy-preserving verification in daily mobile interactions. The paper also discusses potential applications, current limitations, and future directions for broader adoption of such technologies.

title: CAT-Q: Cost-efficient and Accurate Ternary Quantization for LLMs
comment: This work is accepted to ICML 2026 as an oral. The project page: https://github.com/IntelChina-AI/BitTern
summary: In this paper, we present CAT-Q, Cost-efficient and Accurate Ternary Quantization, for compressing and accelerating LLMs. Unlike existing state-of-the-art ternary quantization methods that rely on data-intensive and costly quantization-aware training to mitigate severe performance degradation, CAT-Q is a simple yet effective post-training quantization scheme that is readily applicable to LLMs with diverse architectures and model sizes. It has two key components, learnable modulation (LM) and softened ternarization (ST), which are coupled from an optimization perspective. LM leverages a composition of learnable factors to modulate the distribution of pre-trained high-precision weights and the ternary threshold, making them less sensitive to ternarization. ST further introduces a differentiable transition function to guide the ternarization process toward stable convergence. We show that, for pre-trained LLMs with 1.7B to 8B parameters, CAT-Q can efficiently quantize them into ternary models using only 512 calibration samples, while achieving superior performance than the seminal BitNet 1.58-bit v1 and v2 families (with 1.3B to 7B parameters) trained with 100B tokens, yielding about a 100,000X reduction in training tokens. Moreover, we show for the first time that CAT-Q can quantize much larger pre-trained LLMs having 14B to 235B parameters into leading ternary models within just 8 to 60 hours on 8 A100-80GB GPUs. Code is available at https://github.com/IntelChina-AI/BitTern.

AI.tldr: CAT-Q is a post-training quantization method that compresses LLMs to ternary precision (1.58-bit) using only 512 calibration samples, outperforming models like BitNet that were trained from scratch on 100B tokens. It introduces learnable modulation and softened ternarization to achieve stable, high-accuracy ternary conversion, scaling from 1.7B to 235B parameters within hours on 8 GPUs.
AI.motivation: Existing ternary quantization methods require expensive quantization-aware training (QAT) with massive data to avoid severe accuracy loss, making them impractical for large-scale LLMs. The authors aim to develop a post-training quantization (PTQ) scheme that is data-efficient, cost-effective, and applicable across diverse model architectures and sizes without retraining.
AI.method: CAT-Q employs two key components: (1) Learnable Modulation (LM), which uses learnable factors to modulate the pre-trained weight distribution and ternary threshold, reducing sensitivity to ternarization; (2) Softened Ternarization (ST), a differentiable transition function that smooths the ternarization process for stable convergence. These are jointly optimized using only 512 calibration samples in a PTQ framework.
AI.result: CAT-Q achieves superior performance over BitNet 1.58-bit v1 and v2 (1.3B–7B, trained on 100B tokens) when quantizing pre-trained LLMs of 1.7B–8B parameters, representing a ~100,000× reduction in training tokens. It also successfully quantizes models up to 235B parameters into ternary within 8–60 hours on 8 A100-80GB GPUs, a first for PTQ at this scale.
AI.conclusion: CAT-Q demonstrates that post-training ternary quantization can match or exceed the quality of quantization-aware trained models while dramatically reducing data and compute costs. It opens the door to practical, large-scale ternary LLM deployment.

title: Epiphany-Aware KV Cache Eviction Without the Attention Matrix
summary: As reasoning models emit chains of thought tens of thousands of tokens long, KV cache increasingly becomes a deployment bottleneck. Existing cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention weight, which is a noisy importance proxy in long reasoning traces, and prohibits the use of fused kernels in production inference by forcing the model to materialize the attention matrix. In this work, we instead score tokens with a metric we term the epiphany score: the change in the model's internal representation, read directly from the forward pass with no attention matrix and negligible extra state. Our resulting cache eviction method, EpiKV, requires no training, classifier, or custom kernel, and can be used directly in FlashAttention inference stacks unchanged -- scaling to a 16x longer feasible context than attention-based scoring. upper-mid layers negatively) and remove a positional trend with a causal rolling z-score. At a 4096-token cache EpiKV reaches 72% on MATH-500, matching the strongest attention-based baseline (ThinKV 71%, H2O 67%); a lag-normalized KV variant reaches 37% on AIME-2024 at 8192 tokens against the best of them (33%), at up to 2.8x the speed.

AI.tldr: EpiKV introduces the "epiphany score" — the change in a model's internal representation during forward pass — as a novel, training-free metric for KV cache eviction. It eliminates reliance on noisy attention weights and the attention matrix, integrates seamlessly with FlashAttention, and scales to 16× longer contexts while matching or outperforming attention-based baselines (e.g., ThinKV, H2O) on MATH-500 and AIME-2024 benchmarks with up to 2.8× speedup.
AI.motivation: Long reasoning chains from modern models produce massive KV caches (tens of thousands of tokens), creating a deployment bottleneck. Existing cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention weights, but attention is a noisy importance signal for reasoning traces and forces materialization of the attention matrix, which breaks compatibility with fused kernels like FlashAttention used in production inference.
AI.method: The authors propose the epiphany score: a measure of how much a token changes the model's internal representation, read directly from the forward pass without computing the attention matrix. This requires negligible extra state. EpiKV applies the score for KV cache eviction, corrects for layer-wise biases (upper-mid layers are negatively biased), and removes a positional trend using a causal rolling z-score normalization. The method requires no training, classifier, or custom kernel and works directly in FlashAttention stacks.
AI.result: At a 4096-token cache budget, EpiKV achieves 72% on MATH-500, matching the strongest attention-based baseline (ThinKV 71%, H2O 67%). A lag-normalized KV variant reaches 37% on AIME-2024 at 8192 tokens versus the best baseline at 33%, with up to 2.8× speedup. The method scales to a 16× longer feasible context than attention-based scoring.
AI.conclusion: The epiphany score provides a superior signal for KV cache eviction in long-reasoning deployments — more reliable than attention weights, compatible with fused-kernel inference stacks, and empirically stronger on challenging math reasoning benchmarks while being significantly faster.

title: Content-Based Smart E-Mail Dispatcher Using Large Language Models
summary: Email communication has become an integral part of personal and professional life, but handling its vast volume is still a significant issue for large organisations. Manual perusal of emails and forwarding their contents and attachments to intended recipients using other instant messaging platforms has proved to be error-prone and time-consuming leading to losses in terms of productivity and creating undue stress. The main objective of this paper is to explore an alternative mechanism that is to automate the task of dispatching emails based on their contents to the respective WhatsApp groups of students of various semesters of programs in an engineering college, facilitating a smooth flow of information from one end to another end in an organisation. The dispatcher system is built using agents querying large language models (LLMs) to enable it to analyze the contents of emails and route them to the relevant groups of students for their information and consumption. The system harnesses the capabilities of LLMs in analysing the textual contents for decision-making. With a well-structured agent framework prompt that includes email content as input with instructions and context, the system figures out the relevant groups to which the email message is dispatched, thus providing the required information on time. The proposed system does not rely on labelled datasets and provides several benefits, including enhanced productivity and a reduction in the cognitive load associated with reading emails.

AI.tldr: A system that uses LLM-based agents to automatically analyze email content and forward messages to appropriate WhatsApp student groups, eliminating manual email triage in an engineering college setting.
AI.motivation: Manual email handling in large organizations is error-prone, time-consuming, and creates cognitive overload and productivity losses. There is a need for automated routing of email content to the right recipients on platforms where they actually consume information (WhatsApp).
AI.method: A dispatcher system employing agents that query LLMs to analyze email textual content. A structured agent framework prompt provides the email content alongside instructions and context, enabling the LLM to determine the relevant WhatsApp groups for dispatch without relying on labeled datasets.
AI.result: The system successfully automates email-to-WhatsApp routing across multiple semester groups in an engineering college, delivering timely information while reducing cognitive load and improving productivity.
AI.conclusion: LLM-powered agent frameworks offer a viable, label-free approach to automated cross-platform information routing, with significant gains in organizational productivity and reduced cognitive burden on users.

title: Application of LLMs to Threat Assessment of Foreign Peacekeeping Missions
summary: We present a novel approach for applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to threat assessment in the context of foreign peacekeeping missions. Building on the PINPOINT project and its use case, the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia, we combine an interdisciplinary risk-model with OSINT-based media collection and LLM-supported threat extraction. The proposed workflow maps media contents to mission-relevant threats, extracts structured information and applies several additional LLM-based processing steps to improve relevance and grounding. An evaluation of threats extracted from media documents shows high agreement between automatically generated results and human judgment for core aspects such as threat and mission relevance. These results indicate that LLMs provide a promising approach to support analysts in the context of peacekeeping missions.

AI.tldr: A novel LLM-based pipeline for threat assessment in peacekeeping missions is proposed, combining an interdisciplinary risk model with OSINT media collection. Evaluated on the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia (PINPOINT project), the workflow extracts mission-relevant threats from media documents, yielding high agreement with human judgment.
AI.motivation: Analysts in foreign peacekeeping missions face overwhelming volumes of open-source intelligence (OSINT) from media sources. Manual threat extraction is labor-intensive and does not scale. There is a need for automated, structured, and mission-relevant threat assessment tools that can ground extracted information in a formal risk model.
AI.method: The proposed workflow integrates: (1) an interdisciplinary risk model defining mission-specific threat categories; (2) automated OSINT-based media collection; (3) LLM-supported threat extraction that maps media content to structured threat representations; (4) additional LLM-based post-processing steps to improve relevance filtering and factual grounding. The approach is instantiated within the PINPOINT project for the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia.
AI.result: Evaluation of LLM-extracted threats against human judgments demonstrates high inter-rater agreement on core dimensions — specifically threat identification and mission relevance. The results validate that LLMs can reliably replicate human-level threat assessment in this domain.
AI.conclusion: LLMs offer a promising tool for supporting human analysts in peacekeeping missions by automating threat extraction from open-source media. The approach reduces cognitive load and scales to large media volumes while maintaining alignment with human expert judgment.

title: When Does Quality-Aware Multimodal Fusion Matter? A Leakage-Safe Diagnostic for Decision-Level Dependence
comment: Accepted to INTERSPEECH 2026. 5 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables
summary: Many multimodal systems estimate the reliability of each modality and weight their contributions to the final prediction. However, it remains unclear whether these scores influence model decisions or merely correlate with performance. We propose a simple diagnostic to test whether reliability information is used during inference. After training, the model and inputs are fixed while reliability scores are permuted across test examples. If predictions depend on these scores, performance should degrade. Experiments on StressID for stress recognition and CMU-MOSEI for sentiment analysis show that permuting reliability scores leaves performance unchanged despite substantial potential gains from selecting the best modality per example. In positive controls where reliability signals identify the correct modality, the same frozen fusion rules yield significant improvements, indicating that reliability signals influence fused decisions only when they reliably predict unimodal correctness.

AI.tldr: A diagnostic permutes learned reliability scores post-training; since performance is unaffected, multimodal fusion models do not actually use these scores for decision-making unless the scores reliably predict unimodal correctness.
AI.motivation: To determine whether modality reliability weights in multimodal fusion systems genuinely influence model decisions or are merely correlated with performance without being causally utilized during inference.
AI.method: A simple diagnostic: after training, fix the model and inputs, then randomly permute the reliability scores across test examples. If predictions depend on these scores, performance should degrade. Positive controls are constructed where reliability signals explicitly identify the correct modality. Experiments run on StressID (stress recognition) and CMU-MOSEI (sentiment analysis).
AI.result: Permuting reliability scores leaves performance unchanged despite substantial potential oracle gains from selecting the best modality per example. In positive controls where reliability signals correctly identify the correct modality, the same frozen fusion rules yield significant improvements.
AI.conclusion: Reliability scores in standard multimodal fusion systems are not causally used during inference; they influence fused decisions only when they reliably predict unimodal correctness, which they typically do not. The diagnostic offers a lightweight way to audit whether learned weights are functionally utilized.

title: LLM-based Models for Detecting Emerging Topics in Service Feedback
summary:
Enhancing the analysis of service feedback is essential for public sector organizations, particularly tax administrations, where trust and compliance depend on fair and effective service delivery. As feedback volumes grow, identifying emerging service quality issues and potential disparities across diverse populations becomes increasingly challenging. Traditional approaches often rely on manual review or static expert-defined indicators, limiting scalability and the ability to capture complex patterns in textual feedback.
  This paper presents a novel methodology that integrates large language models (LLMs), statistical techniques, and human-AI collaboration to improve multilingual customer feedback analysis. The primary objective is to detect emerging service quality topics that may also reveal potential inequities in service delivery. Our framework combines fine-tuned, quantized LLMs with expert oversight to produce accurate, computationally efficient, and context-aware analyses.
  The proposed approach was evaluated using similarity analysis and assessments from experienced tax officers, demonstrating stronger alignment with expert judgments than baseline models. By incorporating a human-in-the-loop framework, the methodology reduces LLM fabrication while improving the reliability and relevance of generated insights.
  The results demonstrate the practicality of combining LLMs with human expertise to support scalable, evidence-based decision-making in public sector organizations. This work contributes to the development of responsible AI systems that enhance service quality, responsiveness, fairness, and public trust through more effective analysis of multilingual customer feedback.

AI.tldr: A human-AI collaborative framework combining fine-tuned quantized LLMs with expert oversight to detect emerging service quality issues and potential inequities in multilingual tax administration feedback, outperforming baseline models and reducing LLM fabrication.
AI.motivation: Traditional feedback analysis in public sector (especially tax administrations) relies on manual review or static indicators, which cannot scale or capture complex patterns in growing volumes of multilingual textual feedback, potentially missing emerging service quality issues and demographic disparities.
AI.method: A methodology integrating fine-tuned, quantized large language models (LLMs) with statistical techniques and a human-in-the-loop framework. Expert tax officers provide oversight, and the system is evaluated via similarity analysis and expert assessments against baseline models.
AI.result: The proposed approach demonstrated stronger alignment with expert judgments than baseline models, reduced LLM fabrication (hallucination), and improved the reliability and relevance of generated insights.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs with human expertise is practical and effective for scalable, evidence-based decision-making in public sector organizations, contributing to responsible AI that enhances service quality, fairness, and public trust through multilingual feedback analysis.

title: PRISM: PE Relational Inter-Section Matrix. A 2D Section-Aware Dataset for Static PE Malware Detection
summary:
We introduce PRISM (PE Relational Inter-Section Matrix), an open dataset and feature representation for static Windows PE malware detection. Existing benchmarks such as EMBER, BODMAS, and SOREL-20M represent each PE file as a flat one-dimensional feature vector, discarding the ordering of sections and the relational context between them. PRISM instead encodes every binary as a two-dimensional matrix whose rows are individual PE sections in file order, with a global summary row that preserves compatibility with EMBER-style models. We build the corpus from four malware sources (BODMAS, MalwareBazaar, VirusShare, and CAPE) together with SOREL-20M benign software, yielding 83,633 deduplicated matrices and a family-filtered analysis corpus of 49,204 samples across 684 malware families.
  A formal separability analysis (Fisher Discriminant Ratio, mutual information, and inter-section information gain) shows that the per-section positional structure carries discriminative information that flat representations cannot capture. Under a strictly controlled, sample-matched comparison, a gradient-boosted classifier on the compact PRISM representation recovers nearly all of the binary-detection performance of the same classifier on the much larger EMBER vector, at roughly one-sixth the dimensionality; EMBER retains only a small, consistent advantage confined to the extreme low-false-positive regime, the two being operationally indistinguishable at the decision threshold. We are explicit that this binary task is saturated, so the structural content PRISM preserves is reserved for tasks with greater metric headroom, such as family classification and architectures that exploit the 2D structure directly. The dataset, extraction library, trained models, and full analysis pipeline are released under CC BY-NC-SA and MIT licences.

AI.tldr: PRISM introduces a 2D matrix representation of PE files that preserves section ordering and inter-section relationships, unlike flat feature vectors used in prior benchmarks. A compact gradient-boosted classifier on PRISM matches EMBER's binary detection performance at ~1/6 the dimensionality, with the structural information reserved for tasks like family classification where metric headroom exists.
AI.motivation: Existing PE malware detection benchmarks (EMBER, BODMAS, SOREL-20M) discard section ordering and relational context by representing files as flat 1D feature vectors. This structural information may carry discriminative value that flat representations cannot capture, particularly for tasks beyond saturated binary detection.
AI.method: PRISM encodes each PE binary as a 2D matrix where rows represent individual PE sections in file order, plus a global summary row preserving EMBER compatibility. The corpus aggregates 83,633 deduplicated samples from BODMAS, MalwareBazaar, VirusShare, CAPE, and SOREL-20M, with a family-filtered subset of 49,204 samples across 684 families. Separability is formally analyzed via Fisher Discriminant Ratio, mutual information, and inter-section information gain. A gradient-boosted classifier on PRISM is compared against EMBER under strictly controlled, sample-matched conditions.
AI.result: The per-section positional structure carries discriminative information that flat representations cannot capture (shown by separability analysis). The PRISM classifier recovers nearly all binary-detection performance of the EMBER classifier at roughly 1/6 dimensionality. EMBER retains only a small, consistent advantage in the extreme low-false-positive regime, and the two are operationally indistinguishable at the decision threshold.
AI.conclusion: Binary malware detection is a saturated task; PRISM's preserved structural content is better leveraged for tasks with greater metric headroom, such as family classification and architectures that exploit the 2D structure directly. The dataset, extraction library, models, and analysis pipeline are publicly released under CC BY-NC-SA and MIT licenses.

title: Beyond Logical Forms: LLM-Extracted Patterns for Fallacy Classification
summary: In today's fast-paced information era, logical fallacies, defined as defective patterns of reasoning, inevitably contribute to the growth of information disorder. However, often fallacies appear in nuanced forms that complicate automated classification. In this study, we investigate whether merging abstract logical structures with context-level linguistic cues proves beneficial for fallacy classification, developing a framework that inductively extracts such patterns from fallacious examples and their explanations using Large Language Models (LLMs). We evaluate the impact of these patterns across different LLMs and experimental zero- and one-shot configurations, showing statistically significant improvements over zero-shot baselines and outperforming competing approaches. Cross-dataset experiments validate generalization, establishing data-driven pattern extraction as an effective method for generating logical representations.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether combining abstract logical structures with context-level linguistic cues improves logical fallacy classification. The authors develop an LLM-based framework that inductively extracts such patterns from fallacious examples and their explanations, demonstrating statistically significant improvements over zero-shot baselines and competing approaches across multiple datasets and experimental configurations.
AI.motivation: Logical fallacies contribute to information disorder in the digital age, but their nuanced and often subtle manifestations make automated classification challenging. Existing approaches may rely solely on surface-level linguistic features without capturing the underlying logical structure that defines a fallacy. This motivates the exploration of whether integrating abstract logical patterns with contextual cues can yield more robust classification.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to inductively extract abstract logical patterns from fallacious examples paired with their explanations. These extracted patterns are then merged with context-level linguistic cues and used for fallacy classification. The approach is evaluated under zero-shot and one-shot configurations across different LLMs.
AI.result: The integrated pattern-based approach yields statistically significant improvements over zero-shot baselines and outperforms competing methods. Cross-dataset experiments further validate the generalization capability of the framework, confirming that data-driven pattern extraction is an effective strategy for generating logical representations for fallacy classification.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven extraction of abstract logical patterns, when combined with linguistic context, provides a meaningful representational advance for automated fallacy classification. The approach generalizes across datasets and LLMs, establishing a promising direction for future work on reasoning-aware NLP systems.

title: Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use to a Single Crosscoder Feature
comment: Accepted as a spotlight at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop
summary: Fine-tuning through RL reshapes the internal representations of language models to enable agentic behaviors such as tool use, yet the mechanistic basis of these changes remains poorly understood. While RL substantially improves structured tool-call generation, it is unclear which features emerge, which are preserved, and whether identified features can be leveraged for retraining-free behavioral control. In this work, we show that $\textit{Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC)}$ isolate a compact set of RL-specific features that mediate tool-calling capability in $\texttt{Qwen2.5-3B}$. Across a $48$-crosscoder hyperparameter sweep, encode-decode reconstruction improves the RL model's tool correctness by $+31.1 \pm {9.7}$ pp and passively transfers tool-calling ability to the frozen base model by $+6.8 \pm 5.0$ pp which we call a $\textit{capability spillover}$. Our findings show that DFC partitioning concentrates RL-introduced capability into a minimal, steerable feature set that enables runtime behavioral control of agentic LLMs.

AI.tldr: RL fine-tuning for tool calling in LLMs introduces a compact, isolatable set of features. Using Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC), these features can be extracted and transferred to a frozen base model, improving tool-calling correctness without retraining, and enabling runtime behavioral control.
AI.motivation: While RL fine-tuning demonstrably improves agentic behaviors like structured tool use in language models, the underlying mechanistic changes in internal representations are poorly understood. The authors aim to identify which features emerge or are preserved through RL, and whether these features can be leveraged for behavioral control without additional retraining.
AI.method: The authors propose Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC), a method that isolates a compact set of RL-specific features mediating tool-calling capability. They conduct a 48-crosscoder hyperparameter sweep on Qwen2.5-3B, using encode-decode reconstruction to partition RL-introduced features from the base model's representations.
AI.result: DFC encode-decode reconstruction improves the RL model's tool-call correctness by +31.1 ± 9.7 percentage points. Furthermore, the isolated features passively transfer tool-calling ability to the frozen base model, yielding a +6.8 ± 5.0 pp improvement — a phenomenon termed "capability spillover."
AI.conclusion: DFC partitioning successfully concentrates RL-introduced capabilities into a minimal, steerable feature set. This enables runtime behavioral control of agentic LLMs without retraining, demonstrating that tool-use capabilities can be extracted and transferred through sparse feature manipulation.

title: Autoformalization of Agent Instructions into Policy-as-Code
comment: Accepted at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD), ICML 2026
summary: Agent safety in high-stakes domains requires formal policy enforcement, but most existing approaches either rely on probabilistic guardrails (fine-tuned classifiers, prompt-based steering) that offer no formal guarantees, or on hand-coded symbolic enforcement that does not scale to the breadth of real policy specifications. We present an autoformalization pipeline that translates agent prompts, MCP tool descriptions, and natural language policy documents into formally verified policies using an LLM-based generator-critic loop. The resulting policies are written in the Cedar Policy Language. On the MedAgentBench benchmark, our autoformalized policies cover substantially more of the source natural-language specification than the hand-coded symbolic enforcement in prior work.

AI.tldr: An autoformalization pipeline uses an LLM generator-critic loop to translate natural-language agent prompts, tool descriptions, and policy documents into formally verified Cedar policies, achieving broader specification coverage on MedAgentBench than prior hand-coded symbolic enforcement.
AI.motivation: High-stakes agent safety demands formal policy enforcement with rigorous guarantees. Existing solutions fall short: probabilistic guardrails (fine-tuned classifiers, prompt steering) lack formal guarantees, while hand-coded symbolic enforcement fails to scale to the breadth and complexity of real-world policy specifications.
AI.method: An autoformalization pipeline employing an LLM-based generator-critic loop that ingests agent prompts, MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool descriptions, and natural-language policy documents, and outputs policies written in the Cedar Policy Language. The critic component iteratively verifies and refines the generated policies to ensure formal correctness.
AI.result: On the MedAgentBench benchmark, the autoformalized policies achieve substantially greater coverage of the source natural-language specification compared to hand-coded symbolic enforcement from prior work.
AI.conclusion: Autoformalization via an LLM generator-critic loop offers a scalable path to formally verified policy enforcement for AI agents, overcoming the coverage limitations of manual symbolic encoding while retaining formal guarantees absent from probabilistic approaches.

title: The Observer World: A Cryptographic Extension of Impagliazzo's Five Worlds
summary: Impagliazzo's five worlds classify computational assumptions along a single axis, the existence of cryptographic primitives. All five worlds implicitly assume that every party, including the adversary, observes the full input, that the observer is always $O_{top}$. This assumption is so natural that it is never stated. This work makes it explicit and relaxes it by introducing a second, orthogonal axis, the observational axis, defined by the observer hierarchy introduced in previous work. Relaxing the assumption reveals structural phenomena, such as the collapse $P^{O_{prof}} = NP^{O_{prof}} \subset P$, that the five-world framework cannot express. We prove that this collapse holds unconditionally in all five worlds, showing that observational blindness and computational hardness are independent. We define the Observer World $W_O$, classify all world-observer pairs, identify the labeled cells (a)--(d), and introduce a parametric family $W_O^{\varepsilon}$ modelling partial violations of observational invariants. The framework also interfaces with physical information limits, including thermodynamic, quantum, and cosmological bounds.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a second, orthogonal "observational axis" to Impagliazzo's five worlds, defined by an observer hierarchy. It proves that observational blindness (collapse of P^O_prof = NP^O_prof ⊆ P) holds unconditionally across all five worlds, demonstrates independence between observational and computational hardness, and constructs a parametric family modeling partial violations of observational invariants, linking the framework to physical information bounds.
AI.motivation: Impagliazzo's five worlds classify computational assumptions solely by the existence of cryptographic primitives, but all implicitly assume the adversary has full, top-level observational access (O_top). This assumption is never stated. The authors make it explicit and argue that relaxing it—by introducing an observer hierarchy—reveals structural phenomena invisible to the original five-world framework, such as unconditional collapses and independence results between observational blindness and computational hardness.
AI.method: The authors introduce a second orthogonal axis: the observational axis, defined by an observer hierarchy (O_top, O_prof, etc.) from prior work. They define the Observer World W_O, classify all world-observer pairs into labeled cells, and prove structural results such as P^O_prof = NP^O_prof ⊆ P holding unconditionally across all five worlds. They further introduce a parametric family W_O^ε that models partial violations of observational invariants, and interface the framework with physical information limits (thermodynamic, quantum, cosmological bounds).
AI.result: The key result is that the collapse P^O_prof = NP^O_prof ⊆ P holds unconditionally in all five of Impagliazzo's worlds, demonstrating that observational blindness and computational hardness are independent. The framework successfully classifies all world-observer pairs and identifies labeled cells (a)–(d). The parametric family W_O^ε captures partial violations, and the framework connects to physical constraints on information.
AI.conclusion: The observational axis is independent of the computational hardness axis in Impagliazzo's taxonomy. By making the implicit full-observation assumption explicit and relaxing it, the paper uncovers structural properties—such as unconditional collapses—that the five-world framework alone cannot express. The resulting framework generalizes Impagliazzo's worlds with a richer, two-dimensional classification that also engages physical limits on observation.

title: Retrieval-Warmed Energy-Based Reasoning: A Five-Arm Ablation Methodology for Diffusion-as-Inference on Structured Reasoning Tasks
summary: Warm-started diffusion samplers accelerate iterative inference, but it is rarely clear which part of the pipeline carries the gain. We study \textbf{retrieval-warmed energy-based reasoning (RW-EBR)} -- an IRED energy-based diffusion model \cite{du2024ired} augmented with a Modern Hopfield trajectory memory -- and contribute a \textbf{five-arm ablation methodology} (oracle, best-constant, per-query-random, shuffled, aligned) that separates three confounded effects: class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, and graph-aligned value reuse. The diagnostic decomposition is adapted from LLM-RAG evaluation \cite{ru2024ragchecker}. On \textbf{connectivity-2} (Erdős--Rényi all-pairs reachability), the aligned-vs-shuffled-oracle swing reaches \textbf{$+35$\,pp} balanced accuracy on a fixed 1{,}000-graph validation-set diagnostic, with value distribution and retrieval mechanics fixed, only per-graph alignment destroyed, while per-query random initialisation falls below cold -- per-graph alignment, not bias shift or stochasticity, dominates. Yet the \emph{deployable} cold-prediction pipeline misses the acceptance gate at stored-value quality. The same diagnostic logic, stopped at the key-quality screen, applied to \textbf{Sudoku} with a task-specific key encoder produces a clean negative at a \emph{different} component -- key quality, under the current setup. The decomposition names the first blocking component on each task. The setting -- graph reachability refined by an iterative diffusion sampler, with explainability of failure modes as the lens -- places the work within structured and spatio-temporal reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces retrieval-warmed energy-based reasoning (RW-EBR), combining an IRED diffusion model with a Modern Hopfield memory, and a five-arm ablation methodology to disentangle confounded effects in warm-started diffusion samplers. On graph reachability, per-graph alignment dominates gains (+35pp over shuffled), while on Sudoku, key quality is the bottleneck. The framework isolates failure modes in iterative diffusion reasoning pipelines.
AI.motivation: Warm-started diffusion samplers are known to accelerate inference, but it remains unclear which specific component (class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, or graph-aligned value reuse) actually drives the performance gain. The authors seek to isolate these confounded effects with a principled ablation methodology.
AI.method: The authors propose RW-EBR, an IRED energy-based diffusion model augmented with a Modern Hopfield trajectory memory. They contribute a five-arm ablation methodology (oracle, best-constant, per-query-random, shuffled, aligned) adapted from LLM-RAG evaluation (Ru et al., 2024), which separates three confounded effects: class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, and graph-aligned value reuse. The methodology is applied to two tasks: Erdős–Rényi all-pairs reachability (connectivity-2) and Sudoku, the latter with a task-specific key encoder.
AI.result: On connectivity-2 with a fixed 1,000-graph validation set, aligned retrieval yields a +35pp balanced accuracy swing over shuffled-oracle, with value distribution and retrieval mechanics fixed — only per-graph alignment destroyed. Per-query random initialization falls below the cold baseline, confirming alignment dominates over bias shift or stochasticity. However, the deployable cold-prediction pipeline fails the acceptance gate at stored-value quality. On Sudoku, the same diagnostic reveals a clean negative: key quality — not alignment — is the first blocking component under the current setup.
AI.conclusion: The diagnostic decomposition successfully names the first blocking component on each task: per-graph alignment for graph reachability, key quality for Sudoku. This approach, framed within structured and spatio-temporal reasoning with explainability of failure modes as the lens, provides a principled way to audit and improve warm-started iterative diffusion samplers.

title: SKILL-DISCO: Distilling and Compiling Agent Traces into Reusable Procedural Skills
summary: Agents often repeatedly solve similar task instances from scratch, leading to unnecessary reasoning cost and long execution traces. Prior work has explored workflow reuse and executable skill induction, but it remains unclear which task scenarios admit procedural skills and how the shared procedural structure should be represented across successful traces. We study this problem in FSM-defined scenarios, where successful traces can be viewed as paths in an unknown transition graph, and formulate procedural skills as reusable parameterized control-flow subgraphs. Based on this view, we introduce SkillDisCo, a distillation-and-compilation framework that distills reusable PFSM subgraphs from successful traces and compiles them into callable, executable, and verifiable procedural skills. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebArena show that SkillDisCo improves success rates and reduces agent turns across benchmarks and model scales, demonstrating the benefits of representing shared experience as reusable execution structures.

AI.tldr: SkillDisCo introduces a framework that distills reusable procedural skills from successful agent execution traces by modeling them as parameterized finite-state machine (PFSM) subgraphs, then compiles them into callable, executable, and verifiable skills. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebArena show improved success rates and reduced agent turns.
AI.motivation: Agents waste computational effort by repeatedly solving similar tasks from scratch, producing long execution traces. Existing approaches using workflow reuse or executable skill induction lack clarity on (1) which scenarios admit procedural skills and (2) how shared procedural structure across successful traces should be represented.
AI.method: The authors model FSM-defined task scenarios where successful traces are paths in an unknown transition graph. Procedural skills are formalized as reusable parameterized control-flow subgraphs (PFSMs). The SkillDisCo framework operates in two stages: (1) distillation — extracting reusable PFSM subgraphs from successful traces, and (2) compilation — converting these subgraphs into callable, executable, and verifiable procedural skills that agents can invoke during future tasks.
AI.result: SkillDisCo achieves improved success rates and reduced agent turns across both ALFWorld and WebArena benchmarks, with the benefits generalizing across different model scales.
AI.conclusion: Representing shared experience as reusable execution structures (PFSM-based procedural skills) is an effective approach for improving agent efficiency and performance in FSM-defined task environments.

title: Tilikum: Transaction Fair Ordering on a DAG without Weak Edges
summary: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) applications rely heavily on the order in which transactions are executed, making them susceptible to reordering attacks that enable adversaries to extract Blockchain Extractable Value (BEV). While linear blockchain systems such as Ethereum have inspired extensive research into fair ordering mechanisms, DAG-based consensus protocols have remained largely unprotected despite their growing adoption for scalability and performance. In this paper, we introduce Tilikum, a DAG-based ledger protocol that ensures fair transaction ordering without relying on weak edges. Tilikum achieves ordering linearizability by leveraging median-based timestamp aggregation, or batch order fairness, while maintaining low data redundancy and robust garbage collection. We implemented Tilikum in Rust and evaluated it against representative baselines, namely Narwhal/Tusk, Pompē, Themis and FairDAG. Our results show that Tilikum achieves up to $39\times$ higher throughput than other fair-ordering baselines, while fully blocking state-of-the-art DAG-specific reordering attacks.

AI.tldr: Tilikum is a DAG-based ledger protocol that achieves fair transaction ordering through median-based timestamp aggregation, achieving up to 39× higher throughput than existing fair-ordering baselines while fully blocking DAG-specific reordering attacks.
AI.motivation: DAG-based consensus protocols lack protection against transaction reordering attacks and Blockchain Extractable Value (BEV) extraction, despite their growing adoption for scalability. Existing fair ordering mechanisms are designed for linear blockchains and are not applicable to DAG-based systems.
AI.method: Tilikum employs median-based timestamp aggregation to achieve ordering linearizability and batch order fairness on a DAG structure, without relying on weak edges. It also incorporates low data redundancy and robust garbage collection mechanisms. The protocol was implemented in Rust and evaluated against Narwhal/Tusk, Pompē, Themis, and FairDAG.
AI.result: Tilikum achieves up to 39× higher throughput than other fair-ordering baselines (Narwhal/Tusk, Pompē, Themis, FairDAG) and successfully blocks state-of-the-art DAG-specific reordering attacks.
AI.conclusion: Tilikum demonstrates that fair transaction ordering is achievable on DAG-based ledgers without sacrificing throughput, offering a practical solution for DeFi applications on high-performance DAG consensus protocols.

title: Evaluation Pitfalls and Challenges in Multimedia Event Extraction
summary: Multimedia event extraction aims to jointly identify events and their arguments across multiple modalities, such as text and images, to support more comprehensive event understanding. While recent work reports steady and substantial progress, the reliability and comparability of these results critically depend on consistent and rigorous evaluation. In this work, we present the first systematic analysis of evaluation pitfalls in multimedia event extraction and identify three major sources of issues: inconsistent data processing, inconsistent task assumptions, and overly relaxed evaluation settings. We demonstrate, through a series of controlled experiments under a strict evaluation framework, that minor evaluation choices can cause large performance variations and lead to overestimation of a model's ability to ground real-world events across modalities. Our findings highlight the need for comparable evaluation standards and encourage a shift toward more rigorous evaluation in multimedia event extraction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic analysis of evaluation pitfalls in multimedia event extraction, identifying three major sources of issues — inconsistent data processing, inconsistent task assumptions, and overly relaxed evaluation settings — and demonstrates through controlled experiments that minor evaluation choices can significantly inflate performance, calling for more rigorous and standardized evaluation practices.
AI.motivation: While multimedia event extraction has seen steady progress, the reliability and comparability of reported results are questionable due to inconsistent evaluation practices. The authors recognized that no prior work had systematically examined how evaluation choices affect performance claims, potentially leading to overestimated model capabilities in grounding real-world events across modalities.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic audit of evaluation practices in multimedia event extraction. They identify and taxonomize three categories of pitfalls: (1) inconsistent data preprocessing across studies, (2) incompatible task assumptions (e.g., differing definitions of what constitutes correct argument identification), and (3) overly permissive evaluation metrics. They then design controlled experiments under a strict, unified evaluation framework to isolate and quantify the impact of each evaluation choice on reported performance.
AI.result: Minor variations in evaluation choices — such as data splits, argument matching criteria, or whether partial credit is awarded — produce large swings in reported performance, often substantially overestimating a model's true cross-modal event grounding ability. The strict evaluation framework reveals that models perform considerably worse than previously reported when held to consistent, rigorous standards.
AI.conclusion: The field of multimedia event extraction urgently needs standardized, comparable evaluation protocols. The authors advocate for a shift toward stricter evaluation that more faithfully reflects real-world multimodal event understanding capabilities, rather than artificially inflated metrics driven by lax or inconsistent evaluation practices.

title: What Survives When You Compress a Recursive Reasoner for the Edge?
summary: Recursive reasoning models can solve complex structured tasks with only a few million parameters by repeatedly updating a latent state. Deploying these models on edge hardware requires significant compression, but unlike conventional sequence models, quantization errors compound across recursive reasoning cycles rather than across output tokens. As a result, standard intuitions about compression fail to apply. In this work, we ask what survives when recursive reasoners are compressed. Across a full precision sweep, three tasks, and two recursive architectures, we find that aggressive compression preserves local prediction but destroys global reasoning: cell accuracy holds while puzzle-exact accuracy collapses to zero under naive INT4 pruning, distillation, and linear attention alike. Token-level objectives, including quantization-aware training, cannot repair it. The collapse is architectural -- it strikes MLP-mixing recursion but not attention on the same task -- and we reverse it with per-channel calibrated INT4 without retraining. We also introduce carry-trajectory fidelity, the cosine similarity to the full-precision reasoning path, as a label-free signal that predicts this damage and its recovery before a task evaluation. The combined result is a deployment recipe: flash-streamed embeddings remove a 99.4MB bottleneck, INT8 at one cycle matches full-depth accuracy at 6x fewer FLOPs (8MB SoC), and calibrated INT4 fits a 4MB microcontroller.

AI.tldr: Compressing recursive reasoning models reveals a critical divergence: local token prediction survives aggressive quantization, but global puzzle-solving reasoning collapses. Token-level objectives cannot fix this architectural vulnerability, but per-channel calibrated INT4 without retraining can reverse it. A new metric, carry-trajectory fidelity, predicts the damage label-free.
AI.motivation: Recursive reasoning models are attractive for edge deployment due to their small parameter counts, but compression is necessary for extreme hardware constraints (microcontrollers, SoCs). Unlike standard autoregressive models where quantization error accumulates across output tokens, recursive models compound error across reasoning cycles within the same latent state, making standard compression intuitions inapplicable. The authors aim to understand what aspects of recursive reasoning survive compression and how to mitigate catastrophic failures.
AI.method: The authors conduct a full precision sweep across three tasks and two recursive architectures (MLP-mixing recursion and attention-based recursion). They evaluate naive INT4 pruning, distillation, linear attention approximations, and quantization-aware training (QAT). They introduce per-channel calibrated INT4 (without retraining) as a remedy, and propose "carry-trajectory fidelity" — the cosine similarity between compressed and full-precision latent state trajectories — as a label-free diagnostic metric. Deployment strategies include flash-streamed embeddings, INT8 at one cycle, and calibrated INT4 for microcontrollers.
AI.result: Under aggressive compression, cell-level prediction accuracy holds while puzzle-exact match accuracy collapses to zero — a pattern consistent across naive INT4 pruning, distillation, and linear attention. Token-level objectives including QAT fail to repair this collapse. The collapse is architectural: it affects MLP-mixing recursion but not attention-based models on the same task. Per-channel calibrated INT4 without retraining reverses the collapse. Carry-trajectory fidelity reliably predicts reasoning degradation before any task evaluation. Deployment results: flash-streamed embeddings remove a 99.4MB bottleneck, INT8 at one cycle matches full-depth accuracy at 6× fewer FLOPs (8MB SoC), and calibrated INT4 fits a 4MB microcontroller.
AI.conclusion: Recursive reasoning models exhibit a sharp local-vs-global fidelity tradeoff under compression that standard techniques cannot address. Per-channel calibrated quantization without retraining provides a practical fix, and carry-trajectory fidelity offers a task-agnostic early-warning signal. The combined recipe enables deployment of recursive reasoners down to 4MB microcontrollers.

title: NebulaExp-8B: An Empirical Post-Training Pipeline via Full-Scale Ablation Research
summary: Post-training alignment determines the reasoning and human preference following capabilities of large language models, yet most existing works withhold detailed data construction, filtering rules and training recipes, which hinders community reproducibility and lightweight model optimization. This work presents NebulaExp, a fully transparent, ablation-driven post-training pipeline built on Qwen3-8B-base, covering two orthogonal model branches: general instruct model and complex reasoning-specialized model. We curate a raw corpus of 3.84M multi-source SFT samples and a 200K verifiable RL candidate pool, and design an end-to-end data processing stack including response distillation, multi-dimensional cross-verification filtering, fine-grained difficulty grading, task classification and diversity-aware sampling. For the Instruct branch, our three-stage optimized supervised fine-tuning approach NebulaExp-Ins-SFT improves the average benchmark score from the 55.01 baseline of Qwen3-8B-nothink to 60.99. GRPO reinforcement learning then further elevates the average score to 61.85. For the Reasoning branch, medium-difficulty GRPO RL improves average reasoning score from 73.88 to 75.17. To address RL's dependency on task verifiers, we systematically investigate single-teacher and multi-teacher OPD (MOPD): utilizing merely 4K instruction-following samples and outperforms RL baseline by 3.26 points on IFEval with +4.43 average overall gain; MOPD fuses four domain-specialist teachers with merely 10K samples, lifting average performance by 4.18 over the base model. This report provides a fully reproducible empirical post-training recipe for 8B-scale LLMs, and comprehensively dissects the capability trade-offs among instruction adherence, mathematical reasoning, code generation and general knowledge.

AI.tldr: NebulaExp presents a fully transparent, reproducible post-training pipeline for Qwen3-8B, covering both general instruct and reasoning-specialized models. It details data construction (3.84M SFT samples, 200K RL candidates), multi-stage SFT, GRPO-based RL, and investigates offline policy distillation (OPD/MOPD) as an alternative to RL, providing comprehensive capability trade-off analysis.
AI.motivation: Most existing post-training works withhold critical details on data construction, filtering rules, and training recipes, hindering reproducibility and lightweight model optimization. The authors aim to provide a fully transparent, ablation-driven empirical pipeline to fill this gap.
AI.method: The pipeline builds on Qwen3-8B-base with two branches: (1) Instruct branch using three-stage supervised fine-tuning (NebulaExp-Ins-SFT) followed by GRPO reinforcement learning; (2) Reasoning branch using medium-difficulty GRPO RL. Data processing includes response distillation, multi-dimensional cross-verification filtering, fine-grained difficulty grading, task classification, and diversity-aware sampling from a 3.84M SFT corpus and 200K verifiable RL pool. Additionally, single-teacher and multi-teacher Offline Policy Distillation (OPD/MOPD) are investigated as alternatives to RL, using only 4K–10K samples.
AI.result: For the Instruct branch, SFT improves average benchmark from 55.01 to 60.99; GRPO further lifts it to 61.85. For the Reasoning branch, GRPO improves reasoning score from 73.88 to 75.17. Single-teacher OPD with 4K samples outperforms RL by 3.26 points on IFEval with +4.43 average gain; MOPD with four domain specialists and 10K samples achieves +4.18 average improvement over base.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a fully reproducible post-training recipe for 8B-scale LLMs, with transparent data and training details. It demonstrates that OPD/MOPD can serve as sample-efficient alternatives to RL for instruction following, and provides a thorough dissection of capability trade-offs among instruction adherence, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general knowledge.

title: OPID: On-Policy Skill Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides a stable optimization backbone for language agents, but its sparse trajectory-level rewards provide little guidance on which intermediate decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. On-policy self-distillation offers dense token-level supervision, yet existing skill-conditioned variants often rely on external skill memories or retrieved privileged context, which are costly to maintain and can be mismatched with the state distribution induced by the current policy in multi-turn interaction. We propose \textbf{OPID} (\textbf{O}n-\textbf{P}olicy Sk\textbf{i}ll \textbf{D}istillation), a framework that extracts skill supervision directly from completed on-policy trajectories. OPID represents trajectory hindsight as hierarchical skills: episode-level skills capture global workflows or failure-avoidance rules, while step-level skills capture local decision knowledge at critical timesteps. A critical-first routing mechanism uses step-level skills when critical decisions are identified and falls back to episode-level skills as default guidance otherwise. The selected skill is injected into the interaction history, allowing the old policy to re-score the same sampled response under both original and skill-augmented contexts. The resulting log-probability shift yields a token-level self-distillation advantage, which is combined with the outcome advantage for policy optimization. OPID thus preserves RL as the primary training objective while introducing dense, distribution-matched hindsight supervision. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop and Search-based QA demonstrate that OPID generally improves agent performance, sample efficiency, and robustness over outcome-only RL and existing skill-distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/jinyangwu/OPID/tree/main.

AI.tldr: OPID introduces on-policy skill distillation for language agents, extracting hierarchical skills (episode-level and step-level) directly from completed trajectories. A critical-first routing mechanism selects appropriate skills to augment context, producing token-level self-distillation advantages that complement sparse outcome rewards in RL training.
AI.motivation: Outcome-based RL for language agents suffers from sparse trajectory-level rewards that offer no intermediate guidance. Existing skill-conditioned methods rely on external skill memories or retrieved privileged context, which are costly and suffer from distribution mismatch with the current policy in multi-turn settings.
AI.method: OPID extracts hierarchical skills directly from on-policy trajectories: episode-level skills summarize global workflows/failure-avoidance rules, while step-level skills capture local decision knowledge at critical timesteps. A critical-first routing mechanism uses step-level skills at critical junctures and defaults to episode-level skills otherwise. Selected skills are injected into interaction history, and the old policy re-scores responses under both original and skill-augmented contexts. The resulting log-probability shift produces token-level self-distillation advantages, combined with outcome advantages for policy optimization.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA show OPID improves agent performance, sample efficiency, and robustness over outcome-only RL and existing skill-distillation baselines.
AI.conclusion: OPID demonstrates that dense, distribution-matched hindsight supervision from on-policy trajectories can effectively complement sparse outcome rewards in language agent RL, without requiring external skill memories or privileged context.

title: Learning Probabilistic Filters with Strictly Proper Scoring Rules
summary: Bayesian filtering of partially and noisily observed dynamical systems seeks to infer the evolving conditional distribution of the state of a dynamical system, given observations, in an online fashion. This Bayesian filtering distribution is the natural object for uncertainty quantification, but it is rarely available as a supervised learning target. However, one can often use the forecast model to generate synthetic system trajectories, along with synthetic observations. We introduce the proper scoring ensemble filter (PSEF), an ensemble data assimilation method based on training an analysis map to approximate the filtering distribution using only synthetic state--observation trajectories. The analysis step is represented as a permutation-invariant, transformer-based map that takes as input a forecast ensemble and observations, producing an analysis ensemble. Training is based on strictly proper scoring rules -- with the energy score used in our implementation -- so that probabilistic accuracy is rewarded over the whole probability distribution. We prove that, under a realizability assumption, the population objective is minimized by the true Bayesian filtering distribution. We also derive the finite-ensemble empirical objective used in training and relate its single state--observation trajectory form to the population objective, using a mean-field consistency argument. Numerical experiments show that the learned filter accurately approximates challenging filtering distributions, including nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and multi-modal posteriors, and achieves stronger performance in data assimilation tasks than classical methods or learning-based methods with mean-squared-error objectives. For close-to-Gaussian problems, learning a correction to the EnKF is the best approach, while for highly non-Gaussian problems an end-to-end approach that discards this inductive bias is superior.

AI.tldr: Introduces PSEF, a learned ensemble data assimilation method that trains a transformer-based analysis map using strictly proper scoring rules (energy score) on synthetic data. The method provably recovers the true Bayesian filtering distribution under realizability and outperforms classical and MSE-based learned filters, especially on non-Gaussian and multi-modal problems.
AI.motivation: The Bayesian filtering distribution is the ideal target for uncertainty quantification in sequential data assimilation, but is rarely available as a supervised learning target. Existing learned filters typically use mean-squared-error objectives, which fail to capture full distributional accuracy. The authors aim to leverage synthetic simulation data and proper scoring rules to learn analysis maps that approximate the entire filtering distribution.
AI.method: The PSEF trains a permutation-invariant, transformer-based analysis map that maps a forecast ensemble and observations to an analysis ensemble. Training uses the energy score, a strictly proper scoring rule, computed on synthetic state-observation trajectories. The authors prove the population objective is minimized by the true filtering distribution (realizability), derive the finite-ensemble empirical objective, and establish a mean-field consistency argument linking single-trajectory and population objectives.
AI.result: PSEF accurately approximates challenging filtering distributions including nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and multi-modal posteriors. It outperforms classical methods and MSE-based learned methods in data assimilation tasks. For near-Gaussian problems, learning a correction to the EnKF works best; for highly non-Gaussian problems, an end-to-end approach discarding the EnKF inductive bias is superior.
AI.conclusion: Training analysis maps with strictly proper scoring rules on synthetic data is an effective strategy for learned data assimilation. The energy score provides distributionally accurate filters that outperform MSE-trained alternatives. The choice between correcting EnKF versus end-to-end learning depends on the degree of non-Gaussianity in the problem.

title: Do Safety Guardrails Need to Reason? LeanGuard: A Fast and Light Approach for Robust Moderation
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://ndb796.github.io/LeanGuard ; code and models: https://github.com/ndb796/LeanGuard
