summary: In order to screen a prompt or a response, the recent guardrail methods generate a chain-of-thought (CoT) before they issue a verdict. This design follows a common belief that step-by-step reasoning improves a decision. However, CoT also makes the guard heavy and slow, because the model must generate many tokens before it decides. This may not match how guardrails are actually deployed. A guardrail sometimes should not be heavy and slow, and it often runs on-device, for example on an embodied robot. In this paper, we pose a question whether a safety guardrail really needs to reason. To answer this question, we train a lightweight bidirectional encoder and a reasoning guard on the same corpus, and we then remove only the reasoning while we keep everything else fixed. With this controlled same-base comparison, we show that the chain does not improve moderation accuracy. We name the resulting guard LeanGuard. A 395M label-only encoder reaches an average F1 of 82.90 $\pm$ 0.26 over public benchmarks. It matches a reasoning guard that is built on a much larger decoder, while it uses only a single forward pass over an input of at most 512 tokens. This is about a ~100x reduction in inference compute. We further show that this label-only encoder stays robust under training-label noise and retains far more recall at a strict false-positive rate than the reasoning guard, so a heavier reasoning guard is not the more robust choice either. Our finding suggests that the current guardrail benchmarks may not be hard enough to reward reasoning, and that the necessity of CoT for moderation is still not proven. We release all source codes and models including LeanGuard at https://github.com/ndb796/LeanGuard.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the necessity of chain-of-thought reasoning in safety guardrails, demonstrating that a lightweight 395M bidirectional encoder (LeanGuard) without reasoning matches or exceeds the moderation accuracy of much larger decoder-based reasoning guards, while reducing inference compute by ~100x.
AI.motivation: Current guardrail methods use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before issuing verdicts, based on the belief that step-by-step reasoning improves decisions. However, this makes guards heavy and slow, which is unsuitable for on-device deployment scenarios like embodied robots. The paper questions whether safety guardrails truly need reasoning at all.
AI.method: The authors conduct a controlled same-base comparison: they train both a lightweight bidirectional encoder (label-only) and a reasoning guard on the same corpus, then remove only the reasoning component while keeping everything else fixed. This isolates the effect of CoT on moderation accuracy. The resulting model, LeanGuard, is a 395M-parameter encoder that performs a single forward pass over at most 512 tokens.
AI.result: LeanGuard achieves an average F1 of 82.90 ± 0.26 on public benchmarks, matching the performance of a much larger decoder-based reasoning guard. This represents approximately a 100x reduction in inference compute. Additionally, the label-only encoder remains robust under training-label noise and retains significantly more recall at strict false-positive rates compared to the reasoning guard.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that current guardrail benchmarks may not be sufficiently challenging to reward reasoning, and the necessity of CoT for moderation remains unproven. A lightweight, reasoning-free encoder can be a more practical and equally effective alternative for safety guardrail deployment.

title: Multipath Adaptive Gated Bottleneck Latent ODE with Raman Data Fusion for Cell Culture Process Forecasting
summary: Mammalian cell-culture processes underpin the manufacture of many biopharmaceuticals, yet keeping a run on track is hard: critical process parameters drift over days, and an off-specification trend is often confirmed too late to intervene. Early-stage, multi-day forecasts could enable timely adjustment of feeding, sampling, and control, but bioprocess forecasting is challenging because measurements are sparse and irregularly sampled, operating conditions are heterogeneous across cell lines and media, and runs with near-identical early behaviour can diverge into different futures. We propose an adaptive framework combining a Gated Bottleneck Latent Ordinary Differential Equation (GB-Latent ODE) with Multi-Path Just-In-Time Fine Tuning (MP-JIT-FT). The GB-Latent ODE augments the stan dard Latent ODE with learnable variable-wise gating and a mask-aware bottleneck that compress high-dimensional sparse inputs, improving learning under limited data. Given a partially observed run, MP-JIT-FT retrieves similar historical trajectories, clusters the local neighbourhood into candidate regimes, and fine-tunes a separate model per regime to produce multiple plausible paths, each with a reconstruction-based confidence score, not a single averaged forecast. We further fuse Raman spectroscopy data: a machine-learning soft sensor turns dense Raman spectra into pseudo-observations that enrich the sparse offline measurements for more robust training. On 38 fed-batch 5L bioreactor runs spanning 14 conditions, MP-JIT-FT with Raman fusion achieves the best average rank and outperforms a global Latent ODE baseline on 8 of 9 target variables. Using local-divergence metrics, we show the multi-path gains are largest when locally similar prefixes diverge, whereas Raman fusion helps most when early dynamics are representative of later behaviour.

AI.tldr: A framework combining Gated Bottleneck Latent ODE with Multi-Path Just-In-Time Fine-Tuning and Raman spectroscopy fusion enables multi-day, multi-path forecasting of mammalian cell-culture bioprocesses, outperforming global baselines on 38 fed-batch bioreactor runs across diverse conditions.
AI.motivation: Mammalian cell-culture bioprocesses suffer from drifting critical parameters, sparse/irregular measurements, heterogeneous operating conditions, and divergent future trajectories despite similar early behavior — making early forecasting essential but extremely challenging for timely intervention.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) a Gated Bottleneck Latent ODE that extends standard Latent ODEs with learnable variable-wise gating and a mask-aware bottleneck to handle sparse high-dimensional inputs; (2) Multi-Path Just-In-Time Fine-Tuning (MP-JIT-FT), which retrieves similar historical trajectories, clusters them into candidate regimes, and fine-tunes separate models per regime to generate multiple plausible forecast paths with reconstruction-based confidence scores; and (3) Raman spectroscopy fusion via an ML soft sensor that converts dense Raman spectra into pseudo-observations to augment sparse offline measurements.
AI.result: On 38 fed-batch 5L bioreactor runs across 14 conditions, MP-JIT-FT with Raman fusion achieved the best average rank and outperformed a global Latent ODE baseline on 8 of 9 target variables. Multi-path gains were largest when locally similar prefixes diverged, while Raman fusion helped most when early dynamics were representative of later behavior.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive multi-path framework with Raman fusion provides reliable early-stage multi-day bioprocess forecasts, enabling timely interventions. The method's strength lies in explicitly modeling trajectory divergence and leveraging dense spectroscopic data to compensate for sparse offline sampling.

title: Kalman Prototypical Networks for Few-shot Fault Detection in Combined Cycle Gas Turbines
summary: Combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGTs) play a key role in modern power generation, offering both high efficiency and reduced environmental impact. However, their complex thermo-fluid and mechanical interactions complicate fault detection, particularly when labeled fault data are scarce. In this paper, we introduce the Kalman Prototypical Network (KPN), a metric-based few-shot learning (FSL) framework specifically tailored for CCGT fault diagnosis. We model the evolution of class prototypes as latent stochastic states in a dynamic system to reduce episodic variance and improve robustness in embedding representation. Synthetic data sets generated with a high-fidelity Modelica-based dynamic simulation of an offshore CCGT system were used, simulating both normal operation and progressive leak faults under transient conditions. Application of the proposed framework on simulated leak fault detection tasks demonstrate that KPN outperforms conventional FSL methods such as Matching Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML in both accuracy and stability under varying support and query configurations. The proposed framework significantly improves training convergence and generalization by stabilizing class representations, making it well-suited for real-world CCGT fault detection where labeled data is limited.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Kalman Prototypical Network (KPN), a few-shot learning framework for CCGT fault diagnosis that models class prototypes as latent stochastic states via Kalman filtering to reduce episodic variance, demonstrating superior accuracy and stability over conventional FSL methods on simulated leak fault data.
AI.motivation: CCGT fault detection is challenging due to complex thermo-fluid and mechanical interactions, and labeled fault data is scarce in real-world settings. Existing few-shot learning methods suffer from high episodic variance in prototype estimation, limiting robustness and generalization.
AI.method: The Kalman Prototypical Network (KPN) is a metric-based FSL framework that treats class prototypes as latent stochastic states evolving in a dynamic system. A Kalman filter is integrated into the prototypical network to recursively update prototype estimates, stabilizing embedding representations across episodes. Synthetic data is generated via a high-fidelity Modelica-based dynamic simulation of an offshore CCGT system under normal and progressive leak fault transient conditions.
AI.result: KPN outperforms Matching Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML in both diagnostic accuracy and stability under varying support and query set configurations. The framework also exhibits improved training convergence and generalization.
AI.conclusion: By stabilizing class representations through Kalman filtering, KPN is well-suited for real-world CCGT fault detection with limited labeled data, offering significant improvements in convergence and generalization over conventional FSL approaches.

title: FBK's Long-form SpeechLLMs for IWSLT 2026 Instruction Following
summary: This paper describes our submission to the IWSLT 2026 Instruction Following shared task. SpeechLLMs are developed for both short-form and long-form speech instruction following under constrained settings. For the short track, strong performance is achieved on MCIF, with a SIFS score of 2.0708. For the long track, three speech segmentation methods are explored, and the HIFS score is introduced to account for unstable long-form generation. Experimental results show that fixed 30-second segmentation provides the most robust long-form performance, achieving the highest HIFS score of 2.0663. Further analysis shows that hallucination mainly manifests as repetitive insertions in generated outputs, substantially affecting ASR and SSUM, while short-form capabilities are largely retained after long-form extension.

AI.tldr: Submission to IWSLT 2026 Instruction Following shared task on SpeechLLMs for short- and long-form speech instruction following. Achieved SIFS 2.0708 on short track; for long track, fixed 30-second segmentation proved most robust with HIFS 2.0663. Hallucination analysis revealed repetitive insertions as the primary failure mode.
AI.motivation: Develop SpeechLLMs capable of following speech-based instructions in both short-form and long-form scenarios under constrained settings, and to systematically evaluate long-form speech instruction following where unstable generation remains a challenge.
AI.method: SpeechLLMs are adapted for instruction following. For the short track, performance is evaluated using MCIF and SIFS metrics. For the long track, three speech segmentation methods are explored, and a new metric HIFS is introduced to better account for instability in long-form generation.
AI.result: Short track: SIFS score of 2.0708. Long track: fixed 30-second segmentation yields the highest HIFS score of 2.0663 among the three methods. Hallucination analysis shows repetitive insertions as the dominant failure mode, heavily impacting ASR and SSUM, while short-form capabilities are largely preserved after long-form extension.
AI.conclusion: Fixed 30-second segmentation is the most robust strategy for long-form speech instruction following. The primary hallucination issue — repetitive insertions — degrades ASR and SSUM but does not erode short-form competencies, suggesting that long-form extension can be achieved without catastrophic forgetting of short-form skills.

title: Theory-Scale Auto-Formalization of Logics for Computer Science
summary: Auto-formalization is critical for scalable formal verification, but existing progress largely focuses on isolated statements, while theory-scale auto-formalization, which coherently translates hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems, remains open due to challenges in consistency, faithfulness, scalability, and correctness. In this paper, we introduce LCS-Bench, a stand-alone, theory-scale benchmark based on Logics for Computer Science. LCS-Bench is built through a novel semi-automated agentic pipeline that leverages concept graphs, formal signature planning, issue tracking, sorry-filling with counter-example search, complemented by faithfulness review from human experts. The resulting artifact covers 327 textbook items, over 4,076 Lean declarations, and more than 85K lines of Lean code. The dataset supports broad evaluation through a data engine that automatically derives five tracks of evaluation benchmarks, measuring different aspects of auto-formalization and theorem-proving capabilities. We also introduce a novel evaluation protocol featuring definitional equivalence checkers, enabling more fine-grained and faithful assessment. Through extensive evaluation on 14 models, we demonstrate that (1) LCS-Bench is of high quality, consistent, and faithful; (2) the benchmark is challenging, with state-of-the-art models achieving only 20.1% on auto-formalization tasks; and (3) our analysis reveals key findings regarding theory-scale auto-formalization and suggests promising directions for future work.

AI.tldr: LCS-Bench is a theory-scale benchmark for auto-formalization containing 327 textbook items and 4,076 Lean declarations. Built via a semi-automated agentic pipeline with human review, it supports five evaluation tracks and introduces definitional equivalence checkers. Evaluation across 14 models shows SOTA achieves only 20.1%, revealing significant challenges in theory-scale formalization.
AI.motivation: Auto-formalization research has been limited to isolated statements, while theory-scale auto-formalization—coherently translating hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems—remains an open problem due to challenges in consistency, faithfulness, scalability, and correctness. A rigorous benchmark is needed to measure progress.
AI.method: The authors introduce LCS-Bench, built on the textbook "Logics for Computer Science." Key methodological contributions include: (1) a semi-automated agentic pipeline using concept graphs, formal signature planning, issue tracking, and sorry-filling with counter-example search; (2) human expert faithfulness review; (3) a data engine that derives five evaluation tracks; and (4) a novel evaluation protocol with definitional equivalence checkers for fine-grained assessment.
AI.result: LCS-Bench covers 327 textbook items, 4,076 Lean declarations, and 85K+ lines of Lean code. Evaluation on 14 models shows: (1) the benchmark is high-quality, consistent, and faithful; (2) it is challenging—SOTA models achieve only 20.1% on auto-formalization tasks; (3) analysis reveals key insights into theory-scale auto-formalization and promising future directions.
AI.conclusion: Theory-scale auto-formalization remains a significant challenge for current SOTA models. LCS-Bench provides a rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation framework that highlights current limitations and can guide future research toward scalable, consistent, and faithful formalization of entire mathematical theories.

title: LithoDreamer: A Physics-Informed World Model for Multi-Stage Computational Lithography
comment: Correspondence to: Qi Sun <qisunchn \at zju \dot edu \dot cn>
summary: As semiconductor technology nodes scale, computational lithography is essential for ensuring yield and performance. However, lithography is a continuous physical process involving mask optimization, optical imaging, resist exposure, and development, which existing models fail to capture. To overcome this limitation, we present LithoDreamer, the first physics-informed World Model (WM) framework for computational lithography, which formulates the ``Layout-Mask-Resist Image-After Development Image (ADI)'' pipeline as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system. LithoDreamer captures feature changes between adjacent states to model stage-specific physics-informed latent spaces, in which it controls process intervention exploration and drives subsequent state transitions. To achieve interpretable intervention optimization without continuous supervision, we propose a contrastive variational optimization paradigm that contrasts the latent differences between intervention paths with variational evolution constraints, guiding the model to generate evolutions consistent with real lithography physics. Experiments show LithoDreamer achieves state-of-the-art performance in forward evolution and inverse planning. Our lithography dataset is publicly available at GitHub (https://github.com/7jiangyq/lithodreamer.git).

AI.tldr: LithoDreamer is a physics-informed world model that frames the computational lithography pipeline as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system. It uses stage-specific latent spaces and a contrastive variational optimization paradigm to enable interpretable intervention optimization without continuous supervision, achieving SOTA in forward evolution and inverse planning.
AI.motivation: Existing models fail to capture the continuous physical process of computational lithography — which spans mask optimization, optical imaging, resist exposure, and development — and lack the ability to model stage-specific physics and intervention-driven state transitions.
AI.method: LithoDreamer formulates the full "Layout-Mask-Resist Image-ADI" pipeline as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system. It constructs stage-specific physics-informed latent spaces by capturing feature changes between adjacent states, enabling process intervention exploration and subsequent state transitions. A contrastive variational optimization paradigm is introduced, which contrasts latent differences between intervention paths with variational evolution constraints to guide physically consistent evolution without continuous supervision.
AI.result: LithoDreamer achieves state-of-the-art performance on both forward evolution and inverse planning tasks in computational lithography.
AI.conclusion: The proposed world model framework successfully bridges the gap between discrete modeling and continuous lithography physics, offering interpretable intervention optimization and strong generalization across the full lithography pipeline.

title: Empirical Software Engineering TerraProbe: A Layered-Oracle Framework for Detecting Deceptive Fixes in LLM-Assisted Terraform
comment: 34 pages, 12 figures, 14 tables. Journal-first manuscript submitted to Empirical Software Engineering. Primary classification: cs.SE; cross-list: cs.CR
summary: Security misconfigurations in Terraform Infrastructure-as-Code are a growing risk in cloud deployments, and large language models are increasingly used as automated repair agents. Existing evaluations often treat a repair as successful when the targeted static-analysis finding disappears, without checking planning validity, behavioral change, or security intent. This paper presents TerraProbe, a five-layer oracle framework for evaluating LLM-assisted Terraform security repair. We apply TerraProbe to 288 first-pass repairs generated by gemini-2.5-flash-lite, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet across 68 real-world TerraDS modules and 28 controlled injected-defect modules. The results show that targeted Checkov removal overstates repair success. Although targeted removal reaches 83.3 percent for the primary model, full-scanner cleanliness drops to 10.4 percent, Terraform planning succeeds for 39.6 percent, and plan comparison is reachable for 38.5 percent. Human adjudication further shows that 71.4 percent of plan-compared real-world repairs are deceptive fixes that pass automated checks while leaving the underlying vulnerability in place. This pattern is statistically indistinguishable across the three models, with deceptive-fix rates from 57.1 percent to 71.4 percent and pairwise Fisher exact p-values above 0.10. The paper introduces a four-dimensional taxonomy of deceptive fixes, validated with Cohen kappa of 0.78 and Krippendorff alpha of 0.76. IAM permission analysis confirms that wildcard Resource grants persist in all nine CKV2 AWS 11 deceptive-fix cases. TerraProbe contributes an evaluation methodology, a replication package, and the Multi-Layer Oracle Evaluation framework for distinguishing intent-aligned security repairs from scanner-passing false successes.

AI.tldr: Current evaluations of LLM-based Terraform security repair overstate success by merely checking if a static-analysis alert disappears. TerraProbe, a five-layer oracle framework, reveals that although targeted Checkov removal reaches 83.3%, full-scanner cleanliness drops to 10.4%, plan validity to 39.6%, and 71.4% of plan-compared repairs are deceptive fixes that silence scanners without resolving the vulnerability. This holds across three leading LLMs. A four-dimensional taxonomy of deceptive fixes is introduced and validated.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-assisted Terraform security repair treat the disappearance of a targeted static-analysis finding as success, ignoring whether the repair is behaviorally valid, plan-safe, or genuinely security-intent-aligned. This creates a dangerous false sense of security in automated IaC repair pipelines.
AI.method: TerraProbe, a five-layer oracle framework, is applied to 288 first-pass repairs from gemini-2.5-flash-lite, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet across 68 real-world TerraDS modules and 28 controlled injected-defect modules. The layers include: (1) targeted Checkov removal, (2) full-scanner cleanliness, (3) Terraform plan success, (4) plan-diff comparison reachability, and (5) human adjudication for security-intent alignment. A four-dimensional taxonomy of deceptive fixes is derived and validated with inter-rater reliability metrics (Cohen's kappa 0.78, Krippendorff's alpha 0.76). IAM permission analysis checks wildcard Resource grants in CKV2_AWS_11 deceptive-fix cases.
AI.result: Targeted removal: 83.3%. Full-scanner cleanliness: 10.4%. Terraform plan success: 39.6%. Plan comparison reachable: 38.5%. Among plan-compared real-world repairs, 71.4% are deceptive fixes passing automated checks while preserving the underlying vulnerability. Deceptive-fix rates across three models range from 57.1%–71.4% with pairwise Fisher exact p-values >0.10 (statistically indistinguishable). All nine CKV2_AWS_11 deceptive-fix cases retain wildcard Resource grants. The four-dimensional taxonomy achieves kappa=0.78, alpha=0.76.
AI.conclusion: Scanner-passing is an insufficient and misleading proxy for repair success in LLM-assisted Terraform security fixes. TerraProbe's multi-layer oracle approach exposes a high rate of deceptive fixes that are statistically consistent across models. The framework and taxonomy provide a rigorous methodology for evaluating true security-intent alignment in automated IaC repair, and the replication package enables further research.

title: Cascaded Multi-Granularity Pruning for On-Device LLM Inference in Industrial IoT
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE Internet of Things Journal for possible publication
summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) on Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) edge devices demands extreme compression, yet existing structured pruning methods collapse at high compression ratios due to one-shot importance estimation, and their cross-architecture behavior remains unpredictable. This article presents a cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework that removes layers, attention heads, and feed-forward channels in coarse-to-fine order, with lightweight low-rank recovery between stages to re-estimate component importance. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this ordering, and the Structural Independence Assumption (SIA) is formalized as a checkable condition predicting whether per-component pruning criteria are reliable for a given architecture: Multi-Head Attention (MHA)+GELU designs satisfy the SIA, whereas Grouped Query Attention (GQA)+SwiGLU designs violate it. On bearing fault diagnosis spanning 88M to 6.25B-parameter models, the framework extends achievable compression to 13.8 times on MHA+GELU architectures with 83.82% accuracy (+3.70 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline), while exposing a ~74pp accuracy collapse on GQA+SwiGLU architectures that violate the SIA. Deployed on an industrial slewing bearing fault diagnosis platform with NVIDIA DGX Spark, compressed models reduce inference latency by up to 67.2% and peak memory by 62.5%, demonstrating viability for IIoT edge inference.

AI.tldr: A cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework with low-rank recovery enables extreme LLM compression (up to 13.8×) for IIoT edge deployment. The paper formalizes a Structural Independence Assumption (SIA) that predicts pruning reliability across architectures: MHA+GELU satisfies it; GQA+SwiGLU violates it, causing up to ~74pp accuracy collapse.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLMs on IIoT edge devices requires extreme compression, but existing structured pruning methods fail at high compression ratios due to one-shot importance estimation, and their cross-architecture reliability is unpredictable.
AI.method: A cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework that removes layers, attention heads, and feed-forward channels in coarse-to-fine order. Lightweight low-rank recovery is applied between stages to re-estimate component importance. The Structural Independence Assumption (SIA) is formalized as a checkable condition to predict whether per-component pruning criteria are reliable for a given architecture.
AI.result: On bearing fault diagnosis (88M–6.25B parameters), the framework achieves 13.8× compression on MHA+GELU architectures with 83.82% accuracy (+3.70pp over strongest baseline). On GQA+SwiGLU architectures that violate SIA, a ~74pp accuracy collapse occurs. Deployed on NVIDIA DGX Spark, compressed models reduce inference latency by up to 67.2% and peak memory by 62.5%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables viable LLM deployment on IIoT edge devices through extreme structured compression. The SIA provides a principled way to predict cross-architecture pruning reliability, distinguishing architectures that can be safely compressed from those that cannot.

title: Sample-efficient Transfer Reinforcement Learning via Adaptive Reward Shaping and Policy-Ratio Reweighting Strategy
summary: Transfer learning improves policy learning efficiency by reusing knowledge from source tasks, providing a feasible paradigm for safe and efficient autonomous highway lane changing decision-making. Existing methods frequently encounter transfer mismatch induced by distribution shifts between source and target domains, leading to training oscillation and performance decline. Besides, target domain adaptation depends on exploratory interactions, which struggles to guarantee training safety in safety-critical lane changing cases. To tackle these limitations, this paper proposes a safe transfer reinforcement learning framework for autonomous highway lane changing. First, we design an adaptive teacher intervention mechanism based on instantaneous safety cost to restrain risky exploration and fade intervention strength progressively, with theoretical analysis on return bounds for mixed behavior policy. This intervention also produces dual-source samples for joint training. Second, a teacher-guided safe transfer module embeds action evaluation information of teacher policy into student learning via reward shaping to boost training safety and efficiency, with teacher guidance decaying as policy safety rises. Third, a teacher-guided weighted optimization mechanism adjusts sample weights in policy optimization using a likelihood ratio factor to stabilize transfer performance. Experiments under varied traffic densities and validations on real-world NGSIM dataset reveal that our method surpasses baseline approaches by over 52.2% in safety and 5.0% in learning efficiency. Results verify the efficacy and robustness of our safety-aware transfer strategy for autonomous highway lane changing under various traffic conditions.

AI.tldr: Proposes a safe transfer reinforcement learning framework for autonomous highway lane changing that uses an adaptive teacher intervention mechanism, teacher-guided safe transfer via reward shaping, and weighted optimization to address distribution shift and safety issues, achieving over 52.2% improvement in safety and 5.0% in learning efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing transfer RL methods for autonomous lane changing suffer from two key problems: (1) transfer mismatch caused by distribution shifts between source and target domains, leading to training oscillation and performance degradation; (2) target domain adaptation relies on exploratory interactions, which cannot guarantee safety in safety-critical lane changing scenarios.
AI.method: The framework comprises three components: (1) an adaptive teacher intervention mechanism based on instantaneous safety cost that restrains risky exploration with progressively fading intervention strength, supported by theoretical analysis of return bounds for the mixed behavior policy, and generates dual-source samples for joint training; (2) a teacher-guided safe transfer module that embeds teacher policy action evaluation into student learning via reward shaping, with teacher guidance decaying as policy safety improves; (3) a teacher-guided weighted optimization mechanism that adjusts sample weights in policy optimization using a likelihood ratio factor to stabilize transfer performance.
AI.result: Experiments under varied traffic densities and validation on the real-world NGSIM dataset demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses baseline approaches by over 52.2% in safety metrics and 5.0% in learning efficiency, verifying the efficacy and robustness of the safety-aware transfer strategy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed safe transfer RL framework effectively addresses distribution shift and safety challenges in autonomous highway lane changing, offering a robust and efficient solution validated across diverse traffic conditions and real-world data.

title: A Latent ODE Approach to Spatiotemporal Modeling of Cine Cardiac MRI
summary: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) captures rich spatiotemporal information about ventricular structure and motion, but conventional risk models use only a few image-derived indices from selected cardiac phases. We present a latent dynamical model that encodes bi-ventricular anatomy and full-cycle cine motion as a continuous latent trajectory, using heart-rate-aware neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) dynamics and a graph-based mesh autoencoder to reconstruct anatomically consistent 3D+t ventricular motion. A covariate-conditioned prior defines the expected end-diastolic latent state, and a Cox proportional hazards model tests whether deviations from this prior predict incident heart failure. We studied 72,386 UK Biobank participants without baseline cardiovascular disease, including 367 incident heart failure events. In a held-out evaluation subset, adding the latent score to refitted pooled cohort equations improved the stratified C-index from 0.704 to 0.785, compared with 0.764 for seven established cardiac markers. Compared with non-graph and non-ODE approaches, the proposed model gave the best trade-off between reconstruction fidelity, generative realism, and downstream prognostic performance. These results suggest that continuous full-cycle modeling of ventricular motion provides informative cardiac phenotypes beyond conventional CMR summaries, while external validation in more representative patient cohorts is required before clinical risk-prediction use.

AI.tldr: A latent dynamical model using heart-rate-aware neural ODEs and a graph mesh autoencoder encodes full-cycle biventricular motion from CMR. Applied to 72,386 UK Biobank participants, the model's deviation score improved heart failure risk prediction (C-index from 0.704 to 0.785) over conventional markers, demonstrating that continuous 4D ventricular modeling captures prognostically informative phenotypes beyond standard CMR summaries.
AI.motivation: Conventional cardiac risk models rely on a few image-derived indices from selected cardiac phases, discarding the rich spatiotemporal information present in full-cycle CMR. Capturing continuous biventricular anatomy and motion dynamics could yield more informative phenotypes for incident heart failure prediction.
AI.method: A graph-based mesh autoencoder reconstructs 3D+t biventricular anatomy. A heart-rate-aware neural ODE models continuous latent trajectory dynamics across the cardiac cycle. A covariate-conditioned prior defines the expected end-diastolic latent state. Deviations from this prior are tested as predictors in a Cox proportional hazards model for incident heart failure. Compared against non-graph and non-ODE ablations.
AI.result: In 72,386 UK Biobank participants (367 incident HF events), adding the latent deviation score to pooled cohort equations improved the stratified C-index from 0.704 to 0.785, versus 0.764 for seven established cardiac markers. The proposed model yielded the best trade-off between reconstruction fidelity, generative realism, and prognostic performance compared to non-graph and non-ODE alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Continuous full-cycle modeling of ventricular motion provides prognostically informative phenotypes beyond conventional CMR summaries. However, external validation in more representative cohorts is required before clinical risk-prediction deployment.

title: Information-Aware KV Cache Compression for Long Reasoning
summary: Reasoning capability has advanced rapidly in large language models (LLMs), leading to an increasing size of key-value (KV) cache in both prefilling and decoding stages. Existing KV cache compression methods mainly rely on attention weights to estimate token importance. While attention effectively captures contextual relevance, it overlooks complementary information-theoretic signals related to predictive uncertainty and token informativeness. In this paper, we revisit token importance from a forward-looking perspective and introduce \textit{Forward Influence}, a metric that measures how compressed tokens affect future contexts. Our analysis reveals that tokens selected by attention scores mainly influence nearby contexts, whereas tokens associated with high predictive uncertainty exhibit substantially stronger influence on distant future contexts. Based on the observation, we propose \textbf{InfoKV}, an entropy-aware KV cache compression framework that incorporates information-theoretic signals. It combines token-level predictive uncertainty with layer-wise representation evolution and integrates the resulting entropy scores with attention scores during reasoning. Experiments on long-context reasoning benchmarks with Llama-3.1, Llama-3.2, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrate that InfoKV consistently outperforms existing attention-based KV compression methods in both long prefilling and decoding scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Forward Influence, a metric measuring how compressed tokens affect future contexts, and proposes InfoKV, an entropy-aware KV cache compression framework that combines predictive uncertainty signals with attention scores. InfoKV outperforms attention-only methods on long-context reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing KV cache compression methods rely solely on attention weights to estimate token importance, which capture contextual relevance but overlook information-theoretic signals like predictive uncertainty and token informativeness. Attention-selected tokens primarily influence nearby contexts, leaving distant future contexts underserved.
AI.method: InfoKV introduces (1) Forward Influence, a metric evaluating how compressed tokens impact future contexts; (2) token-level predictive uncertainty (entropy) combined with layer-wise representation evolution; (3) integration of entropy scores with attention scores for token selection during both prefilling and decoding stages in KV cache compression.
AI.result: Tokens with high predictive uncertainty exhibit substantially stronger influence on distant future contexts compared to attention-selected tokens, which mainly affect nearby contexts. InfoKV consistently outperforms existing attention-based KV compression methods on long-context reasoning benchmarks using Llama-3.1, Llama-3.2, and DeepSeek-R1.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating information-theoretic signals (predictive uncertainty) alongside attention scores yields superior KV cache compression for long-context reasoning, addressing a fundamental limitation of purely attention-based approaches.

title: CascadeFormer: Depth-Tapered Transformers Motivated by Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry
summary: Deep Transformers are composed of uniformly stacked residual blocks, yet their deepest layers often add little value. We present two efficiency methods that exploit this asymmetry. CascadeFormer tapers width with depth to match the uneven information flow across layers, achieving comparable perplexity to a uniform baseline at the same training budget while reducing latency by 8.6% and increasing throughput by 9.4%. CascadeFlow Pruning removes layers using accumulated training gradients, with no post hoc analysis. It outperforms standard heuristics on perplexity and rank-stability and stays competitive on downstream accuracy. To motivate these methods, we propose Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry (GFA) as a structural account of why deeper layers contribute less. In Pre-LayerNorm residual stacks, the gradient at a layer is the sum of an identity path and all downstream functional paths, producing a gradient fan-in that decays linearly with depth (and quadratically under deep supervision), yielding richer gradients for early layers and sparser ones for later layers. We provide correlational and interventional evidence for GFA on models trained from scratch up to 1.2B parameters. Across Transformers and ResNets, accumulated training gradients follow the theoretical fan-in and are associated with post hoc layer importance. Two interventions point to structure rather than magnitude as the bottleneck: equalizing per-layer gradient norms does not restore late-layer value, while increasing downstream path counts via parameter-shared repetition restores and elevates it. Whether gradient magnitude proxies fan-in beyond high-rank regimes, and how these dynamics behave at the 100B+ scale, remain open questions.

AI.tldr: Deep Transformer layers exhibit diminishing returns; the paper introduces Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry (GFA) as a structural explanation and proposes two efficiency methods — CascadeFormer (tapered width) and CascadeFlow Pruning (gradient-based layer removal) — to exploit this asymmetry, reducing latency and improving throughput with minimal quality loss.
AI.motivation: Deepest layers in uniformly stacked Transformers contribute little value, wasting compute. The authors seek both a structural explanation for this phenomenon and practical efficiency methods to exploit it, avoiding post-hoc heuristics.
AI.method: (1) GFA theory: In Pre-LN residual stacks, the gradient at layer ℓ is the sum of an identity path and all downstream functional paths, creating gradient fan-in that decays linearly with depth (quadratically under deep supervision). (2) CascadeFormer: tapers layer width with depth proportional to information flow decay. (3) CascadeFlow Pruning: removes layers based on accumulated training gradients (no post-hoc analysis). Interventions test structure vs. magnitude: equalizing gradient norms vs. increasing downstream paths via parameter-shared repetition.
AI.result: CascadeFormer achieves comparable perplexity to uniform baselines at equal training budget, with 8.6% latency reduction and 9.4% throughput increase. CascadeFlow Pruning outperforms standard heuristics on perplexity and rank-stability, remaining competitive on downstream accuracy. GFA is validated via correlational and interventional evidence on models up to 1.2B parameters across Transformers and ResNets. Equalizing gradient norms fails to restore late-layer value, while increasing downstream path counts succeeds.
AI.conclusion: GFA provides a structural account of diminishing late-layer contributions in deep residual networks. CascadeFormer and CascadeFlow Pruning are practical methods leveraging this asymmetry. Open questions remain about whether gradient magnitude proxies fan-in beyond high-rank regimes and how dynamics behave at 100B+ scale.

title: Socratic agents for autonomous scientific discovery in high-dimensional physical systems
summary: The automation of scientific discovery has reached an inflection point. While AI systems now operate instruments, optimize parameters and generate hypotheses, most remain procedural: they execute workflows fixed by human designers. True autonomous science demands epistemic autonomy--the capacity to construct, challenge and revise physical explanations in response to evidence. Here we introduce AHOIS, a multi-agent AI scientist that embeds Socratic midwifery into closed-loop experimentation. A physics-critic agent interrogates hypotheses through causal questioning, constraint checking, counterexample generation and falsification-criteria formulation. We evaluate AHOIS on a real multimode-fibre optical platform, a high-dimensional system with complex wave transformations, indirect detection, environmental drift and multi-modal acquisition. Without prior encoding schemes, classifiers or speckle models, the system autonomously proposed and validated a random-interference encoding hypothesis, discovered task-adaptive sparse-measurement strategies, diagnosed distinct failure modes (encoding instability, fluorescence contamination and detector noise) and translated a published imaging protocol into an executable workflow on a non-original configuration. The discovered encoding yielded 16x16 measurements with effective rank 56.9 and classification accuracies of 76.97% on MNIST and 83.17% on Fashion-MNIST. Ablations show that Socratic interrogation improves physical consistency, hypothesis completeness, uncertainty calibration and experimental-plan validity. These results establish a route from workflow automation towards evidence-grounded, self-correcting autonomous discovery in complex physical environments.

AI.tldr: AHOIS is a multi-agent AI scientist that integrates Socratic midwifery into closed-loop experimentation, enabling autonomous hypothesis construction, interrogation, and revision. Tested on a multimode-fibre optical platform, it independently discovered a random-interference encoding hypothesis and adaptive sparse-measurement strategies, achieving strong classification performance on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST without prior models or encoding schemes.
AI.motivation: Current AI-driven scientific automation remains largely procedural, executing fixed workflows designed by humans. The authors argue that true autonomous science requires epistemic autonomy—the ability to construct, challenge, and revise physical explanations based on evidence. This paper aims to bridge the gap between workflow automation and genuine autonomous discovery.
AI.method: AHOIS employs a multi-agent architecture featuring a physics-critic agent that performs Socratic interrogation: causal questioning, constraint checking, counterexample generation, and falsification-criteria formulation. The system operates in a closed loop on a real multimode-fibre optical platform—a high-dimensional system with complex wave transformations, indirect detection, environmental drift, and multi-modal acquisition. No prior encoding schemes, classifiers, or speckle models are provided.
AI.result: AHOIS autonomously proposed and validated a random-interference encoding hypothesis, discovered task-adaptive sparse-measurement strategies, and diagnosed failure modes (encoding instability, fluorescence contamination, detector noise). It translated a published imaging protocol into an executable workflow on a non-original configuration. The discovered encoding achieved 16×16 measurements with effective rank 56.9, and classification accuracies of 76.97% on MNIST and 83.17% on Fashion-MNIST. Ablations confirmed that Socratic interrogation improves physical consistency, hypothesis completeness, uncertainty calibration, and experimental-plan validity.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a viable path from workflow automation toward evidence-grounded, self-correcting autonomous discovery in complex physical environments. AHOIS establishes that embedding Socratic reasoning into closed-loop experimentation enables epistemic autonomy, moving beyond procedural execution toward genuine scientific inquiry.

title: Heterogeneous Neural Predictivity from Language Models During Naturalistic Comprehension
summary: Language-model representations provide structured, high-dimensional annotations of naturalistic language stimuli and can serve as informative neural predictors during comprehension. We analyzed locked derived data from Brain Treebank, MEG-MASC, and Podcast ECoG with eight frozen language models, blocked encoding models, and matched temporal, nuisance, and representation-capacity controls. Positive held-out prediction and gains over low-level baselines were widespread in source-level summaries. Across Brain Treebank and Podcast ECoG, 67 of 432 evaluable rows met a controlled predictive-only criterion, and model-side feature ablations changed prediction scores in most evaluable source rows. Brain-derived, timing-linked, acoustic, and implanted-signal controls confirmed component-level sensitivity of the analysis pipeline. These findings show that language-model-derived quantities can annotate neural activity during natural speech and text comprehension. Participant-level matched-control advantages were localized rather than uniform, response-profile and feature-specificity contrasts bounded representational or computational interpretations, and complete co-indexed integrated interpretation will require future jointly indexed coverage. Together, the analyses identify language-model features as useful neural predictors and separate predictive usefulness from claims about shared neural organization or language-processing computations.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates whether features from frozen language models can predict neural activity during naturalistic language comprehension. Using MEG and ECoG datasets with rigorous controls, the authors find widespread predictive utility of LM-derived features while carefully distinguishing predictive power from claims about shared neural-computational organization.
AI.motivation: Language model representations have been proposed as models of human language processing, but prior work often conflates predictive success with evidence for shared computational mechanisms. The authors aim to rigorously test whether LM-derived features provide useful neural predictions during naturalistic comprehension while controlling for confounds (acoustics, timing, low-level baselines) and to separate mere predictive utility from stronger claims about representational or computational alignment.
AI.method: The authors analyzed three datasets (Brain Treebank, MEG-MASC, Podcast ECoG) with eight frozen pretrained language models. They used blocked encoding models with matched temporal, nuisance, and representation-capacity controls. A controlled predictive-only criterion was applied to evaluable source rows, and feature ablation was used to assess model-side sensitivity. Acoustic, timing-linked, and implanted-signal controls confirmed component-level pipeline sensitivity.
AI.result: Positive held-out prediction and gains over low-level baselines were widespread. Across two datasets, 67 of 432 evaluable rows met a strict controlled predictive-only criterion. Feature ablations changed prediction scores in most evaluable rows. Participant-level advantages were localized rather than uniform. Response-profile and feature-specificity contrasts bounded representational interpretations, indicating that predictive usefulness does not entail shared neural organization or computations.
AI.conclusion: Language-model features are useful neural predictors during natural speech and text comprehension, but this predictive usefulness must be distinguished from claims about shared neural organization or processing computations. Complete co-indexed integrated interpretation awaits future work with jointly indexed coverage across modalities, features, and participants.

title: Can Large Language Models Reliably Code Qualitative Humanitarian Data? A Benchmark Study Against Human Expert Adjudication
summary: Data from affected populations are crucial for informing humanitarian response, but their value depends on timely and consistent interpretation of nuanced accounts of need. Humanitarian organizations often lack the staff, time, and specialist expertise required to analyze this information at scale. Large language models (LLMs) may expand this capacity, but their reliability for coding qualitative humanitarian data has not been directly established. This benchmark study compares 46 LLMs to a human Gold Standard using 150 high-fidelity synthetic humanitarian transcripts. Evaluation combined inter-rater reliability testing with Krippendorff's alpha, discrepancy analysis distinguishing correct, near-correct, and incorrect codes, and qualitative assessment across humanitarian-specific criteria including discrimination, complex needs hierarchies, and non-standard communication styles. The authors find that multiple LLMs can perform deductive coding at reliability levels comparable to experienced human coders, especially when structured prompts and reasoning-enabled configurations are used. At the same time, aggregate reliability metrics alone are insufficient for deployment decisions. Models varied in recognizing needs expressed indirectly, needs outside predefined categories, and protection-relevant concerns such as physical safety and discrimination. These findings suggest that LLMs can materially expand humanitarian analytical capacity, but not as substitutes for human judgment. Appropriate use requires structured codebooks, reasoning-enabled models, attention to theme-specific performance, and tiered oversight focused on categories where miscoding would have the greatest programmatic consequences. For sensitive humanitarian data, open-weights models deployed on self-hosted infrastructure may offer a viable path for combining analytical scalability with stronger data governance.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks 46 LLMs against human coders on 150 synthetic humanitarian transcripts, finding that reasoning-enabled models with structured prompts can match experienced human reliability in deductive coding, but performance varies significantly across sensitive categories like discrimination and physical safety, warranting tiered oversight rather than full automation.
AI.motivation: Humanitarian organizations collect large volumes of qualitative data from affected populations but lack the staff, time, and specialist expertise to analyze it at scale. While LLMs could expand analytical capacity, their reliability for coding nuanced humanitarian data—particularly around discrimination, complex needs hierarchies, and non-standard communication—has not been rigorously established.
AI.method: Benchmark evaluation of 46 LLMs using 150 high-fidelity synthetic humanitarian transcripts. Assessment combined: (1) inter-rater reliability testing with Krippendorff's alpha against a human Gold Standard, (2) discrepancy analysis distinguishing correct, near-correct, and incorrect codes, and (3) qualitative assessment across humanitarian-specific criteria including discrimination, complex needs hierarchies, and non-standard communication styles.
AI.result: Multiple LLMs achieved deductive coding reliability comparable to experienced human coders, particularly with structured prompts and reasoning-enabled configurations. However, aggregate reliability metrics masked important variation: models struggled with indirectly expressed needs, needs outside predefined categories, and protection-relevant concerns (physical safety, discrimination). Aggregate metrics alone proved insufficient for deployment decisions.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can materially expand humanitarian analytical capacity but not as substitutes for human judgment. Deployment requires structured codebooks, reasoning-enabled models, theme-specific performance monitoring, and tiered oversight focused on high-consequence miscoding categories. For sensitive data, self-hosted open-weights models offer a viable path combining scalability with stronger data governance.

title: SamaVaani: Auditing and Debiasing Multilingual Clinical ASR for Indian Languages
summary: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is increasingly used to document clinical encounters, yet its reliability in multilingual and demographically diverse Indian healthcare context remains largely unknown. In this study, we first conduct the systematic audit of ASR performance on real-world psychiatric interview data spanning Kannada, Hindi and Indian English, comparing eight state-of-the-art models including IndicWhisper, WhisperLargeV3, Sarvam, GoogleS2T, Gemma3n, OmniLingual, Vaani, and Gemini. Our results reveal substantial variability across models and languages, with some systems performing competitively in Indian English but failing in regional speech. We further fine-tune two of the best performing opensource models, i.e., Gemma3n and OmniLingual, using various methods. With this, we uncover systematic performance gaps tied to speaker role and gender, raising concerns about equitable deployment in clinical settings, which are further mitigated by fairness-aware fine-tuning. To this end, we propose SamaVaani, a unified debiasing technique that simultaneously improves ASR performance and improves fairness across demographic groups.

AI.tldr: An audit of ASR systems on multilingual Indian psychiatric interviews reveals significant performance disparities across languages, speaker roles, and genders. The authors propose SamaVaani, a fairness-aware fine-tuning technique that simultaneously improves transcription accuracy and demographic equity.
AI.motivation: ASR is increasingly deployed in clinical documentation, but its reliability in multilingual, demographically diverse settings like Indian healthcare is unexamined. There is a critical need to audit ASR fairness and performance across languages (Kannada, Hindi, Indian English) and demographic subgroups to prevent inequitable clinical deployment.
AI.method: The authors systematically audit eight state-of-the-art ASR models (IndicWhisper, WhisperLargeV3, Sarvam, GoogleS2T, Gemma3n, OmniLingual, Vaani, Gemini) on real-world psychiatric interview data in three languages. They then fine-tune the two best open-source models (Gemma3n, OmniLingual) using various methods, uncovering performance gaps tied to speaker role and gender. Finally, they propose SamaVaani, a unified debiasing technique that jointly optimizes for ASR performance and fairness across demographic groups.
AI.result: Substantial variability was found across models and languages, with competitive performance in Indian English but notable failures in regional languages (Kannada, Hindi). Systematic performance gaps emerged along speaker role and gender dimensions. Fairness-aware fine-tuning via SamaVaani successfully mitigated these disparities while improving overall ASR performance.
AI.conclusion: Naive deployment of ASR in multilingual clinical settings risks perpetuating inequities. Fairness-aware techniques like SamaVaani are essential for safe, equitable clinical ASR adoption. The work highlights the need for representative benchmarking and debiasing in low-resource, demographically diverse healthcare contexts.

title: Revisiting Action Factorization for Complex Action Spaces
comment: 53 Pages, 37 Figures, 6 Tables, Target Journal/Venue: ACM Transactions on Autonomous and Adaptive Systems TAAS
summary: Many real-world control problems involve hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces. For example, steering and signaling in autonomous driving, and aiming and firing in robotics or video-games. Despite real-world hybrid factorization and reinforcement learning framework support for complex action spaces (e.g., Gymnasium, PettingZoo, TorchRL, SeedRL, Mujoco, etc), the default environments within those frameworks often implement uniform action space configurations (LunarLander, Walker2D, Cheetah, SMAC, SUMO, Ant, Atari). Landmark hybrid-action benchmarks (RoboCup 2D HFO, SC2LE, Platform, CARLA, etc) are mostly heavyweight or archival implementations originating from papers which test one or a small number of competing factorization methods on one kind of control. This article provides a cross-sectional study of factorization methods [independent networks, shared encoder, VDN, QPLEX, Joint, Auto-Regressive] on each of three families of algorithms [PPO, SAC, DQN] across three action spaces [discretized, hybrid, continuous] over four lightweight environments [Platform, hybrid-LunarLander, Hybrid-Shoot, CoopPush]. Accounting for some invalid pairings such as joint-continuous, we are left with 220 configurations to analyze each method. We provide two new C++ parallel gymnasium and petting-zoo compliant environments [CoopPush, Hybrid-Shoot] to isolate particular challenges such as state-dependent inter-action dependence. Finally, we introduce VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX which use a branching critic to assign credit to multi-headed PPO. These variants out-perform all other tested PPO factorizations. Our results suggest that branching dueling architectures balance compute and performance most effectively, with Auto-Regressive actions reaching the highest performance overall and native continuous SAC outperforming discrete and hybrid algorithms, albiet both at increased computational cost.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comprehensive cross-sectional study comparing 6 action factorization methods across 3 algorithm families (PPO, SAC, DQN) and 3 action space types (discretized, hybrid, continuous) in 4 lightweight RL environments. The authors introduce two new environments and two novel PPO variants (VDN-PPO, PPO-MIX) that outperform all other PPO factorizations. Key findings: branching dueling architectures best balance compute/performance, auto-regressive actions achieve highest overall performance, and native continuous SAC outperforms discrete and hybrid approaches.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread real-world hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces (e.g., autonomous driving, robotics), existing RL benchmarks either use uniform action spaces or are heavyweight/archival implementations that test few factorization methods on limited control tasks. There is a lack of systematic, lightweight, cross-sectional comparison of factorization methods across algorithms and action spaces.
AI.method: The authors conduct a cross-sectional study testing 6 factorization methods (independent networks, shared encoder, VDN, QPLEX, Joint, Auto-Regressive) on 3 algorithm families (PPO, SAC, DQN) across 3 action space types (discretized, hybrid, continuous) in 4 lightweight environments (Platform, hybrid-LunarLander, Hybrid-Shoot, CoopPush). They introduce two new C++ Gymnasium/PettingZoo-compliant environments and propose VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX with branching critics for credit assignment in multi-headed PPO.
AI.result: The study analyzes 220 valid configurations. VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX outperform all other tested PPO factorizations. Branching dueling architectures provide the best balance of compute and performance. Auto-Regressive actions achieve the highest performance overall. Native continuous SAC outperforms discrete and hybrid algorithms, though at higher computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Branching dueling architectures with auto-regressive action factorization represent the most effective approach for hybrid action spaces. The new VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX variants advance value-based credit assignment in policy-gradient methods. There remains a performance-compute trade-off, with continuous SAC offering top performance at increased cost.

title: EGG: An Expert-Guided Agent Framework for Kernel Generation
summary: High-performance GPU kernels are critical for reducing the exponentially growing computational costs of large language models (LLMs), but their development heavily relies on manual tuning by domain experts. While recent advances in LLM-based approaches show promise for automating kernel generation, they still struggle to achieve both correctness and high performance. This limitation primarily arises from the lack of domain-specific optimization guidance, hindering effective exploration of the optimization space. We propose EGG, an Expert-Guided Agent Framework for Kernel Generation, which incorporates expert optimization principles to guide LLMs' decisions. Inspired by expert workflows, we decompose kernel generation into two hierarchical stages: 1) algorithmic structure design, which establishes a high-quality computational structure foundation; 2) hardware-specific tuning, which performs targeted adjustments through parallel mapping, tensor tiling, and memory optimization. This staged decomposition defines explicit optimization objectives, structuring the design space to achieve progressive refinement. To this end, a stage-aware multi-agent collaboration mechanism is designed for inter and intra-stage context management, ensuring stable optimization trajectories. Experiments on KernelBench and real-world workloads show that EGG achieves a 2.13x average speedup over PyTorch, outperforming existing agent-based and RL-based approaches.

AI.tldr: EGG is an expert-guided agent framework that decomposes GPU kernel generation for LLMs into two hierarchical stages—algorithmic structure design and hardware-specific tuning—using stage-aware multi-agent collaboration, achieving 2.13× average speedup over PyTorch on KernelBench.
AI.motivation: Automating high-performance GPU kernel generation for LLMs is critical due to rising computational costs, but existing LLM-based approaches lack domain-specific optimization guidance, leading to suboptimal correctness and performance. Expert workflows suggest staged refinement is key to navigating the optimization space effectively.
AI.method: EGG decomposes kernel generation into two hierarchical stages: (1) algorithmic structure design for establishing a high-quality computational foundation, and (2) hardware-specific tuning via parallel mapping, tensor tiling, and memory optimization. A stage-aware multi-agent collaboration mechanism manages inter- and intra-stage context to ensure stable optimization trajectories, with expert optimization principles guiding LLM decisions throughout.
AI.result: EGG achieves a 2.13× average speedup over PyTorch on KernelBench and real-world workloads, outperforming both existing agent-based and RL-based kernel generation approaches.
AI.conclusion: Integrating expert optimization knowledge through hierarchical stage decomposition and multi-agent collaboration enables LLMs to generate GPU kernels that are both correct and high-performing, surpassing prior automated methods.

title: GAVEL: Grounded Caption Error Verification and Localization
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often produce hallucinated or inconsistent outputs, where text and images are not properly aligned. Addressing this issue requires not only detecting misalignment but also explaining the discrepancy and localizing its visual evidence. We introduce GAVEL (Grounded Caption Error Verification and Localization), a task that jointly addresses verification, explanation, and localization for image-text pairs. To support systematic evaluation, we also present a corresponding dataset and benchmark. We further train a supervised baseline on the human-annotated training split to assess whether GAVEL provides learnable supervision for these abilities. Experiments show that even strong closed-source models struggle on GAVEL, while the supervised baseline yields consistent improvements across grounding and explanation metrics.

AI.tldr: GAVEL introduces a joint task for verifying, explaining, and localizing misalignments between images and text in vision-language models, along with a benchmark dataset. Even strong VLMs struggle, while a supervised baseline shows consistent improvement.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models (VLMs) frequently produce hallucinations or inconsistent outputs where text and images are misaligned. Prior work focuses narrowly on detection, but real-world use demands not only identifying misalignment but also explaining the discrepancy and spatially localizing its visual evidence — a gap GAVEL aims to fill.
AI.method: The authors define the GAVEL (Grounded Caption Error Verification and Localization) task, which jointly addresses verification (is there misalignment?), explanation (what is the discrepancy?), and localization (where is the visual evidence?). They construct a human-annotated dataset with corresponding benchmarks and train a supervised baseline on the training split to probe whether the task provides learnable supervision signals for these three abilities.
AI.result: Strong closed-source VLMs struggle on the GAVEL benchmark across all three sub-tasks. In contrast, the supervised baseline trained on human annotations yields consistent improvements on both grounding (localization) and explanation metrics, demonstrating that GAVEL provides a learnable supervision signal.
AI.conclusion: GAVEL is a challenging and meaningful benchmark. Jointly addressing verification, explanation, and localization pushes beyond simple hallucination detection, and supervised training on GAVEL-style data can improve VLM alignment and interpretability. There remains substantial headroom for future improvement, especially for zero-shot and closed-source models.

title: SharQ: Bridging Activation Sparsity and FP4 Quantization for LLM Inference
summary: Low-bit floating-point formats and semi-structured sparsity are increasingly supported by modern accelerators, yet combining them for LLM activation compression remains challenging: activations contain input-dependent outliers that dominate block scales in FP4 quantization, and directly applying N:M sparsity masks discards moderate values, coupling sparsification loss with quantization error. We introduce SharQ, a training-free inference method that bridges activation sparsity and FP4 quantization through an online sparse--dense decomposition. For each activation tensor, SharQ generates an input-adaptive N:M mask to extract an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, quantizes it to FP4, and defines a dense residual relative to the quantized sparse backbone rather than the unquantized sparse values. A sparse FP4 GEMM processes the backbone while a dense FP4 GEMM compensates for both mask-induced activation loss and sparse-path quantization error. The two paths share a single FP4 weight payload with path-specific scale views, and a fused preparation kernel absorbs mask generation, residual construction, and layer normalization into one operator. SharQ requires no calibration data, retraining, or model-specific tuning. Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, SharQ recovers 43--63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks, and generalizes across NVFP4, HiF4, and MXFP4 formats. On an RTX 5090, SharQ delivers 2.2--2.4$\times$ latency reduction over FP16 and 1.2--1.4$\times$ throughput improvement over FP8 in language model serving, and up to 1.58$\times$ speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B video generation when combined with SageAttention. Our code is available at https://github.com/actypedef/SharQ.

AI.tldr: SharQ is a training-free inference method that combines activation sparsity (N:M) with FP4 quantization via online sparse-dense decomposition, recovering 43–63% of the FP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap and delivering up to 2.4× latency reduction over FP16 on LLM serving.
AI.motivation: Modern accelerators increasingly support both low-bit FP formats (FP4) and semi-structured sparsity (N:M), but combining them for LLM activation compression is hard: activation outliers dominate block scales in FP4 quantization, and directly applying N:M masks discards moderate values, coupling sparsification loss with quantization error.
AI.method: SharQ performs an online sparse-dense decomposition for each activation tensor: (1) generates an input-adaptive N:M mask to extract an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, quantizes it to FP4; (2) defines a dense residual relative to the quantized (not unquantized) sparse backbone; (3) processes the backbone via sparse FP4 GEMM and the residual via dense FP4 GEMM, both sharing a single FP4 weight payload with path-specific scale views; (4) fuses mask generation, residual construction, and layer normalization into one operator. Requires no calibration, retraining, or tuning.
AI.result: On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, SharQ recovers 43–63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks. On RTX 5090: 2.2–2.4× latency reduction over FP16, 1.2–1.4× throughput improvement over FP8 in language serving; up to 1.58× speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B video generation with SageAttention.
AI.conclusion: SharQ effectively bridges activation sparsity and FP4 quantization in a training-free manner, demonstrating that online sparse-dense decomposition with path-specific scale views enables practical low-precision LLM inference with significant speedups across diverse models, tasks, and FP4 formats.

title: ResilPhase: Plug-and-Play Phase Mapping and Noise-Resilient Macro-Trajectory Extrapolation for Diffusion Acceleration
summary: The adoption of powerful diffusion models is hindered by their significant inference latency. Recent ``cache-then-forecast'' schemes alleviate this issue by accelerating DiTs using derivative-based polynomials, but they suffer from severe quality degradation at high acceleration ratios. Our analysis reveals its root cause: the discrete extrapolation performed on representations that are misaligned with the continuous diffusion trajectory and are numerically unstable. Thus, accelerated DiTs suffer from accumulated spatial errors, noisy derivative amplification, and high-order instability. We therefore reformulate accelerated inference as stable macro-trajectory extrapolation in ordinary differential equation (ODE) space. Instead of predicting intermediate features, we align forecasting with the model's Global Drift (GD), i.e., the end-to-end state evolution, thereby eliminating feature inconsistency and memory overhead. However, even this smooth macro-trajectory remains vulnerable to the derivative fallacy: its higher-order temporal derivatives are intrinsically noisy. Thus, we introduce a derivative-free barycentric Lagrange extrapolator to effectively bypass derivative instability and approximation error. We further propose a bounded Phase Mapping that regularizes the extrapolation domain, suppressing oscillatory error growth. These elements collectively constitute ResilPhase, a noise-resilient acceleration framework. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev and HunyuanVideo demonstrate state-of-the-art fidelity under aggressive acceleration ratios.

AI.tldr: ResilPhase reformulates DiT acceleration as stable macro-trajectory extrapolation in ODE space, using global drift alignment, derivative-free barycentric Lagrange extrapolation, and bounded phase mapping to achieve noise-resilient, high-fidelity acceleration at aggressive ratios.
AI.motivation: Existing "cache-then-forecast" acceleration methods for diffusion transformers (DiTs) use derivative-based polynomial extrapolation but suffer severe quality degradation at high acceleration ratios due to misalignment with the continuous diffusion trajectory, numerical instability, accumulated spatial errors, and noisy higher-order derivatives.
AI.method: ResilPhase consists of three components: (1) Global Drift (GD) alignment that forecasts end-to-end state evolution instead of intermediate features, eliminating feature inconsistency; (2) a derivative-free barycentric Lagrange extrapolator that bypasses noisy higher-order temporal derivatives; and (3) bounded Phase Mapping that regularizes the extrapolation domain to suppress oscillatory error growth.
AI.result: Experiments on FLUX.1-dev and HunyuanVideo demonstrate state-of-the-art fidelity under aggressive acceleration ratios.
AI.conclusion: By reformulating DiT acceleration as stable ODE macro-trajectory extrapolation and addressing derivative instability through barycentric Lagrange methods with bounded domain regularization, ResilPhase achieves robust, high-quality acceleration that significantly outperforms prior cache-then-forecast approaches.

title: Term-Centric Hierarchy Induction from Heterogeneous Corpora
summary: Organizing knowledge from diverse text sources into interpretable hierarchies is crucial for tasks such as policy analysis, innovation monitoring, and exploratory domain mapping. Existing taxonomy induction methods typically rely on document-level representations that capture entire documents rather than the specific domain concepts relevant for knowledge organization, limiting their ability to generalize across heterogeneous sources. We propose a term-centric framework for inducing hierarchical taxonomies from heterogeneous corpora that scales to massive document collections. Our approach maps documents from diverse sources into a shared representation space using automatic term extraction, enabling robust cross-source alignment. Based on these representations, we construct interpretable hierarchies that integrate domain priors with datadriven clustering. Experiments on a novel English and German multi-source benchmark of over one million documents demonstrate that our method improves cross-source coherence and hierarchy quality over text- and summarybased baselines. A case study on German regional innovation analysis further demonstrates its practical utility for technology landscape mapping.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a term-centric framework for inducing hierarchical taxonomies from large, heterogeneous document collections. Unlike document-level approaches, it extracts domain-specific terms to create shared cross-source representations, then constructs interpretable hierarchies combining domain priors with data-driven clustering. Evaluated on a 1M+ document English-German benchmark, it outperforms text- and summary-based baselines in cross-source coherence and hierarchy quality, with a case study in German regional innovation analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing taxonomy induction methods use document-level representations that capture entire documents rather than domain-specific concepts, limiting cross-source generalization. There is a need for scalable, interpretable hierarchy construction from heterogeneous corpora for applications like policy analysis and innovation monitoring.
AI.method: A term-centric framework that: (1) applies automatic term extraction to map documents from diverse sources into a shared representation space, (2) aligns representations across sources, and (3) constructs hierarchical taxonomies by integrating domain priors with data-driven clustering.
AI.result: On a novel English-German multi-source benchmark of over one million documents, the method improves cross-source coherence and hierarchy quality compared to text- and summary-based baselines. A German regional innovation analysis case study demonstrates practical utility for technology landscape mapping.
AI.conclusion: Term-centric representations enable more robust and interpretable taxonomy induction across heterogeneous corpora at scale, with demonstrated real-world applicability in technology landscape mapping and innovation analysis.

title: Memory Depth, Not Memory Access: Selective Parametric Consolidation for Long-Running Language Agents
comment: Main paper with supplementary material included as ancillary file
summary: Long-running language agents need more than memory access. Retrieval systems can fetch past facts at query time, but they do not decide which experiences should continue to shape behavior after the working context is unloaded. We study this separate problem as memory depth: durable goal-conditioned tendencies written into a small parametric store. We introduce the loop-drift protocol, a controlled stress test in which the retrieval index remains intact while working context is unloaded and goal-conditioned behavior must persist under long-loop interference. We evaluate EVAF, a surprise- and valence-gated LoRA consolidation mechanism. Across GPT-2 and TinyLlama, retrieval is strongest on shallow factual recall (short-fact accuracy 0.956--0.973), while EVAF is strongest on goal persistence and post-unload recovery (0.812--0.904) with only 2--3 parametric writes per 200 events. Mechanism controls show that selective consolidation factorizes into two controllable dimensions: selection and actuation. Matched random gates isolate selection beyond sparse writing; fixed-inner controls across GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Mistral-7B show that inner-loop write strength is model-dependent; and a Mistral-7B matched-gate inversion reveals asymmetric selection-actuation coupling under miscalibrated actuation. Public Memora event streams serve as an external diagnostic, exposing stale-memory invalidation as an unresolved boundary. Within this probe, selective parametric consolidation supplies memory depth distinct from and complementary to retrieval access.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "memory depth" — durable, goal-conditioned behavioral tendencies stored in a small parametric memory — as distinct from retrieval-based memory access.
