Alternatively, if LLMs reason based on content, they should flexibly switch strategies when appropriate. Across two experiments with nine state-of-the-art LLMs and 100 human participants, we show humans and LLMs fail on this paradigm in opposite directions. LLMs were far more accurate on genuine riddles than on riddle riddles (84.9% vs. 50.7%); whereas humans showed the reverse effect (50.5% vs. 80.5%). Error analysis shows that 90.8% of LLM errors on riddle riddles (the condition where they show diminished performance) were due to inappropriate use of inventive reasoning while only 57.6% of human errors on genuine riddles were due to overextending literal reasoning. Thus, while both groups make mistakes, reasoning mistakes are made more often by LLMs than by humans. Overall, LLMs' strong performance on genuine riddles may reflect memory retrieval rather than flexible strategy selection, and without stimuli designed to elicit this contrast, it becomes easy to conflate LLM-generated outputs that look like reasoning with genuine reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "riddle riddle" paradigm to test whether LLMs genuinely reason flexibly or merely pattern-match. While LLMs excel at genuine riddles, they fail dramatically on riddle riddles (which require literal interpretation), over-relying on inventive reasoning strategies. Humans show the opposite pattern. The findings suggest LLM performance reflects memory retrieval rather than flexible reasoning.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLMs' strong performance on cognitive tasks stems from genuine flexible reasoning or superficial pattern matching from training data. Existing benchmarks may conflate outputs that resemble reasoning with actual reasoning.
AI.method: The authors created the "riddle riddle" paradigm: word problems that mimic the surface structure of popular riddles but are altered so correct answers require only literal interpretation (not inventive thinking). Two experiments tested nine state-of-the-art LLMs and 100 human participants on both genuine riddles and riddle riddles, comparing accuracy and error types (inappropriate inventive reasoning vs. inappropriate literal reasoning).
AI.result: LLMs scored 84.9% on genuine riddles but only 50.7% on riddle riddles; humans showed the reverse (50.5% vs. 80.5%). 90.8% of LLM errors on riddle riddles came from wrongly applying inventive reasoning, while only 57.6% of human errors on genuine riddles came from overextending literal reasoning. LLMs' reasoning mistakes were thus more frequent and systematic.
AI.conclusion: LLMs' strong riddle performance likely reflects memory retrieval of training data rather than flexible, content-driven strategy selection. Without carefully controlled stimuli like riddle riddles, LLM outputs that mimic reasoning can easily be mistaken for genuine cognitive flexibility.

title: Structure Before Collapse: Transient semantic geometry in next-token prediction
summary: Neural Collapse predicts that balanced one-hot classification pushes model representations to be equally far from each other; a symmetric configuration that depends only on the output label and ignores any semantic similarity in the inputs. This creates a puzzle: next-token prediction language models are trained predominantly (as context length increases) with one-hot labels: the same context is very unlikely to appear twice in training with different labels. However, they clearly learn latent structural features. That is, despite the one-hot training regime, a language model's contextual embeddings represent the fact that the next word in ''Mary broke the ___'' is likely to be filled by tokens in the latent classes of a) medium-sized, b) rigid, c) inanimate nouns. How does gradient descent find such categorical semantic structure when co-occurrence statistics collapse to one-hot sparsity, eliminating any shared next-tokens among different contexts? To investigate this tension we identify three synthetic controlled settings where inputs have latent semantic factors but are mapped to distinct one-hot labels. We find that semantic geometry emerges early in training, and that representations cluster by shared attributes despite receiving no explicit supervision to do so. This structure is transient: with sufficient capacity and time, the model eventually reaches the predicted symmetric state where all representations are equally separated. We study this phase transition through Gram matrix analysis and propose a preliminary modification to the commonly used unconstrained features model to capture the emergent semantic geometry.

AI.tldr: Neural Collapse theory predicts one-hot classification yields symmetric, equally-spaced representations ignoring input semantics. Yet LMs trained with one-hot next-token prediction learn latent semantic structure. This paper shows that semantic geometry emerges early in training as a transient phase before collapsing to symmetric Neural Collapse, and proposes a modified unconstrained features model to capture this phenomenon.
AI.motivation: Resolve the tension between Neural Collapse theory—which predicts that one-hot classification leads to symmetric representations where all classes are equidistant—and the empirical observation that language models trained with one-hot next-token prediction learn semantically meaningful latent structure. Co-occurrence statistics in such training collapse to one-hot sparsity, eliminating shared next-tokens among contexts, so how does gradient descent discover categorical semantic structure?
AI.method: The authors construct three synthetic controlled settings where inputs possess latent semantic factors but are assigned distinct one-hot labels. They then analyze the training dynamics by tracking representation geometry over time, using Gram matrix analysis to study the phase transition from emergent semantic clustering to the symmetric Neural Collapse state. They also propose a preliminary modification to the standard unconstrained features model to account for the emergent semantic geometry.
AI.result: Semantic geometry emerges early in training: representations cluster by shared attributes without explicit supervision. This structure is transient—with sufficient capacity and training time, the model eventually transitions to the predicted symmetric Neural Collapse state where all representations are equally separated.
AI.conclusion: The semantic clustering observed in LM representations is a transient phase in the optimization trajectory, eventually giving way to symmetric Neural Collapse. This suggests that the useful semantic features exploited in practice arise from early-stage training dynamics, and the unconstrained features model can be adapted to capture this phenomenon.

title: Generative Retrieval via Diffusion Transformer with Metric-Ordered Sequence Training and Hybrid-Policy Preference Optimization
summary: Embedding-based retrieval ranks items by their similarity to a query in a shared vector space and usually aims to return the highest-scoring items. In many production settings this is not what is wanted: given a seed set that expresses a fine-grained pattern, one needs more items that both satisfy a target attribute and stay within that pattern. We formalize this as pattern-preserving attribute retrieval. The two goals pull against each other: averaging the seeds preserves the pattern but stays in a low-attribute region, while global attribute retrieval drifts to unrelated patterns. We approach the task with continuous generative retrieval, where a model reads a sequence of item embeddings and generates query embeddings for nearest-neighbor search. We propose MO-DiT+HPPO, a staged framework with raw-sequence pretraining, multi-domain metric-ordered continuation pretraining, tail-centroid fine-tuning, and HPPO. Metric-ordered training turns sparse online retrieval labels into in-pattern trajectories ordered from low to high predicted attribute density, teaching one model the metric-improvement direction across domains. HPPO aligns the generated query distribution with the true online objective by labeling a hybrid candidate pool with the online intersection metric and applying reference-anchored preference optimization. A Pareto pair filter keeps only winner pairs that do not lower same-pattern purity, raising the attribute metric without sacrificing the pattern. Across four attribute domains under item- and pattern-holdout protocols, metric-ordered DiT improves the intersection metric over a pretrained generative retriever, and HPPO improves it further, with significant gains on seven of eight domain-split cells and a marginal tie on the hardest split. Metric-predictor validation, order ablations, CPT/SFT comparisons, and a candidate-policy ablation show where the gains come from.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "pattern-preserving attribute retrieval": given a seed set expressing a fine-grained pattern, retrieve items that satisfy a target attribute while staying within that pattern. They propose MO-DiT+HPPO, a staged framework combining metric-ordered continuation pretraining on Diffusion Transformer (DiT) and Hybrid Preference Policy Optimization, achieving significant gains across multiple attribute domains.
AI.motivation: Standard embedding-based retrieval either averages seeds (preserving pattern but landing in low-attribute regions) or optimizes purely for attributes (drifting to unrelated patterns). There is a need for retrieval that simultaneously preserves the seed pattern and maximizes a target attribute — a tug-of-war that existing methods fail to resolve.
AI.method: A staged framework called MO-DiT+HPPO: (1) raw-sequence pretraining on item embeddings, (2) multi-domain metric-ordered continuation pretraining that converts sparse online labels into trajectories ordered from low to high predicted attribute density, teaching the DiT model metric-improvement direction across domains, (3) tail-centroid fine-tuning, and (4) HPPO — Hybrid Preference Policy Optimization that aligns generated query distributions with the online intersection metric via reference-anchored preference optimization on a hybrid candidate pool, plus a Pareto pair filter to retain only winner pairs that do not degrade same-pattern purity.
AI.result: Metric-ordered DiT improves the intersection metric over a pretrained generative retriever baseline, and HPPO yields further improvements. Significant gains are reported on seven of eight domain-split cells, with a marginal tie on the hardest split. Gains are validated via metric-predictor validation, order ablations, CPT/SFT comparisons, and candidate-policy ablation.
AI.conclusion: The staged MO-DiT+HPPO framework effectively balances the dual objectives of pattern preservation and attribute maximization in embedding-based retrieval. Metric-ordered continuation pretraining and HPPO are both critical contributors, and the Pareto pair filter ensures attribute gains without sacrificing pattern purity.

title: Forecasting With LLMs: Improved Generalization Through Feature Steering
summary: Successful forecasting involves identifying patterns between historical and future states of the world which generalize to future observations. We apply LLMs to a variety of forecasting tasks and inspect their internal states using sparse autoencoders to understand whether they appear to rely on time-specific pieces of knowledge versus generalizable patterns. Our analyses identify features associated with both time-aware reasoning and look-ahead-biased reasoning. We then apply the LLMs to an entirely different domain and intervene on these features. We find that amplifying time-awareness features substantially reduces look-ahead bias on forecasting prompts while preserving general reasoning performance. In contrast, steering the candidate look-ahead-bias features does not produce an effect. These results suggest that interpretable temporal features can be used to causally shift LLMs toward more historically grounded reasoning.

AI.tldr: LLMs contain interpretable temporal features that, when amplified via sparse autoencoders, causally reduce look-ahead bias in forecasting tasks without harming general reasoning. Surprisingly, directly suppressing candidate bias features has no effect, suggesting time-awareness features are the more effective intervention target.
AI.motivation: LLMs used for forecasting risk incorporating look-ahead bias — using information from future time periods that would be unavailable at the historical prediction point. The authors aim to understand whether LLMs rely on time-specific knowledge versus generalizable patterns, and whether interpretable temporal features can be causally manipulated to produce more historically grounded forecasts.
AI.method: The authors apply LLMs to forecasting tasks and probe internal representations using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify two categories of features: (1) time-aware reasoning features and (2) look-ahead-biased reasoning features. They then perform causal intervention experiments — amplifying or suppressing these features — and evaluate the effect on both forecasting accuracy/bias and general reasoning performance. They also test generalization by applying the same interventions in a different domain.
AI.result: Amplifying time-awareness features significantly reduces look-ahead bias on forecasting prompts while preserving general reasoning capabilities. In contrast, steering candidate look-ahead-bias features produces no measurable effect. The intervention effects transfer to an entirely different domain, indicating robustness.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable temporal features discovered via sparse autoencoders can be causally manipulated to shift LLMs toward more historically grounded reasoning. This demonstrates a practical use case for mechanistic interpretability in improving LLM reliability for forecasting applications.

title: Batch-Invariant Spectral Intelligence for Robust and Explainable Insect Authentication
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables (excluding supplementary materials, submitted to journal
summary: Edible insects offer an efficient source of alternative protein, requiring less land, water and emitting less greenhouse gas than conventional livestock. However, their successful integration into the food supply chain demands reliable species authentication to control allergen exposure, prevent adulteration, and meet regulatory standards. Near-infrared spectroscopy provides a rapid analytical tool, but its performance drops when applied to production batches unseen during training due to batch-to-batch variation in spectral measurements. We introduce the Batch-Invariant Spectral Network (BISN), an end-to-end framework that combines a learnable preprocessing module, initialised with Savitzky-Golay filtering, with an entropy-regularised adversarial objective to suppress batch-specific spectral variation. In contrast to Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks, which enforce domain adaptation only after feature extraction, BISN suppress batch-effects before species-specific features are learned. Using 2,700 spectra from three species (Acheta domesticus, Hermetia illucens, and Tenebrio molitor) collected across three independent production batches, BISN achieves a mean leave-one-batch-out accuracy of 0.93 (standard deviation 0.04), outperforming the strongest baseline by four percent. Further insights gained by using explainable AI confirm that model decisions consistently rely on the lipid and protein absorption regions across all folds, connecting predictive performance to known insect biochemistry. BISN addresses both cross-batch robustness and biochemical interpretability for automated insect species authentication under realistic industrial conditions. The source code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/majharB/bisn.

AI.tldr: BISN, a Batch-Invariant Spectral Network, introduces a learnable preprocessing module with adversarial training to suppress batch-specific variation in NIR spectra before feature learning, achieving 0.93 accuracy for edible insect species authentication across independent production batches.
AI.motivation: Edible insects are a sustainable alternative protein source, but industrial adoption requires reliable species authentication. NIR spectroscopy is a rapid tool, yet its performance degrades across unseen production batches due to batch-to-batch spectral variation. Existing domain adaptation methods like DANN address batch effects only after feature extraction, which limits robustness.
AI.method: The Batch-Invariant Spectral Network (BISN) is an end-to-end framework with two key innovations: (1) a learnable preprocessing module initialized with Savitzky-Golay filtering to handle spectral variation at the input level, and (2) an entropy-regularized adversarial objective that suppresses batch-specific effects before species-specific features are learned. This contrasts with Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks (DANN), which enforce domain adaptation post-feature extraction. The method was validated on 2,700 NIR spectra from three insect species across three independent batches using leave-one-batch-out cross-validation.
AI.result: BISN achieved a mean leave-one-batch-out accuracy of 0.93 (SD 0.04), outperforming the strongest baseline by four percentage points. Explainable AI analysis confirmed that model decisions consistently rely on lipid and protein absorption regions across all folds, aligning with known insect biochemistry.
AI.conclusion: BISN effectively addresses both cross-batch robustness and biochemical interpretability for automated insect species authentication under realistic industrial conditions. The code and dataset are publicly released.

title: Learning to Recover Task Experts from a Multi-Task Merged Model
summary: Multi-task model merging aims to consolidate several task-specific experts into a unified model, yet static merging consistently suffers from parameter interference. While dynamic merging models aim to bridge this gap, many works rely on the costly storage and loading of redundant expert components at inference. In this work, from the perspective of task expert, we view parameter interference as parameter perturbation introduced to each expert during merging process. We show that such parameter perturbations can be modeled as affine transformation, which can be approximated as additive offsets. Motivated by these, we propose Recover Task eXpert (ReTeX), a framework that predicts those offsets, in order to undo parameter interference and recover task-expert performance from a single merged checkpoint. To recover the appropriate expert when task identity is unknown, we introduce a router-free task identifier based on SVD subspace signatures computed offline before inference. At inference, the identifier selects the task whose subspace yields the smallest projection residual for a given input. As a result, ReTeX recovers over 95% of individual-expert performance in both vision and NLP domains, while significantly improving generalization to unseen tasks. Crucially, we also show that the parameter offset prediction leads to emergent adaptive interpolation of expert knowledge for out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. ReTeX adaptively interpolates seen expert knowledge to handle unseen tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/BAIKLAB/ReTeX

AI.tldr: ReTeX proposes a framework that recovers task-expert performance from a single merged checkpoint by predicting additive parameter offsets that undo parameter interference, using SVD-based task identification without a router, achieving >95% expert recovery and emergent OOD generalization.
AI.motivation: Multi-task model merging suffers from parameter interference that degrades individual task performance. Dynamic merging methods mitigate this but require costly storage/loading of redundant expert components at inference. The authors aim to recover expert performance from a single merged model without storing multiple experts.
AI.method: The authors model parameter interference as affine transformations (approximated as additive offsets) introduced to each expert during merging. ReTeX predicts these offsets to recover task-specific experts. For task identification without a router, they use SVD subspace signatures: at inference, the input is projected onto pre-computed task subspaces, and the task with the smallest projection residual is selected. The framework enables adaptive interpolation of expert knowledge for OOD tasks.
AI.result: ReTeX recovers over 95% of individual-expert performance in both vision and NLP domains and significantly improves generalization to unseen (OOD) tasks through emergent adaptive interpolation of expert knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Parameter interference in model merging can be effectively modeled and reversed as additive offsets. ReTeX achieves strong expert recovery from a single merged checkpoint while enabling emergent OOD generalization, eliminating the need for storing multiple expert components at inference.

title: Syntactic Belief Update as the Driver of Garden Path Processing Difficulty
summary:
Garden path sentences present a processing difficulty for humans -- the sentence prefix leads the listener towards one interpretation, until the listener hears a critical word that shows that the initial interpretation was wrong. Lexical surprisal, a measure that usually predicts sentence processing difficulty quite well, fails to provide good predictions for garden path sentences.
  We propose an alternative that actively predicts a probability distribution over syntactic trees (its syntactic belief) and updates that distribution after each new word. If a processor is led down a garden path, syntactic beliefs will be wrong and will require a large update at the critical word. The magnitude of the update is measured with a generalized Rényi divergence. Crucially, this metric is dependent on lexical items, but is fully independent of the probability of lexical items. This Syntactic Belief Update provides a better fit to the human reading time data on garden path sentences. This suggests a new research direction examining purely non-lexical alternatives to surprisal for psycholinguistics.

AI.tldr: Garden path sentences challenge standard lexical surprisal models. This paper proposes Syntactic Belief Update — a metric using generalized Rényi divergence to measure how much a processor's syntactic tree distribution shifts at each word — which better predicts human reading times on garden path sentences than surprisal.
AI.motivation: Lexical surprisal, despite being a strong predictor of sentence processing difficulty in general, fails to account for the processing difficulty observed in garden path sentences. This gap motivates the search for a non-lexical, syntax-driven alternative.
AI.method: The authors propose a processor that maintains a probability distribution over syntactic trees (a syntactic belief), updating it incrementally word-by-word. When a garden path is disambiguated, the belief requires a large revision. The magnitude of this revision is quantified using generalized Rényi divergence. Crucially, this metric depends on syntactic structure and lexical items but is independent of lexical item probabilities, isolating syntactic processing difficulty from lexical prediction.
AI.result: The Syntactic Belief Update metric provides a better fit to human reading time data on garden path sentences compared to lexical surprisal.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest that purely non-lexical, syntax-based metrics represent a promising new research direction for psycholinguistic models of sentence processing, complementing or replacing surprisal-based accounts.

title: Escaping Iterative Parameter-Space Noise: Differentially Private Learning with a Hypernetwork
summary: Differentially private (DP) training of neural networks is often hindered by the large amount of noise required by gradient-based methods such as DP-SGD, which repeatedly inject high-dimensional noise in parameter space throughout training. In this paper, we propose a new framework for DP learning that avoids iterative optimization in parameter space. Instead of updating the target model using privatized gradients, we employ a hypernetwork trained on public datasets to map a private dataset to the parameters of the target model. Specifically, each example is embedded into a low-dimensional representation, the embeddings are aggregated and perturbed to obtain a DP dataset embedding, and the hypernetwork generates the target model parameters from this noisy embedding. Because privacy noise is injected only once into a low-dimensional dataset representation, our approach can significantly reduce the adverse effect of noise. We theoretically show in a synthetic setting that, under a fixed privacy budget, models produced by our approach achieve higher utility than those trained with DP-SGD. Moreover, we apply our approach to LoRA fine-tuning of diffusion models and show that it achieves lower FID than LoRA models trained with DP-SGD and other public-data-guided methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes a DP learning framework that uses a hypernetwork trained on public data to generate model parameters from a single, low-dimensional DP embedding of the private dataset, avoiding iterative DP-SGD noise accumulation.
AI.motivation: DP-SGD injects high-dimensional noise repeatedly throughout training, severely degrading model utility. The authors aim to reduce noise impact by privatizing only once in a low-dimensional space.
AI.method: A hypernetwork is pretrained on public datasets. Private examples are embedded into low-dimensional vectors, aggregated, then perturbed with DP noise (e.g., Gaussian) to form a DP dataset embedding. The hypernetwork maps this noisy embedding to target model parameters in a single forward pass.
AI.result: Theoretically, under fixed privacy budget, their method achieves higher utility than DP-SGD in synthetic settings. Empirically, applied to LoRA fine-tuning of diffusion models, it achieves lower FID than DP-SGD-trained LoRA and other public-data-guided baselines.
AI.conclusion: One-shot DP noise injection into low-dimensional dataset embeddings via hypernetworks substantially mitigates the utility loss typical of DP-SGD, offering a promising direction for DP learning when public data is available.

title: Diagnosing Task Insensitivity in Language Agents
summary: Large language models can serve as capable long-horizon agents, but their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains weak. We identify a key source of this failure as task insensitivity: when faced with similar but distinct tasks, models might apply patterns learned during training and fail to solve the task at hand. We show that models often continue with actions aligned with the original task even when the instruction is semantically corrupted and cannot be directly answered. We further find that, when we replace the task description in a trained prompt with another similar but distinct task, the model may still output the same action. This behavior is accompanied by a consistent training-time attention drift away from task tokens and toward local observations, suggesting an optimization bias toward shortcuts. To mitigate this problem, we propose Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization, a lightweight contrastive regularizer that explicitly encourages action dependence on the task instruction. Extensive evaluations show that our intervention improves task sensitivity and OOD generalization while preserving more stable attention to task tokens.

AI.tldr: LLMs acting as long-horizon agents suffer from OOD generalization failures due to task insensitivity — models default to learned action patterns even when task instructions are corrupted or swapped. The authors trace this to an attention drift away from task tokens toward local observations during training, and propose a contrastive regularizer (Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization) that improves task sensitivity and OOD generalization.
AI.motivation: Large language models deployed as long-horizon agents exhibit poor out-of-distribution generalization. The authors identify a core mechanism behind this brittleness: models become insensitive to the specific task instruction, instead relying on spurious shortcuts learned during training. This manifests as models producing the same actions when instructions are semantically corrupted or replaced with different tasks.
AI.method: The authors first diagnose task insensitivity through two probes: (1) semantic corruption of task instructions, and (2) replacement with similar but distinct tasks. They observe a consistent attention drift from task tokens to local observations during training. To address this, they propose Task-Perturbed NLL (Negative Log-Likelihood) Optimization — a lightweight contrastive regularizer that explicitly penalizes the model when its action distribution is invariant to task perturbation, thereby enforcing dependence on the task instruction.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed regularizer improves task sensitivity, enhances OOD generalization, and yields more stable attention allocation to task tokens throughout training.
AI.conclusion: Task insensitivity is a key failure mode for LLM-based agents, driven by an optimization shortcut that shifts attention away from task instructions. The proposed contrastive regularizer effectively mitigates this issue, offering a practical intervention for building more robust, task-aware agents.

title: Paved with True Intents: Intent-Aware Training Improves LLM Safety Classification Across Training Regimes
summary: We argue that safety classifiers should model user intent as an explicit signal between the prompt and the final label. To study this, we introduce AIMS, a human-annotated dataset of 1,724 difficult safety prompts, each paired with an intent description and harm label. We use AIMS to evaluate intent-aware training across supervised fine-tuning, preference learning, reasoning distillation, and reinforcement learning. Despite its size, AIMS enables competitive safety classifiers across training regimes: DPO from model-generated intent errors improves over SFT, and intent-conditioned distillation outperforms reasoning-only distillation in most teacher-student pairs. Most notably, directly rewarding intent faithfulness with GRPO yields the strongest average performance across five external safety benchmarks, while our intent-aware models form the inference latency-F1 Pareto frontier. These results show that faithful intent modeling is a compact, high-quality supervision signal for more robust safety classifiers.

AI.tldr: AIMS introduces a dataset of 1,724 safety prompts with human-annotated intent descriptions to train safety classifiers that explicitly model user intent. Intent-aware training — especially GRPO-based reinforcement learning — yields superior performance across external benchmarks and forms the Pareto frontier for inference latency vs. F1.
AI.motivation: Current safety classifiers typically map prompts directly to harm labels without modeling the user's underlying intent, which can lead to brittle or overbroad safety decisions. The authors argue that explicitly incorporating user intent as an intermediate signal can produce more robust and faithful safety classification.
AI.method: The authors construct AIMS, a human-annotated dataset of 1,724 difficult safety prompts with intent descriptions and harm labels. They evaluate intent-aware training across four paradigms: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), preference learning (DPO using model-generated intent errors), reasoning distillation (intent-conditioned), and reinforcement learning (GRPO with direct intent-faithfulness rewards).
AI.result: DPO from intent errors improves over SFT; intent-conditioned distillation outperforms reasoning-only distillation in most teacher-student pairs; GRPO with intent-faithfulness rewards achieves the strongest average performance across five external safety benchmarks. Intent-aware models form the inference latency–F1 Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: Faithful intent modeling provides a compact, high-quality supervision signal that yields more robust safety classifiers, consistently outperforming intent-agnostic approaches across diverse training regimes and benchmarks.

title: Reproducibility Study of "AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models"
summary: Fang et al. (2025) introduced a null-space constrained projection, named AlphaEdit, for locate-then-edit knowledge editing methods, theoretically guaranteeing that edits do not disrupt previously preserved knowledge, and reports substantial gains over existing editing methods on LLaMA3, GPT2-XL, and GPT-J. In this work, we present a reproducibility study of AlphaEdit, reproducing its reported results under the original experimental setup and extending the evaluation along three axes: new model architectures, additional downstream benchmarks, and substantially longer sequential editing horizons. We successfully reproduce AlphaEdit's reported metrics across the original models, though we identify a discrepancy in the reported fluency and consistency metric. Extending AlphaEdit to newer model families, we find that its advantage does not generalize uniformly, which we trace to architectural assumptions in the locate-then-edit paradigm that are violated by these newer models. We further stress-test AlphaEdit's central sequential-editing claim by extending the number of edits well beyond those evaluated in the original paper, and find that performance, which is stable at the originally reported scale, degrades as edits reach a much higher count, indicating that the null-space projection's protection against catastrophic forgetting is bounded rather than unconditional. Finally, we extend evaluation of edited models on three extra benchmarks, namely, BoolQ, HellaSwag, and XSTest, and we find that large-scale sequential editing degrades both general downstream task competence and safety-relevant refusal behavior. Our results confirm that AlphaEdit performs as reported within its original scope, while showing that its core theoretical guarantees are sensitive to model architecture and editing scale in ways that have practical implications for its deployment.

AI.tldr: A reproducibility study of AlphaEdit confirms its original results but reveals that its null-space projection advantage does not generalize to newer model architectures, degrades under substantially longer editing horizons, and negatively impacts downstream task performance and safety refusal behavior at scale.
AI.motivation: AlphaEdit claims theoretical guarantees against catastrophic forgetting during sequential knowledge editing via null-space constrained projection. The authors aim to verify these claims through reproduction and stress-test the method beyond its original scope.
AI.method: The study reproduces AlphaEdit under the original experimental setup on LLaMA3, GPT2-XL, and GPT-J, then extends evaluation along three axes: (1) newer model architectures, (2) additional downstream benchmarks (BoolQ, HellaSwag, XSTest), and (3) substantially longer sequential editing horizons well beyond the originally reported scale.
AI.result: Original metrics were successfully reproduced, but a fluency/consistency discrepancy was found. AlphaEdit's advantage fails to generalize to newer model families due to violated architectural assumptions. Performance degrades under extended editing counts, revealing the null-space protection is bounded. Large-scale editing also degrades general downstream competence and safety refusal behavior.
AI.conclusion: AlphaEdit performs as reported within its original scope, but its core theoretical guarantees are sensitive to model architecture and editing scale, carrying practical implications for real-world deployment.

title: Where Do CoT Training Gains Land in LLM based Agents?
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is widely used in language-model agents, but prior work has shown that verbalized CoT is not always faithful and may instead reflect post-hoc reasoning, which means the model already knows the answer before reasoning. We therefore ask what CoT training is actually improving: is the model getting better at changing its action through generated reasoning, or is it getting better at predicting the action directly from the prompt? We study this question by comparing \emph{prompt actions} (predicting action without CoT) with CoT actions (predicting action with CoT). Across checkpoints, prompt-action quality improves substantially. While interacting with the environment, the relative advantage of CoT actions over prompt actions remains similar, showing that CoT training does not widen the advantage of CoT reasoning, and it helps to improve the quality of prompt actions. We further find that later checkpoints are less likely to revise the action in response to CoT, suggesting greater reliance on the prompt. Motivated by these patterns, we selectively mask action-token supervision on a fraction of training examples. This intervention improves out-of-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether chain-of-thought training actually improves the reasoning process or merely enhances direct action prediction from prompts. Findings show CoT training primarily improves prompt-action quality rather than widening CoT's relative advantage, and later checkpoints rely more on prompts. Masking action-token supervision on some training examples improves out-of-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Prior work has shown that verbalized chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful and may reflect post-hoc rationalization — the model already knows the answer before generating the reasoning trace. This raises a fundamental question: what is CoT training actually improving? The authors aim to disentangle whether CoT training genuinely improves the model's ability to reason through generated chains, or whether it simply improves direct (prompt-based) action prediction.
AI.method: The authors compare two types of actions across training checkpoints: (1) **prompt actions** — predicting the action directly without generating CoT, and (2) **CoT actions** — predicting the action after generating a CoT reasoning trace. They measure how each improves over the course of training, analyze whether later checkpoints revise actions in response to CoT, and conduct an intervention where they selectively mask action-token supervision on a fraction of training examples to test whether reducing reliance on CoT-then-act improves generalization.
AI.result: Across checkpoints, prompt-action quality improves substantially. The relative advantage of CoT actions over prompt actions remains similar throughout training, indicating CoT training does not widen CoT's advantage — it primarily improves prompt-action quality. Later checkpoints are less likely to revise their action in response to CoT, suggesting greater reliance on the prompt alone. The selective masking intervention (removing action-token supervision on some examples) improves out-of-domain generalization performance.
AI.conclusion: CoT training largely serves to improve the model's internal, direct action-prediction capability rather than enhancing the contribution of the reasoning chain itself. This suggests that much of the benefit attributed to CoT may actually come from training on action tokens within a structured reasoning format, rather than from faithful step-by-step deliberation. The masking intervention provides a practical method to mitigate over-reliance on the prompt and improve generalization.

title: Compositionality and the lexicon in evolutionary semantics
summary: Formal semantics has shown that sentence meanings arise by recursively composing lexical meanings, yet much of the literature on semantic universals models either lexicons with fixed signal structures or holistic composition without interpretable lexical parts. We introduce a framework that integrates this fundamental insight of formal semantics in evolutionary modeling, by allowing lexical meanings and a composition function to co-evolve under pressures for conceptual simplicity and communicative accuracy. We apply this framework to the evolution of quantificational meaning. Analyzing the Pareto frontier, we find that the most well-known semantic universal, conservativity, emerges as an efficient system-wide abstraction. The account is sensitive to syntactic structure and helps reconcile tensions between empirical evidence on quantifier learnability and prior evolutionary models. More broadly, the results demonstrate that the picture of sentential meaning developed in formal semantics can be productively combined with evolutionary modeling. The framework offers a template for studying universals that involve global compression within a grammatical category, semantic specialization of syntactic arguments, and the co-evolution of lexical and compositional meaning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an evolutionary framework where lexical meanings and a composition function co-evolve under pressures for simplicity and accuracy. Applied to quantificational meaning, it shows that the semantic universal of conservativity emerges as an efficient system-wide abstraction on the Pareto frontier, reconciling empirical learnability data with prior models and demonstrating how formal compositional semantics can be integrated with evolutionary modeling.
AI.motivation: Prior work on semantic universals has typically modeled either lexicons with fixed signal structures or holistic composition without interpretable lexical parts, ignoring the core insight of formal semantics that sentence meanings arise from recursive composition of lexical meanings. The authors aim to bridge this gap by incorporating compositional structure into evolutionary models of semantic universals.
AI.method: The authors introduce a co-evolutionary framework where lexical meanings and a composition function evolve simultaneously under dual pressures: conceptual simplicity (favoring compressible, systematic representations) and communicative accuracy (favoring faithful meaning transmission). They apply this to the domain of quantificational meaning, analyzing the resulting Pareto frontier to identify which semantic properties emerge as optimal trade-offs.
AI.result: Conservativity — the most well-known semantic universal for quantifiers — emerges as an efficient system-wide abstraction on the Pareto frontier. The account is sensitive to syntactic structure and helps reconcile tensions between empirical findings on quantifier learnability and predictions from prior evolutionary models that lacked compositional structure.
AI.conclusion: Formal compositional semantics can be productively combined with evolutionary modeling. The framework provides a general template for investigating universals involving global compression within grammatical categories, semantic specialization of syntactic arguments, and the co-evolution of lexical and compositional meaning.

title: AIGP: An LLM-Based Framework for Long-Term Value Alignment in E-Commerce Pricing
comment: Accepted by KDD 2026 Applied Data Science Track (Oral presentation)
summary: Traditional dynamic pricing models in large-scale e-commerce suffer from limited interpretability, poor utilization of unstructured information, and misalignment with long-term business objectives such as cumulative Gross Merchandise Value (GMV), Return on Investment (ROI) and milestone achievement. We propose AIGP, a novel framework that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) prompted with domain knowledge, structured data and textual context to make interpretable, knowledge-aware pricing decisions. For efficient deployment while maintaining high-quality outputs, we employ supervised fine-tuning for knowledge distillation. Central to AIGP is the Long-Term Value Estimator (LTVE), trained via offline reinforcement learning on historical data, which serves as a reward model to score candidate pricing actions and select preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), thereby aligning the pricing policy with long-term business objectives. Extensive offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B tests on Tao Factory demonstrate that AIGP achieves significant improvements: +13.21% in GMV, +7.59% in ROI, and +8.20% in milestone achievement rate over 14 days compared to the production baseline, while simultaneously providing interpretable and transparent pricing rationales.

AI.tldr: AIGP is an LLM-based dynamic pricing framework for large-scale e-commerce that combines domain knowledge prompts with a Long-Term Value Estimator (LTVE) trained via offline RL. It uses DPO to align pricing with long-term objectives (GMV, ROI, milestones). Deployed on Tao Factory, it achieved +13.21% GMV, +7.59% ROI, and +8.20% milestone achievement over the production baseline.
AI.motivation: Traditional dynamic pricing models suffer from three key limitations: (1) limited interpretability of pricing decisions, (2) poor utilization of unstructured textual information, and (3) misalignment with long-term business objectives such as cumulative GMV, ROI, and milestone achievement, as opposed to short-term revenue optimization.
AI.method: AIGP uses an LLM prompted with domain knowledge, structured data, and textual context for interpretable pricing. Knowledge distillation is achieved via supervised fine-tuning for efficient deployment. The core component, the Long-Term Value Estimator (LTVE), is trained via offline reinforcement learning on historical data and serves as a reward model to score candidate pricing actions. Preference pairs are selected using LTVE scores for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), aligning the pricing policy with long-term business objectives.
AI.result: In extensive offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B tests on Tao Factory over 14 days, AIGP delivered: +13.21% GMV, +7.59% ROI, and +8.20% milestone achievement rate compared to the production baseline, while providing interpretable pricing rationales.
AI.conclusion: AIGP demonstrates that LLM-based pricing frameworks, when combined with offline RL-trained reward models and DPO alignment, can significantly outperform traditional production baselines on long-term e-commerce metrics while maintaining interpretability — making the approach both effective and practically deployable at scale.

title: Look-Before-Move: Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention in Dynamic 3D Story Worlds
summary: As embodied AI and world models increasingly operate in dynamic 3D environments, visual perception must move beyond passively interpreting given observations toward actively deciding what to observe. We study this problem through camera planning in dynamic 3D story worlds, where the camera must not only generate smooth motion, but also decide what visual evidence should be acquired before it moves. We formulate this capability as Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention, where the camera acts as an embodied observer that determines what to observe, how to compose the observation, and how to shift attention over time under narrative intent and physical 3D constraints. To realize this capability, we propose Look-Before-Move, a camera planning framework that separates observation specification from motion execution. It first builds a Semantic Observation Contract to convert directorial intent into executable visual constraints, then performs Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search to find narrative-compliant and geometrically feasible viewpoints, and finally applies Semantic Trajectory Grounding to connect selected viewpoints into continuous, collision-aware, and temporally coherent camera motion. We further construct a dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark based on StoryBlender, covering 50 stories, 457 scenes, and 1585 shots with animated characters, semantic scene configurations, and executable 3D environments. Experiments show that our framework improves subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality over representative baselines, demonstrating the importance of organizing visual attention before generating camera motion.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Look-Before-Move, a camera planning framework for dynamic 3D story worlds that separates observation specification from motion execution. It introduces Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention as a formulation where an embodied observer decides what to observe, how to compose it, and how to shift attention under narrative and physical constraints. A benchmark of 50 stories with 457 scenes and 1585 shots is also contributed.
AI.motivation: As embodied AI and world models operate in dynamic 3D environments, visual perception must evolve from passive interpretation of given observations toward active decision-making about what to observe. Existing camera planning approaches focus primarily on smooth motion generation but neglect the critical question: what visual evidence should be acquired before the camera moves. This gap motivates the work.
AI.method: The framework, Look-Before-Move, operates in three stages: (1) Semantic Observation Contract — converts directorial intent into executable visual constraints; (2) Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search — finds viewpoints that are both narrative-compliant and geometrically feasible; (3) Semantic Trajectory Grounding — connects selected viewpoints into continuous, collision-aware, temporally coherent camera motion. The approach decouples observation specification from motion execution.
AI.result: The authors construct a Dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark using StoryBlender, comprising 50 stories, 457 scenes, and 1585 shots with animated characters, semantic scene configurations, and executable 3D environments. Experiments demonstrate that Look-Before-Move improves subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality over representative baselines.
AI.conclusion: Organizing visual attention before generating camera motion is crucial for camera planning in narrative-grounded 3D environments. The decoupled design of Look-Before-Move — specifying observations first, then executing motion — proves effective for achieving narrative-compliant, physically feasible, and temporally coherent camera trajectories.

title: CARVE: Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency for Chunk-Parallel Linear Attention
comment: 27 pages, 2 figures, multiple tables. Submitted to arXiv. Primary category: cs.LG; cross-list: cs.CL
summary:
Recurrent models must forget in order to remember, yet the state of the art decides what to erase without consulting what is stored -- the gate sees only the arriving token, not the memory it is about to modify. This memory-blind gating is one of three coupled defects in the leading delta-rule architecture (GDN-2): the value-axis erase mask wastes parameters at the scale of the value projection, and -- as we prove -- mathematically prevents the WY-form triangular chunk solver that makes recurrent training competitive with Transformers.
  We introduce CARVE (Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency), which resolves all three problems through one principle: erase only on the key axis. This is provably necessary and sufficient for the WY-form solver to remain valid. Within it, CARVE reuses the recurrent output tensor -- already written to GPU memory -- as a free content signal for the erase gate, and replaces the per-value write-gate projection with a single scalar per head. At initialisation CARVE is bit-identical to GDN-2; any quality difference emerges from what the content gate learns.
  At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens, CARVE achieves WikiText perplexity 15.72 (minus 0.18 vs. GDN-2, a 4.5-sigma effect), leads every recurrent baseline on nine common-sense reasoning benchmarks, and sets state of the art on every RULER retrieval probe -- at 0.4% throughput overhead, 13% lower peak memory, and 19% fewer parameters. Six formal theorems cover memory capacity, Lyapunov stability, gradient flow, expressivity separation, Pareto-optimal chunk size, and hybrid optimality.

AI.tldr: CARVE introduces content-aware gating for recurrent architectures by restricting erasure to the key axis, reusing the recurrent output as a free content signal for the erase gate, and replacing per-value write-gate projections with scalar-per-head parameters. This fixes three defects in GDN-2: memory-blind gating, wasted value-axis parameters, and incompatibility with the WY-form chunk solver. At 1.3B/100B tokens, CARVE outperforms GDN-2 and all recurrent baselines on perplexity, reasoning, and retrieval benchmarks with lower memory and fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing delta-rule architectures like GDN-2 suffer from three coupled defects: (1) the erase gate is "memory-blind" — it decides what to forget based only on the incoming token without consulting the stored memory state; (2) applying the erase mask on the value axis wastes parameters; and (3) this value-axis erasure mathematically breaks the WY-form triangular chunk solver, which is critical for making recurrent training competitive with Transformers. All three problems stem from erasing on the wrong axis.
AI.method: CARVE resolves all three defects through a single design principle: erase only on the key axis. This is proven necessary and sufficient for the WY-form solver to remain valid. Within this constraint, CARVE (1) reuses the recurrent output tensor already in GPU memory as a free content signal for the content-aware erase gate, and (2) replaces the per-value write-gate projection with a single scalar per head. At initialization, CARVE is bit-identical to GDN-2, so any performance differences derive purely from what the content gate learns during training.
AI.result: At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens, CARVE achieves WikiText perplexity of 15.72 (0.18 improvement over GDN-2, a 4.5-sigma effect). It leads all recurrent baselines on nine common-sense reasoning benchmarks and sets state of the art on every RULER retrieval probe. These gains come with only 0.4% throughput overhead, 13% lower peak GPU memory, and 19% fewer parameters. The paper also provides six formal theorems covering memory capacity, Lyapunov stability, gradient flow, expressivity separation, Pareto-optimal chunk size, and hybrid optimality.
AI.conclusion: CARVE demonstrates that content-aware, key-axis-only erasure is both theoretically grounded and empirically superior for recurrent architectures, fixing fundamental defects in delta-rule models while maintaining compatibility with efficient WY-form training. The approach yields consistent improvements across language modeling, reasoning, and long-context retrieval with negligible overhead.

title: Reasoning Quality Emerges Early: Data Curation for Reasoning Models
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a small, high-quality set of long reasoning traces is an effective approach for eliciting strong reasoning capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing methods for curating high-quality SFT data rely heavily on strong reasoning models to filter examples based on diversity and difficulty, making the curation process costly while often yielding suboptimal data quality. In this work, we show that diverse and challenging reasoning examples can be identified using only the initial reasoning tokens. Specifically, we demonstrate that difficult problems can be reliably detected based on the loss of the first 100 reasoning tokens evaluated at a randomly perturbed checkpoint of the pretrained model. We further show that examples exhibiting similar loss patterns over their first 1k reasoning tokens across a small number of perturbed checkpoints extrapolating along the fine-tuning trajectory provably induce similar gradients. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B models on the M23K medical reasoning and OpenThoughts-Math datasets. Our method outperforms existing baselines by up to 1.7% while being 91% more token efficient.

AI.tldr: Diverse and challenging reasoning examples for SFT can be identified using only initial reasoning tokens, by detecting difficulty via loss on the first 100 tokens at a randomly perturbed checkpoint, and grouping examples with similar loss patterns across perturbed checkpoints to ensure gradient diversity. The method outperforms existing baselines by up to 1.7% while being 91% more token-efficient.
AI.motivation: Existing SFT data curation methods depend on strong reasoning models to filter examples by diversity and difficulty, which is costly and yields suboptimal quality. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency by identifying high-quality reasoning examples directly from pretrained model signals.
AI.method: (1) Difficulty detection: use the loss over the first 100 reasoning tokens at a randomly perturbed checkpoint of the pretrained model to reliably identify difficult problems. (2) Diversity selection: examples with similar loss patterns over the first 1k reasoning tokens across a small set of perturbed checkpoints (extrapolated along the fine-tuning trajectory) provably induce similar gradients, enabling efficient diversity-based selection without full reasoning traces.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B fine-tuned on M23K (medical reasoning) and OpenThoughts-Math datasets show the method outperforms existing baselines by up to 1.7% while achieving 91% token efficiency gains.
AI.conclusion: Initial reasoning tokens carry sufficient signal for both difficulty estimation and diversity-based data selection, enabling high-quality SFT data curation without reliance on strong reasoning models, dramatically reducing computational cost.

title: Einstein World Models
summary: Does intelligence require the ability to reason about phenomena beyond direct experience? It is natural to suspect that some complex thought cannot be captured through language alone. However, of particular concern to this work, is whether visualising counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought. We ask whether LLMs can be trained to utilise such visualisation mechanisms, in a way that benefits their reasoning abilities. Motivated by this question, we propose Einstein World Models. EWMs are a blueprint for LLM-based reasoning systems that place visual-temporal rollouts inside the reasoning trace, allowing them to reason in ways that text alone may not support well. In an EWM, the LLM calls a world-module (not to be confused with a world model), to produce short rollouts of scenes under consideration. The returned rollout is treated not as the answer, but as an inspectable hypothesis that can support later reasoning. Einstein World Models extend the capability of LLMs for tool calling (such as web search or code execution), into the domain of visual thought experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Einstein World Models (EWMs), a blueprint for LLM-based reasoning systems that integrate visual-temporal rollouts (visual thought experiments) into the reasoning trace, extending tool-calling capabilities beyond text to visual counterfactual simulation, aiming to enhance complex reasoning that text alone may not adequately support.
AI.motivation: The authors are motivated by the question of whether complex reasoning requires abilities beyond language — specifically, whether visualizing counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought. They investigate whether LLMs can be trained to utilize such visualization mechanisms to improve their reasoning abilities, addressing the concern that some complex thought cannot be captured through language alone.
AI.method: The paper proposes Einstein World Models, a blueprint architecture where an LLM calls a "world-module" to generate short visual-temporal rollouts of scenes under consideration. These rollouts are not treated as final answers but as inspectable hypotheses that support later reasoning steps. This extends the existing LLM tool-calling paradigm (e.g., web search, code execution) into the domain of visual thought experiments, placing visual simulations directly inside the reasoning trace.
AI.result: The abstract presents EWMs as a proposed blueprint/architecture rather than reporting experimental results. It frames the contribution as extending LLM tool-calling capabilities into visual counterfactual reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that EWMs offer a promising direction for enabling LLMs to reason through visual counterfactual simulation, suggesting that visual-temporal rollouts inside the reasoning trace can complement text-based reasoning for complex thought that may exceed the expressive or inferential limits of language alone.

title: Bridging Talk and Thought: Understanding Dialogue Dynamics Across Collaborative Problem-Solving Contexts
summary: We present a conceptual framework for analyzing dialogue in collaborative problem-solving contexts, with an emphasis on the emerging dynamics of human-AI and multi-agent collaboration. As intelligent systems become active agents capable of autonomous reasoning and strategic cooperation, understanding the dialogic interaction during collaborative problem solving is increasingly important for optimizing and evaluating such partnerships. Our framework addresses key limitations in current analytical approaches through a hierarchical two-layer coding scheme that integrates cognitive and non-cognitive problem solving with metacognitive regulatory mechanisms. We demonstrate its effectiveness and generalizability across nine datasets spanning multiple domains, and provide insights into how humans and agents coordinate their knowledge, skills, and efforts to solve complex problems, showing in particular that metacognitive regulation can be an essential discriminator of deeper collaboration.

AI.tldr: A two-layer hierarchical coding framework is proposed to analyze dialogue in collaborative problem-solving, covering cognitive/non-cognitive dimensions and metacognitive regulation. Tested across nine datasets, it reveals metacognitive regulation as a key discriminator of deeper collaboration in human-AI and multi-agent settings.
AI.motivation: Current analytical approaches for studying dialogue in collaborative problem-solving lack the ability to jointly capture task-oriented problem-solving moves and the metacognitive regulation that governs them. As AI systems become autonomous collaborative partners, there is a pressing need for a comprehensive framework that can evaluate and optimize human-AI and multi-agent dialogic interactions.
AI.method: The authors propose a conceptual framework with a hierarchical two-layer coding scheme. The first layer addresses cognitive and non-cognitive problem-solving dimensions. The second layer captures metacognitive regulatory mechanisms — processes such as planning, monitoring, and evaluation that govern the collaboration. The framework is validated across nine datasets from multiple domains to test its effectiveness and generalizability.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates effectiveness and generalizability across nine diverse datasets. Analysis reveals how humans and agents coordinate knowledge, skills, and efforts. A key finding is that metacognitive regulation serves as an essential discriminator of deeper, more effective collaboration.
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-layer coding scheme offers a robust, generalizable tool for analyzing collaborative problem-solving dialogue. Metacognitive regulation emerges as a critical dimension for distinguishing surface-level from deep collaboration, with implications for designing and evaluating future human-AI and multi-agent collaborative systems.

title: Quantization in Federated Learning: Methods, Challenges and Future Directions
summary: Federated Learning (FL) has become a foundational paradigm for privacy-preserving distributed intelligence, yet its scalability remains fundamentally constrained by communication bottlenecks, device heterogeneity, and the challenges of training under statistically non-IID data. Quantization is one of the most effective mechanisms for mitigating these limitations, reducing both uplink/downlink payloads and on-device computation. This paper provides the first FL-centric systematic review of quantization, introducing a novel taxonomy organized around FL-specific dimensions, including client heterogeneity, aggregation consistency, communication-scheduling adaptation, non-IID robustness, privacy/security integration, and hardware/energy co-optimization. Beyond cataloging existing methods, we analyze how quantization interacts with core FL behaviors such as client drift, partial participation, convergence stability, secure aggregation, and differential privacy. We further identify cross-method insights, open research gaps, and design guidelines for practitioners deploying quantized FL on mobile, IoT, and edge platforms. This survey thus establishes quantization not merely as a compression technique, but as a fundamental systems component shaping the performance, robustness, and practicality of modern FL.

AI.tldr: A systematic survey that redefines quantization in Federated Learning as a core systems component, introducing a novel FL-centric taxonomy and analyzing its interaction with client drift, convergence, privacy, and hardware constraints.
AI.motivation: FL scalability is constrained by communication bottlenecks, device heterogeneity, and non-IID data. While quantization is effective for compression, no prior survey has systematically examined it through FL-specific dimensions or treated it as a fundamental systems element rather than a mere compression technique.
AI.method: The authors conduct the first FL-centric systematic review of quantization, proposing a novel taxonomy organized around six FL-specific dimensions: client heterogeneity, aggregation consistency, communication-scheduling adaptation, non-IID robustness, privacy/security integration, and hardware/energy co-optimization. They also analyze interactions between quantization and core FL phenomena.
AI.result: The survey catalogs existing quantization methods, identifies cross-method insights, reveals open research gaps, and provides design guidelines for practitioners deploying quantized FL on mobile, IoT, and edge platforms.
AI.conclusion: Quantization should be understood not merely as compression but as a fundamental systems component that shapes the performance, robustness, and practicality of modern FL, with significant implications for future FL system design.

title: Adaptive Utility driven Resource Orchestration for Resilient AI (AURORA-AI)
comment: Accepted at IEEE Research and Technologies for Society and Industry 2026 conference
summary: Modern AI systems are increasingly deployed under non-stationary computational, demographic, and operational conditions in which static resource allocation strategies degrade both predictive performance and human-centric properties such as fairness and explainability. This paper presents AURORA-AI, an Adaptive Utility-driven Resource Orchestration framework for Resilient AI that unifies Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman feedback control, Lyapunov-based stability monitoring, and a fairness-aware composite utility into a single closed-loop policy.The framework continuously redistributes computational budget across a population of heterogeneous AI models so that the global utility, defined jointly over predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability, remains maximised under disruption. The framework is evaluated in a stress-rich discrete-time simulation that concurrently injects demographic bias shocks, gradual concept drift, and abrupt black-swan disruptions, and is compared against five established controllers including Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, and a deep reinforcement-learning agent based on Proximal Policy Optimisation. AURORA-AI achieves immediate recovery from the black-swan event compared to eighty-eight time steps for the Static baseline and twenty-two for Proximal Policy Optimisation, lifts the alpha-quantile and the super-quantile by twenty-nine and twenty-five percent respectively, simultaneously reduces the mean and maximum demographic parity gap, and increases the fraction of Lyapunov-stable operating steps. These results indicate that fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory is a practical and theoretically motivated path toward resilient human-centric AI deployment.

AI.tldr: AURORA-AI is a closed-loop resource orchestration framework that uses HJB control and Lyapunov stability to maximize a composite utility (performance, fairness, cost, latency, robustness, interpretability) under non-stationary conditions, significantly outperforming static and learning-based baselines in recovery speed, fairness, and stability.
AI.motivation: Modern AI deployments face non-stationary conditions where static resource allocation degrades both predictive performance and human-centric properties (fairness, explainability). Existing controllers lack a unified theoretical framework that simultaneously optimizes multiple objectives under disruption while providing stability guarantees.
AI.method: AURORA-AI integrates Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) feedback control for optimal resource allocation, Lyapunov-based stability monitoring to ensure safe operation, and a fairness-aware composite utility function covering predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability. The framework continuously redistributes computational budget across a heterogeneous model population in a closed loop.
AI.result: Evaluated under stress-rich simulation (demographic bias shocks, concept drift, black-swan disruptions), AURORA-AI recovered from black-swan events immediately vs. 88 steps (Static) and 22 steps (PPO). It improved the alpha-quantile by 29% and super-quantile by 25%, reduced mean and maximum demographic parity gap, and increased the fraction of Lyapunov-stable operating steps. Benchmarks included Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, and PPO-based DRL.
AI.conclusion: Fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory offers a practical, theoretically principled path toward resilient, human-centric AI deployment under diverse disruptions.

title: LMs as Task-Specific Knowledge Bases: An Interpretability Analysis
summary: Language models (LMs) capture large amounts of factual knowledge applicable to a wide range of tasks, motivating the view of their parameters as a knowledge base. An important property of knowledge bases is that different queries for the same fact return consistent results, drawing on a single source of truth. We investigate whether LMs satisfy this property through behavioral and mechanistic analyses. Our results suggest that they encode knowledge in a task-specific manner. Behaviorally, facts acquired on one task frequently fail to co-emerge on others during training. Parameter localization experiments suggest a mechanistic explanation, revealing distinct parameter subsets underlying different tasks for the same fact. Finally, we show that chain-of-thought reasoning draws part of its effectiveness from engaging task-specific parameters beyond those tied to the evaluation task. Our findings suggest that what the model knows and how it is asked are intertwined in parameter space, undermining the "knowledge base" analogy and carrying implications for the reliability and controllability of factual knowledge in LMs.

AI.tldr: LMs do not encode factual knowledge as a unified knowledge base; instead, they store facts in a task-specific manner, meaning the same fact may or may not be retrieved depending on how it is queried, with distinct parameter subsets underlying different tasks.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the prevailing analogy that LM parameters function as a coherent knowledge base with a single source of truth. If true, different queries for the same fact should yield consistent results. The authors investigate whether this consistency property actually holds in LMs.
AI.method: The authors employ a dual approach: (1) behavioral analysis — tracking whether facts acquired during training on one task (e.g., open-domain QA) co-emerge on semantically equivalent but differently formatted tasks (e.g., fill-in-the-blank); and (2) mechanistic analysis — using parameter localization experiments to identify which parameter subsets are causally responsible for factual recall under different task formats, plus analyzing how chain-of-thought reasoning engages task-specific parameters.
AI.result: Behaviorally, facts learned on one task frequently fail to transfer to other tasks during training. Mechanistically, distinct parameter subsets are implicated for the same fact across different task formats. Chain-of-thought reasoning partially derives its effectiveness by recruiting task-specific parameters beyond those used for the final evaluation task.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge in LMs is not stored in a task-agnostic, unified manner. How a model is asked and what it knows are entangled in parameter space, which undermines the knowledge-base analogy and raises concerns about factual reliability and controllability in LMs.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Learning for Parametric Prophet Inequalities
summary: We study learning in prophet inequalities with i.i.d. rewards drawn from an exponential-type parametric family with an unknown parameter $θ$, a class that includes exponential, Pareto, and bounded-support power-family distributions. We first characterize the optimal full-information asymptotic competitive ratio for this family. In the unbounded-support case, the limit is $ {\left(θ/({θ-c_+})\right)^{c_+/θ}}/ {Γ(1-c_+/θ)},$ while in the bounded-support case, the limit is $1$. We then propose a confidence-based dynamic-programming policy for online learning. By exploiting the explicit parametric structure, the policy achieves the same optimal asymptotic competitive ratio using only online observations, without external offline samples. We further derive distribution-specific convergence rates for canonical examples. Finally, numerical experiments on synthetic instances illustrate the performance of our algorithm.

AI.tldr: The paper studies online learning for prophet inequalities where i.i.d. rewards come from an exponential-type parametric family with unknown parameter θ. It characterizes the optimal asymptotic competitive ratio, proposes a confidence-based dynamic programming policy that achieves this ratio using only online observations, derives convergence rates, and validates with numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: Classical prophet inequalities assume known reward distributions, which is unrealistic in practice. This work addresses the online learning setting where the distribution belongs to a known parametric family but the parameter θ is unknown, requiring the decision-maker to simultaneously learn the parameter and make accept/reject decisions to maximize expected reward.
AI.method: The authors first derive the optimal full-information asymptotic competitive ratio for exponential-type families (including exponential, Pareto, and bounded power-law distributions). They then design a confidence-based dynamic programming (CBDP) policy that constructs confidence intervals around the unknown parameter θ from past observations and solves an optimistic dynamic programming problem within the confidence region to determine thresholds. The analysis proves this policy achieves the same asymptotic optimal ratio as the full-information benchmark.
AI.result: For unbounded-support distributions, the optimal asymptotic competitive ratio is (θ/(θ−c₊))^(c₊/θ) / Γ(1−c₊/θ); for bounded-support, the limit is 1. The CBDP policy matches these ratios using only online observations. Distribution-specific convergence rates are derived for canonical examples. Numerical experiments on synthetic data confirm the theoretical findings.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that for exponential-type parametric families, optimal asymptotic prophet inequality performance can be achieved without prior knowledge of the distribution parameter, bridging the gap between full-information and online learning settings. The explicit parametric structure is key to the method's success.

title: How Surprising Is Historical Italian to Language Models? Tokenization Tax, Comprehension Tax, and a Simple Mitigation
comment: The 22nd Conference on Information and Research Science Connecting to Digital and Library Science
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly critical to digital library workflows, yet their ability to process historical language remains poorly understood. Historical difficulty is typically treated as a monolithic barrier, conflating orthographic variation, linguistic distance, and pretraining exposure. In this paper, we propose a diagnostic framework that decomposes this difficulty into four distinct dimensions: tokenization cost, predictive uncertainty (surprisal), semantic robustness, and context sensitivity.
  We evaluate this framework on three datasets spanning three centuries: (1) a newly curated corpus of 17th-century Italian texts (1610-1689) digitized from original page images; (2) canonical 19th-century Italian "I Promessi Sposi" serving as a high-exposure control; and (3) 18th-century Russian civil print books as a contrastive orthographic stress test.
  Our results reveal a distinct dissociation between encoding cost and comprehension. While Russian and early modern Italian incur comparable tokenization penalties (25-30% inflation), their predictive difficulty diverges sharply. 17th-century Italian is on average 2.4 times more surprising than its modern equivalent - with academic prose reaching 3.2 times - whereas Russian shows only a modest increase. But predictive uncertainty does not imply representational degradation: embedding similarity remains robust (> 0.85) across all datasets, confirming that models can represent historical meaning even when generation is unstable.
  Finally, we demonstrate that a minimal temporal context prompt reduces historical surprisal by approximately 60%, offering a simple, model-agnostic mitigation. These findings suggest that while historical text imposes a consistent encoding tax, digital libraries can safely deploy LLMs for semantic retrieval tasks, provided that generative applications are carefully adapted.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a four-dimensional diagnostic framework for evaluating LLM performance on historical texts, revealing that while historical language incurs a consistent "encoding tax" (tokenization cost), semantic representation remains robust. A minimal temporal context prompt significantly reduces predictive uncertainty, guiding safe LLM deployment in digital libraries.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in digital library workflows, but their ability to process historical language is poorly understood. Existing approaches treat historical difficulty as a monolithic barrier, conflating distinct challenges like orthographic variation, linguistic distance, and pretraining exposure. The authors aim to systematically disentangle these factors.
