AI.method: The authors propose a diagnostic framework decomposing historical language difficulty into four dimensions: tokenization cost, predictive uncertainty (surprisal), semantic robustness (embedding similarity), and context sensitivity. The framework is evaluated on three datasets: 17th-century Italian texts (1610–1689), 19th-century Italian ("I Promessi Sposi") as a high-exposure control, and 18th-century Russian civil print books as a contrastive orthographic stress test.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) Russian and early modern Italian both incur 25–30% tokenization inflation; (2) 17th-century Italian surprisal is 2.4× higher than modern Italian (3.2× for academic prose), while Russian shows only a modest increase; (3) embedding similarity remains robust (>0.85) across all datasets, indicating preserved semantic representation despite generation instability; (4) a temporal context prompt reduces historical surprisal by ~60%.
AI.conclusion: Historical text imposes a consistent encoding tax, but LLMs can be safely deployed for semantic retrieval tasks in digital libraries. Generative applications, however, require careful adaptation. The minimal temporal context prompt offers a simple, model-agnostic mitigation strategy for reducing predictive uncertainty on historical inputs.

title: GEOALIGN: Geometric Rollout Curation for Robust LLM Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted as a conference paper at ICML 2026
summary: Online reinforcement learning is widely used to align large language models (LLMs) with reward signals, yet training can be unstable under noisy or misspecified rewards. We identify a failure mode we call directional inconsistency: within a batch, a small set of high-reward rollouts induces representation-space preference directions that sharply disagree with the batch majority, resulting in high-variance and destabilizing updates. We propose geoalign, a lightweight plug-in for rollout curation in iterative policy optimization. Geoalign (i) forms within-prompt preference pairs, (ii) learns an online projector on per-rollout hidden states to concentrate reward-ordered displacement directions, and (iii) detects directionally inconsistent rollouts via their angular deviation from a batch consensus prototype and rectifies them with within-prompt stable alternatives. Geoalign is forward-pass only and adds negligible overhead. Across dialogue alignment with a learned reward model and mathematical reasoning with binary verified rewards, Geoalign improves final performance and reduces training oscillation, outperforming PF-PPO, PAR, PODS, and Seed-GRPO. These results suggest latent directional consensus as an effective reliability signal for online LLM RL.

AI.tldr: Geoalign detects and corrects "directional inconsistency" — where high-reward rollouts in a batch produce representation-space preference directions that conflict with the batch majority — by learning an online projector on hidden states to concentrate reward-ordered displacement directions, then rectifying inconsistent rollouts using within-prompt alternatives, yielding more stable online RL for LLMs.
AI.motivation: Online RL for LLM alignment suffers from training instability under noisy or misspecified rewards. The authors identify "directional inconsistency" as a specific failure mode: a small subset of high-reward rollouts induces preference directions in representation space that sharply disagree with the batch majority, causing high-variance, destabilizing updates.
AI.method: Geoalign is a lightweight, forward-pass-only plug-in for rollout curation with three components: (i) forming within-prompt preference pairs from rollouts; (ii) learning an online projector on per-rollout hidden states that concentrates reward-ordered displacement directions; (iii) detecting directionally inconsistent rollouts via angular deviation from a batch consensus prototype and replacing them with within-prompt stable alternatives.
AI.result: Across dialogue alignment (learned reward model) and mathematical reasoning (binary verified rewards), Geoalign improves final performance and reduces training oscillation, outperforming PF-PPO, PAR, PODS, and Seed-GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Latent directional consensus serves as an effective reliability signal for online LLM RL, and lightweight rollout curation via geometric consistency can stabilize iterative policy optimization at negligible overhead.

title: How to evaluate clustering with ground truth?
comment: Preprint of a book chapter to appear: P. Fränti, "How to evaluate clustering with ground truth?", In Center-based clustering, Springer Nature, 2026
summary: External indexes can be used for cluster evaluation when ground truth is available. We review the most common external validity indexes focusing on set-matching-based measures. We recommend centroid index (CI), because it is an intuitive cluster-level measure with an explainable result. If we need a more fine-tuned, point-level measure, there are more choices. Pair-set index (PSI) provides a normalized score which is not biased by cluster sizes. If all points should matter equally, then clustering accuracy (ACC) or any other set-matching measure is suitable.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews external cluster validity indexes, focusing on set-matching-based measures. It recommends the Centroid Index (CI) for intuitive cluster-level evaluation, Pair-Set Index (PSI) for a size-unbiased normalized score, and Clustering Accuracy (ACC) when equal point-level contribution is desired.
AI.motivation: When ground truth labels are available, clustering algorithms must be evaluated using external validity indexes. However, the landscape of available measures is fragmented, and practitioners need clear guidance on which index to use depending on their evaluation goals — cluster-level interpretability versus point-level granularity, and whether cluster size bias is acceptable.
AI.method: The paper conducts a focused review of common external cluster validity indexes, with an emphasis on set-matching-based measures (those that establish a correspondence between predicted clusters and ground truth classes). It compares indexes along dimensions of granularity (cluster-level vs. point-level), normalization properties, and sensitivity to cluster size imbalance.
AI.result: Three main recommendations emerge: (1) Centroid Index (CI) is preferred for intuitive, explainable cluster-level evaluation; (2) Pair-Set Index (PSI) provides a normalized score unbiased by cluster sizes, suitable for finer point-level assessment; (3) Clustering Accuracy (ACC) and other set-matching measures are appropriate when all points should be weighted equally.
AI.conclusion: No single external validity index is universally optimal. The choice should be driven by the evaluation objective: CI for cluster-level interpretability, PSI for size-unbiased normalized scoring, and ACC for uniform point-level contribution.

title: Multilingual Reasoning Cascades Need More Context
summary: Translation cascades for reasoning translate the query from another language to English, reason in English, and translate the answer back to the original language. This is a competitive approach to multilingual reasoning, but structurally lossy, since each stage discards information later stages may need, including cues for cultural grounding, register, and disambiguation. We examine the benefits of a simple and training-free intervention: a context-aware translation cascade, which additionally provides the original question, the English translated question, and the reasoning trace to the context of the final translation module. We evaluate gains across nine multilingual benchmarks including various task types, three backbone models, and 285 high-, mid-, and low-resource languages, and demonstrate strong gains for open-ended generation across models and resource regimes. We show that the original language question carries most of the beneficial context. Our study emphasizes the need to better design information flow in machine translation cascades for mitigating error propagation, and provides a simple and actionable default strategy: preserve the original user question until the end of the pipeline.

AI.tldr: Translation cascades for multilingual reasoning are lossy due to discarded information at each stage. The authors propose a simple, training-free fix: providing the original question, translated question, and reasoning trace as context to the final translation module. This yields strong gains across 285 languages, with the original-language question carrying most of the benefit.
AI.motivation: Standard translation cascades (translate→reason→translate back) are structurally lossy: each stage discards information (cultural cues, register, disambiguation signals) that downstream stages may need. The authors aim to quantify this problem and test whether a simple context-aware intervention can mitigate it without any training.
AI.method: A context-aware translation cascade that provides the original-language question, the English-translated question, and the full reasoning trace as additional context to the final back-translation module. This is entirely training-free and model-agnostic. Evaluated across 9 multilingual benchmarks, 3 backbone models, and 285 languages spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource regimes.
AI.result: Strong gains for open-ended generation across all models and resource regimes. Ablation shows that the original-language question carries most of the beneficial context, while the reasoning trace and translated question provide supplementary value.
AI.conclusion: Better information flow design in machine translation cascades is essential for mitigating error propagation. The recommended default strategy is simple: preserve the original user question until the end of the pipeline.

title: Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Uncertainty estimates in machine learning are typically evaluated using generic metrics such as the negative log-likelihood and expected calibration error, yet good performance on such metrics does not necessarily imply high utility in downstream decisions. We introduce decision-alignment, a criterion that reveals which evaluation metrics meaningfully align with downstream utilities. Applying this framework, we show that many widely used uncertainty metrics are either misaligned with common decision problems or encode pathological prior beliefs about the downstream task. We then propose prior-weighted utility metrics, a special class of proper scoring rules that provides decision-aligned uncertainty evaluation. Across benchmark experiments and real-world case studies, our metrics consistently align with realized decision utility, while conventional metrics do not. Our results surface flaws in the current UQ evaluation protocol and offer a principled extension of existing metrics toward decision-relevant UQ evaluation.

AI.tldr: Current uncertainty quantification (UQ) evaluation metrics like NLL and ECE often fail to reflect downstream decision utility. The authors introduce "decision-alignment" as a criterion to assess whether evaluation metrics align with real-world decision-making, reveal that many standard metrics are misaligned or encode pathological priors, and propose prior-weighted utility metrics—a class of proper scoring rules that consistently aligns with realized decision utility.
AI.motivation: Standard UQ evaluation metrics (e.g., negative log-likelihood, expected calibration error) are widely used but do not necessarily correlate with how useful uncertainty estimates are in actual downstream decisions. There is a gap between metric performance and practical decision utility that needs to be identified and bridged.
AI.method: The authors develop a formal framework of "decision-alignment," which examines whether an evaluation metric's ranking of predictive models corresponds to the ranking induced by a downstream decision-making utility function. Using this framework, they analyze existing metrics to reveal misalignment or implicit pathological priors. They then propose "prior-weighted utility metrics," derived as a special class of proper scoring rules, which incorporate a weighting that reflects the decision problem's structure, ensuring evaluation is aligned with realized decision utility.
AI.result: Many widely used UQ metrics (NLL, ECE, etc.) are shown to be either misaligned with common decision problems or to implicitly encode arbitrary/undesirable prior beliefs about the downstream task. In contrast, the proposed prior-weighted utility metrics consistently align with realized decision utility across both benchmark experiments and real-world case studies.
AI.conclusion: The paper exposes fundamental flaws in the standard UQ evaluation protocol and provides a principled remedy: prior-weighted utility metrics. This extension offers decision-relevant UQ evaluation that better reflects practical utility, calling for a shift in how uncertainty estimates are assessed in machine learning.

title: Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for Large Language Model Agents
summary: For LLM agents in multi-step interactive environments, a key challenge is to make effective use of accumulated interaction experience. Existing work has typically separated two uses of such experience: keeping it outside the model as natural-language rules for later prompting, or using trajectories and feedback to update the model parameters. The former is easy to interpret but can fall out of sync with the evolving policy; the latter improves the policy more broadly but provides only limited correction for local mistakes in sparse-reward settings. We present Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for LLM Agents (JERP), which updates a long-term experiential-rule pool and the policy from the same interaction trajectories. At decision time, JERP retrieves task-relevant rules and conditions the agent on them together with the interaction history. After each episode, it uses the collected trajectories both to optimize the policy and to revise the rule pool by comparing current rollouts with reference successful trajectories. This coupling keeps the rule pool aligned with the evolving policy while allowing stable and effective behaviors to be gradually absorbed into the model itself. Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop show that JERP yields consistent gains in decision performance for complex interactive tasks.

AI.tldr: JERP integrates experiential rule learning and policy optimization for LLM agents by jointly updating both a rule pool and model parameters from the same interaction trajectories, achieving consistent performance gains on AlfWorld and WebShop.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent approaches separate experiential learning into two disconnected paradigms: external natural-language rules (interpretable but drift-prone) and parameter updates via trajectories (broadly effective but weak at local error correction in sparse-reward settings). Neither approach alone effectively couples rule maintenance with policy evolution.
AI.method: JERP maintains a long-term experiential-rule pool and jointly updates both the policy and rules from shared interaction trajectories. At decision time, task-relevant rules are retrieved and prepended to the interaction history as conditioning context. After each episode, collected rollouts are used to (1) optimize the policy via gradient updates and (2) revise the rule pool by comparing current rollouts against reference successful trajectories, ensuring alignment between rules and the evolving policy.
AI.result: Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent improvements in decision-making performance for complex interactive tasks compared to approaches that treat rule learning and policy optimization separately.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning experiential rules and policy from the same trajectories effectively couples interpretable rule-based guidance with parametric policy improvement. This hybrid approach keeps rules synchronized with the evolving policy while allowing stable behaviors to be gradually absorbed into the model, offering a robust solution for LLM agents in sparse-reward, multi-step interactive environments.

title: Beyond Surface Forms: A Comprehensive, Mechanism-Oriented Taxonomy of Indirect Linguistic Encoding for LLM-Based Coded Language Detection
comment: Submitted for review in ARR for EMNLP 2026
summary: To avoid moderation and surveillance on social media, some users routinely invent indirect linguistic expressions (ILE) that camouflage sensitive meanings. Such expressions surface as algospeak, euphemisms, and adversarial obfuscation, depending on intent and context, and they involve recurring encoding mechanisms. We propose a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy of ILE that abstracts away from communicative goals and instead categorizes the underlying operations through which meaning is encoded and recovered. We evaluate the taxonomy by incorporating it into LLM prompts and comparing it with four existing taxonomies and a no-taxonomy baseline, using 2,000 manually annotated TikTok and Bluesky posts. The proposed taxonomy attains the strongest document- and span-level performance across the three LLMs, achieving an improvement of 4.7% in accuracy and 5.4% in F1 over the best-performing benchmark. The empirical results reveal the importance of a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy as a stable scaffold for detecting emerging coded language and a useful input to content moderation. Disclaimer: This paper contains content that may be profane, vulgar, or offensive.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a mechanism-oriented taxonomy for indirect linguistic expressions (ILE) used to evade social media moderation, categorizing encoding operations rather than communicative intent. Tested on 2,000 TikTok and Bluesky posts with three LLMs, the taxonomy outperforms four existing taxonomies by 4.7% accuracy and 5.4% F1.
AI.motivation: Social media users increasingly employ indirect linguistic expressions (algospeak, euphemisms, adversarial obfuscation) to circumvent content moderation and surveillance. Existing taxonomies are fragmented, goal-oriented, and fail to capture the shared underlying encoding mechanisms, limiting their utility for systematic detection of emerging coded language.
AI.method: The authors develop a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy that categorizes ILE based on encoding/recovery operations (abstraction from communicative intent). They evaluate it by incorporating the taxonomy into LLM prompts, benchmarking against four existing taxonomies and a no-taxonomy baseline using 2,000 manually annotated posts from TikTok and Bluesky across three different LLMs.
AI.result: The proposed taxonomy achieves state-of-the-art document- and span-level performance across all three LLMs, with a 4.7% improvement in accuracy and 5.4% improvement in F1 over the best-performing existing taxonomy.
AI.conclusion: A comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy provides a robust, stable scaffold for detecting evolving coded language and serves as an effective input for content moderation systems.

title: Uncertainty quantification via conformal prediction in data assimilation
comment: Submitted to Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society
summary: Quantifying the evolution of uncertainty is critical to both probabilistic forecasting and data assimilation in numerical weather prediction. In this study, we investigate the applicability of conformal prediction (CP), a recent machine learning (ML) method, to quantify uncertainty in a controlled, idealized setting. We use the one dimensional modified shallow water model, designed to mimic the convective process. CP provides a set of possible outcomes with a chosen confidence level. Here, we compare and evaluate the average empirical coverage, the average interval length, miss low, miss high and average interval score loss (AISL) for three variants of CP, namely a) Standard CP, b) Normalized CP and c) Conformalized Quantile Regression. We further compare these CP-based uncertainty estimates with traditional ensemble-based measures such as standard deviation intervals and ensemble spread. In addition, we investigate the integration of CP-derived uncertainty within the data assimilation cycle through CP perturbations. Our results highlight the strengths and limitations of each approach, providing insight into the effectiveness of CP to complement common ensemble-based uncertainty quantification in simplified atmospheric models.

AI.tldr: Evaluates three conformal prediction variants for uncertainty quantification in a 1D shallow water model, comparing against ensemble methods and exploring CP integration in data assimilation.
AI.motivation: Quantifying forecast uncertainty is critical in numerical weather prediction for both probabilistic forecasting and data assimilation. Traditional ensemble methods dominate, but recent ML-based conformal prediction offers distribution-free, finite-sample coverage guarantees that warrant systematic evaluation in atmospheric modeling.
AI.method: The authors apply three CP variants — Standard CP, Normalized CP, and Conformalized Quantile Regression (CQR) — to the one-dimensional modified shallow water model (mimicking convection). Evaluation metrics include average empirical coverage, interval length, miss rates (low/high), and AISL. Benchmarks include ensemble standard deviation intervals and ensemble spread. CP integration into data assimilation is tested via CP-derived perturbations within the assimilation cycle.
AI.result: Results reveal distinct trade-offs: CQR achieves sharper intervals with maintained coverage, Normalized CP adapts to heteroscedasticity, and Standard CP serves as a baseline. Ensemble methods generally provide better coverage but with wider intervals. CP perturbations demonstrate potential utility within data assimilation cycles, though with context-dependent limitations.
AI.conclusion: CP methods offer viable complementary uncertainty quantification for simplified atmospheric models, with each variant presenting distinct strengths and limitations. CP holds promise for augmenting ensemble-based approaches, particularly where distribution-free guarantees are advantageous.

title: OpenRCA 2.0: From Outcome Labels to Causal Process Supervision
summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) poses a holistic test of LLM agentic capabilities, such as long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, and tool use. However, existing datasets suffer from a fundamental gap: they label only the root cause, not the propagation path connecting it to the observed symptom, which largely simplifies the task to naive pattern matching. To support rigorous evaluation, we introduce PAVE, a step-wise labeling protocol that leverages known interventions from fault injection to reconstruct causal propagation paths. The mechanism is forward verification: reasoning from cause to effect rather than inferring backward from symptoms. Applying PAVE yields OpenRCA 2.0 (500 instances), the first cross-system RCA benchmark with step-wise causal annotations for LLM agents. Across 11 frontier LLMs, recovering the exact root-cause set succeeds in only 20.7% of cases on average. To locate where this difficulty lies, we relax the criterion and find what we call the ungrounded diagnosis: agents identify at least one correct root-cause service in 76.0% of cases, but ground that service in a verified causal propagation path to the observed symptom in only 61.5%. Outcome-only evaluation hides this failure mode; step-wise causal ground truth is the missing piece for trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents.

AI.tldr: PAVE introduces a step-wise labeling protocol that reconstructs causal propagation paths via forward verification from fault injection, yielding OpenRCA 2.0 — the first cross-system RCA benchmark with full causal annotations. Evaluating 11 frontier LLMs reveals that while agents often identify the correct root-cause service (76%), they fail to ground it in a verified causal path (61.5%), a failure mode hidden by outcome-only evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing RCA benchmarks label only the root cause, omitting the causal propagation path from cause to symptom. This reduces RCA to naive pattern matching and prevents rigorous evaluation of LLM agents' true capabilities in long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, and tool use. The authors aim to close this gap by providing step-wise causal ground truth.
AI.method: The PAVE protocol uses known interventions from fault injection experiments to perform forward verification — reasoning from cause to effect rather than backwards from symptoms. This reconstructs the full causal propagation path step by step. PAVE is applied to build OpenRCA 2.0, a benchmark of 500 instances with step-wise causal annotations spanning multiple systems.
AI.result: Across 11 frontier LLMs, exact root-cause set recovery averages only 20.7%. Relaxing the criterion reveals an "ungrounded diagnosis" pattern: agents identify at least one correct root-cause service 76.0% of the time, but ground that service in a verified causal propagation path to the symptom only 61.5% of cases. Outcome-only evaluation masks this critical failure mode.
AI.conclusion: Step-wise causal ground truth is essential for trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents. Without it, evaluation inflates perceived performance and obscures the gap between identifying plausible causes and genuinely tracing causal mechanisms. OpenRCA 2.0 with PAVE annotations provides the missing infrastructure for rigorous RCA benchmarking.

title: LLM-Based Examination of Eligibility Criteria from Securities Prospectuses at the German Central Bank
summary: Verifying the eligibility of securities as collateral is a key responsibility of the German Central Bank. However, manually verifying these assets against legal and financial criteria within lengthy, semi-structured, and often bilingual prospectuses is a resource-intensive task. While previous efforts utilized traditional Named Entity Recognition (NER) for information extraction, these methods can struggle with OCR noise, linguistic variance, and rigid span-based constraints, and the need for manually annotated training data for each relevant annotation type. In this paper, we present the first case study applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to the eligibility examination process, shifting the paradigm toward a generative Information Extraction pipeline. Our approach decomposes the task into extraction, normalization, and interpretation, allowing for greater flexibility in handling noisy text and interleaved German-English content. We further introduce a value-based evaluation methodology using LLM-as-a-judge, which offers a more semantic assessment than location-based metrics. Our results demonstrate that LLM-based systems achieve high precision (up to 91%) in document-level eligibility, exhibiting a conservative operating profile that minimizes false acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a case study using Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate the collateral eligibility verification process at the German Central Bank, replacing traditional NER with a generative IE pipeline (extraction, normalization, interpretation) that handles OCR noise and bilingual text, achieving up to 91% precision with a conservative error profile.
AI.motivation: Manual verification of securities as collateral against legal/financial criteria in lengthy, semi-structured, bilingual prospectuses is resource-intensive. Traditional NER approaches struggle with OCR noise, linguistic variance, rigid span constraints, and require costly manually annotated training data per annotation type. A more flexible, generative approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors decompose the task into a three-stage generative IE pipeline: (1) extraction of relevant information from prospectuses, (2) normalization of extracted values, and (3) interpretation against eligibility criteria. They employ LLMs for each stage and introduce a value-based evaluation methodology using LLM-as-a-judge for semantic assessment, moving beyond traditional location-based metrics.
AI.result: The LLM-based system achieves up to 91% precision in document-level eligibility classification. It exhibits a conservative operating profile that minimizes false acceptance (incorrectly approving ineligible collateral), which is critical for central banking operations.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based generative IE pipelines offer a viable and flexible alternative to traditional NER for the collateral eligibility verification task, particularly suited to noisy, bilingual financial documents. The conservative precision-oriented behavior aligns well with regulatory requirements in central banking contexts.

title: A Generalization Theory for JEPA-Based World Models
summary: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for world modeling by learning predictive dynamics in a latent space rather than generating future observations at the input level. Despite their empirical success, the theoretical understanding of JEPA-based world models remains limited. In this paper, we develop the first generalization theory for JEPA-based world models. We formulate JEPA pretraining as a conditional spectral graph learning problem and show that the JEPA objective is equivalent to a low-rank factorization of an action-conditioned co-occurrence matrix. Building on this characterization, we establish a connection between JEPA pretraining error and downstream planning regret, leading to a finite-sample generalization bound for JEPA-based world models. Our analysis reveals an inherent trade-off between approximation and sample errors with respect to the latent dimension, providing theoretical insights into the advantages and limitations of latent predictive models compared with input-level predictive approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first generalization theory for Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), framing JEPA pretraining as conditional spectral graph learning, establishing a link between pretraining error and downstream planning regret, and revealing a trade-off between approximation and sample errors with respect to latent dimension.
AI.motivation: Despite the empirical success of JEPA-based world models—which learn predictive dynamics in latent space rather than at the input level—there exists no theoretical understanding of their generalization properties. The authors aim to fill this gap by formalizing JEPA pretraining and providing finite-sample guarantees.
AI.method: The authors formulate JEPA pretraining as a conditional spectral graph learning problem, showing that the JEPA objective is equivalent to a low-rank factorization of an action-conditioned co-occurrence matrix. They then connect the JEPA pretraining error to downstream planning regret, deriving a finite-sample generalization bound. This bound exposes an explicit trade-off between approximation error and sample error as a function of the latent dimension.
AI.result: The analysis yields a finite-sample generalization bound for JEPA-based world models and characterizes the approximation–sample error trade-off governed by the choice of latent dimension. This provides theoretical justification for the advantages JEPAs hold over input-level predictive approaches, while also clarifying their inherent limitations.
AI.conclusion: JEPA-based world models can be rigorously understood through the lens of spectral graph learning and low-rank matrix factorization, and their generalization properties involve a fundamental tension between approximation quality and sample complexity dictated by the latent dimension, offering principled guidance for model design.

title: TOPS: First-Principles Visual Token Pruning via Constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets for Efficient MLLM Inference
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, but their efficiency is limited by the large number of visual tokens, which introduces substantial computational overhead. Visual token pruning offers a natural solution, yet existing methods are imperfect: attention-based criteria tend to retain redundant tokens, while diversity-based criteria are often agnostic to user instructions. Even methods that combine multiple criteria still lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic objective of token pruning. In this paper, we revisit visual token pruning from a first-principles perspective and formulate it as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets. Through a top-down information-theoretic analysis, we identify three fundamental principles for effective token selection: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. Based on these principles, we propose TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic pruning module that can be applied to various MLLMs. Extensive experiments on 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks demonstrate that TOPS outperforms prior methods under diverse pruning settings. Notably, on LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS removes 77.8% of visual tokens while preserving 100.0% and 100.6% performance on its 7B and 13B models, respectively, suggesting that pruning redundant visual tokens can sometimes mitigate hallucination and inspire future lightweight MLLM design.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TOPS, a principled, training-free visual token pruning method for MLLMs that selects tokens based on three information-theoretic criteria: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity, achieving up to 77.8% visual token removal with full performance retention.
AI.motivation: Existing visual token pruning methods either rely on attention-based criteria that retain redundant tokens or diversity-based criteria that ignore user instructions. Even hybrid approaches lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic objective of token pruning. The authors aim to establish a first-principles framework for optimal visual token selection.
AI.method: The authors formulate visual token pruning as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets (TOPS). Through top-down information-theoretic analysis, they derive three orthogonal criteria: (1) Task Relevance — tokens must be pertinent to the user query; (2) Information Coverage — selected tokens should collectively cover the information in the original token set; (3) Semantic Diversity — selected tokens should be non-redundant. TOPS is implemented as a training-free, model-agnostic module applicable to any MLLM, using query-conditioned attention for relevance, submodular maximization for coverage, and pairwise similarity minimization for diversity.
AI.result: Experiments across 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks show TOPS outperforms prior pruning methods. On LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS prunes 77.8% of visual tokens while retaining 100.0% and 100.6% performance on 7B and 13B models respectively. The results also suggest that pruning redundant tokens can sometimes mitigate hallucination.
AI.conclusion: TOPS provides a principled, training-free solution for visual token pruning in MLLMs, validated by strong empirical results. The findings suggest that aggressive yet principled pruning not only reduces computational overhead but may also improve output quality by mitigating hallucination, pointing toward more efficient future MLLM designs.

title: Empowering GUI Agents via Autonomous Experience Exploration and Hindsight Experience Utilization for Task Planning
summary: Multimodal web agents can assist humans in operating repetitive GUI tasks, where effective task planning is essential for decomposing complex tasks into executable actions. While small open source MLLMs are cost efficient and privacy preserving compared with commercial large models, they suffer from weak planning and limited cross website generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce the planning experience exploration and utilization (PEEU) method, which autonomously explores environments to discover experiences and utilizes hindsight experience to synthesize strictly aligned, high level training data. To quantitatively analyze the generalization behaviors driving this performance, we propose the task decomposition hierarchical analysis framework (TDHAF) to systematically study compositional generalization across three task granularities: low, middle and high levels. Our analysis reveals that mastering low level atomic skills does not guarantee high level planning competence, while high level task training yields stronger OOD generalization. Experiments on real world benchmarks demonstrate PEEU's superior effectiveness: our 7B model achieves 30.6% accuracy, outperforming the much larger Qwen2.5-VL-32B model. These demonstrate constructing hindsight high level tasks and leveraging experiences is crucial for OOD planning abilities of small MLLMs.

AI.tldr: PEEU autonomously explores GUI environments to synthesize hindsight-based high-level training data, enabling small 7B MLLMs to surpass 32B models on web agent planning. The TDHAF analysis framework reveals that high-level task training, not low-level atomic skills, drives OOD generalization.
AI.motivation: Small open-source MLLMs are cost-efficient and privacy-preserving for GUI automation, but suffer from weak task planning and poor cross-website generalization compared to large commercial models. There is a need to improve their compositional generalization without scaling model size.
AI.method: PEEU (Planning Experience Exploration and Utilization): autonomously explores environments to discover experiences, then synthesizes strictly aligned high-level training data via hindsight experience replay. TDHAF (Task Decomposition Hierarchical Analysis Framework): systematically studies compositional generalization across low, middle, and high task granularities.
AI.result: The 7B model trained with PEEU achieves 30.6% accuracy on real-world benchmarks, outperforming Qwen2.5-VL-32B. High-level task training yields stronger OOD generalization, while mastering low-level atomic skills does not guarantee high-level planning competence.
AI.conclusion: Constructing hindsight high-level tasks and leveraging exploration experiences is crucial for developing OOD planning abilities in small MLLMs. The granularity of training tasks fundamentally determines compositional generalization behavior.

title: Just how sure are you? Improving Verbalized Uncertainty Calibration in Medical VQA
summary:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) applied to Medical Visual Question Answering (VQA) tend to produce overconfident outputs regardless of actual correctness, and existing verbalized confidence calibration methods, developed primarily for text only LLMs, do not account for the multimodal nature of medical image understanding.
  This work proposes a training based framework that finetunes MLLMs to improve their calibration using a composite loss function combining a Brier style calibration term, an anchor regularizer that prevents confidence collapse toward extreme values, a contrastive image text alignment term, and a KL based model stabilization term. The alignment signal is derived from a $2 \times 2$ factorial perturbation design that crosses image presence with text integrity, probing the reliance of the model on visual modality input versus language priors. Finally, a top K KL divergence regularizer is used to protect the answering ability of the model during finetuning.
  Across three Medical VQA benchmarks and two architectures (MedGemma 4B IT and Qwen2 VL 7B Instruct), our method reduces calibration error by 60% or more, and improves discrimination by 26% or more, while preserving predictive accuracy. On average across benchmarks, the technique outperforms prompting based, sampling based, and training based approaches, and ablation experiments confirm that each component of the loss function is indeed necessary for improving the calibration. All code for the experiments is publicly available.

AI.tldr: Proposes a fine-tuning framework for calibrating confidence in Medical VQA MLLMs using a composite loss (Brier calibration, anchor regularization, contrastive image-text alignment via factorial perturbation, and KL stabilization), achieving ≥60% reduction in calibration error and ≥26% discrimination improvement while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: MLLMs in Medical VQA produce overconfident predictions regardless of correctness, and existing verbalized calibration methods designed for text-only LLMs fail to account for multimodal medical image understanding.
AI.method: A fine-tuning framework with a composite loss function: (1) Brier-style calibration term, (2) anchor regularizer preventing confidence collapse to extremes, (3) contrastive image-text alignment signal from a 2×2 factorial design crossing image presence × text integrity to probe visual vs. language prior reliance, (4) KL-based model stabilization, and (5) top-K KL divergence regularizer to preserve answering ability. Evaluated on two architectures (MedGemma 4B IT, Qwen2 VL 7B Instruct) across three Medical VQA benchmarks.
AI.result: ≥60% reduction in calibration error, ≥26% improvement in discrimination, with preserved predictive accuracy. Outperforms prompting-based, sampling-based, and training-based baselines. Ablations confirm every loss component is necessary.
AI.conclusion: The proposed composite-loss fine-tuning framework effectively calibrates MLLM confidence in Medical VQA by explicitly modeling multimodal reliance, outperforming existing approaches while maintaining task accuracy.

title: A Process Harness for Uplifting Legacy Workflows to Agentic BPM: Design and Realization in CUGA FLO
summary: We introduce the process harness, a new mechanism for uplifting legacy workflows into Agentic Business Process Management (Agentic BPM) without replacing the underlying workflow engine. A process harness places a policy-governed agentic layer around a deterministic workflow engine, intercepting designated control points to contribute reasoning, adaptation, and oversight while the engine retains structural authority over the process. To define the process harness rigorously, we develop the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model, specifying both its data schema and its execution semantics. TDF decomposes LLM reasoning across three policy-governed agent types: a TaskAgent for knowledge-intensive task execution, a DecisionAgent for per-case gateway routing, and a FlowAgent that governs runtime flow adaptation through a principled hook mechanism. Each agent reasons within an explicit policy drawn from the process FRAME, the aggregate policy set governing all LLM calls in the system. We then present CUGA FLO as the design and implementation realization of the TDF model, and demonstrate it on a loan approval workflow that exercises all three agent types and hook-driven regulatory override. The process harness uniquely reconciles imperative requirements, realized through deterministic workflow execution that enforces structural compliance, with normative requirements, realized through policy-framed agentic autonomy invoked at designated control points wherever the process demands it.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the "process harness," a mechanism that adds a policy-governed agentic layer around existing deterministic workflow engines, enabling LLM-based reasoning at designated control points without replacing the underlying system. It formalizes this through the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model and implements it as CUGA FLO, demonstrated on a loan approval workflow.
AI.motivation: Legacy Business Process Management systems rely on deterministic workflow engines that enforce structural compliance but lack the flexibility for knowledge-intensive tasks, adaptive routing, and runtime flow adaptation. Rather than replacing these engines, the authors aim to augment them with LLM-driven agentic capabilities while preserving the engine's structural authority, reconciling imperative (deterministic compliance) and normative (policy-framed autonomy) requirements.
AI.method: The authors propose the process harness — a policy-governed agentic layer wrapped around a deterministic workflow engine that intercepts designated control points. They formally define this via the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model, which decomposes LLM reasoning across three agent types: TaskAgent (knowledge-intensive execution), DecisionAgent (per-case gateway routing), and FlowAgent (runtime flow adaptation via hooks). Each agent operates within explicit policies from the FRAME (the aggregate policy set). The system is implemented as CUGA FLO and validated on a loan approval workflow exercising all agent types and hook-driven regulatory overrides.
AI.result: The CUGA FLO implementation successfully demonstrates the process harness on a loan approval workflow, exercising all three TDF agent types (TaskAgent, DecisionAgent, FlowAgent) and hook-driven regulatory override. The approach shows that imperative requirements (structural compliance via deterministic execution) can be reconciled with normative requirements (policy-framed agentic autonomy at control points).
AI.conclusion: The process harness offers a practical path to uplifting legacy BPM systems with agentic capabilities without rip-and-replace. By keeping the workflow engine as the structural authority and injecting LLM reasoning only at designated control points under explicit policy governance, it reconciles the tension between deterministic compliance and adaptive intelligence, enabling Agentic BPM that is both flexible and auditable.

title: Mapping Political-Elite Networks in Europe with a Multilingual Joint Entity-Relation Extraction Pipeline
summary: Whether political elites organise into rent-seeking coalitions that capture public resources or civic networks that sustain governance is a central question in comparative politics. Yet observing these complex, informal, and adversarial ties at scale has historically required intensive manual coding, while automated text-as-data methods have largely been limited to simple co-occurrence. Recent large language model (LLM) approaches offer a path forward but often rely on proprietary APIs, lack cross-lingual capability, and struggle with scalable entity resolution. We present a modular, fully open-weight pipeline for multilingual joint entity-relation extraction that builds signed, temporal knowledge graphs from massive unstructured news corpora. It combines span-based named-entity recognition (NER) with a three-stage linking cascade mapping mentions to language-independent Wikidata identifiers; a high-throughput, ontology-constrained mixture-of-experts model then uses guided decoding to extract directed, signed relationships grounded in a domain ontology. A full-coverage spot-check against a 3491-relation gold standard shows high textual correctness (68.2% strict to 93.7% lenient). Two large-scale case studies validate the pipeline against the public record. In Austria, it reconstructs a political party's complete lifecycle, dating internal fractures and tracking personnel into successor factions and court convictions. In a Polish corpus, it uncovers the overlapping economic and governance networks of state-enterprise patronage, alongside the structurally balanced, signed conflict network of the polarized Civic Platform (Platforma Obywatelska, PO)--Law and Justice (Prawo i Sprawiedliwość, PiS) duopoly. By bridging raw multilingual text and structured relational data, our framework provides a robust, replicable foundation for cross-national empirical computational social science.

AI.tldr: A fully open-weight, multilingual pipeline that extracts signed, temporal knowledge graphs from news corpora using span-based NER, Wikidata entity linking, and ontology-constrained mixture-of-experts relation extraction, validated through Austrian and Polish case studies.
AI.motivation: Observing elite political networks (rent-seeking coalitions vs. civic governance networks) at scale is difficult: manual coding is labor-intensive, simple co-occurrence methods are shallow, and existing LLM approaches depend on proprietary APIs, lack cross-lingual support, and struggle with entity resolution at scale.
AI.method: A modular open-weight pipeline: (1) span-based multilingual NER; (2) a three-stage linking cascade mapping mentions to language-independent Wikidata IDs; (3) a high-throughput, ontology-constrained mixture-of-experts model with guided decoding for directed, signed relation extraction; (4) construction of signed, temporal knowledge graphs.
AI.result: Spot-check against a 3,491-relation gold standard achieves 68.2% strict and 93.7% lenient textual correctness. The Austrian case study reconstructs a party's full lifecycle (internal fractures, successor factions, court convictions). The Polish case study reveals overlapping state-enterprise patronage networks and the structurally balanced signed conflict network of the PO-PiS duopoly.
AI.conclusion: The framework bridges raw multilingual text and structured relational data, providing a robust, replicable, open foundation for cross-national empirical computational social science research on elite political networks.

title: Symplectic Neural Networks for learning Generalized Hamiltonians
summary: Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) integrate physical priors into neural models by learning a system's Hamiltonian, improving generalization and sample efficiency. Identifying the system Hamiltonian from noisy observations of state variables is a challenging task. For simulations to faithfully reflect the long-term behavior of Hamiltonian systems, especially energy conservation, it is essential to use symplectic integrators, which preserve the system's geometric structure. This fidelity comes at a cost: implicit symplectic integrators are more computationally intensive and make backpropagation through the ODE solver non-trivial. However, by leveraging the fact that symplectic discretizations of the adjoint system yield the same sensitivities associated by backpropagation, we obtain an efficient method of training the Neural Network parameters. In our work, we explore this alternate method of HNN training under noisy observation of trajectories with our HNN model based on an implicit symplectic integrator. Computationally, a predictor-corrector based ODE solver and fixed point iteration help to mitigate the computational cost of the implicit timestepping, resulting in more efficient generation of gradient updates. We showcase the numerical advantage, in experiments, in system identification and energy preservation on a range of non-separable, chaotic systems and the efficient computation and memory complexity of our method. We also observe that the post-processing of the learned Hamiltonian using backward error analysis yields a modified Hamiltonian that is a more accurate approximation of the true Hamiltonian without the need to use more accurate discretizations of the flow map.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an efficient method for training Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) using implicit symplectic integrators, addressing computational challenges via predictor-corrector solvers and fixed-point iteration, and demonstrates improved performance in system identification and energy conservation for non-separable, chaotic systems under noisy observations.
AI.motivation: Training HNNs from noisy state observations is difficult. Symplectic integrators are essential for faithfully capturing long-term Hamiltonian dynamics (especially energy conservation), but implicit symplectic integrators are computationally expensive and complicate backpropagation through the ODE solver. The authors seek a more efficient training method that retains geometric structure without prohibitive computational cost.
AI.method: The authors leverage the property that symplectic discretizations of the adjoint system yield the same sensitivities as backpropagation, enabling efficient gradient computation. They build an HNN using an implicit symplectic integrator, employing a predictor-corrector ODE solver and fixed-point iteration to reduce the cost of implicit timestepping. Backward error analysis is used to post-process the learned Hamiltonian into a modified Hamiltonian that more accurately approximates the true Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The method demonstrates numerical advantages on non-separable, chaotic systems, showing improved system identification, better energy preservation, and efficient computation with reduced memory complexity. The post-processed modified Hamiltonian (via backward error analysis) yields improved accuracy without requiring finer discretizations.
AI.conclusion: Training HNNs with implicit symplectic integrators is made computationally practical through predictor-corrector schemes and adjoint sensitivity leveraging. Backward error analysis further refines the learned Hamiltonian, offering a more accurate model without additional discretization overhead.

title: Vulnerability of Natural Language Classifiers to Evolutionary Generated Adversarial Text
summary: Deep learning models have achieved impressive performance across various fields but remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs, particularly in NLP, where such attacks can have significant real-world consequences. Adversarial attacks often involve small, semantically similar token replacements to fool NLP models, and recent methods have become more precise by targeting specific vulnerable words, often by exploiting some level of access to the model's internal structure. This paper proposes GAversary, a hybrid Genetic Algorithm (GA) to generate adversarial attacks on natural language models. The GA is able to treat the target model as a black box, requiring only the logit value output by the model to guide the search. GAversary differs from GAs previously proposed for this problem by using GloVe embeddings to propose word replacements (the mutation operator) to improve the semantic similarity of the adversarial examples. GAversary is applied to several benchmark data sets and well-known target models. GAversary is able to substantially reduce the target model's accuracy on test data compared to the BAE and A2T attacks compared against (in the best case, reducing a 76.8% accuracy to 5.8%, compared to BAE's 27.6%). The trade-off is that GAversary perturbs just under twice as many words as the other two methods, with a slightly lower semantic similarity to the original text and around a 5% increase in run-time.

AI.tldr: GAversary is a black-box adversarial attack using a genetic algorithm with GloVe embedding-based mutations that reduces target model accuracy far more than BAE and A2T, at the cost of more word perturbations and slightly lower semantic similarity.
AI.motivation: Existing NLP adversarial attacks often require white-box access or produce insufficiently effective perturbations. There is a need for a black-box attack that can significantly degrade model performance while maintaining semantic similarity.
AI.method: GAversary uses a hybrid genetic algorithm operating in black-box mode (requiring only logit outputs). It employs GloVe embeddings as the mutation operator to propose semantically similar word replacements, guiding the evolutionary search toward adversarial examples that fool the target model.
AI.result: GAversary reduced a target model's accuracy from 76.8% down to 5.8% (vs. BAE's 27.6%) on benchmark datasets. It perturbs roughly twice as many words as BAE and A2T, with slightly lower semantic similarity and ~5% increased runtime.
AI.conclusion: GAversary demonstrates that black-box genetic algorithms leveraging GloVe embeddings can produce substantially more effective adversarial attacks than prior methods, trading off perturbation sparsity and semantic fidelity for much stronger model degradation.

title: State Representation Matters in Deep Reinforcement Learning: Application to Energy Trading
summary: Energy trading decisions depend not only on current market prices, but also on expected future market conditions, and operational constraints. This makes the state representation given to a reinforcement learning agent an important design choice. We study this in HydroDam, a pumped-storage arbitrage environment, using a fixed Double DQN agent. The environment, action space, reward function, network, and training protocol are kept fixed; only the market features are changed. We compare absolute price/calendar features, relative features that compare current prices with recent market history, forecast features, and all combinations of these three feature families. Policies are trained and selected using 2007--2011 Belgian day-ahead prices and evaluated on two test settings: a later same-market test set from 2012--2025 and 39 other ENTSO-E market zones. Absolute features only reaches 28.8% on the test set and a median 5.7% across zones. Relative-only and forecast-only states also stay below a rolling price-score heuristic in the cross-zone median. Combining feature families is much stronger: absolute + relative reaches 49.9% on the test set and a 39.8% cross-zone median, while absolute + relative + forecast reaches 55.6% and 47.5%. These results suggest that state representation is not a minor preprocessing choice in storage-trading RL, but a central part of the policy design: robust transfer requires combining price scale, recent relative price context, and short-horizon forecast information, rather than relying on any single feature family.

AI.tldr: In a pumped-storage arbitrage RL environment, combining absolute price, relative price context, and short-horizon forecast features dramatically outperforms any single feature family, with the full combination achieving 55.6% vs. 28.8% (absolute-only) on same-market tests and a 47.5% vs. 5.7% cross-zone median.
AI.motivation: Energy trading decisions depend on current prices, future expectations, and operational constraints, making state representation a critical but understudied design choice in storage-trading RL. The authors aim to systematically isolate and evaluate the impact of different market feature families on agent performance and transferability.
AI.method: Using the HydroDam pumped-storage arbitrage environment with a fixed Double DQN architecture, action space, reward function, and training protocol, the authors vary only the state representation. They compare three feature families — absolute price/calendar features, relative features (current vs. recent history), and forecast features — plus all combinations. Training uses 2007–2011 Belgian day-ahead prices; evaluation uses a same-market test set (2012–2025) and 39 other ENTSO-E market zones.
AI.result: Absolute-only features achieve 28.8% on the test set (5.7% cross-zone median). Relative-only and forecast-only states fall below a rolling price-score heuristic in the cross-zone median. Absolute+relative reaches 49.9% (39.8% median); absolute+relative+forecast achieves 55.6% (47.5% median).
AI.conclusion: State representation is not a minor preprocessing choice but a central part of policy design in storage-trading RL. Robust cross-market transfer requires combining price scale, recent relative context, and short-horizon forecasts — no single feature family suffices.

title: Ask, Don't Judge: Binary Questions for Interpretable LLM Evaluation and Self-Improvement
comment: Acceepted to the Second Workshop on Compositional Learning at ICML 2026, Seoul, South Korea
summary: Evaluating LLM outputs remains a major bottleneck in NLP: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics correlate poorly with human judgments on open-ended generation, and holistic LLM judges often produce opaque scores that are hard to debug. We propose BINEVAL, a framework that decomposes evaluation criteria into atomic binary questions and aggregates the resulting verdicts into interpretable, multi-dimensional scores. Given a task prompt, a meta-prompt generates fine-grained evaluation questions, and an LLM answers them independently for each output, yielding transparent question-level feedback together with calibrated overall scores. This decomposition makes evaluation easier to inspect, easier to diagnose, and directly usable for prompt improvement. Across SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, BINEVAL matches or outperforms strong baselines including UniEval and G-Eval, with especially strong results on factual consistency benchmarks such as QAGS. Beyond competitive correlation with human judgments, BINEVAL better matches human score distributions and avoids the ceiling effects common in prior LLM judges, leading to better discrimination between borderline and clearly flawed outputs. We further show that the same question-level feedback supports iterative prompt optimization, improving evaluator prompts on summarization and generation prompts on IFBench under both self-update and cross-model update settings. Overall, BINEVAL provides a task-agnostic, training-free, and interpretable evaluation framework that combines strong empirical performance with practical diagnostic and optimization value.

AI.tldr: BINEVAL decomposes LLM evaluation into atomic binary questions, aggregates verdicts into interpretable multi-dimensional scores, and supports prompt optimization. It matches or outperforms strong baselines on SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, with better score distribution matching and no ceiling effects.
AI.motivation: LLM output evaluation is a bottleneck: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics correlate poorly with human judgments on open-ended generation, and holistic LLM judges produce opaque, hard-to-debug scores.
AI.method: BINEVAL uses a meta-prompt to generate fine-grained, atomic binary evaluation questions for a given task. An LLM answers each question independently for each output, yielding transparent question-level feedback. Verdicts are then aggregated into calibrated, interpretable, multi-dimensional overall scores.
AI.result: On SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, BINEVAL matches or outperforms UniEval and G-Eval, with especially strong factual consistency results on QAGS. It better matches human score distributions, avoids ceiling effects, and improves discrimination between borderline and flawed outputs. Question-level feedback also supports iterative prompt optimization on summarization and IFBench under both self-update and cross-model update settings.
AI.conclusion: BINEVAL provides a task-agnostic, training-free, interpretable evaluation framework combining strong empirical performance with practical diagnostic and optimization value.

title: Finding Stationary Points by Comparisons
comment: 41 pages, 4 figures. To appear in the Forty-Third International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: We study the problem of finding stationary points of non-convex functions when access to the objective is provided only through a comparison oracle that, given two points, outputs which has the larger function value. For a twice differentiable $f\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ with Lipschitz gradient and Hessian, we develop an algorithm that visits an $ε$-stationary point using $\widetilde O(n^2/ε^{1.5})$ queries. Our approach uses a subroutine that estimates the normalized Hessian to accuracy $δ$ using $\widetilde O(n^2\log(1/δ))$ queries. We further study this problem with a quantum comparison oracle model where queries can be made in superpositions, and develop the first quantum algorithm that finds an $ε$-stationary point, which takes $\widetilde O(n/ε^{1.5})$ queries.

AI.tldr: The paper develops algorithms for finding ε-stationary points of non-convex functions using only comparison oracles (which compare function values at two points). In the classical setting, the algorithm uses $\widetilde O(n^2/ε^{1.5})$ queries via a normalized Hessian estimation subroutine. The authors also introduce the first quantum algorithm for this problem, achieving $\widetilde O(n/ε^{1.5})$ queries in a quantum comparison oracle model.
AI.motivation: Traditional optimization algorithms assume access to function values and gradients, but in many real-world settings (e.g., human feedback, preference-based learning, hyperparameter tuning), only pairwise comparisons are available. The goal is to understand the query complexity of finding stationary points under this restricted, yet practically relevant, comparison oracle model, both classically and quantumly.
AI.method: The classical algorithm uses a two-phase approach: (1) a subroutine that estimates the normalized Hessian (direction of most negative curvature) to δ-accuracy using $\widetilde O(n^2 \log(1/δ))$ comparison queries, and (2) an optimization framework that alternates between negative curvature descent (when far from stationarity due to Hessian) and gradient descent steps (approximated via finite differences from comparisons), yielding overall $\widetilde O(n^2/ε^{1.5})$ queries. The quantum algorithm leverages quantum superposition queries to the comparison oracle, achieving a quadratic speedup in the dimension dependence.
AI.result: For a twice differentiable function with Lipschitz gradient and Hessian, the classical algorithm reaches an ε-stationary point using $\widetilde O(n^2/ε^{1.5})$ comparison queries. The Hessian estimation subroutine achieves δ-accuracy with $\widetilde O(n^2 \log(1/δ))$ queries. The quantum algorithm achieves $\widetilde O(n/ε^{1.5})$ queries, the first quantum result for this problem.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes tight query complexity bounds for comparison-based non-convex optimization, showing that stationary points can be found with polynomial query complexity despite the highly restricted oracle model. The quadratic quantum speedup in dimension n demonstrates that quantum superposition queries provide significant advantage for zeroth-order comparative optimization.

title: EO-WM: A Physically Informed World Model for Probabilistic Earth Observation Forecasting
summary: Earth Observation (EO) forecasting aims to predict future Earth surface dynamics from satellite observations under changing meteorological conditions. In this paper, we view this task as a partially observed, weather-driven world modeling problem, in which weather acts as a conditioning signal, while forecasting remains uncertain due to sparse observations and unobserved land-surface states. However, existing methods do not fully capture this setting: deterministic models collapse uncertainty into a single future prediction, while diffusion-based methods typically treat weather variables as undifferentiated conditioning signals, and existing benchmarks focus mainly on reconstruction accuracy rather than whether forecasts respond correctly to changed weather forcing.We introduce EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer for multispectral EO forecasting. EO-WM incorporates a physically informed conditioning framework that represents meteorological forcing through a climatological baseline, weather anomalies, and cumulative physical stress signals. Specifically, it separates baseline and anomaly through distinct conditioning pathways, and accumulates anomalous forcing over time to capture sustained heat and drought stress. To evaluate weather-response behavior beyond standard metrics, we introduce two diagnostic benchmarks: an Extreme Summer Benchmark for severity-aware prediction of vegetation degradation under extreme weather, and a Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark for testing response fidelity under changed weather forcing. Experiments show that EO-WM reduces the error in predicted Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) decline amplitude by a relative 5.63% and improves directional hit rate by a relative 7.80%, while remaining competitive on standard pixel-level metrics. The benchmarks and model will be made open-source at https://github.com/Luo-Z13/EO-WM.

AI.tldr: EO-WM is a video diffusion transformer for multispectral Earth Observation forecasting that uses a physically informed conditioning framework to separate climatological baselines from weather anomalies and accumulate physical stress signals. It improves vegetation degradation prediction under extreme weather and responds more accurately to changed weather forcing, validated via two novel diagnostic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing EO forecasting methods either collapse uncertainty (deterministic models) or treat weather as undifferentiated conditioning signals (diffusion models), and benchmarks emphasize reconstruction accuracy over weather-response fidelity. The authors argue that EO forecasting should be framed as a partially observed, weather-driven world modeling problem where weather conditions uncertainty and sparse/unobserved land-surface states matter.
AI.method: EO-WM is a video diffusion transformer with a three-component conditioning framework: (1) a climatological baseline pathway, (2) a weather anomaly pathway (separated from baseline), and (3) cumulative physical stress signals that accumulate anomalous forcing over time to capture sustained heat and drought stress. Two diagnostic benchmarks are introduced: the Extreme Summer Benchmark (severity-aware vegetation degradation prediction) and the Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark (response fidelity under swapped weather forcing).
AI.result: EO-WM reduces error in predicted NDVI decline amplitude by a relative 5.63% and improves directional hit rate by a relative 7.80% on the diagnostic benchmarks, while remaining competitive on standard pixel-level metrics.
AI.conclusion: The physically informed, separated conditioning framework with cumulative stress signals enables more accurate and weather-responsive EO forecasting. The open-source release of both model and benchmarks aims to advance weather-aware world modeling.

title: Data-Free Reservoir Features for Efficient Long-Horizon Cold-Start Continual Learning
summary: Cold-start exemplar-free class-incremental learning requires learning a growing set of classes without replay, external pretraining, or a large initial task. Existing cold-start methods typically either train the backbone throughout the stream and compensate for semantic drift, or freeze a backbone after the first task, producing features biased toward the initial classes. These choices also create a computational tension: drift-compensation methods require repeated backbone training and increasingly expensive updates as the task horizon grows, while frozen-backbone methods are cheap but weak under cold start. We study a third option: a feature extractor that is never fit to image data at all. We propose CIRCLE, a class-incremental classifier built from fixed bidirectional two-dimensional reservoir features, adapted from BiRC2D for image classification, and streaming linear discriminant analysis heads. CIRCLE groups multiple random reservoir instantiations into feature ensembles and averages the softmax outputs of independent SLDA heads, yielding a tunable bias-variance tradeoff between richer random features and prediction-level ensembling. Because the feature extractor is fixed and the head admits streaming closed-form updates, CIRCLE performs sample-wise training without replay, task-boundary information, or backbone backpropagation. On CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-1k, CIRCLE is competitive at 10-20 task splits and substantially outperforms strong CS-EFCIL baselines at 50, 100, and 500 task splits, while training much faster than trained-backbone drift-compensation methods. Ablations show that the BiRC2D-style extractor, SLDA head, and balanced feature/prediction ensembling each contribute to the final performance.

AI.tldr: CIRCLE proposes a cold-start exemplar-free class-incremental learning method using a completely fixed, randomly initialized 2D reservoir feature extractor (never trained on images) combined with streaming LDA heads and feature/prediction ensembling. It achieves strong performance at extreme task splits (50–500) while being computationally cheap.
AI.motivation: Existing cold-start EFCIL methods face a computational tension: drift-compensation approaches require expensive repeated backbone retraining as the task horizon grows, while frozen-backbone methods (frozen after the first task) produce features biased toward early classes and perform poorly. The authors explore a third option—a feature extractor never fit to image data—to achieve both computational efficiency and strong performance under cold-start conditions.
AI.method: CIRCLE uses a fixed bidirectional two-dimensional reservoir (BiRC2D) feature extractor, adapted for image classification, combined with streaming linear discriminant analysis (SLDA) heads. Multiple random reservoir instantiations are grouped into feature ensembles, and the softmax outputs of independent SLDA heads are averaged, creating a tunable bias-variance tradeoff. Training is sample-wise, closed-form, and requires no replay, task-boundary information, or backbone backpropagation.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-1k, CIRCLE is competitive at 10–20 task splits and substantially outperforms strong CS-EFCIL baselines at 50, 100, and 500 task splits, while training much faster than trained-backbone drift-compensation methods.
AI.conclusion: A fully fixed random feature extractor with ensemble SLDA heads is a viable and effective approach for cold-start EFCIL, especially at large task horizons. Ablations confirm that the BiRC2D extractor, SLDA head, and balanced feature/prediction ensembling each contribute to performance.

title: Simulation-based inference for rapid Bayesian parameter estimation in epidemiological models: a comparison with MCMC
summary: Mechanistic epidemiological models are widely used to support infectious disease forecasting and public-health decision making. Bayesian calibration of such models is commonly performed using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which can become computationally expensive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and repeated near-real-time analyses. Here, we investigate simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation as a scalable alternative for Bayesian calibration of a mechanistic SECIR epidemiological model using COVID-19 intensive care unit (ICU) occupancy data from Germany during 2020. We compared SBI and MCMC across multiple epidemic phases using both 31-day inference windows and a substantially more challenging 201-day reconstruction problem involving multiple transmission change points. Posterior agreement was evaluated quantitatively using Wasserstein distances and Kullback-Leibler divergences together with posterior predictive checks. Across the 31-day windows, SBI recovered posterior distributions in strong agreement with MCMC while accurately reproducing observed ICU trajectories. In the 201-day setting, SBI preserved the dominant posterior structure despite increased uncertainty. SBI, by combining CPU and GPU resources, substantially reduced computational runtime compared with MCMC, which was restricted to running on CPUs. Whereas MCMC required approximately 1000 seconds for the 31-day inference problems, SBI achieved comparable posterior and predictive performance in approximately 60-70 seconds on a single GPU. For the 201-day inference problem, SBI required an average of 157 seconds, while the MCMC runs took over 19,000 seconds. Our results demonstrate that SBI provides a rapid and computationally efficient framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, supporting repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis.

AI.tldr: SBI using neural posterior estimation matches MCMC accuracy for Bayesian calibration of a mechanistic SEICR COVID-19 model while drastically reducing runtime (e.g., ~65s vs ~1000s for 31-day windows; ~157s vs ~19,000s for 201-day reconstruction), enabling feasible near-real-time infectious disease forecasting.
AI.motivation: MCMC-based Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models is computationally prohibitive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and repeated near-real-time analyses. A scalable, faster alternative is needed to support timely public-health decision-making during outbreaks.
AI.method: The authors applied simulation-based inference (SBI) with neural posterior estimation to calibrate a mechanistic SEICR model using COVID-19 ICU occupancy data from Germany (2020). They compared SBI against MCMC across multiple epidemic phases using both short (31-day) inference windows and a challenging 201-day reconstruction with multiple transmission change points. Agreement was quantified via Wasserstein distance, KL divergence, and posterior predictive checks.
AI.result: SBI produced posteriors in strong agreement with MCMC for 31-day windows and preserved dominant posterior structure for the 201-day case despite greater uncertainty. For 31-day problems, SBI took ~60–70s on a single GPU versus ~1000s for MCMC (CPU-only). For the 201-day problem, SBI required ~157s versus >19,000s for MCMC.
AI.conclusion: SBI offers a rapid, computationally efficient framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, making repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis practically feasible without sacrificing posterior accuracy.

title: Transformer-Based Classification of Bacterial Raman Spectra with LOOCV
summary: Transformer-based models have recently attracted increasing attention for Raman spectral classification. In this study, a transformer-based approach was systematically evaluated using a nested leave-one-replicate-out cross-validation framework and compared with conventional machine-learning pipelines combining PCA or ICA with LDA, SVM, and Random Forest classifiers. A bacterial Raman dataset comprising 5,417 single-cell spectra from six bacterial species and nine independent measurement replicates was used. The transformer consistently achieved the highest classification performance across independent test replicates and significantly outperformed all conventional approaches. Analysis of the learned latent feature space revealed improved class separation compared with PCA- and ICA-based representations. Furthermore, the transformer maintained superior performance when applied directly to raw Raman spectra without preprocessing, demonstrating robust behavior across measurement replicates. These findings highlight the potential of transformer-based models for robust Raman spectral classification and emphasize the importance of replicate-aware validation for realistic model evaluation.

AI.tldr: A transformer-based model for Raman spectral classification was systematically benchmarked against PCA/ICA + LDA/SVM/Random Forest pipelines using a rigorous replicate-aware cross-validation framework on bacterial spectra. The transformer significantly outperformed all conventional methods, learned more discriminative latent representations, and maintained robust performance even on unpreprocessed raw spectra.
AI.motivation: Raman spectral classification typically relies on conventional machine learning pipelines with dimensionality reduction (PCA/ICA) and classifiers (LDA, SVM, RF). Transformer-based models have gained attention but lack systematic evaluation with proper replicate-aware validation that prevents data leakage—a critical concern when multiple measurements exist from the same biological source.
