AI.method: A transformer-based classification model was evaluated on a bacterial Raman dataset (5,417 single-cell spectra, 6 species, 9 independent measurement replicates). Nested leave-one-replicate-out cross-validation ensured that all spectra from a given replicate were held out together during testing. Conventional pipelines combining PCA or ICA with LDA, SVM, and Random Forest served as baselines. Both preprocessed and raw spectra were used to assess robustness.
AI.result: The transformer consistently achieved the highest classification accuracy across all independent test replicates, significantly outperforming all conventional combinations (PCA/ICA + LDA/SVM/RF). Latent space analysis showed superior class separation compared to PCA and ICA representations. The transformer also maintained strong performance on raw, unpreprocessed spectra, demonstrating robustness to replicate-to-replicate variation.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based architectures offer substantial promise for robust Raman spectral classification, outperforming conventional pipelines while eliminating the need for separate dimensionality reduction and preprocessing steps. The study underscores that replicate-aware validation is essential for realistic, generalizable model evaluation in spectroscopic applications.

title: Prompt Injection in Automated Résumé Screening with Large Language Models: Single and Multi-Injection Settings
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to screen and rank job applicants, creating incentives for candidates to strategically manipulate algorithmic hiring systems. We study prompt injection in automated résumé screening, defined as subtle self-promotional text that introduces no new qualifications but is designed to influence LLM evaluations. Using controlled experiments, we show that prompt injection reliably improves applicant rankings when résumé quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject. However, its effectiveness rapidly diminishes as more candidates inject, collapsing when manipulation becomes widespread. When candidate quality is heterogeneous, prompt injection is less effective on average, but can occasionally allow lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones, raising fairness concerns. Overall, LLM-based screening is most vulnerable when manipulation is rare and candidate quality differences are small. Code and resources are publicly available at: https://github.com/preetb1199/Prompt_Injection_ACL26

AI.tldr: Prompt injection in LLM-based résumé screening boosts rankings when manipulation is rare and candidates are similarly qualified, but its effectiveness collapses under widespread use and is less reliable when candidate quality varies, raising fairness concerns.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed for automated hiring, candidates have incentives to strategically manipulate these systems. Understanding the effectiveness and limits of prompt injection—subtle self-promotional text that adds no real qualifications—is critical for assessing the robustness and fairness of LLM-based screening.
AI.method: Controlled experiments simulating LLM-based résumé screening under two conditions: (1) homogeneous candidate quality, varying the proportion of candidates using prompt injection; (2) heterogeneous candidate quality, testing whether prompt injection can cause lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones.
AI.result: Prompt injection reliably improves rankings when résumé quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject, but effectiveness collapses as injection becomes widespread. Under heterogeneous quality, injection is less effective on average but can occasionally enable lower-quality candidates to surpass higher-quality ones, raising fairness issues.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based screening is most vulnerable to prompt injection when manipulation is rare and candidate quality differences are small. The findings highlight both the fragility of LLM evaluators under sparse attacks and the fairness risks when injection distorts merit-based rankings.

title: Heavy-Ball Q-Learning with Residual Weighting Correction
summary: This paper proposes a corrected heavy-ball Q-learning method for reinforcement learning (RL) and establishes its convergence. It also identifies conditions under which the method is theoretically guaranteed to converge faster than standard Q-learning. The same construction is then extended to Q-learning with linear function approximation, where analogous convergence and acceleration statements are derived. The analysis is based on a switched linear system (SLS) representation of Q-learning algorithms and on the joint spectral radius (JSR) of the associated switching families. This SLS viewpoint is not commonly used in standard analyses of Q-learning, and it provides a complementary framework and new insight into how heavy-ball momentum can accelerate Q-learning.

AI.tldr: Proposes a heavy-ball momentum variant of Q-learning with convergence guarantees and provable acceleration over standard Q-learning, extended to linear function approximation, analyzed via switched linear systems and joint spectral radius.
AI.motivation: Standard Q-learning can suffer from slow convergence. Heavy-ball momentum has proven effective for acceleration in optimization, but its theoretical underpinnings for reinforcement learning—particularly convergence and acceleration guarantees—remain underexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a rigorous analysis of momentum-accelerated Q-learning.
AI.method: The authors propose a corrected heavy-ball Q-learning algorithm. The analysis employs a switched linear system (SLS) representation of the Q-learning updates, departing from conventional stochastic approximation or ODE-based analyses. Convergence and acceleration are characterized via the joint spectral radius (JSR) of the associated switching families, establishing conditions under which the JSR of the momentum-augmented system is strictly smaller than that of standard Q-learning. The framework is extended to linear function approximation.
AI.result: Convergence of the corrected heavy-ball Q-learning method is established. Theoretical conditions are identified under which the proposed method provably converges faster than standard Q-learning. Analogous convergence and acceleration results are extended to the linear function approximation setting.
AI.conclusion: The SLS/JSR framework offers a complementary and insightful lens for analyzing momentum in Q-learning, distinct from traditional approaches. The corrected heavy-ball method provides theoretically grounded acceleration for both tabular and linear function approximation settings.

title: When Does Combining Language Models Help? A Co-Failure Ceiling on Routing, Voting, and Mixture-of-Agents Across 67 Frontier Models
summary:
Multi-model LLM systems such as routing, voting, cascades, fusion, and mixture-of-agents are used to beat single-model accuracy. We show that their gain is capped by a quantity the field rarely reports. For any policy whose output is one member model answer, accuracy cannot exceed one minus beta, where beta is the rate at which every model is wrong on the same query. In contrast, the usual diagnostic, average pairwise error correlation rho, cannot identify beta: error laws with identical marginals and pairwise correlations can have different all-wrong rates. A Clopper-Pearson bound on beta gives a finite-sample certificate on the largest gain any router, vote, or cascade could deliver before training a router.
  Across 67 models from 21 providers, a tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor model still underprices the all-wrong tail: on open-ended mathematics, observed beta is 0.052 versus 0.023 under the full 67-model Gaussian copula, about 2.5 times underpricing, with 90 percent CI 1.7 to 3.4 and k equals 17. The effect recurs on execution-graded code, where beta is 0.079. Re-asking the same GPQA-Diamond questions in free-response rather than multiple-choice form reopens the tail, with beta 0.127 and a five-judge panel with kappa 0.73 to 0.92, locating co-failure in answer format rather than subject. At matched quality, low-rho heterogeneous ensembles beat high-rho Self-MoA, but on checkable tasks in our pool, combining models rarely beats the single best model without a strong query-level routing signal. Gains come from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models.

AI.tldr: Multi-model LLM systems have accuracy gains fundamentally capped by the "all-wrong" rate (beta) — the probability all models fail simultaneously on a query. Average pairwise error correlation (rho) fails to capture this. Empirical analysis across 67 models shows the all-wrong tail is substantially underpriced by standard copula models, and combining models rarely beats the single best model without strong query-level routing.
AI.motivation: The field routinely uses multi-model LLM systems (routing, voting, cascades, MoA) to improve accuracy but relies on pairwise error correlation (rho) as a diagnostic. The authors argue this is insufficient: rho cannot identify the all-wrong rate (beta), which is the true upper bound on achievable accuracy for any policy selecting among member models. Without reporting beta, the community lacks a proper understanding of the ceiling on multi-model gains.
AI.method: The paper formally derives that for any policy outputting one member model's answer, max accuracy ≤ 1 − beta, where beta = P(all models wrong). It distinguishes beta from average pairwise error correlation rho, showing that identical marginals and rho can yield different beta values. A Clopper-Pearson confidence bound provides finite-sample certification of the maximum possible gain. Empirically, 67 models from 21 providers are evaluated on open-ended mathematics, execution-graded code generation, and free-response GPQA-Diamond (with five-judge panel, kappa 0.73–0.92). A tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor Gaussian copula is used to model the all-wrong tail and compared against observed beta.
AI.result: The Gaussian copula underprices beta by ~2.5× on mathematics (observed 0.052 vs. modeled 0.023; 90% CI [1.7, 3.4], k=17). On code, beta = 0.079. Switching GPQA-Diamond from multiple-choice to free-response reopens the tail (beta = 0.127), locating co-failure in answer format rather than subject matter. Low-rho heterogeneous ensembles outperform high-rho Self-MoA at matched quality. Critically, on checkable tasks, combining models rarely beats the single best model without strong query-level routing signals. Gains stem from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models.
AI.conclusion: The all-wrong rate beta is the correct diagnostic for multi-model system ceilings, not pairwise correlation rho. Standard copula models systematically underpredict co-failure. Free-response formats expose co-failure that multiple-choice masks. For checkpointable tasks, heterogeneous low-rho ensembles with strong query-level routing are necessary to exceed single-best-model performance; merely adding models provides diminishing returns.

title: Cross-Head Attention Uplift Network with Inverse Propensity Score under Unobserved Confounding
summary: Uplift modeling, crucial for estimating individual treatment effects (ITE), faces dual challenges: flexibly leveraging inter-group similarity to enhance discriminative power and debiasing under unobserved confounding scenarios. In this paper, we propose the Cross-Head Attention Uplift Network (CHAUN) and Robust Adversarial Inverse Propensity Score (RA-IPS) method to address these limitations. CHAUN employs shared feature embeddings and cross-head attention mechanisms to dynamically integrate treatment-specific and control-specific representations, enhancing inter-group correlation modeling. Theoretically, we prove that access to the true propensity scores ensures ITE identifiability even with unobserved confounders. For practical scenarios lacking true propensity scores, RA-IPS adversarially optimizes propensity weights within constrained uncertainty sets to mitigate bias from unobserved variables. Experiments on public datasets (CRITEO-UPLIFT, LAZADA) and a production e-commerce dataset demonstrate CHAUN's superiority over state-of-the-art uplift models, achieving relative improvements of up to 25.6% in QINI scores. RA-IPS further enhances robustness, outperforming standard IPS by 5.4% under unobserved confounding. The results validate the effectiveness of our proposed methods in real-world causal inference tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CHAUN (Cross-Head Attention Uplift Network) for uplift modeling with cross-head attention to dynamically integrate treatment/control representations, and RA-IPS (Robust Adversarial Inverse Propensity Score) for debiasing under unobserved confounding via adversarially optimized propensity weights within uncertainty sets. CHAUN achieves up to 25.6% QINI improvement over SOTA; RA-IPS outperforms standard IPS by 5.4% under unobserved confounding.
AI.motivation: Uplift modeling faces two key challenges: (1) flexibly leveraging inter-group similarity between treatment and control groups to improve discriminative power, and (2) debiasing estimates when unobserved confounders are present, which standard methods fail to address adequately.
AI.method: CHAUN uses shared feature embeddings with cross-head attention mechanisms to dynamically fuse treatment-specific and control-specific representations, modeling inter-group correlations. Theoretically, the authors prove that true propensity scores guarantee ITE identifiability under unobserved confounding. For practical settings without true propensity scores, RA-IPS adversarially optimizes propensity weights within constrained uncertainty sets to mitigate hidden confounding bias.
AI.result: On CRITEO-UPLIFT, LAZADA, and a production e-commerce dataset, CHAUN achieves up to 25.6% relative improvement in QINI scores over state-of-the-art uplift models. RA-IPS improves robustness, surpassing standard IPS by 5.4% under unobserved confounding conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CHAUN and RA-IPS methods are effective for real-world causal inference tasks, demonstrating both superior discriminative performance in uplift modeling and enhanced robustness against unobserved confounding.

title: Language-Based Digital Twins for Elderly Cognitive Assistance
comment: Accepted and published in the Proceedings of the ACM International Conference on PErvasive Technologies Related to Assistive Environments (PETRA 2026). The final published version is available through the ACM Digital Library
summary: Digital twins have emerged as a promising paradigm for personalized healthcare, enabling modeling of individual behavior and health trajectories. In cognitive health, early detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) remains challenging, where language and conversational patterns serve as non-invasive biomarkers. In this work, we propose a language-based digital twin framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to mimic the conversational behavior of elderly individuals by incorporating stylometric cues and contextual metadata. To evaluate fidelity and cognitive consistency, we introduce a multi-head conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) that jointly measures reconstruction quality and predicts cognitive scores. Experiments on the I-CONECT dataset show that the digital twin preserves identity-specific characteristics and achieves reconstruction and MoCA prediction errors comparable to real data, while outperforming baseline GPT-generated responses. These results highlight the potential of language-based digital twins as a scalable and non-invasive approach for personalized and continuous cognitive health monitoring.

AI.tldr: A language-based digital twin framework using LLMs and a multi-head cVAE to mimic elderly conversational behavior for cognitive health monitoring, validated on the I-CONECT dataset with MoCA prediction.
AI.motivation: Early detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is challenging; language and conversational patterns offer non-invasive biomarkers, but existing methods lack personalized, continuous monitoring. Digital twins can fill this gap by modeling individual cognitive trajectories.
AI.method: A language-based digital twin framework that uses LLMs to generate conversational responses mimicking elderly individuals, incorporating stylometric cues and contextual metadata. A multi-head conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) jointly evaluates reconstruction fidelity and predicts MoCA cognitive scores.
AI.result: On the I-CONECT dataset, the digital twin preserved identity-specific characteristics, achieved reconstruction quality and MoCA prediction errors comparable to real data, and outperformed baseline GPT-generated responses.
AI.conclusion: Language-based digital twins represent a scalable, non-invasive approach for personalized and continuous cognitive health monitoring, with strong potential for early MCI detection.

title: Kolmogorov Arnold networks (KAN) for aerodynamic prediction: a comparison with MLPs and GNNs
summary: Kolmogorov Arnold networks (KAN) have recently been introduced as a (deep) neural network architecture whose trainable parameters adapt the activation functions, instead of the coefficients of the affine transformations at the core of traditional architectures such as deep multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). This architecture builds on the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem, which endows it with universal approximation properties. While the advent of KANs has been received with excitement, there is a current debate about the possible KAN supremacy over deep multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) for classic fields such as symbolic regression, generic-purpose machine learning, natural language processing or computer vision. Here we assess the performance of KANs --and its nuanced comparison against MLPs and graph neural networks (GNNs)-- in the realm of fluid dynamics surrogate modelling. To that aim, we consider the task of predicting the surface pressure distribution over subsonic and transonic airfoils, a canonical task in aerodynamics. Our results show that KAN models show good performance in predicting the whole pressure coefficients and is able to interpolate across Mach numbers and angles of attack, however its performance is comparable --marginally inferior-- to a suitably trained MLP, where best performance is achieved by a GNN at the expense or requiring lengthier training. While the optimal KAN model have typically much lower complexity than MLP and GNN --hence resulting in faster training--, we find that KANs suffer from training instabilities, and their performance is highly dependent on a proper hyperparameter optimisation.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) against MLPs and GNNs for aerodynamic surrogate modeling of airfoil surface pressure distributions. KANs perform comparably but marginally worse than MLPs, with GNNs achieving best results at higher training cost. KANs offer lower model complexity and faster training but suffer from training instability and hyperparameter sensitivity.
AI.motivation: To rigorously assess whether KANs offer genuine advantages over traditional MLPs and GNNs in the specific domain of fluid dynamics surrogate modeling, especially given the ongoing debate about KAN supremacy in various machine learning fields.
AI.method: The authors benchmark KANs, MLPs, and GNNs on the canonical aerodynamic task of predicting surface pressure coefficients over subsonic and transonic airfoils, testing interpolation capability across varying Mach numbers and angles of attack.
AI.result: KANs achieve good predictive performance but are marginally inferior to well-tuned MLPs. GNNs deliver the best overall accuracy at the cost of longer training. KANs exhibit lower parameter complexity and faster training, yet are plagued by training instabilities and require careful hyperparameter optimization.
AI.conclusion: KANs do not demonstrate clear superiority over MLPs in aerodynamic surrogate modeling; their practical adoption is hindered by training instability and hyperparameter sensitivity despite attractive efficiency properties.

title: fTNN: a tensor neural network for fractional PDEs
summary: We develop the fTNN, a deterministic tensor neural network subspace method for problems involving the fractional Laplacian on bounded domains, taking the fractional Poisson equation and time-dependent fractional advection-diffusion equation as typical representatives. The work employs a geometry-adapted integration split featuring a spatially dependent near-field radius, which decomposes the fractional Laplacian into three contributions: a singular near field, a regular interior far field, and an analytical exterior far field. Then the singular radial integrals are treated by Gauss-Jacobi quadrature, the regular radial integrals by Gauss quadrature, and the angular variables by deterministic angular quadrature, yielding a fully deterministic integration framework of the fractional Laplacian operator. To accurately resolve low-regularity solutions and the associated loss functional, we construct boundary-singularity-aware trial functions enriched with explicit boundary features, and propose two strategies for automatically selecting the leading exponent and evaluating the loss function from the singularity structure induced by the fractional operator, or jointly by the fractional operator and the source term. For time-dependent fractional PDEs, we design a spatiotemporally separable neural network that factorizes the time-space residual into a sum of low-dimensional temporal and spatial integrals, and we integrate this representation with an alternating neural network subspace optimization strategy for efficient training. Numerical experiments show that the proposed framework attains high accuracy on the tested benchmarks and improves substantially over existing fPINN and Monte Carlo baselines, particularly for problems with strong boundary singularities and long-time simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces fTNN, a deterministic tensor neural network method for fractional Laplacian problems on bounded domains. It uses a geometry-adapted integration split (near-field, interior far-field, exterior far-field) with deterministic quadrature rules, boundary-singularity-aware trial functions with automatic exponent selection, and a spatiotemporally separable architecture for time-dependent problems. The method significantly outperforms fPINN and Monte Carlo baselines, especially on problems with strong boundary singularities and long-time simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for fractional PDEs (e.g., fPINNs, Monte Carlo) suffer from low accuracy and inefficiency, particularly when solutions exhibit low regularity near boundaries and for long-time simulations. There is a need for a deterministic, high-accuracy framework that can handle the singular integrals of the fractional Laplacian and resolve boundary singularities without stochastic noise.
AI.method: The fTNN framework consists of three main components: (1) A geometry-adapted integration split that decomposes the fractional Laplacian into singular near-field, regular interior far-field, and analytical exterior far-field contributions, with Gauss-Jacobi quadrature for singular radial integrals, Gauss quadrature for regular ones, and deterministic angular quadrature. (2) Boundary-singularity-aware trial functions enriched with explicit boundary features, plus two strategies for automatic selection of the leading exponent from the singularity structure. (3) A spatiotemporally separable neural network for time-dependent problems that factorizes the time-space residual, combined with alternating neural network subspace optimization.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on the fractional Poisson equation and time-dependent fractional advection-diffusion equation demonstrate that fTNN achieves high accuracy and substantially improves over fPINN and Monte Carlo baselines, with particularly strong gains on problems featuring strong boundary singularities and long-time simulations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fTNN framework provides a fully deterministic, highly accurate method for fractional Laplacian problems on bounded domains. Its geometry-adapted integration, singularity-aware trial functions, and separable space-time architecture collectively overcome key limitations of existing stochastic and PINN-based approaches, making it a robust tool for fractional PDEs with low-regularity solutions.

title: Stochastic Gradient Optimization with Model-Assisted Sampling
summary: This work addresses the problem of variance in stochastic gradient estimation for machine learning optimization. Deep learning relies on mini-batch methods such as stochastic gradient descent, which approximate full gradients but introduce noise, creating trade-offs between convergence stability, speed, and generalization. Existing methods, including variance reduction techniques (e.g., SVRG and SAG) and adaptive optimizers, aim to mitigate gradient noise but may introduce additional computational overhead. We propose a model-assisted sampling framework that interprets mini-batch gradients through survey sampling theory, treating the dataset as a fixed finite population and gradients as sample-based estimates. Our aim is to bridge machine learning optimization and survey sampling theory by combining their perspectives on sample-based estimation and variance reduction. By incorporating auxiliary gradient-prediction models, we construct more efficient gradient estimators, with uniform sampling arising as a special case when no auxiliary information is used. Our approach integrates easily with existing optimizers, improving efficiency without altering their dynamics. Empirical results on synthetic and six benchmark datasets show performance gains in 71-86% of the experiments, particularly for medium-sized input spaces in our benchmarks. Notably, with momentum-based optimizers such as AdamW, the proposed estimator achieves clearly better generalization in roughly half the training epochs compared to baseline estimator.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a model-assisted sampling framework that applies survey sampling theory to mini-batch gradient estimation, using auxiliary gradient-prediction models to construct more efficient gradient estimators for deep learning optimization, achieving performance gains in 71–86% of experiments.
AI.motivation: Stochastic gradient estimation in deep learning introduces noise from mini-batch sampling, creating trade-offs between convergence stability, speed, and generalization. Existing variance reduction techniques (SVRG, SAG) and adaptive optimizers mitigate gradient noise but incur additional computational overhead. The authors identify an unexplored connection between machine learning optimization and survey sampling theory that could yield more principled, efficient gradient estimators.
AI.method: The authors frame mini-batch gradient computation as a finite population sampling problem, treating the full dataset as a fixed population and mini-batch gradients as sample-based estimates of the population gradient. They introduce auxiliary gradient-prediction models and apply model-assisted survey sampling techniques to construct more efficient gradient estimators. Uniform sampling emerges as a special case when no auxiliary information is used. The framework integrates transparently with existing optimizers (e.g., SGD, AdamW) without altering their core dynamics.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on synthetic and six benchmark datasets shows the proposed estimator outperforms baselines in 71–86% of experimental configurations. Gains are particularly pronounced for medium-sized input spaces. With momentum-based optimizers like AdamW, the estimator achieves comparable or better generalization in roughly half the training epochs required by the baseline estimator.
AI.conclusion: The model-assisted sampling framework successfully bridges survey sampling theory and machine learning optimization, offering a principled variance reduction approach that integrates seamlessly with existing optimizers and yields significant efficiency and generalization improvements.

title: RecallRisk-BERT: A Multi-Task Framework for Post-Report Medical Device Recall Triage
summary: Medical device recalls are a critical regulatory mechanism for protecting patient safety. The growing volume of FDA recall records presents challenges in post-report recall triage, severity assessment, and root-cause interpretation. Existing studies mostly address recall occurrence prediction or root-cause analysis separately, while joint modeling of recall severity and root-cause categories has received limited attention. We develop an automated recall triage framework using 54,165 FDA medical device recall records from openFDA, covering the period from 2002 to October 2025. We first evaluate classical machine learning and boosting-based models for recall severity and root-cause category prediction. We then develop RecallRisk-BERT, a multi-task model that combines PubMedBERT-based textual representations of recall narratives with embedding-based representations of structured categorical features, including product code, regulation number, and medical specialty. The model simultaneously predicts recall severity (Class I/II/III) and a consolidated root-cause category (9 classes). Performance was evaluated using accuracy, macro-averaged precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. In single-task severity prediction, our LightGBM-based text--tabular configuration achieved the strongest performance, with an accuracy of 0.963, macro-F1 of 0.856, and ROC-AUC of 0.974. In the multi-task setting, RecallRisk-BERT substantially outperformed the single-task PubMedBERT baseline. Model-derived risk rankings were strongly consistent with observed root-cause severity patterns (rho = 0.983, p = 1.936e-6). These findings indicate that text--tabular learning can support scalable post-report recall triage, regulatory decision support, and model-based root-cause risk analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper presents RecallRisk-BERT, a multi-task model combining PubMedBERT with structured categorical features to jointly predict FDA medical device recall severity (Class I/II/III) and root-cause categories, achieving strong performance and enabling automated post-report recall triage.
AI.motivation: The growing volume of FDA medical device recall records creates challenges in triage, severity assessment, and root-cause interpretation. Existing work treats recall occurrence prediction and root-cause analysis separately, leaving a gap in joint modeling of severity and root-cause categories.
AI.method: Using 54,165 FDA recall records (2002–2025) from openFDA, the authors first benchmark classical ML and boosting models for severity and root-cause prediction, then develop RecallRisk-BERT — a multi-task architecture that fuses PubMedBERT-derived textual embeddings of recall narratives with embedding-based representations of structured categorical features (product code, regulation number, medical specialty) to jointly predict recall severity (3 classes) and consolidated root-cause category (9 classes). Evaluation uses accuracy, macro-averaged precision/recall/F1, and ROC-AUC.
AI.result: The LightGBM text–tabular configuration achieved 0.963 accuracy, 0.856 macro-F1, and 0.974 ROC-AUC in single-task severity prediction. RecallRisk-BERT substantially outperformed the single-task PubMedBERT baseline in the multi-task setting. Model-derived risk rankings correlated strongly with observed root-cause severity patterns (Spearman's ρ = 0.983, p = 1.936e-6).
AI.conclusion: Text–tabular multi-task learning can effectively support scalable post-report recall triage, regulatory decision support, and model-based root-cause risk analysis for FDA medical device recalls.

title: Automating Potential-based Reward Shaping with Vision Language Model Guidance
summary: Sparse rewards are inherently challenging for reinforcement learning agents as they lack intermediate feedback to guide exploration and to correctly attribute the sparse success rewards to relevant parts of the trajectory. Naive reward shaping can induce reward hacking, yielding policies that exploit auxiliary signals instead of solving the intended task. Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) guarantees preservation of the optimal policy set, but requires the definition of a heuristic potential function over the state space. In this work, we introduce the VLM-guided PBRS framework VLM-PBRS that learns the potential function directly from vision language model (VLM) feedback. We query a lightweight VLM to obtain preferences over image pairs and train a model of the potential function using these preferences. As this approach is based on potential-based reward shaping, it preserves the original optimal policies, and removes the need for expert-designed reward shaping terms. Because large VLMs are prohibitively expensive to invoke repeatedly during policy learning, we employ smaller, more computationally efficient VLMs. Although the resulting preference labels are less accurate, empirical evidence shows that the preference labels can still be used to accelerate learning. We validate our method empirically in the Meta-World and Franka Kitchen environments and highlight the connection between VLM preference label accuracy and sample efficiency improvements. Our contributions are threefold: (1) the first application of VLM preference-based learning to synthesize a potential function for PBRS, (2) a principled, low-cost solution that leverages small VLMs, and (3) extensive empirical demonstration of improved sample efficiency and robustness to reward hacking.

AI.tldr: VLM-PBRS uses small vision-language models to learn potential functions for potential-based reward shaping, preserving optimal policies while improving sample efficiency in sparse-reward RL without expert-designed heuristics.
AI.motivation: Sparse rewards challenge RL agents due to lack of intermediate feedback. Naive reward shaping risks reward hacking, while classical PBRS requires handcrafted potential functions. Large VLMs are too expensive for repeated queries during policy learning.
AI.method: VLM-PBRS queries a lightweight VLM for preferences over image pairs, trains a potential function model from those preferences, and uses it for potential-based reward shaping — preserving optimal policy invariance while providing dense intermediate rewards.
AI.result: Empirical validation in Meta-World and Franka Kitchen shows that even with less accurate preference labels from small VLMs, sample efficiency improves and robustness to reward hacking is maintained compared to naive shaping baselines.
AI.conclusion: Small VLM preference labels, despite lower accuracy, are sufficient to accelerate sparse-reward RL via PBRS. The approach is principled, low-cost, and eliminates the need for expert-designed potential functions.

title: Explaining Temporal Graph Neural Networks via Feature-induced Information Flow
summary: Event-based Temporal Graph Neural Networks (ETGNNs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of applications, including social network analysis, epidemic tracing, recommender systems, and political event forecasting. However, their increasing complexity poses significant challenges for explainability. Existing explanation methods focus only on a subset of the information flow within ETGNNs, typically tracing contributions from the event-related embeddings to the output. Consequently, they overlook the important pathways through event-induced variables, which mediate interactions between nodes and thereby play a central role in capturing long-range temporal dependencies. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel attribution method that analyzes the \emph{entire} information flow through all event-associated variables. Our method is built upon the recent Normalized Relevance Measure (NRM) framework, which enables explicit quantification of information flow originating from event embeddings as well as information flow passing through event-induced variables. It also ensures comparability of latent variables across layers, and supports higher-order analysis of interactions between events. To handle the architectural complexity of ETGNNs, we extend the NRM framework with a modular decomposition procedure that facilitates the systematic construction of relevance structure for complex neural architectures. We evaluate our approach on two synthetic datasets for epidemic tracing and social dynamics, as well as a real-world dataset of political event networks. Our qualitative and quantitative experiments show that our method consistently outperforms existing explanation approaches while producing more human-interpretable explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel attribution method for Event-based Temporal Graph Neural Networks (ETGNNs) that analyzes the entire information flow, including often-overlooked event-induced variables. Built on the Normalized Relevance Measure framework, it uses modular decomposition to handle architectural complexity, outperforming existing methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing explanation methods for ETGNNs only trace contributions from event-related embeddings to the output, overlooking critical pathways through event-induced variables that mediate inter-node interactions and capture long-range temporal dependencies. This incomplete coverage limits explainability for increasingly complex ETGNN architectures.
AI.method: The authors propose an attribution method built on the Normalized Relevance Measure (NRM) framework that explicitly quantifies both (1) information flow from event embeddings and (2) information flow through event-induced variables. It ensures cross-layer comparability of latent variables and supports higher-order event interaction analysis. A modular decomposition procedure extends NRM to systematically construct relevance structures for complex ETGNN architectures.
AI.result: The method was evaluated on two synthetic datasets (epidemic tracing and social dynamics) and one real-world political event network dataset. Both qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrated consistent outperformance over existing explanation approaches, with more human-interpretable explanations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method provides the first complete attribution analysis for ETGNNs by accounting for all event-associated variables. This yields superior and more interpretable explanations compared to prior approaches, advancing the explainability of temporal graph neural networks.

title: Graph Neural Networks Applications Across Domains: All Insights You Need
summary: Graph neural networks have moved from a niche representation-learning technique to the default model class wherever data carry relational structure. The interesting question is no longer whether message passing helps on a given dataset, but where graph structure earns its computational cost and where it does not. This survey organises the field around a single design space, derives the spectral and spatial formulations from shared first principles, and connects expressive power to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy with explicit statements of what current architectures can and cannot separate. Against that methodological backbone we examine twelve application domains, among them recommendation and social networks, knowledge graphs and language-model integration, drug discovery and molecular property learning, healthcare and neuroscience, computer vision, traffic and urban computing, power and renewable-energy systems, wireless and sixth-generation networks, fraud and cybersecurity, industrial prognostics, materials science, and climate modelling. For each domain we specify the graph-construction choices and their costs, identify which architecture families dominate and why, and separate reported gains from artefacts of weak baselines or favourable splits. A cross-domain comparison exposes recurring patterns: heterophily and scale undercut the same models almost everywhere, temporal graphs remain harder than their static counterparts, and the architectures that top public leaderboards are seldom the ones that reach deployment. We treat over-smoothing, over-squashing, robustness, distribution shift, fairness, and explainability not as a closing checklist but as the constraints that decide adoption.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey organizing graph neural networks around a unified design space, deriving spectral/spatial formulations from first principles, linking expressiveness to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, and systematically evaluating architectures across twelve application domains to identify where graph structure provides genuine value versus where it incurs unjustified computational cost.
AI.motivation: GNNs have become the default model for relational data, but the field lacks a systematic understanding of when graph structure actually helps versus when it merely adds overhead. The survey aims to move beyond the settled question of whether message passing works, toward identifying precisely where graph structure earns its cost, while separating genuine architectural advances from gains attributable to weak baselines or favorable data splits.
AI.method: The survey organizes the GNN field around a single design space, deriving both spectral and spatial formulations from shared first principles. It maps expressive power explicitly to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, specifying what current architectures can and cannot separate. Twelve application domains are examined — recommendation/social networks, knowledge graphs/LM integration, drug discovery/molecular property learning, healthcare/neuroscience, computer vision, traffic/urban computing, power/renewable energy, wireless/6G networks, fraud/cybersecurity, industrial prognostics, materials science, and climate modeling. For each domain, graph construction choices, costs, dominant architecture families, and reasons for dominance are analyzed. Cross-domain patterns are identified, and deployment-relevant constraints (over-smoothing, over-squashing, robustness, distribution shift, fairness, explainability) are treated as adoption-deciding factors rather than afterthoughts.
AI.result: Several recurring cross-domain patterns emerge: (1) heterophily and scale undermine the same models across almost all domains; (2) temporal graphs remain significantly harder than static counterparts; (3) architectures dominating public leaderboards are rarely those that reach actual deployment. The survey also identifies that reported performance gains in many domains are often attributable to weak baselines or favorable data splits rather than genuine architectural improvements.
AI.conclusion: The GNN field has matured beyond proving message passing works; the critical frontier is determining precisely where graph structure justifies its computational cost. Deployment success depends not on leaderboard performance alone but on satisfying constraints around over-smoothing, over-squashing, robustness, distribution shift, fairness, and explainability. These constraints, rather than being a closing checklist, should be treated as primary filters determining whether a GNN solution is adopted in practice.

title: The Geometry of Updates: Fisher Alignment at Vocabulary Scale
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306. 64 pages total (main paper plus appendix), 4 figures, 29 tables
summary: Training-free source selection for LLM families with shared vocabularies arises in scientific string domains such as SMILES, protein, and genomic sequences, where candidate corpora share a tokenizer but differ in prediction targets. This creates an activation-dark regime: representation-similarity metrics can be uninformative without assumptions about label-conditioned error geometry, while classical update-geometry metrics are computationally prohibitive at vocabulary scale. We show that, in a shared-output head setting, representation metrics (e.g., CKA) are non-identifiable for transfer; models can share identical representations yet have orthogonal head updates. The key identity is that head Fisher alignment is exactly a cosine between kernel mean embeddings in the joint activation-error space, exposing activation, error, and coupling factors rather than requiring a materialized Fisher matrix. FisherSketch estimates this cosine directly in a single streaming pass, making K=128,256 head Fisher alignment practical with a 16 KB task signature (m=4096) and a 192 KB per-task streaming state, small enough to store next to a model hash, but encoding transfer-relevant update structure. Beyond source selection, the same signatures and marginals provide a diagnostic instrument for studying whether LLM task similarity is driven by activations, errors, or their coupling; shared-parameter and internal-layer validations, together with Llama-3.1-8B verbalizer-shift experiments, show that FisherSketch remains informative when activation similarity cannot distinguish tasks.

AI.tldr: FisherSketch enables efficient, training-free source selection for LLM families with shared vocabularies by estimating head Fisher alignment via a streaming cosine between kernel mean embeddings in joint activation-error space, using only a 16 KB task signature, and reveals transfer structure where activation similarity (e.g., CKA) fails.
AI.motivation: In scientific string domains (SMILES, protein, genomic sequences), LLM families share tokenizers but have different prediction targets, creating an "activation-dark" regime where representation similarity metrics like CKA are uninformative for transfer learning, and full Fisher-based update geometry is computationally prohibitive at vocabulary scale. A lightweight, training-free method is needed to assess task similarity and select sources.
AI.method: The authors prove that head Fisher alignment equals the cosine between kernel mean embeddings in the joint activation-error space, decomposing into activation, error, and coupling factors. FisherSketch estimates this cosine in a single streaming pass using sketching techniques (K=128,256), producing a compact 16 KB task signature (m=4096) and 192 KB per-task streaming state, without materializing the full Fisher matrix.
AI.result: FisherSketch successfully identifies transfer-relevant task structure where activation similarity (CKA) cannot distinguish tasks. Validations include shared-parameter and internal-layer experiments, plus Llama-3.1-8B verbalizer-shift experiments, demonstrating the method remains informative in activation-dark regimes.
AI.conclusion: FisherSketch provides a practical, storable diagnostic tool for training-free source selection in shared-vocabulary LLM families, and doubles as an analytical instrument for understanding whether LLM task similarity is driven by activations, errors, or their coupling.

title: Effective Covariance Dynamics in Solvable High-Dimensional GANs
summary: We study a solvable high-dimensional model of generative adversarial network (GAN) training in which a linear generator learns a low-dimensional subspace from data with structured latent covariance. Prior solvable GAN analyses assume unconditional signals with diagonal latent covariance; we extend the multi-feature discriminator setting to class-dependent, correlated, and non-zero-mean latent structure. For the quadratic energy discriminator, all such heterogeneity enters the dynamics through a probability-weighted effective second moment. We prove that the stochastic microscopic training process converges, in the high-dimensional limit, to deterministic ordinary differential equations governed by this effective covariance. In the matched-covariance specialization, the stability analysis yields a mode-wise solvable interval determined by the learning rates and noise level: learning begins when the leading effective eigenvalue crosses the lower threshold, while full recovery requires all relevant effective modes to remain within the interval. This reveals a signal-boosting mechanism: low-rank correlations can lift weak directions above the learnability threshold, whereas overly strong correlations destabilize recovery. Numerical simulations validate the ODE, phase boundary, and boosting mechanism. Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 further show that informed generator covariance improves alignment with the data-driven reference subspace.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a solvable high-dimensional GAN model with a linear generator and structured (class-dependent, correlated, non-zero-mean) latent covariance, extending prior diagonal-covariance analyses. The dynamics converge to ODEs governed by a probability-weighted effective second moment, revealing a signal-boosting mechanism where low-rank correlations aid learnability but overly strong correlations destabilize recovery.
AI.motivation: Prior solvable GAN analyses are limited to unconditional signals with diagonal latent covariance, which fails to capture the structured heterogeneity (class dependence, correlations, non-zero means) present in real-world data. The authors aim to understand how such structured latent covariance affects GAN training dynamics and learnability.
AI.method: The authors analyze a high-dimensional GAN model with a linear generator learning a low-dimensional subspace from data with structured latent covariance, using a quadratic energy discriminator with multi-feature settings. They prove that the stochastic microscopic training process converges in the high-dimensional limit to deterministic ODEs governed by a probability-weighted effective second moment. Stability analysis is performed for the matched-covariance case, yielding mode-wise solvable intervals determined by learning rates and noise levels.
AI.result: The dynamics depend on heterogeneity solely through the effective second moment. A mode-wise solvable interval emerges: learning begins when the leading effective eigenvalue exceeds a lower threshold, and full recovery requires all relevant modes to stay within this interval. A signal-boosting mechanism is revealed: low-rank correlations lift weak directions above the learnability threshold, while overly strong correlations destabilize recovery. Numerical simulations validate the ODE, phase boundary, and boosting mechanism. Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 show informed generator covariance improves alignment with data-driven reference subspaces.
AI.conclusion: Structured latent covariance fundamentally shapes GAN training dynamics through the effective second moment. The mode-wise solvable interval provides a precise phase boundary for learnability. The signal-boosting mechanism demonstrates that moderate low-rank correlations aid learning, but excessive correlation strength is detrimental — offering practical guidance for covariance-informed generator initialization in real-world GAN training.

title: RSPC: A Benchmark for Modeling Stress and Psychiatric Conditions in Digitally Mediated Relationships using Psychiatrist Annotations
summary: In NLP, mental health conditions are often modeled as isolated phenomena, without interpersonal context. We use Reddit posts about long-distance relationships to capture both mental health distress and associated relational triggers. We introduce the Relational Stress and Psychiatry Corpus (RSPC) containing 1,799 Reddit posts annotated by psychiatrists for diagnostic categories, including the most prevalent mood disorders (anxiety and depression), relational stressor triggers, and indications of relationship phase. We benchmark seven fine-tuned transformer models and five large language models across multi-label disorder classification, relational trigger detection, and temporal phase prediction tasks. We find clear task-dependent differences between model families, with Claude-3-Haiku achieving the best disorder classification performance (Macro-F1 = 0.538) and GPT-4o obtaining the strongest relational trigger detection performance (Macro-F1 = 0.519), suggesting distinct model capabilities. We further find strong associations between anxiety disorders and chronic relational uncertainty. Overall, RSPC establishes a benchmark for NLP tasks that consider relational context and supports a shift from individual-centric to context-aware mental health modeling that captures the social and temporal dynamics of distress.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RSPC, a Reddit corpus annotated by psychiatrists for mental health disorders, relational triggers, and relationship phases in long-distance relationships. Benchmarking transformer models and LLMs reveals task-dependent performance differences, with Claude-3-Haiku best for disorder classification and GPT-4o best for trigger detection. The work advocates shifting from individual-centric to context-aware mental health NLP modeling.
AI.motivation: Current NLP approaches to mental health model conditions as isolated phenomena, ignoring the interpersonal and relational context in which distress arises. The authors argue that understanding the social and temporal dynamics of relationships is critical for more accurate and clinically meaningful mental health modeling.
AI.method: The authors construct the Relational Stress and Psychiatry Corpus (RSPC) — 1,799 Reddit posts from long-distance relationship communities, annotated by psychiatrists for: (1) multi-label diagnostic categories (anxiety, depression, and other mood disorders), (2) relational stressor triggers, and (3) relationship phase indications. They benchmark seven fine-tuned transformer models and five large language models (LLMs) across these three tasks, evaluating with Macro-F1.
AI.result: Claude-3-Haiku achieved the best disorder classification performance (Macro-F1 = 0.538), while GPT-4o obtained the strongest relational trigger detection (Macro-F1 = 0.519). A strong association was found between anxiety disorders and chronic relational uncertainty. Model performance was task-dependent, with different model families showing distinct strengths across the three tasks.
AI.conclusion: RSPC establishes a benchmark for context-aware mental health NLP that incorporates relational and temporal dimensions. The findings support moving beyond individual-centric models toward approaches that capture the social embeddedness of psychological distress, with implications for both clinical understanding and computational modeling.

title: BetXplain: An Explanation-Annotated Dataset for Detecting Manipulative Betting Advertisements on Social Media
summary: The promotion of betting applications on social media platforms has increased significantly in recent years. Many of these advertisements use persuasive techniques that may mislead users, encourage risky behavior, and potentially influence users' mental well-being. However, research on the automated detection of manipulative and deceptive betting advertisements remains limited due to the lack of publicly available annotated datasets. In this work, we introduce a new dataset of betting-related advertisements collected from two widely used social media platforms, Instagram and Reddit. The advertisements were manually annotated for manipulative and deceptive advertising practices. In addition to classification labels, the dataset includes human-provided explanations that describe the reasoning behind each annotation, enabling research into explainable approaches to detecting manipulative advertising. Furthermore, we analyze the strategies commonly used in betting advertisements and examine how these persuasive tactics may impact users' mental health. The proposed framework can also enable practical applications such as browser plugins that warn users about manipulative betting advertisements and automated web crawlers that help regulatory authorities monitor and detect such promotions online.

AI.tldr: A new manually annotated dataset of betting advertisements from Instagram and Reddit is introduced, targeting the detection of manipulative and deceptive advertising practices, with human explanations provided to support explainable AI approaches and mental health impact analysis.
AI.motivation: Betting advertisements on social media increasingly employ persuasive and deceptive techniques that may harm users' mental well-being, yet automated detection research is hindered by the absence of publicly available annotated datasets.
AI.method: The authors collected betting-related advertisements from Instagram and Reddit, then manually annotated them for manipulative and deceptive advertising practices, including classification labels and human-written explanations justifying each annotation. They also conducted an analysis of common persuasive strategies and their potential mental health impacts.
AI.result: A novel annotated dataset with classification labels and human explanations was created. Analysis revealed common persuasive tactics in betting advertisements and their potential adverse effects on users' mental health. The framework supports practical downstream applications such as browser warning plugins and automated regulatory monitoring crawlers.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and framework enable future research in explainable detection of manipulative betting advertisements and offer practical tools for user protection and regulatory oversight.

title: How Good Can Linear Models Be for Time-Series Forecasting?
summary: Time-series forecasting research has been moving steadily toward larger architectures, from specialized transformers to general-purpose foundation models, on the assumption that capacity is what unlocks accuracy. We take the opposite position: most of the gap can be closed at far lower cost by tuning preprocessing rather than scaling models. We use Ridge regression as the testbed, since it has a closed-form solution and interpretable weights, which let the optimal hyperparameters be read off the search directly. We search over context length, local normalization, regularization, and augmentation on eight standard benchmarks and find three patterns. (1) Optimal lookback is strongly series-specific and often non-monotonic in forecast horizon, with fitted power-law exponents ranging from $+0.46$ on ETTm2 to $-0.19$ on Exchange and Traffic, challenging the convention that longer horizons need longer history. (2) Normalizing over a learned trailing fraction of the context, rather than its entirety, is almost universally preferred. (3) Series within the same dataset often disagree on hyperparameters; the optimal degree of cross-series sharing varies from fully shared to fully per-series. The resulting models beat prior linear forecasters on most dataset-horizon entries and exceed Transformer, MLP, and CNN baselines on six of eight benchmarks. The optimized hyperparameters also serve as a diagnostic on the data itself, revealing structures that larger models absorb silently into their learned parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the trend of scaling up model architectures for time-series forecasting, showing that optimizing preprocessing (context length, normalization, regularization, augmentation) in a simple Ridge regression model can match or exceed complex Transformer/MLP/CNN baselines on most benchmarks at far lower cost.
AI.motivation: The dominant assumption in time-series forecasting is that larger, more complex models (transformers, foundation models) are necessary for accuracy. The authors question this, hypothesizing that much of the performance gap can be closed by better understanding and tuning of preprocessing choices rather than scaling model capacity.
AI.method: The authors use Ridge regression with a closed-form solution as a transparent testbed. They conduct a structured hyperparameter search over four axes: (1) context length, (2) local normalization strategy (learned trailing fraction vs. full context), (3) L2 regularization strength, and (4) data augmentation. The search is performed on eight standard benchmarks, and optimal hyperparameters are read directly from fitted weights due to the model's interpretability.
AI.result: Three key findings emerge: (1) Optimal lookback is strongly series-specific and often non-monotonic with forecast horizon — fitted power-law exponents range from +0.46 (ETTm2) to −0.19 (Exchange, Traffic), refuting the convention that longer horizons always need longer history. (2) Normalizing over a learned trailing fraction of the context is almost universally preferred over full-context normalization. (3) Series within the same dataset often disagree on optimal hyperparameters; the best degree of cross-series sharing ranges from fully shared to fully per-series. The resulting Ridge models beat prior linear forecasters on most entries and exceed Transformer, MLP, and CNN baselines on six of eight benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Preprocessing optimization is an underappreciated lever in time-series forecasting, capable of closing most of the accuracy gap attributed to model scale. The interpretable nature of Ridge regression allows optimal hyperparameters to serve as a diagnostic tool, revealing structural properties of the data that larger models absorb opaquely into their parameters.

title: Recovering Governing Equations from Solution Data: Identifiability Bounds for Linear and Nonlinear ODEs
summary: Learning governing equations from observed solution data is a fundamental challenge in scientific machine learning \cite{bruntonDiscoveringGoverningEquations2016,kovachkiNeuralOperatorLearning2023,longPDENetLearningPDEs2018,rudyDatadrivenDiscoveryPartial2017,raonicConvolutionalNeuralOperators2023}, yet the theoretical conditions under which a ground-truth ODE can be uniquely and stably identified from multiple solution observations remain largely undeveloped, and no quantitative analysis of the sample complexity of such learning tasks exists in the literature. To address this gap, we introduce the Hausdorff distance on solution sets as the natural metric for comparing differential equations, since it captures the worst-case separation between two equations over all admissible initial conditions and thus encodes the minimax structure of the identification problem. We establish identifiability bounds for governing ODEs across a wide class of structure equations--ranging from linear ODEs to nonlinear classes with Lipschitz (Hölder)-continuous vector fields--characterizing precisely when two distinct equations can be distinguished from solution data. Using this metric, we derive metric entropy estimates for the relevant ODE classes and analyze sample complexity bounds, quantifying how many solution observations are needed to reliably recover the governing equation.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes theoretical foundations for identifying ODEs from solution data by introducing the Hausdorff distance as a natural metric on solution sets, deriving identifiability conditions across linear to Hölder-continuous nonlinear ODE classes, and providing the first sample complexity bounds for this learning problem via metric entropy estimates.
AI.motivation: Despite growing interest in data-driven discovery of governing equations, no theoretical framework exists for determining when an ODE can be uniquely and stably identified from multiple solution trajectories, nor are there quantitative sample complexity analyses. This gap hinders rigorous understanding of fundamental limits in scientific machine learning.
AI.method: The authors propose the Hausdorff distance on solution sets (over all admissible initial conditions) as the natural metric for comparing differential equations. They derive identifiability bounds characterizing when distinct equations are distinguishable, covering linear ODEs through nonlinear classes with Lipschitz/Hölder-continuous vector fields. Using this metric, they compute metric entropy estimates for ODE function classes and translate these into sample complexity bounds for reliably recovering the governing equation from observed data.
AI.result: The paper establishes precise identifiability conditions showing when two distinct ODEs can be distinguished from solution data. It provides metric entropy estimates for the relevant ODE classes and the first quantitative sample complexity bounds specifying how many solution observations suffice for reliable recovery of the governing equation.
AI.conclusion: The Hausdorff distance framework provides a theoretically principled foundation for analyzing the sample complexity and identifiability of ODE learning tasks, offering rigorous guarantees that were previously absent in the scientific machine learning literature.

title: Designing Reward Signals for Portable Query Generation: A Case Study in Industrial Semantic Job Search
comment: Accepted to KDD 2026 Workshop on AI Agent for Information Retrieval (Agent4IR)
summary:
Job-search platforms rely on low-bandwidth query interfaces that often fail to capture the high-dimensional complexity of candidate profiles. We present an end-to-end RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback) framework to generate \emph{portable} job search queries, terms that abstract away seeker-specific identifiers while preserving generalizable qualifications. This task introduces a highly adversarial reward surface where policy optimization frequently exploits flaws in LLM-as-judge rubrics, resulting in degenerate verbatim-copying behaviors.
  We conducted comprehensive empirical experiments to isolate the impact of optimization mechanics against structured reward engineering. Our results demonstrate that for critic-free optimizers, performance is overwhelmingly dictated by robust reward shaping, rendering the specific choice of algorithm largely immaterial. While critic-free per-rollout baseline methods (RLOO and REINFORCE++) natively resist reward-hacking, the group-relative advantage normalization in GRPO appears uniquely sensitive to spurious reward signals, making it disproportionately susceptible to exploitation. We show that introducing a deterministic, rule-based reward floor to correct for rewards assigned to verbatim copying mitigates this failure mode, resulting in a substantial $+0.147$ quality improvement on a cross-family evaluation judge. Ultimately, we show that the training-time reward model inflates performance gains by $2.4\times$, confirming that the training success is fundamentally dependent on enforcing reward-shaping disciplines rather than selecting alternative optimizers.

AI.tldr: RLAIF-based portable query generation faces adversarial reward surfaces causing verbatim-copying collapse. The study shows reward shaping dominates optimizer choice: GRPO is uniquely vulnerable to reward hacking due to group-relative advantage normalization, but a deterministic rule-based reward floor mitigates this, yielding +0.147 quality improvement. Training-time reward models inflate gains 2.4×.
AI.motivation: Job-search platforms use low-bandwidth query interfaces that inadequately represent high-dimensional candidate profiles. The authors aim to generate "portable" queries — terms that abstract away personal identifiers while retaining generalizable qualifications — using RLAIF. The core challenge is an adversarial reward landscape where policy optimization exploits flaws in LLM-as-judge rubrics, leading to degenerate verbatim-copying rather than genuine abstraction.
AI.method: The authors propose an end-to-end RLAIF framework for portable job-search query generation. They conduct a comprehensive empirical study comparing critic-free policy-gradient optimizers: RLOO (REINFORCE Leave-One-Out), REINFORCE++, and GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). The key methodological interventions are: (1) isolating optimizer mechanics from reward engineering, (2) analyzing how group-relative advantage normalization in GRPO creates unique sensitivity to spurious reward signals, and (3) introducing a deterministic, rule-based reward floor to correct verbatim-copying rewards. Cross-family evaluation judges are used to measure generalization.
AI.result: Critic-free per-rollout baseline methods (RLOO, REINFORCE++) natively resist reward hacking. GRPO's group-relative advantage normalization makes it disproportionately susceptible to reward exploitation. The rule-based reward floor intervention successfully mitigates this failure mode, yielding a +0.147 quality improvement on cross-family evaluation. Critically, the training-time reward model inflates performance gains by 2.4× compared to cross-family evaluation, confirming that training success depends fundamentally on reward-shaping disciplines rather than optimizer selection.
AI.conclusion: For critic-free RL optimizers in this adversarial RLAIF setting, robust reward shaping overwhelmingly determines performance — the choice of optimization algorithm is largely immaterial when rewards are well-structured. GRPO's group-relative advantage mechanism is uniquely fragile and requires explicit corrective reward engineering. The 2.4× performance inflation by the training reward model underscores the necessity of cross-family evaluation for honest assessment of RLAIF-generated outputs.

title: A Multi-Fidelity Convolutional Autoencoder-Transfer Learning Framework for Guided-Wave-Based Damage Diagnosis Using Large Simulated and Limited Experimental Datasets
summary: Guided wave-based structural health monitoring (GWSHM) with onboard transducers offers significant potential for the early diagnosis of damage in engineering structures. However, the practical deployment of deep learning models is often hindered by the limited availability of labelled experimental data and the high computational cost of generating large-scale high-fidelity simulation datasets. This study presents a multifidelity transfer learning framework that integrates lightweight physics-based simulations, convolutional autoencoder (CAE)-based deep feature learning, a feed-forward neural network, and limited experimental measurements for accurate damage localisation and sizing in plate-like structures instrumented with piezoelectric transducers. A computationally efficient one-dimensional time-domain spectral element model is employed to generate a large synthetic dataset for pretraining, while transfer learning adapts the model to experimental domains using only a small amount of labelled data. The CAE-based transfer learning framework significantly outperforms its CNN-based counterpart in damage localisation accuracy. The model achieves excellent predictive performance with $R^2$ scores exceeding 0.93 for damage localisation and 0.99 for damage sizing. Its generalisation capability is demonstrated on previously unseen data, showing high prediction accuracy for damage scenarios not represented during pretraining or fine-tuning. The results establish the proposed framework as an accurate, computationally efficient, and practically viable solution for real-world GWSHM applications.

AI.tldr: A multifidelity transfer learning framework combining lightweight 1D spectral element simulations, convolutional autoencoders, and limited experimental data achieves high-accuracy damage localization (R² > 0.93) and sizing (R² > 0.99) in plate-like structures for guided wave SHM.
AI.motivation: Deep learning for guided wave SHM is constrained by scarce labeled experimental data and the prohibitive computational cost of generating large-scale high-fidelity simulation datasets. A practical solution must bridge the simulation-to-experiment gap efficiently.
AI.method: The framework uses a computationally cheap 1D time-domain spectral element model to generate a large synthetic pretraining dataset. A convolutional autoencoder (CAE) performs deep feature learning, paired with a feed-forward neural network for prediction. Transfer learning adapts the pretrained model to the experimental domain using minimal labeled experimental data.
AI.result: The CAE-based transfer learning approach significantly outperforms a CNN-based counterpart in damage localization. R² scores exceed 0.93 for localization and 0.99 for sizing. Strong generalization is demonstrated on unseen damage scenarios not included in pretraining or fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework is an accurate, computationally efficient, and practically viable solution for real-world guided wave SHM, effectively overcoming data scarcity and simulation fidelity gaps.

title: Blackwell Approachability and Gradient Equilibrium are Equivalent
comment: 30 pages, 1 figure, accepted for presentation at COLT 2026
summary: Gradient equilibrium (GEQ) is a recently introduced online optimization framework that generalizes first-order stationarity from offline optimization and abstracts problems like online conformal prediction. While GEQ has curious similarities with known online learning frameworks, namely regret minimization, prior work has shown that GEQ error and regret are incomparable objectives, leaving open a precise understanding of how GEQ fits into the broader online learning landscape. In this work, we show that GEQ is equivalent to Blackwell approachability in the algorithmic sense. That is, a Blackwell approachability problem can always be solved using queries to a black-box GEQ oracle, with no asymptotic loss in the oracle's error rate, and vice versa. Taken together with known equivalences between approachability, regret minimization, and calibration, these results imply that GEQ is equivalent to these frameworks, as well. Our reductions are efficient and can be used to transfer refined guarantees, such as optimism and strong adaptivity, from regret minimization to GEQ. Along the way, we also identify necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ, and establish reductions between different notions of GEQ with unconstrained and constrained decision sets.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes that Gradient Equilibrium (GEQ) is algorithmically equivalent to Blackwell approachability, and consequently to regret minimization and calibration, enabling the transfer of refined guarantees across these frameworks.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that GEQ error and regret are incomparable objectives, leaving GEQ's precise relationship to the broader online learning landscape unclear. The authors seek to resolve this by formally situating GEQ within established frameworks.
AI.method: The authors prove bidirectional black-box reductions between GEQ and Blackwell approachability with no asymptotic loss in error rate, then leverage known equivalences to connect GEQ to regret minimization and calibration. They also derive necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ and reductions between constrained and unconstrained GEQ variants.
AI.result: GEQ is equivalent to Blackwell approachability, regret minimization, and calibration in the algorithmic sense. The reductions are efficient and allow transfer of properties like optimism and strong adaptivity from regret minimization to GEQ. Necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ are also identified.
AI.conclusion: GEQ is not a distinct paradigm but rather fundamentally equivalent to established online learning frameworks, providing a unified perspective and enabling cross-pollination of algorithmic guarantees between them.

title: Beyond the Hard Budget: Sparsity Regularizers for More Interpretable Top-k Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a leading tool for interpreting the representations of vision foundation models, decomposing their polysemantic activations into a larger set of sparse, more monosemantic features. The Top-$k$ SAE, a now-standard variant, enforces sparsity architecturally through its activation function, retaining only the $k$ most active latents per input. Because it was designed precisely to avoid the $\ell_1$ penalty used by earlier SAEs and its known drawbacks, it has not been combined with an explicit sparsity regularizer, despite retaining limitations of its own, such as a budget $k$ that is fixed regardless of input complexity and a tendency to overfit to the training value of $k$. We introduce two sparsity regularizers compatible with the Top-$k$ architecture, both acting on the activations before the Top-$k$ selection: an $\ell_1$ penalty on the unselected (off-support) units, and a scale-invariant $\ell_1/\ell_2$-ratio penalty that concentrates the code onto fewer effective units. Both penalties are applied only to the batch-active units, those selected by the Top-$k$ operator at least once within the batch. Across two datasets, three vision foundation models, and a range of $k$, both regularizers consistently improve monosemanticity at no cost to reconstruction quality. The $\ell_1/\ell_2$ penalty further concentrates information into fewer latents, making reconstruction more robust to the inference-time choice of $k$ and improving small-budget linear probing. Our central finding is that hard architectural sparsity and soft sparsity regularization are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes combining Top-k sparse autoencoders (SAEs) — which enforce architectural sparsity — with explicit sparsity regularization penalties (ℓ₁ on off-support units and a scale-invariant ℓ₁/ℓ₂ ratio). The authors show that hard architectural sparsity and soft regularization are complementary, improving monosemanticity without harming reconstruction, making reconstruction more robust to inference-time k, and enhancing small-budget linear probing.
AI.motivation: Top-k SAEs avoid the ℓ₁ penalty's known drawbacks but have their own limitations: a fixed sparsity budget k regardless of input complexity and overfitting to the training k. Prior work assumed architectural sparsity eliminated the need for explicit regularization. The authors challenge this assumption, hypothesizing that soft regularization can complement hard architectural constraints.
AI.method: Two sparsity regularizers are applied to activations before Top-k selection: (1) an ℓ₁ penalty on unselected (off-support) units, and (2) a scale-invariant ℓ₁/ℓ₂ ratio penalty that concentrates code onto fewer effective units. Both penalties are applied only to batch-active units (those selected by Top-k at least once in the batch). Evaluated across two datasets, three vision foundation models, and a range of k values.
AI.result: Both regularizers consistently improve monosemanticity at no cost to reconstruction quality. The ℓ₁/ℓ₂ penalty further concentrates information into fewer latents, making reconstruction more robust to inference-time k variation and improving small-budget linear probing performance.
AI.conclusion: Hard architectural sparsity (Top-k) and soft sparsity regularization are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Combining them yields better SAEs than either approach alone.

title: Hallucination in World Models is Predictable and Preventable
comment: Interactive paper, live demo, code, dataset, and models: https://www.nicklashansen.com/mmbench2
summary:
Modern generative world models render increasingly realistic action-controllable futures, yet they frequently hallucinate: rollouts remain visually fluent while drifting from the ground-truth dynamics. We hypothesize that hallucination concentrates in low-coverage regions of the state-action space, where lightweight data-centric signals can both detect it and guide mitigation.
