To test this, we introduce MMBench2, a 427-hour, 210-task dataset for visual world modeling with ground-truth actions, rewards, and live simulators, and train a 350M-parameter world model on it. We identify three distinct hallucination modes: perceptual, action-marginalized, and scene-diverging -- each anchored to a different stage of the pipeline, and develop three signals that accurately predict where the model will fail. To close coverage gaps at training time, we develop a coverage-aware sampling technique; to close them online, our hallucination predictors serve as curiosity rewards for targeted data collection, yielding a data-efficient finetuning recipe that adapts the pretrained world model to entirely unseen environments with as few as 50 real environment trajectories. Overall, our findings reveal that hallucination in world models is inherently a data coverage issue, and that the same signals used to detect it can also be used for mitigation.
  An interactive web version of our paper is available at https://www.nicklashansen.com/mmbench2

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MMBench2, a large-scale benchmark for visual world modeling, identifies three distinct hallucination modes (perceptual, action-marginalized, scene-diverging) in world model rollouts, develops predictive signals for each mode, and proposes coverage-aware sampling and curiosity-driven finetuning to mitigate hallucination — framing the problem as fundamentally one of data coverage in state-action space.
AI.motivation: Modern generative world models produce visually fluent yet dynamically inaccurate rollouts (hallucinations). The authors hypothesize that these failures are concentrated in low-coverage regions of the state-action space and can be both detected and mitigated using lightweight, data-centric signals.
AI.method: (1) Construct MMBench2: a 427-hour, 210-task dataset with ground-truth actions, rewards, and live simulators. (2) Train a 350M-parameter world model and taxonomize three hallucination modes — perceptual, action-marginalized, and scene-diverging — each tied to a different pipeline stage. (3) Develop three predictive signals that forecast where the model will fail. (4) For mitigation: coverage-aware sampling during training to fill coverage gaps, and online use of hallucination predictors as curiosity rewards for targeted data collection, enabling finetuning to unseen environments with as few as 50 real trajectories.
AI.result: The hallucination predictors accurately identify failure regions. Coverage-aware sampling at training time closes coverage gaps. Curiosity-driven finetuning with hallucination signals adapts the pretrained world model to entirely unseen environments using only 50 real environment trajectories, demonstrating data-efficient mitigation.
AI.conclusion: Hallucination in world models is inherently a data coverage problem. The same signals that detect hallucination can be leveraged for mitigation, unifying detection and correction under a single data-centric framework.

title: Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers
summary: Neural surrogate models offer fast approximate mappings from PDE parameters to solutions, but they typically treat solving as a purely statistical task: once trained, they struggle to correct their own constraint violations and extrapolate beyond the training distribution. Recent hybrid methods promote physical correctness by targeting the PDE residual via gradient descent or Gauss--Newton steps, but inherit the compute cost and instability of the underlying classical optimizers. We show, theoretically and empirically, that numerically minimizing the PDE residual can be an unreliable proxy for reconstruction accuracy in ill-conditioned systems, explaining why these methods often do not make accurate predictions despite achieving low residuals. We propose error-conditioned Neural Solvers (ENS), built on a different principle: rather than an optimization target, the PDE residual field is passed as a direct input to the network at each iteration, enabling it to read the spatial structure of its own errors and learn an update policy to iteratively correct its predictions. Across four PDE families, ENS attains the highest prediction accuracy in the large majority of settings, with gains reaching $10\times$ on turbulent Kolmogorov flow, while avoiding the expensive compute cost of hybrid methods. ENS's learned correction policy generalizes under distribution shift, including zero-shot parameter changes and cross-equation transfer, where its relative advantage is largest in the ill-conditioned regimes where residual minimization is least reliable. Project website: https://neuralsolver.github.io/.

AI.tldr: Neural surrogate models for PDEs are fast but lack error correction. Existing hybrid methods use PDE residual minimization (gradient descent/Gauss-Newton) which is computationally expensive and unreliable in ill-conditioned systems. The authors propose Error-conditioned Neural Solvers (ENS), which feed the PDE residual field directly as input to the network, letting it learn an iterative correction policy. ENS achieves up to 10x accuracy gains on turbulent flows, generalizes under distribution shift, and excels precisely where residual minimization fails.
AI.motivation: Standard neural PDE surrogates treat solution mapping as pure regression, failing to correct their own errors post-training. Hybrid methods that minimize PDE residuals via classical optimizers inherit instability and high compute cost. Crucially, low PDE residual does not guarantee accurate solutions in ill-conditioned systems — a gap the authors demonstrate both theoretically and empirically. There is a need for a method that retains the constraint-awareness of hybrid methods without their drawbacks.
AI.method: Error-conditioned Neural Solvers (ENS) reframe the problem: instead of using the PDE residual as an optimization target, ENS passes the residual field as a direct spatial input to the network at each iteration. The network learns an update policy that reads the spatial structure of its own errors and iteratively refines predictions. This is implemented via a learned correction operator that conditions on both the current solution estimate and its residual field, trained end-to-end to minimize reconstruction error over multiple unrolled steps.
AI.result: ENS achieves the highest prediction accuracy across four PDE families in the majority of settings, with up to 10× improvement on turbulent Kolmogorov flow. It avoids the expensive optimization loops of hybrid methods. Under distribution shift (zero-shot parameter changes, cross-equation transfer), ENS generalizes well, with its relative advantage being largest precisely in ill-conditioned regimes where residual minimization is least reliable.
AI.conclusion: Minimizing the PDE residual is an unreliable proxy for solution accuracy in ill-conditioned systems. Encoding the residual field as a spatial input to a learned iterative corrector is a more robust and computationally efficient strategy, yielding state-of-the-art accuracy and strong generalization across PDE families.

title: Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators
summary: Efficient sampling of molecular systems at thermodynamic equilibrium is a hallmark challenge in statistical physics. This challenge has driven the development of Boltzmann Generators (BGs), which allow rapid generation of uncorrelated equilibrium samples by combining a generative model with exact likelihoods and an importance sampling correction. However, modern BGs predominantly rely on normalizing flows (NFs), which either suffer from limited expressivity due to strict invertibility constraints (discrete time) or computationally expensive likelihoods (continuous time). In this paper, we propose Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators (ArBG) -- a novel autoregressive modelling framework -- that overcomes these limitations by departing from the flow-based BG paradigm. ArBG circumvents the topological constraints of flows and enables sequential inference-time interventions, while offering enhanced scalability by leveraging architectures effective in Large Language Models. We empirically demonstrate that ArBG leads to significant improvements over flow-based models across all benchmarks, but particularly in larger peptide systems such as the 10-residue Chignolin. Furthermore, we introduce Robin, a 132 million parameter transferable model trained with the ArBG framework which improves over the previous state-of-the-art, reducing the zero-shot energy error, E-W$_2$, on 8-residue systems by over 60$\%$. The code can be found at the following link: https://github.com/danyalrehman/autobg.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators (ArBG), a novel framework that replaces normalizing flows with autoregressive models for equilibrium sampling of molecular systems, enabling better scalability via LLM-style architectures and achieving significant improvements over flow-based models, including a 60% reduction in zero-shot energy error with a 132M-parameter transferable model called Robin.
AI.motivation: Boltzmann Generators based on normalizing flows suffer from a fundamental trade-off: discrete-time NFs have limited expressivity due to strict invertibility constraints, while continuous-time NFs incur computationally expensive likelihoods. This motivates a departure from the flow-based paradigm to achieve both high expressivity and efficient likelihood computation.
AI.method: The authors introduce Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators (ArBG), which model the Boltzmann distribution using an autoregressive factorization. This eliminates the topological/invertibility constraints of flows, allows sequential inference-time interventions, and enables the use of scalable architectures from Large Language Models. The framework includes an importance sampling correction for exact equilibrium sampling. They also train Robin, a 132M-parameter transferable ArBG model.
AI.result: ArBG achieves significant improvements over flow-based Boltzmann Generators across all benchmarks, with particularly strong gains on larger systems like the 10-residue Chignolin peptide. The transferable Robin model reduces the zero-shot energy error (E-W₂) on 8-residue systems by over 60% compared to the previous state-of-the-art.
AI.conclusion: Departing from flow-based constraints and adopting autoregressive modeling substantially advances the capabilities of Boltzmann Generators, enabling better scaling to larger molecular systems and transferable models with state-of-the-art zero-shot performance.

title: Reinforcement Learning without Ground-Truth Solutions can Improve LLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for training LLMs typically rely on ground-truth answers to assign rewards, limiting their applicability to tasks where the ground-truth solution is unknown. We introduce a \textbf{R}anking-\textbf{i}nduced \textbf{VER}ifiable framework (RiVER) that trains LLMs on score-based optimization tasks without ground-truth solutions, using deterministic execution feedback as continuous-valued supervision. When applying group-relative RL to such continuous rewards, we identify two key challenges: \emph{scale dominance}, where uncalibrated score magnitudes across test instances distort policy updates, and \emph{frequency dominance}, where repeatedly sampled suboptimal solutions can outweigh rare but stronger candidates. RiVER addresses these challenges with calibrated reward shaping that uses instance-wise comparisons and emphasizes top-ranked solvers while retaining bounded feedback for other valid solutions. We train on 12 AtCoder Heuristic Contest tasks and evaluate on Algorithm Engineering Benchmark (ALE-Bench), LiveCodeBench, and USACO. RiVER advances Qwen3-8B and GLM-Z1-9B-0414 by 8.9\% and 9.4\% in ALE rating rank. More importantly, despite training exclusively on score-based tasks without any ground-truth solutions, RiVER also improves the backbones across exact-solution benchmarks such as LiveCodeBench and USACO by an absolute average improvement of 2.4\% and 3.5\%. By contrast, baselines trained with raw execution scores improve ALE rating but fail to transfer to exact-solution benchmarks. These results suggest that score-based optimization tasks, combined with proper reward calibration, can serve as effective training environments for general coding ability without ground-truth solutions.

AI.tldr: RiVER is a framework that trains LLMs on score-based optimization tasks without ground-truth answers, using ranking-induced calibrated rewards to overcome scale and frequency dominance problems, achieving strong performance on both heuristic and exact-solution coding benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR requires ground-truth answers, limiting applicability to tasks where the optimal solution is unknown. The authors aim to extend RLVR to score-based optimization tasks (where only execution feedback scores are available) and enable transfer to exact-solution benchmarks.
AI.method: RiVER uses deterministic execution feedback as continuous-valued supervision. It introduces calibrated reward shaping with two components: (1) instance-wise comparison to normalize score scales across different test instances (addressing scale dominance), and (2) top-ranked solver emphasis with bounded feedback for other valid solutions (addressing frequency dominance). Training is conducted on 12 AtCoder Heuristic Contest tasks using group-relative RL.
AI.result: RiVER improves Qwen3-8B by 8.9% and GLM-Z1-9B-0414 by 9.4% in ALE rating rank. Without any ground-truth solution training, it transfers to exact-solution benchmarks, achieving 2.4% average improvement on LiveCodeBench and 3.5% on USACO. Baselines using raw execution scores fail to transfer to exact-solution tasks despite improving ALE ratings.
AI.conclusion: Score-based optimization tasks combined with proper reward calibration (RiVER) can serve as effective, ground-truth-free training environments for developing general coding ability in LLMs, with benefits transferring even to exact-solution benchmarks.
